# [Roadmap][NPU][Multimodal] Ascend model support and serving features (2026 Q4)

This issue tracks the Q4 2026 multimodal workstream under the [NPU development roadmap](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/25598). It also aligns with the broader [Q4 development roadmap](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/42473). We will link implementation PRs and validation results to the items below as they land.

## 1. Model adaptation

SGLang already has implementations for these models. The work here is to make their intended paths run correctly on Ascend, validate outputs, and add reproducible NPU coverage.

- [ ] **GLM-OCR** (`zai-org/GLM-OCR`): validate model loading, image preprocessing, vision encoding, and OCR generation on Ascend. Add representative document-image tests and compare results with a reference implementation. Document a working NPU launch configuration. [SGLang model guide](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/52edb89d2daf5b27f151f1bafa707c3da6dcb2e5/docs/cookbook/autoregressive/GLM/GLM-OCR.mdx).
- [ ] **Qwen-Image-2.1** (`Qwen/Qwen-Image-2.1`): adapt the existing SGLang Diffusion pipeline for Ascend. Cover text-to-image and image-editing requests, validate generated outputs with fixed inputs and seeds, and add an NPU server test and deployment recipe. [Existing pipeline](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/52edb89d2daf5b27f151f1bafa707c3da6dcb2e5/python/sglang/multimodal_gen/configs/pipeline_configs/qwen_image21.py).
- [ ] **GLM-5.3-Flash** (`zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash`): validate the model's hybrid attention, MoE, vision path, and checkpoint loading on Ascend. Cover text, image, and video requests where supported by the checkpoint, then add correctness tests and a reproducible multi-NPU deployment recipe. [SGLang model guide](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/52edb89d2daf5b27f151f1bafa707c3da6dcb2e5/docs/cookbook/autoregressive/GLM/GLM-5.3-Flash.mdx).

**Completion criteria:** Each model has a documented NPU launch command, representative end-to-end outputs checked against a reference, and an automated regression test on the target Ascend configuration. Model support and performance claims will be reported separately.

## 2. Shared multimodal serving features

- [ ] **JPEG decoding on NPU:** add an Ascend device-side path for eligible JPEG inputs, with a CPU fallback for unsupported inputs or decode failures. Check decoded output consistency and measure decode time, data movement, and end-to-end latency before claiming a speedup. Today the fast path is [guarded by CUDA](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/98fce73d5bd0a25afe7d68443d314190b1c47e64/python/sglang/srt/utils/common.py#L1896-L1952).
- [ ] **Single-node device-side feature transport:** provide an NPU-capable alternative to CUDA IPC for transferring multimodal feature tensors between local processes. Cover bounded memory use, tensor lifetime, cancellation, pool exhaustion, and fallback to the existing CPU/shared-memory path. Compare transfer cost and time to first token under workloads where features are already on device. The current [`cuda_ipc` option requires NVIDIA CUDA](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/98fce73d5bd0a25afe7d68443d314190b1c47e64/python/sglang/srt/arg_groups/serving_hook.py#L853-L865).
- [ ] **Cross-request ViT batching:** enable and validate batching of eligible image-encoding cache misses across requests on NPU. Preserve request-to-image association and the existing per-request fallback; cover mixed cache hits/misses, multiple images, memory pressure, and concurrent requests. Report ViT calls, batch sizes, throughput, and latency. The current [scheduler keeps NPU on the per-request path](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/98fce73d5bd0a25afe7d68443d314190b1c47e64/python/sglang/srt/managers/mm_schedule.py#L596-L630).

**Completion criteria:** Each feature has correctness and fallback coverage plus measurements against the existing NPU path. We will publish the supported input and deployment conditions with the implementation.

## Tracking

We will update this issue with the PR, tested model revision, Ascend hardware/configuration, and validation result for each completed item. Suggestions for additional workloads are welcome.

items.title: [Bug] Transcription multipart upload has no application-level size limit
items.author: JPengLi
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

The OpenAI-compatible transcription endpoint reads an entire multipart upload into memory before model or format validation:

```python
# python/sglang/srt/entrypoints/http_server.py:1856-1884
@app.post("/v1/audio/transcriptions")
async def openai_v1_audio_transcriptions(
    raw_request: Request,
    file: UploadFile = File(...),
    ...
):
    ...
    audio_data = await file.read()
```

There is no `Content-Length` check, streaming size limit, or application-level maximum multipart body size on this route. `await file.read()` accumulates all bytes in one Python object regardless of whether the content is valid audio.

This is distinct from the decoder issue: exhaustion happens before audio decoding or model dispatch.

### Reproduction

On an isolated worker with no external upload limit, create a file larger than the intended application cap:

```bash
dd if=/dev/zero of=not-audio.bin bs=1M count=2048 status=none
```

Submit it as a normal multipart form field:

```bash
curl -sS -i http://127.0.0.1:30000/v1/audio/transcriptions \
  -F model=default \
  -F file=@not-audio.bin \
  -F response_format=json
```

Monitor tokenizer/HTTP worker RSS and cgroup memory. The request need not contain valid audio. The endpoint still buffers the entire upload before rejecting it as audio.

A negative control can set an explicit application limit (for example, 64 MiB) and verify that the same upload is rejected while a small valid WAV file succeeds.

### Evidence

Source on `51686cf8e7fee0ae773c5c9b8ede356507abef7b`:

```python
file: UploadFile = File(...)
...
audio_data = await file.read()
```

A repository search found no application-level max-body or upload-size middleware for this endpoint. Existing `media_url_max_file_size_mb` applies to remote media downloads, not this multipart route.

Therefore the effective cap, if any, comes from an external reverse proxy. A direct worker request or a proxy configured without body limits has no application guard.

### Impact

**Availability: High.**

A caller with access to the transcription endpoint can force the HTTP worker to buffer arbitrary request bytes. Concurrent oversized uploads can exhaust memory and impair both transcription and other requests served by the same process. An invalid payload is sufficient; no audio model execution is required.

Prerequisites:

- Reachability to `/v1/audio/transcriptions`.
- No outer proxy enforcing a sufficiently small request-body limit.

### Environment

```
$ docker exec sglang-v0519-prefill-134 python3 -m sglang.check_env
Python: 3.12.3 (main, Jul 15 2026, 23:46:41) [GCC 13.3.0]
CUDA available: True
GPU 0: NVIDIA A100 80GB PCIe
GPU 0 Compute Capability: 8.0
CUDA_HOME: /usr/local/cuda
NVCC: Cuda compilation tools, release 13.0, V13.0.88
CUDA Driver Version: 590.48.01
PyTorch: 2.13.0+cu130
sglang: 0.5.19
sglang-kernel: 0.4.6.post1
flashinfer_python: 0.6.18
flashinfer_cubin: 0.6.18
flashinfer_jit_cache: 0.6.18+cu130
triton: 3.7.1
transformers: 5.12.1
numpy: 2.3.5
aiohttp: 3.14.3
fastapi: 0.141.1
huggingface_hub: 1.30.0
modelscope: 1.39.1
orjson: 3.12.0
pydantic: 2.13.5
python-multipart: 0.0.32
uvicorn: 0.52.4
uvloop: 0.22.1

ulimit soft: 1024
```

items.title: [Bug][ROCm] NGRAM speculative decoding on a DSA model (GLM-5.3, gfx942): HSA 0x1016 on every rank after the first ~50k-token prompt
items.author: skimanwhite
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

With the HIP routing gap from #43328 worked around, `--speculative-algorithm NGRAM` boots and serves short prompts on gfx942 with GLM-5.3, then every TP rank dies with a GPU hardware exception on the first decode step after a ~50k-token prompt. The same server without speculative decoding serves prompts up to 1M tokens without a fault.

### Environment

8x MI300X (gfx942), `lmsysorg/sglang:v0.5.21-rocm720-mi30x` (sglang 0.5.21 at `e00930c`, ROCm 7.2.0, torch 2.9.1+rocm7.2.0, amd-aiter 0.1.22.dev120+gacf8fdf93), model `zai-org/GLM-5.3` (FP8, `GlmMoeDsaForCausalLM`), `--tp-size 8 --dsa-prefill-backend tilelang --dsa-decode-backend tilelang --kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3 --chunked-prefill-size 32768 --mem-fraction-static 0.80`, `SGLANG_USE_AITER=1`.

### Reproduction

Server args as above plus:

```
--speculative-algorithm NGRAM --speculative-num-draft-tokens 2 --speculative-num-steps 1
--speculative-ngram-min-bfs-breadth 1 --speculative-ngram-max-bfs-breadth 1
--speculative-ngram-match-type BFS --speculative-ngram-max-trie-depth 8
```

1. Stock v0.5.21: dies on the first forward with `AttributeError: '_OpNamespace' 'sgl_kernel' object has no attribute 'reconstruct_indices_from_tree_mask'` - this is exactly what #43328 describes.
2. Work around it by routing HIP to a device implementation of the tree reconstruction. **Caveat:** we routed HIP to the Triton `reconstruct_indices_from_tree_mask_triton` (the XPU branch), not to the JIT `tree` module that #43328 uses, so this report has not been re-verified on top of #43328 itself.
3. Send a chat completion with an ~8k-token prompt: served normally.
4. Send a chat completion with a ~50k-token prompt (`max_tokens=8`, `temperature=1, top_p=0.95`, streaming): the prefill batch completes and the HTTP response starts (`200 OK`), then all ranks abort.

### Error

```
:0:rocdevice.cpp:3586: Callback: Queue 0x... aborting with error : HSA_STATUS_ERROR_EXCEPTION: An HSAIL operation resulted in a hardware exception. code: 0x1016
[TPn] Scheduler hit an exception: Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
  File ".../managers/scheduler.py", line 1956, in pop_and_process
    self.process_batch_result(tmp_batch, tmp_result)
  File ".../managers/scheduler_components/batch_result_processor.py", line 927, in process_batch_result_decode
  File ".../torch/cuda/streams.py", line 231, in synchronize
torch.AcceleratorError: HIP error: unspecified launch failure
```

The Python frame is where the asynchronous fault is observed (a stream synchronize in the overlap scheduler), not necessarily where it is raised.

### What it does not depend on

| variation | 8k prompt | ~50k prompt |
|---|---|---|
| `--chunked-prefill-size 32768` (prompt = 2 chunks) | ok | 0x1016 |
| `--chunked-prefill-size 131072` (prompt = 1 chunk of 50,720) | ok | 0x1016 |
| `--page-size 32` | ok | 0x1016 |

On v0.5.19 (ROCm 7.2.0) we saw the identical fault with a pure-torch fallback for the tree reconstruction, and `--speculative-attention-mode decode` failed identically at the same point, so neither the reconstruction implementation nor the attention mode looks like the cause. It is length-dependent: 8k is fine on every variation, ~50k faults on every variation. We have not bisected the threshold between those two.

### Not yet tried

`AMD_SERIALIZE_KERNEL=3` + `HIP_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1` to name the faulting kernel, and a re-run on top of #43328's JIT route. Happy to run either, or any other diagnostic, on this hardware.

items.title: [RFC]: Limit the use of envvars in vLLM
items.author: zhuohan123
items.body_excerpt:
### Motivation.

vLLM's envvars are on the edge of getting out of control. There are many envvars should instead be configs. Like the attention backend, all2all kernel backend, and even there is a flag to control KV cache layout. envvars are evil because:

1. It is equivalent of using global variables everywhere in the code, which is a bad programming practice.
2. envvars have no advanced structure like, hierarchy, typechecks, etc. 

In summary, I think envvars are the kind of thing that is very easy to add so people tend to add envvars as the shortest path to implement their feature, but this can quickly becomes unmanageable and makes the project very hard to use. 

### Proposed Change.

I think we should:

1. Spend some effort on reviewing the current envvars and move many of them to configs.
2. Have very strict bar on what can be an envvar and question every new envvars in vllm.

### Feedback Period.

_No response_

_No response_

_No response_

items.title: [Docs] Document NIXL KV connector metrics aggregation semantics
items.author: NickLucche
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

The NIXL KV connector logs transfer metrics periodically:

```
KV Transfer metrics: Num successful transfers=4, Avg xfer time (ms)=1.381, P90 xfer time (ms)=2.601, Avg post time (ms)=0.672, P90 post time (ms)=0.801, Avg MB per transfer=2.25, Throughput (MB/s)=1629.549, Avg number of descriptors=72.0
```

Currently there is no documentation explaining what these metrics represent, especially in the context of **multi-rank (TP > 1) deployments**. This has already caused confusion among users.

## Current behavior

All metrics are **aggregated across all TP ranks** before summary stats are computed:

1. Each TP rank independently records per-transfer telemetry (`transfer_duration`, `post_duration`, `bytes_transferred`, `num_descriptors`) via `NixlKVConnectorStats.record_transfer()` in [`stats.py`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/nixl/stats.py).
2. Stats from all ranks are concatenated via `aggregate()` (`list.extend()`).
3. `reduce()` computes averages, percentiles, and throughput over the **combined** pool of observations from all ranks.

This means:
- **"Num successful transfers"** is the total count across all ranks, not per-rank.
- **"Avg MB per transfer"** is the average over all individual rank-level transfers, not the total bytes moved for a single KV cache transfer operation.
- **"Throughput (MB/s)"** is `total_MB_all_ranks / total_time_all_ranks` — effectively an average per-rank throughput, not the aggregate system throughput.
- **Percentiles (P90)** are computed over the combined distribution of all ranks' transfer times.

This is unintuitive because users may expect metrics to reflect per-engine totals or aggregate system throughput.

## What needs to be documented

1. **Docstrings in `stats.py`**: Add clear documentation to `NixlKVConnectorStats` explaining that stats are aggregated across all TP ranks and what each metric represents in that context.
2. **Inline comments in `reduce()`**: Clarify the semantics of throughput and averages — that they are per-rank averages over the combined observation pool.
3. **Docstrings in `metrics.py`**: Document the `observe()` → `aggregate()` → `reduce()` → `log()` pipeline and the fact that stats arrive pre-aggregated across workers.
4. **(Optional) Docs page**: Add a section to the disaggregated serving documentation explaining how to interpret the KV Transfer metrics log line.

## Relevant files

- `vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/nixl/stats.py` — `NixlKVConnectorStats` (recording, aggregation, reduction)
- `vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/metrics.py` — `KVConnectorLogging` (observe/log pipeline), `KVConnectorStats` (base class)

## Context

See related discussion: metrics are aggregated across ranks rather than reported per-rank or per-engine. This is a deliberate design choice (fire-and-forget from workers), but it needs to be clearly documented so users can correctly interpret the numbers.

items.title: [RFC]: Per-Layer Parallelism Policy
items.author: sungsooha
items.body_excerpt:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

## 1. Motivation

PR #36287 introduced TPA (tensor-parallel-size-attention) to vLLM, and review feedback from Lucas Wilkinson — *"the design shouldn't be attention-specific"* — pointed to a more general need: a per-layer parallelism policy that lets layers declare what they are and have the framework resolve their plan.

## 2. The idea

A single function, owned by the framework, that turns a layer's identity into its parallelism plan:

```
                                ┌─────────────────────────────┐
   (layer instance, prefix) ──▶ │  framework-owned resolver   │──▶  plan
                                │  (consults config + layer)  │
                                └─────────────────────────────┘
```

Layers consult the resolver in `__init__` instead of reading global TP accessors. A *plan* is whatever the layer needs to make local decisions — its TP width, its rank within that group, its communication backend, etc. The plan schema is open-ended; the call shape stays the same as new fields are added.

The plan being a function of the layer is what makes the design non-attention-specific. The resolver doesn't know it's an attention layer — it knows it's *this* layer at *this* prefix and consults config to decide. New strategies (Q-replication, hybrid attention, MTP, future ideas) become resolver-and-config changes, not N-model changes.

## 3. How the policy expresses different models

The mechanism in §2 is one resolver and one plan dataclass. The breadth comes from what the policy declares for which layers. To make the schema concrete, here are illustrative configurations for different model architectures. The exact field names are not part of this RFC's ask — the question is whether the *shape* (named axes, rules with matchers, per-layer-kind plans) covers the architectural patterns we want to support.

### 3.1 Llama family — uniform GQA

```yaml
parallelism_rules:
  axes:
    tp: 16
    attn_tp: 4      # TPA: attention layers narrower than full TP
    dcp: 4          # required by TPA invariant: dcp = tp / attn_tp
  rules:
    - match: { kind: attention }
      plan: { tp_size: attn_tp, dcp_size: dcp }
    - match: { kind: mlp }
      plan: { tp_size: tp }
```

One attention rule, one MLP rule. Every block matches the same two rules. Every derivative (Mistral, Phi3, NemotronNAS, TeleChat2, GLM) reuses this verbatim.

### 3.2 Nemotron-H, Jamba — hybrid attention + SSM

```yaml
parallelism_rules:
  axes:
    tp: 16
    attn_tp: 4
    dcp: 4
  rules:
    - match: { kind: attention }
      plan: { tp_size: attn_tp, dcp_size: dcp }
    - match: { kind: mamba }
      plan: { tp_size: tp }     # SSM has no attention heads to TPA-shard
    - match: { kind: mlp }
      plan: { tp_size: tp }
```

The resolver dispatches by layer kind, which HF config already declares via `hybrid_override_pattern`. No new metadata source needed — the heterogeneity signal already exists in the model config.

### 3.3 DSV4 — MLA + MoE + sparse indexer

```yaml
parallelism_rules:
  axes:
    tp: 16
    attn_tp: 1      # MLA has 1 effective KV head → TPA collapses to DCP-only
    dcp: 16
    ep: 8           # expert parallel for MoE layers
  rules:
    - match: { kind: attention, attention_flavor: mla }
      plan: { tp_size: tp, dcp_size: dcp }
    - match: { kind: indexer }
      plan: { tp_size: 1 }                  # replicate across TP
    - match: { kind: moe }
      plan: { tp_size: tp, ep_size: ep }
    - match: { kind: mlp }
      plan: { tp_size: tp }
```

Three distinct layer-kind rules within one model. MLA attention, sparse indexer, and MoE experts each get a different plan; all expressed through the same schema.

### 3.4 MTP heads — speculative decoding

```yaml
parallelism_rules:
  rules:
    - match: { prefix_pattern: "mtp_*" }
      plan: { tp_size: 1 }      # replicate each MTP head
```

The matcher can target by `prefix` when the architecture attaches sub-modules. The rule applies regardless of the main model's parallelism choices, because the resolver dispatches on `(layer, prefix)` independently for each layer.

## 4. Backward compatibility

Three properties of the design enforce backward compatibility by construction:

- **Sentinel-fallback at every consult site.** The resolver returns a "no policy active" plan by default. Layers fall back to today's global TP accessors and behave bit-identically. Adding the resolver call to a parallel layer is safe in isolation.
- **Whitelist gate per architecture.** A model opts into per-layer policy only when its migration is verified. Non-whitelisted models keep their current global-TP wiring; per-layer CLI flags are rejected at config-validation time with a clear error.
- **Per-strategy delivery.** Each new strategy lands resolver-native for the model families it targets, independently. Existing global parallelism (TP, PP, EP, DCP) stays where it is; existing globals become the resolver's fallbacks for those fields if and when a per-layer override is genuinely needed.

A user who upgrades vLLM and changes no CLI flags sees no behavior change. A user who opts into a per-layer flag on a whitelisted model gets the new behavior. There is no third state.

## 5. Roadmap

What we commit to deliver, with TPA-GQA as the concrete reference:

- **TPA + FlashAttention + Llama family** *(rebased [PR #36287])*. Resolver scaffold, `QKVParallelLinear` consult site, `--tensor-parallel-size-attention` flag, Llama-family migration, FA backend integration, whitelist gate. Enables TPA-GQA on Llama family and its derivatives (Mistral, Phi3, NemotronNAS, TeleChat2, GLM). GSM8K parity vs pure-TP baseline validates both the per-rank semantics and the backward-compat property.
- **TPA + FlashInfer + Llama family**. Backend-specific DCP-wrapper audit. The FA path already validates the policy mechanism; this enables the FlashInfer backend for already-whitelisted models.
- **DSV4 with Q-rep (MLA family)**. Q-rep ships as the second concrete po

items.title: [Spec Decode][dflash] Drafter KV group is never identified, so prefix-cache reuse is silently disabled for the Mamba groups
items.author: Karl0007
items.body_excerpt:
AI-authored (disclosed): produced and verified on our live CMP 170HX cluster; the account owner is a user, not a vLLM dev.

### Summary

With `method="dflash"` the drafter's KV cache group is never identified, so the consumer falls back to treating **every** group as a draft group -- including the Mamba/GDN groups -- and prefix-cache reuse across requests is silently disabled for those layers. The warning is printed on every start:

```
Speculative decoding (method=dflash) is enabled but no KV cache group could be
identified as the draft model's, so every group -- including Mamba groups [0, 1, 2, 3]
-- will be treated as a draft group. A Mamba group cannot satisfy the widened lookup
window that implies, so prefix-cache reuse across requests will be disabled ...
```

`_uses_trailing_mtp_layers()` (the positional fallback generalized in #55390) is gated on `spec_config.method == "mtp"`. `dflash` drafts reuse the target's decoder-layer architecture, so their attention spec is indistinguishable from the target's and the spec-driven rule cannot find them either.

### Measured consequence -- corrected

**Correction (2026-09-16, see the validation comment below):** this section originally attributed the
36.4 s prefix-child TTFT to the missing draft-group annotation. That attribution is wrong. With the
annotation patch applied (`xiaoba17/vllm@40681e0c9d`) the same 35-36 s reproduces and the engine's
prefix-cache counters are byte-identical; the annotation fix is correct and worth carrying, but it does
not gate this symptom.

What does gate it is the **Mamba checkpoint retention policy** plus prefill chunk granularity. On the
same box, same payload: `--prefix-cache-retention-interval 832` takes the 51.8k prefix child from
35.15 s to 5.83 s (+74,880 reused tokens = 10 x 7,488), and `--max-num-batched-tokens 1664` takes it to
1.47 s (= an exact re-send) for ~13 % extra on the cold parent prefill. The default
`prefix_cache_retention_interval=0` keeps only semantic replay boundaries, so a child that extends a
cached parent resumes from a much earlier checkpoint. For reference, an **identical** re-send resumes
in 1.5 s in every configuration -- which is why the original comparison looked like an annotation
problem.

### Ask

Extend the trailing-layer positional fallback (with the `_groups_partition_layers_exactly` guard added in #55390) to `method == "dflash"`, or state why it cannot apply there. If dflash drafts are guaranteed to register their KV layers after every target layer the same way MTP drafts do, the rule should transfer; if they are not, some other annotation path is needed, because the flag-all fallback quietly costs the Mamba-group reuse in any dflash deployment.

### Environment / evidence

- vLLM v0.13.0 line (fork image `vllm/vllm-backport:cmp170hx`, sha256 `2d27fe8655b0c57b953dc3dff72034df0a98abf2a1ff07387e48f6a0af886a2a`), V2 GPU model runner.
- Reproducible on every start; no special flags beyond the ones above. Raw server logs, per-request TTFT/JSONL and the harness are kept on the machine and available on request.

---
AI-authored contribution (omp agent). The account owner is a user running these models in production: they reported the failure, asked for the fix, and run it live today. They are not a vLLM developer and do not vouch for the code -- please verify it independently (logs, configs and image digests on request). Thanks for the maintainer work, and apologies for the review load that AI-written reports add; if you would rather not get them, say so and we will stop. If our fix causes trouble, we will keep driving it.

items.title: [Feature]: Per-request prefix-cache miss attribution (prompt divergence vs. eviction)
items.author: sachinworks
items.body_excerpt:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

Automatic prefix caching is one of the biggest cost and latency wins for RAG and agent workloads, where every request re-sends a long, mostly identical scaffold (system prompt, tool schemas, few-shot examples).

vLLM already reports per-request cached tokens (`num_cached_tokens`, `usage.prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens`), so you can tell roughly *where* the cache hit ended. What you can't tell is *why* it ended there. That matters because the fix is completely different:

- **The prompt changed.** A timestamp or request ID in the system prompt, tool definitions serialized in a different order, a user name injected near the top. Each one invalidates every block after it. The fix is in the application.
- **The block was evicted.** The prefix was cached earlier but got pushed out under memory pressure. The fix is capacity, routing or cache offload, not the prompt.

Today both look identical from the outside: a short cache hit. Telling them apart means diffing tokenized prompts by hand and guessing about eviction.

**Proposal:** optional per-request diagnostics, disabled by default:

- a **miss reason** for the first uncached block after the longest hit: `evicted` (its hash was cached recently and evicted, tracked with a small bounded set of recently evicted hashes) or `no_match` (no matching block key was seen recently). `no_match` covers both changed prompt tokens and changed extra keys mixed into the block hash (`cache_salt`, LoRA adapter, multimodal inputs), so on its own it is not proof that the text changed.
- a third outcome, `lookup_limit`, when the hit length reached the lookup cap (`num_tokens - 1`, rounded down to a full block). vLLM always recomputes the last prompt token for logits, so that next block is never probed; it is recomputed by design, not missed, and gets no miss reason
- the **kinds of extra keys** included in that block's hash (e.g. `cache_salt`, `lora`, `mm`), names only and never values, so users can rule out salt or adapter differences first
- optionally, an opt-in **comparison against a reference request** that returns a short decoded snippet around the first differing token, off by default for privacy

_Updated after discussion below: renamed `not_cached` to `no_match` and added extra-key kinds (`cache_salt` edge case), and added `lookup_limit` so fully cached prompts at a block boundary are not reported as misses. Test controls: 16/17/32/33-token prompts with block size 16._

These could be surfaced in debug-level logs and/or request-level metrics.

**Why it helps:** teams could catch cache-hostile prompt construction in CI or staging, and tie TTFT regressions to the right cause: a prompt change versus cache pressure in the serving stack.

### Alternatives

- Diffing tokenized prompts by hand against a known-good request. Works for divergence, but is slow, needs the exact tokenized input, and says nothing about eviction.
- Correlating with KV cache events (block stored / removed) externally. Possible, but requires running an event consumer and joining block hashes to requests outside vLLM.
- Re-hashing prompts client-side. This duplicates vLLM's block-hashing logic and drifts whenever that changes (block size, hash function, multimodal or LoRA extra keys).

### Additional context

Related: #43711 proposed a lower-level debug event at the lookup point (`KVCacheManager.get_computed_blocks`, right after `find_longest_cache_hit`). It was closed for inactivity without maintainer feedback. That lookup point looks like the natural place to compute the miss reason above.

Happy to work on a PR if maintainers agree on the approach.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

items.title: [Feature]: Allow pooling tasks (token_embed / token_classify) to reuse prefix cache while returning full hidden-state sequences
items.author: xxyyy
items.body_excerpt:
### The problem

On vLLM 0.29.0, pooling requests with `task="token_embed"` or `task="token_classify"` are **forcefully excluded from prefix-cache reads**, even when prefix caching is explicitly enabled and the caller explicitly requests it.

The mandatory behavior is in `vllm/pooling_params.py` (`_merge_default_parameters`, present in v0.29.0 through current `main`):

```python
if self.skip_reading_prefix_cache is None:
    # If prefix caching is enabled,
    # the output of all pooling may less than n_prompt_tokens,
    # we need to skip reading cache at this request.
    if self.task in ["token_embed", "token_classify"]:
        self.skip_reading_prefix_cache = True
    else:
        self.skip_reading_prefix_cache = False
```

When the caller leaves `skip_reading_prefix_cache` as `None` (the default), it is forced to `True` for these two tasks. There is no supported way for an application to opt in to cache reads while keeping the pooling task.

### Why full hidden states + prefix caching are needed together

Our workload is multi-candidate classification with a sequence-classification adapter (`vllm-jev`, serving Open-Jev-2B style decision heads). For each HTTP request:

1. The prompt is built as `fixed instructions + fixed candidate list (up to ~18 candidates) + per-request state`, so **the leading ~400+ tokens are identical across requests** and only the trailing state differs.
2. The adapter submits one pooling request per candidate (or a deduplicated set of shared-prefix sequences) with `task="token_embed"`, because the decision head needs **the hidden states at specific readout positions** of the full sequence — a scalar `classify` output is not sufficient.
3. Many candidates share the same leading tokens, and the fixed instruction/criteria block is repeated across every request. This is exactly the workload prefix caching is designed for.

With the forced skip, every request recomputes the entire prompt. Measured on an RTX 4090 (vLLM 0.29.0, prefix caching enabled, same `cache_salt`, identical prompts re-submitted back-to-back):

- `metadata.cached_tokens` is always `0` for both `token_embed` and `classify` pooling requests;
- the engine-level `Prefix cache hit rate` metric does occasionally report small non-zero values (2.6%–5.1%), so the cache subsystem itself is alive — but per-request `num_cached_tokens` stays 0 and our throughput matches the "no reuse" expectation;
- using `--decision-template` style reordering so that the fixed text truly leads the prompt does not change this (the skip happens before any block matching).

With the forced skip, every request recomputes the entire prompt. Measured on an RTX 4090 (vLLM 0.29.0, prefix caching enabled, same `cache_salt`, identical prompts re-submitted back-to-back):

- `metadata.cached_tokens` is always `0` for both `token_embed` and `classify` pooling requests;
- the engine-level `Prefix cache hit rate` metric does occasionally report small non-zero values (2.6%–5.1%), so the cache subsystem itself is alive — but per-request `num_cached_tokens` stays 0 and our throughput matches the "no reuse" expectation;
- using `--decision-template` style reordering so that the fixed text truly leads the prompt does not change this (the skip happens before any block matching).

If prefix-cache reads were allowed for `token_embed` requests, the shared leading blocks (instructions + candidate list ≈ 400+ tokens per request, ×18 candidate variants deduplicated by shared prefixes) would be served from cache, which for our benchmark shape roughly halves the per-request prefill compute.

### Why full hidden states + prefix caching are needed together — the general pattern

The pattern behind this request is **"encode once, read out at many positions"**: a decoder runs the prompt once, and lightweight heads (linear probes, small MLPs) read the hidden states at one or more token positions to produce decisions. This is how a growing family of classification/routing models works on top of decoder backbones. For these models:

- a scalar `classify` output is insufficient — the head needs hidden vectors at specific positions;
- the prompts typically share a large fixed prefix (instructions, schema, candidate definitions) with only a small varying payload;
- request rate is high (classification/routing/moderation workloads), so prefill compute dominates.

All three properties make prefix-cache reuse the single biggest performance lever for this model class, which is why the current forced skip hurts disproportionately.

### Why simply forcing `skip_reading_prefix_cache = False` breaks today

We understand the guard exists for a reason. With cache hits, the scheduler marks the hit tokens as already computed, and the pooling runner processes only the non-cached tail — so `token_embed` would return hidden states for fewer positions than the prompt has tokens, while downstream consumers (decision heads over readout positions, token-level classifiers) require **one hidden vector per prompt token, position-aligned**.

So the missing piece is not just the flag: the V1 pooling path (`vllm/v1/worker/gpu/pool/pooling_runner.py`) has no mechanism to reconstruct position-aligned full-sequence hidden outputs when part of the prompt was served from cache.

### Proposed solutions (any one would unblock this workload)

1. **Fill the gap in the pooling runner**: when a `token_embed`/`token_classify` request has prefix-cache hits, still run (or reconstruct) the hidden states for the cached prefix positions so the output remains position-aligned with the full prompt. Conceptually the KV cache already contains the states for those tokens; the runner would need to re-emit their hidden activations from cache rather than skipping them.
2. **Opt-in flag**: expose `skip_reading_prefix_cache=False` as a documented, caller-owned choice for pooling tasks (as it already is for generation tasks), with a clear caveat that the caller must tolerate/align partial hidden outputs. Applic

items.title: [Bug] GLM hybrid-SSM + MTP: deep-ctx agent session sharply degrades (fabricated tool args, self-amnesia) exactly when a concurrent request arrives — persists after #58454/#58368
items.author: ming616
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

On a hybrid-SSM model (GLM-5.3-Flash) served with MTP speculative decoding + prefix caching, a real long-horizon agent session ran cleanly for ~97 tool-loop rounds and then **abruptly degenerated within a single turn boundary** — empty tool-call arguments, fabricated file paths that never appeared anywhere in the session, and amnesia about its own ~60 completed edits — **at the exact second a second concurrent request entered the engine**.

This phenotype **persists after applying upstream #58454 and #58368** (the rejected-draft/SSM-state × prefix-cache pollution fixes), so we believe there is a remaining sibling gap in the spec-decode × hybrid-SSM-state × concurrency path. We have not yet been able to reproduce it synthetically; we are filing the forensics in case the pattern is recognizable.

## Environment

- Engine: vLLM **v0.13.1 lineage** on Ampere (via the wtdcode/vllm-backport fork; single-GPU-arch backport of upstream, sm_80) + the backport of upstream **#58454** and **#58368** (applied 2026-10-11)
- Model: **GLM-5.3-Flash-AWQ** (MoE, hybrid linear-attention SSM + full attention layers)- Serving: TP4 on 4×A800, `--max-model-len 1048576` (1M), `--speculative-config {method:mtp, num_speculative_tokens:3}`, prefix caching on (default), chunked prefill on, cudagraph_mode=FULL_DECODE_ONLY (capture sizes ≤32), block_size 256, max_num_seqs 4, max_num_batched_tokens 8192
- Client: an agent harness (ZCode) doing OpenAI-compatible chat completions with tools; single stream; conversation grew 69K → 231K prompt tokens over 123 model calls; prefix cache hit ~99%

## Incident forensics

**Token/behavior timeline** (from client-side model-io logs, 123 calls):

- Rounds 1–97 (input 69K → 225K): all outputs sane (correct edits, greps, valid tool JSON). Same client, same link — client-side quoting/encoding issues ruled out.
- **Round 98 (input 225,354) is the sharp onset**: `Edit` tool call with **empty arguments `{}`**; next rounds produced fabricated paths (`E:\github\placeholder`, `/h/mnt/mnt`, `.swk\app`) and hallucinated files (`pipeline_chapter.py`) that no part of the conversation ever contained.
- Degenerate state persisted for the remaining ~26 rounds (short 15–200 token outputs, futile loops).
- Final round: the model stated *"I haven't actually done anything yet — I've only read files in this session"*, despite ~60 completed edits in its (verified) full history. The full payload WAS being sent: input=231,487 tokens, cached=229,120.

**Server-side correlation** (10s-interval engine loggers):

- At the corruption-onset second the engine logged **`Running: 2 reqs`** — the proxy access log confirms two interleaved client streams at that moment. Onset is sharp and coincides with the concurrent request; the preceding ~2h of single-request service was clean.
- During the degenerate window, spec-decode metrics oscillate oddly: **mean acceptance length drops to 1.5–1.8 (15–27% per-position acceptance)** while garbage is generated, then long later outputs show **92–98% acceptance** (suspiciously predictable — repetitive-generation signature).
- The engine was **completely silent**: zero errors, zero preemptions, zero aborts, repetition-detection never fired.

## What we ruled out

1. **Context depth alone**: a synthetic dual probe on the same engine/weights passed at every depth (8K baseline; 52K/88K/124K/354K/399K): needle retrieval 3/3 at all depths, generation dup8 0.016–0.039, arithmetic correct, all finish=stop.
2. **Cross-session leakage** (the #57128/#58454/#58368 phenotype): donor/victim canaries pass with leak=0 at 114K and 450K; the incident output contained **no other-session content** — this is a fabrication/corruption phenotype, not leakage.
3. **Quantized weights**: the same weights produce large volumes of clean output (97 rounds + all probes above); cloud serving of the same model shows no such behavior.
4. **Client-side corruption**: outputs are server-generated tool-call JSON; client unchanged across the clean/degenerate boundary.

## Reproduction attempts (negative so far)

- **Single-shot concurrency**: 305K-token victim with a tools file-creation task × 2 solo controls + 6 rounds with a concurrent 305K donor — all 8 victim outputs byte-clean.
- **Multi-turn concurrency**: victim multi-turn loop at ~400K growing prefix with a donor request concurrent every turn, 20 turns — no hard corruption.
- Exact replay is impossible for us (client log redacts message bodies).

The trigger appears to need the real agent mix (2h session tail, hundreds of spec-decode turn boundaries, real tool content) plus the precise interleaving of the second request.

## Relation to known issues

- #57128 (`MambaManager.find_longest_cache_hit` ignores `drop_eagle_block` — unfixed at the time we checked) — same subsystem.
- #58454 / #58368 — **applied on our fork before this incident**; this phenotype survives them.
- #53912 (Suppressor72's minimal honor-drop patch shown unsafe at three sites) — more evidence this state-management corner is delicate.

**Workaround that works**: `spec=0` (MTP off). Every incident we have ever observed on this lane required `spec >= 1`; with MTP off we have had zero recurrences (but a ~2× decode cost).

## Ask

Is this pattern — *sharp mid-session generation corruption at deep ctx coinciding with a concurrent request*, under MTP + prefix caching on hybrid-SSM — known or explainable from the current state-management code? We can share: the full client-side model-io log of the incident (123 requests, per-request timing/tokens), engine 10s-logger excerpts around onset, and our (negative) repro harness.

Happy to run instrumented builds if someone points at where to add assertions (draft/SSM state rollback paths, kpool recycling, or prefix-cache invalidation on preemption).

items.title: L1 eviction races async L2 store: chunks discarded before offload are never stored (persistent re-prefill under L1 pressure)
items.author: ShreyasBaasri07
items.body_excerpt:
**Label**
Bug

**Describe the bug**
In LMCache v0.5.5 (MP mode), under L1 (CPU) memory pressure, freshly-computed KV chunks can be evicted from L1 before the asynchronous store controller offloads them to L2, so they are silently dropped and never written to L2 — even when L2 is large enough to hold the entire working set and has no eviction configured.

The result: with a shared-prefix (prefix-caching-style) workload, ~19% of requests permanently retrieve only the shared prefix (first half of the prompt) and re-prefill the unique tail on every recurrence, indefinitely. The half-hits persist through the whole run, not just warmup.

Root cause (confirmed in v0.5.5 source):

L1 eviction destination defaults to EvictionDestination.DISCARD — L1 eviction does not offload to L2 (lru.py, eviction_controller.py:193).
The StoreController offloads L1→L2 by reserve_read-ing keys received from an L1_WRITE_FINISHED notification. If a key was already discard-evicted in the meantime, reserve_read returns KEY_NOT_EXIST, the key is silently skipped from the store (only surfaced as an L1_READ_FAILED / lmcache_mp.l1_read_failure "not_found" anomaly), and it never reaches L2 (lmcache/v1/distributed/storage_controllers/store_controller.py:600-627).
So there is a race between L1 DISCARD eviction and the async L2 offload; the loser is silently never stored.

**To Reproduce**
Environment: LMCache v0.5.5, MP mode, L1 + L2 where L2 is sized to hold the full working set and has no L2 eviction, and L1 is smaller than the shared-prefix working set.

Start the LMCache MP server with a small L1 and one large L2 adapter (e.g. S3/filesystem), no L2 eviction:
lmcache server --host 0.0.0.0 --port 6555 --chunk-size 256 \
  --l1-size-gb 60 --eviction-policy LRU \
  --l2-adapter '{"type":"s3", ... ,"max_capacity_gb":500}'

Start vLLM with LMCacheMPConnector (kv_role: kv_both), --no-enable-prefix-caching --enforce-eager.
Run a shared-prefix benchmark whose prefix pool exceeds L1. With aiperf/genai-perf
--prefix-prompt-length 4096 --num-prefix-prompts 150 \
--isl 4096 --osl 100 --num-dataset-entries 200 \
--concurrency 10 --random-seed 42 --benchmark-duration 1200

Here 150 prefixes × 4096 tokens ≈ 75 GB of prefix KV > 60 GB L1. Each request = 8192 tokens (4096 shared prefix + 4096 unique tail).

Grep the server log for Retrieved N tokens.

Observed — persistent prefix-only half-hits throughout the run (not just warmup)
Half-hits occur at ~20–32/min even in steady state, long after every one of the 200 fixed prompts has been served many times. Since retrieval is a contiguous match from token 0, Retrieved 4096 means "prefix found, tail missing → prefill." (Optionally, lmcache_mp.l1_read_failure / L1_READ_FAILED "not_found" events fire in the same window.)

Control: setting --num-prefix-prompts 10 (prefix pool now fits in L1) eliminates the half-hits — all requests become full 8192-token hits. So the trigger is specifically L1 < shared-prefix pool.

**Expected behavior**
Once a chunk is computed and admitted to L1, it should reliably be offloaded to L2 and remain retrievable regardless of L1 pressure. A chunk should not be silently dropped from the L2 store just because it was evicted from L1 before the async offload read it. Subsequent requests for the same prompt should be full L2 hits, not re-prefills, when L2 has capacity and no eviction.

**Screenshots**
N/A (server-side KV-cache behavior; log evidence included above).

**Desktop (please complete the following information):**
OS: Linux
LMCache: v0.5.5
vLLM: 0.26.0
PyTorch: 2.11.0+cu130
Python: 3.12.3
GPU: NVIDIA L40S
Mode: MP (LMCacheMPConnector, kv_role: kv_both), --chunk-size 256, --l1-size-gb 60, L2 sized to hold full working set with no L2 eviction

**Smartphone (please complete the following information):**
N/A (not a mobile/browser issue)

**Additional context**
Add any other context about the problem here.

items.title: [Bug] P2P load timeout can report terminal failure while the transfer is still active
items.author: 0andy
items.body_excerpt:
**Describe the bug**

`P2PL2Adapter.query_load_result()` returns a terminal all-zero `Bitmap` as soon as `load_timeout_s` expires, without querying or cancelling the underlying `TransferChannelClient` read ([p2p_l2_adapter.py#L333-L336](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/8d7d2c47e1edb8c107033ae709722b2c3a05dec4/lmcache/v1/distributed/l2_adapters/p2p_l2_adapter.py#L333-L336)). The read may still be in flight at that point, so the adapter reports "finished (failed)" for a load whose transfer has not reached a terminal state.

The existing test `test_load_deadline_expired_yields_failure` asserts exactly this behaviour, so I am raising it as a contract question rather than a regression: is a terminal load result allowed to precede the end of the transfer?

**To Reproduce**

On `dev` @ 8d7d2c47, add this test to `tests/v1/distributed/l2_adapters/test_p2p_l2_adapter.py`:

```python
def test_load_deadline_does_not_report_terminal_while_read_is_in_flight():
    keys = [_key(0)]
    now = [100.0]
    in_flight = TransferChannelReadResult(finished=False)
    with (
        _adapter(load_timeout_s=0.01) as (adapter, _mq, _tc_ctx, tc_client, _n),
        patch.object(p2p_mod.time, "monotonic", side_effect=lambda: now[0]),
    ):
        adapter._remote_addresses[keys[0]] = TransferChannelAddress(offset=100, size=10)
        tc_client.submit_read.return_value = 123
        tc_client.query_read_status.return_value = in_flight
        task_id = adapter.submit_load_task(
            keys, [MagicMock(shm_offset=0, shm_byte_length=10)]
        )
        now[0] = 100.02  # past the 0.01 s load deadline
        assert not in_flight.is_finished()
        assert adapter.query_load_result(task_id) is None
```

```
pytest -v tests/v1/distributed/l2_adapters/test_p2p_l2_adapter.py -k "deadline or not_finished"
```

Result (CPU-only build, transfer channel mocked):

```
>           assert adapter.query_load_result(task_id) is None
E           assert 0 is None
E            +  where 0 = query_load_result(0)

LMCache WARNING: P2P load task 0 timed out; treating as a failure (p2p_l2_adapter.py:335)

test_lookup_deadline_expired_yields_miss PASSED
test_load_not_finished_returns_none PASSED
test_load_deadline_expired_yields_failure PASSED
test_load_deadline_does_not_report_terminal_while_read_is_in_flight FAILED
1 failed, 3 passed
```

(`0` is the repr of a one-key, all-zero `Bitmap`, i.e. a terminal failure.)

This test only demonstrates the current behaviour; its assertion would need adjusting depending on which direction below is preferred.

**Expected behavior**

Either the adapter does not report a terminal load result while its transfer-channel read may still access the destination buffers, or the contract states explicitly that a terminal result does not imply the transfer has quiesced and callers handle that.

**Additional context**

To be clear about what is and is not shown:

*Reproduced (unit test above):* the read is modelled as unfinished, and after the deadline `query_load_result()` returns a terminal failure.

*Derived from reading the code, not reproduced:*
- On that result, `PrefetchController._poll_load_results()` calls `finish_write_and_delete()` for the failed keys and then `submit_unlock()` ([prefetch_controller.py#L1389-L1395](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/8d7d2c47e1edb8c107033ae709722b2c3a05dec4/lmcache/v1/distributed/storage_controllers/prefetch_controller.py#L1389-L1395)); for P2P, `submit_unlock()` sends `p2p_unlock_objects` to the peer ([#L277-L280](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/8d7d2c47e1edb8c107033ae709722b2c3a05dec4/lmcache/v1/distributed/l2_adapters/p2p_l2_adapter.py#L277-L280)). So both the destination staging buffer and the source-side lock are released.
- The NIXL transfer channel registers the whole L1 buffer once ([nixl_impl.py#L344](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/8d7d2c47e1edb8c107033ae709722b2c3a05dec4/lmcache/v1/distributed/transfer_channel/impl/nixl_impl.py#L344)). This creates a window in which a late read may write into memory that has since been reassigned to another key.
- After the timeout the adapter no longer queries the read, so the `NixlTransferChannelClient._tasks` entry and its xfer handle are only released on `close()` ([#L178-L181](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/8d7d2c47e1edb8c107033ae709722b2c3a05dec4/lmcache/v1/distributed/transfer_channel/impl/nixl_impl.py#L178-L181), [#L202-L206](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/8d7d2c47e1edb8c107033ae709722b2c3a05dec4/lmcache/v1/distributed/transfer_channel/impl/nixl_impl.py#L202-L206)).

*Not reproduced:* actual stale or corrupted KV data end to end. I have not run a two-instance NIXL test for this.

**Possible directions** (not proposing a specific fix yet)

- **A. Stay pending until the transfer is terminal.** After the deadline, keep polling `query_read_status()` and only report once it finishes. Simple ownership model; a hung transfer would hold its buffers and locks indefinitely.
- **B. Add per-task cancellation to `TransferChannelClient`** ([abstract.py#L52-L88](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/8d7d2c47e1edb8c107033ae709722b2c3a05dec4/lmcache/v1/distributed/transfer_channel/abstract.py#L52-L88) has only `submit_read`, `query_read_status`, `close`), and report terminal only once the cancel is confirmed. For NIXL this would map to `releaseXferReq`, which the BackendGuide says "can return error, meaning it was not successful in aborting the request", so it still needs A as a fallback. The Mooncake wrapper has no cancel today; I have not checked the engine itself.
- **C. Drop the adapter-level load deadline** and rely on the controller-level deadline from #5255, which already keeps late loads' buffers and locks until the load result arrives.

The P2P adapter is the runtime caller of `submit_read()`; the transfer-channel benchmark also calls it directly, so an API change in B would touch both.

**Related**

- #5263 — same ownership family, on the shutdown / TTL paths rat
items.author_work_intent: If maintainers agree this is a contract gap, I'm happy to work on the fix. I'd especially appreciate guidance on whether the preferred direction is to keep timed-out reads pending until terminal, add a TransferChannel cancell

comments.author: holtwood
comments.body:
I checked another timeout case at [`1ca53a8`](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/1ca53a8aadca1d054f171fd67350be35797cfddc/lmcache/v1/distributed/l2_adapters/p2p_l2_adapter.py#L326-L347) using the original query methods with mocked dependencies. I haven't run a real NIXL transfer.

Even when the transfer is already marked `DONE`, polling after the deadline returns a zero bitmap without calling `query_read_status`. The adapter removes its task, so later adapter polls return `None`. The client's `close()` still has a separate cleanup path.

This seems worth covering in the timeout tests, including cleanup of an already-completed transfer. I can help add that case if it's useful.

items.title: [Bug] HiCacheFile scans the whole store directory on every existence check, so the scheduler stalls as the store grows
items.author: Yunzez
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

With `--hicache-storage-backend file`, every prefix-existence check walks the **entire** store directory:

```python
# python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/hicache_storage.py:590
        if self.metadata_cache is None:
            existing_files = set()
            with os.scandir(self.file_path) as entries:     # O(files in the store)
                for entry in entries:
                    if entry.is_file() and entry.name in target_files:
                        existing_files.add(entry.name)
            return existing_files
```

`target_files` holds a handful of names. The branch below it does the right thing — `os.path.exists` per target key, O(len(keys)) — but it is only taken when `metadata_cache` is not None, and

```python
# python/sglang/srt/environ.py:723
    SGLANG_HICACHE_FILE_BACKEND_ENABLE_METADATA_CACHE = EnvBool(False)
```

so **a stock file-backend server takes the scanning branch**.

Every block is one file in one flat directory (`os.path.join(self.file_path, f"{key}.bin")`, no sharding), and the store grows continuously while serving. Under `--hicache-storage-prefetch-policy wait_complete` the lookup is synchronous on the request path, so as the store grows the scheduler stalls: the waiting queue stays non-empty while nothing is running.


Ask claude to measure if this is a real issue: 

It ran SGLang 0.5.19, `Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B`, one RTX 4090, 40-minute cells, identical seed, identical workload and the same single contract. The only difference is the L3 file tier:

| arm | server flags | iterations | scheduler stalls | latency spikes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| file tier | `--enable-hierarchical-cache --hicache-ratio 2.0 --hicache-write-policy write_through --hicache-storage-backend file --hicache-storage-prefetch-policy wait_complete --hicache-storage-backend-extra-config '{"prefetch_threshold":64}' --max-total-tokens 8192` | 96 | **10** | 9 |
| host tier only (control) | the same **without** the three `--hicache-storage-*` flags, ratio 8.0 | **353** | **0** | **0** |

The control did **3.7x** the work -- 353 iterations and 7,663 requests against 96 and 1,884 -- and stalled zero times, with zero latency spikes and zero KV-leak rows. Its single contract was also judged 45 times against 2 on the file arm, because a lookup that returns promptly leaves room to judge. A stall is "the waiting queue was non-empty continuously for ≥3 s after the running queue drained to zero"; p99 TTFT on the file arm reached 36,975 ms at concurrency 3.

**Dose-response**, which is what points at the directory scan rather than at slow storage in general, same cell, same budget, differing only in how full the store was at the start:

| store at start | first stall | stalls in the run |
|---|---|---|
| 43 GB / 398,543 files (grown by a previous run) | iteration **13** | 17 |
| empty | iteration **37** | 10 |

The store reaches ~1.2 GB/min while serving; the two runs left 43 GB and 48 GB behind.


## Suggested fix
Either:

1. **Default `SGLANG_HICACHE_FILE_BACKEND_ENABLE_METADATA_CACHE` to true.** The correct code path already exists and is already tested; only the default keeps it out of reach.
2. Drop the scanning branch entirely and always use the per-key `os.path.exists` path. `os.scandir` over the whole store to find ≤ `len(keys)` names is never the better plan, it is strictly more work than stat-ing the names you are looking for.
3. Shard the store into subdirectories by key prefix, so no single directory grows without bound. Worth doing regardless of 1 and 2, since the directory is also enumerated elsewhere (`_scan_existing_files_to_metadata_cache`, the clear path).

### Reproduction

[repro_sglang_hicache_file_scandir.py](https://gist.github.com/Yunzez/b3de5dd240a2588cc515c2778bd3c5c9#file-repro_sglang_hicache_file_scandir-py)

items.title: [Bug]: Paused streaming sessions deadlock the scheduler when the KV cache is full
items.author: damienlaine
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment

Scheduler-level repro on CPU, no model or GPU needed. Main at `89a00995c9`. Also hit on GPU with Voxtral realtime, V1 and V2 model runners.

### 🐛 Describe the bug

A paused streaming session (`resumable`, `WAITING_FOR_STREAMING_REQ`) keeps its KV blocks. When its next chunk arrives it goes through `kv_holding_waiting`. If the pool is full, `allocate_slots` fails and the waiting loop breaks. Preemption only takes from `running`, which is empty because every session is between chunks. Nothing gets freed, and every session stays waiting forever.

So once the sessions' KV goes over the pool, all of them freeze, not only the one that doesn't fit.

Repro (4 sessions, 7 usable blocks of 16 tokens, each chunk adds one block):

```python
from unittest.mock import MagicMock

import torch

from vllm.config import DeviceConfig, VllmConfig
from vllm.sampling_params import SamplingParams
from vllm.v1.core.sched.scheduler import Scheduler
from vllm.v1.kv_cache_interface import FullAttentionSpec, KVCacheConfig, KVCacheGroupSpec
from vllm.v1.outputs import ModelRunnerOutput
from vllm.v1.request import Request
from vllm.v1.structured_output import StructuredOutputManager

STOP = 128001
BLOCK = 16
NUM_BLOCKS = 8
NUM_SESSIONS = 4


def make_scheduler():
    cfg = VllmConfig(device_config=DeviceConfig("cpu"))
    cfg.model_config = MagicMock()
    cfg.model_config.skip_tokenizer_init = True
    cfg.model_config.is_multimodal_model = False
    cfg.model_config.supports_multimodal_inputs = False
    cfg.model_config.is_encoder_decoder = False
    cfg.model_config.is_diffusion = False
    cfg.model_config.max_model_len = 1024
    cfg.model_config.enable_return_routed_experts = False
    cfg.cache_config = MagicMock()
    cfg.cache_config.num_gpu_blocks = NUM_BLOCKS
    cfg.cache_config.enable_prefix_caching = False
    kv = KVCacheConfig(
        num_blocks=NUM_BLOCKS,
        kv_cache_tensors=[],
        kv_cache_groups=[KVCacheGroupSpec(["layer"], FullAttentionSpec(
            block_size=BLOCK, num_kv_heads=1, head_size=1, dtype=torch.float32))],
    )
    return Scheduler(vllm_config=cfg, kv_cache_config=kv, log_stats=False,
                     structured_output_manager=StructuredOutputManager(cfg),
                     block_size=BLOCK, hash_block_size=BLOCK)


def chunk(rid, n):
    # One streaming update: n new prompt tokens, generation stops after 1 token.
    return Request(request_id=rid, prompt_token_ids=list(range(1, n + 1)),
                   sampling_params=SamplingParams(stop_token_ids=[STOP], max_tokens=16),
                   pooling_params=None, resumable=True)


s = make_scheduler()
ids = [f"s{i}" for i in range(NUM_SESSIONS)]
for rid in ids:
    s.add_request(chunk(rid, BLOCK - 1))

for step in range(12):
    out = s.schedule()
    sched = list(out.num_scheduled_tokens)
    free = s.kv_cache_manager.block_pool.get_num_free_blocks()
    print(f"step {step}: scheduled={sched} free_blocks={free} "
          f"waiting={len(s.waiting) + len(getattr(s, 'kv_holding_waiting', []))}")
    if not sched:
        continue
    # Every scheduled session ends its chunk (STOP) and pauses, keeping its KV.
    s.update_from_output(out, ModelRunnerOutput(
        req_ids=sched, req_id_to_index={r: i for i, r in enumerate(sched)},
        sampled_token_ids=[[STOP] for _ in sched], logprobs=None,
        prompt_logprobs_dict={}, pooler_output=[]))
    # The client sends the next chunk for each of them.
    for rid in sched:
        s.add_request(chunk(rid, BLOCK))
```

```
step 0: scheduled=['s0', 's1', 's2', 's3'] free_blocks=3 waiting=0
step 1: scheduled=['s0', 's1', 's2'] free_blocks=0 waiting=1
step 2: scheduled=[] free_blocks=0 waiting=4
...
step 11: scheduled=[] free_blocks=0 waiting=4
```

On GPU, Voxtral-Mini-4B-Realtime with a 256 sliding window (~128 MiB KV per session) and `--kv-cache-memory 1GiB`: 7 sessions run fine, with 9 every session stops after a few seconds, 0 tok/s, no preemption, all 9 transcriptions cut. `--max-num-seqs 7` avoids it, the extra sessions just wait.

Expected: preempt a paused session (free its KV, recompute on resume) instead of blocking the queue.

Related: #58776 (a preempted resumable session is dropped). The encoder cache has the same pattern: a paused session keeps its last multimodal item cached until it resumes, and when the cache can't hold them all the waiting loop breaks the same way (seen with a small encoder cache in #45022).

comments.author: he-yufeng
comments.body:
Reproduced on current main (`31e2443c90`, CPU scheduler-level, exact script from the report): deadlock from step 2 on, `scheduled=[]` for the remaining 10 steps with `free_blocks=0` and all 4 sessions waiting.

This is the deadlock #59339 already fixes: it reclaims KV blocks from paused/`kv_holding` sessions at the waiting loop's allocation-failure point, which is the gap described here (preemption only scans `running`, and `running` is empty). I ran the same repro on #59339's head (`a0f422aa`): continuous progress from step 2 through 8 as paused sessions get reclaimed and resumed. The repro then stalls again at steps 9-11, but that is genuine capacity exhaustion, not deadlock: each session's prompt grows one block per round, so by then a single chunk needs ~9 blocks against an 8-block pool and nothing can legitimately fit.

One note for whoever picks up review: #59339's only red check is the pre-run gate (author has 2 merged PRs, needs a `verified`/`ready` label), not a code failure.

comments.author: divyuuu
comments.body:
Checked this on current main (`1e5d0ea`).

Static trace matches the report: the running-loop only preempts from `self.running` (`vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py:776-782`), and the waiting-loop `allocate_slots` failure path just `break`s (`1241-1248`) with no reclaim from `kv_holding_waiting`. So once all sessions are paused holding KV and `running` is empty, every `schedule()` stalls with nothing scheduled and nothing freed.

I also checked #59339 (reclaim at the waiting-loop failure point, updated Oct 6) to avoid duplicating it. Validating next whether it covers this exact 4-session repro on a Linux runner (my Windows host can't build vLLM -- no AMD64 precompiled wheel, only manylinux). Repro script ready from the issue body.

If a regression-test gap remains after #59339, may I take it? Happy to contribute the repro as a scheduler regression test. AI assistance used for the trace; will run the repro and tests before any PR per the contribution guide.

comments.author: damienlaine
comments.body:
Ran #59339 (`a0f422aa`) against its base (`21d93d0d8c`) on GPU with Voxtral realtime: RTX 4090, 256/256 sliding windows, `--max-num-batched-tokens 256`, `--kv-cache-memory-bytes 1GiB` (11,915 tokens), 120 s streams sent in real time.

| | completed | generation | words/stream |
|---|---|---|---|
| base, 9 sessions | 0/9, stalled after ~20 s | 0 tok/s | ~15 |
| #59339, 9 sessions | 0/9 | 65 → ~7 tok/s (~110 needed) | ~60 |
| #59339, 8 sessions | 0/8 | ~6 tok/s | ~80 |
| #59339, 7 sessions (fit in pool) | 7/7 | same output as reference | ~275 |
| default pool (49,152 tokens), 9 sessions | 9/9 | 112 tok/s | ~280 |

The stall is gone and reclaimed sessions produce correct output (97-100% word match with the reference on the same audio). Under overcommit, throughput collapses for all sessions, not only the extra one: a reclaimed session restarts from `num_computed_tokens = 0` and recomputes its full history, encoder included, so the cost per reclaim grows with session age.

Also tried restricting victims to sessions with lower `(priority, arrival_time)` than the requester, as the running-loop preemption does: 0/8 and 0/9, ~10 tok/s, and it breaks 3 of #59339's tests. Victim selection is not the issue.

Regression tests for this case are already in #59339 (14 tests, pass locally).

items.title: [SM120] Field report: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash in production on 8x RTX PRO 6000 (PCIe, no NVLink) - working config, measured throughput, rejected topologies
items.author: Lei-010
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

Field data from running **DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash** as a production SGLang backend on **8× RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Max-Q (SM120, 96 GB, PCIe-only — no NVLink)**, including the *only* topology we could get to start, measured prefill/decode, a speculative-decoding A/B, and the configuration traps that cost us real experiments. Posting because SM120 + V4.1-Flash users currently have to rediscover all of this from scratch.

Full write-up (with methodology and reproduction artifacts): https://github.com/Lei-010/hermes-agent/blob/main/docs/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-SM120-Performance-and-Production-Config.md

Related: vLLM field report https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/56700 (same hardware, vLLM side), vLLM https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/56892 (SM120 bug/perf tracker).

## What works

```bash
docker run --gpus all -d --name dsv41 \
  --shm-size=64g --ipc=host --network host \
  --restart unless-stopped \
  -e TP_SIZE=8 -e DP_SIZE=1 -e EP_SIZE=8 \
  -e SPEC_ALGORITHM=dspark -e DSPARK_BLOCK_SIZE=6 \
  -e CHUNKED_PREFILL_SIZE=2048 \
  -v /ssd/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash:/model \
  <sglang image>
```

Effective `server_args` (verified at runtime via `/get_server_info`):

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| `tp_size` / `ep_size` / `dp_size` | 8 / 8 / 1 |
| `speculative_algorithm` | DSPARK, `speculative_dspark_block_size = 6` |
| `chunked_prefill_size` | 2048 |
| `context_length` | 1,048,576 |
| `kv_cache_dtype` | `fp8_e4m3` |
| `mem_fraction_static` | 0.72 |
| `max_running_requests` | 16 |
| `attention_backend` / `moe_runner_backend` | `dsv4` / `flashinfer_mxfp4` |
| CUDA graph decode / prefill | full (max_bs 16) / **disabled** |

**TP8/EP8 is not a preference — it is the only layout that starts** (see "Topologies SGLang rejects" below).

## Measured throughput (cold, single stream, tokens from `usage`, not SSE chunk counts)

128K cold prefill:

| Config | tok/s |
|---|---|
| `chunked_prefill_size=2048` (production) | **6,853** |
| same config re-run | 6,765 (−1.3%) |
| flashmla prefill backend | 6,845 |
| fused-MoE all-reduce | 6,828 |
| `chunked_prefill_size=4096` | 6,301 |
| `chunked_prefill_size=1024` | 6,012 |

32K prompt: ≈7,196 tok/s. GPU util ≈87% at 220 W of 600 W → **communication-bound on PCIe**, not compute-bound. ~7K tok/s looks like the ceiling for this board without NVLink.

Radix/prefix cache is the only large multiplier: cache-hit prefill **0.34 s for a 112K-token prefix ≈ 325K tok/s (≈39×)**.

Decode (client path over SSH tunnel, production config): prose 93.9 tok/s, structured/JSON 134.1 tok/s, TTFT 143–169 ms.

## DSPARK A/B (block_size=2, clean legs, each verified via `server_info` + acceptance length)

| Prompt class | DSPARK ON | DSPARK OFF |
|---|---|---|
| prose | 76.5–78.9 tok/s | 36.4–36.5 tok/s |
| structured | 120.3–120.5 tok/s | 36.5 tok/s |
| `accept len` | 3.0 tokens/step | 1.0 |

With DSPARK off the model flattens to ~36.5 tok/s regardless of prompt class — speculation is the difference between usable and unusable latency on this hardware. Production ships `block_size=6` (structured ≈237–252 tok/s vs 120 at block 2).

## Traps that cost us experiments (SGLang-specific)

1. **`--enable-expert-parallel` is a vLLM flag** — SGLang takes `ep_size`; the vLLM spelling is rejected outright.
2. **`docker run` must pass `TP_SIZE`/`DP_SIZE`/`EP_SIZE` explicitly.** Without `-e`, the container silently serves TP8 defaults and your "new" config never happens (we recorded a full sweep of false data this way before adding a config gate).
3. **`ep_size ≤ tp_size`** or the MoE rank computation divides by zero: `moe_ep_rank = tp_rank % (tp_size // moe_dp_size) // (tp_size // moe_dp_size // ep_size)`.
4. **DSPARK + DP attention requires `--enable-dp-lm-head`** — but is unreachable on this model anyway (next section).

## Topologies SGLang rejects on this model

| Attempt | Result |
|---|---|
| DP2 × TP4 (any EP) | `ValueError: V4.1 vision currently supports TP/EP without DP, CP, PP or MoE A2A` — both replicas die within ~70 s |
| prefill context-parallel | same class of rejection |
| `--enable-dp-attention` alone | silently no DP group (`dp_size: 1`) — looks fine, isn't |

Other SM120 gaps we hit: MSCCL++ (`_tune` kernel crash), FlashInfer all-reduce fusion, `flashmla_sparse_q8`, and CUDA-graph capture for **prefill** (crashes even with DSPARK off, i.e. unrelated to speculation).

## Operational notes

- A defunct container can survive a single `docker rm -f`; the next `docker run` then fails on the name conflict while an orphaned engine process keeps the port and answers health checks — which silently mislabels the next experiment. Loop `docker rm -f` until the container is gone **and** nothing listens on the port.
- A parse failure must never satisfy an "expected config" assertion, or a server that has not started yet gets recorded as "spec disabled".
- Verify intended config from the server (`/get_server_info`) before timing anything; discard legs that fail the gate rather than recording them.

## Not established

No 24 h soak (numbers come from a working day of production use), block sizes 4/8/12 not re-measured with the fixed sweep tool, and >32K prefill/long-context degradation not characterised.

items.title: [RFC] Torch Ops Improvements and Backend Routing
items.author: hlin99
items.body_excerpt:
## Background

Today, Torch ops and C ops are separate implementations. This RFC proposes to:

1. Close the functional gap between Torch ops and C ops.
2. Reorganize the Torch ops file layout to align with C ops.
3. Route ops through per-device `DeviceOps` implementations.

## Step 1: Close the Gap Between Torch Ops and C Ops (https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/pull/4370)

The first step is to complete the missing Torch ops functionality and close the gap with C ops. A related PR already exists.

### Motivation

1. **Hybrid model convergence**

   Complete Torch ops support is required for converging hybrid models in the LMCache engine-driven path.

2. **Complete fallback support for device vendors**

   A complete Torch ops implementation provides a functional fallback, allowing device vendors to evaluate LMCache software support quickly before implementing or optimizing native C ops.

## Step 2: Reorganize the Torch Ops File Layout

The second step is to reorganize the Torch ops file layout and align it with the C ops layout.

### Motivation

Currently, Torch ops are concentrated in a single large file. The file is difficult to maintain and becomes increasingly hard to extend as more ops are added.

Aligning the Torch ops layout with C ops will improve maintainability and make the relationship between the two implementations clearer.

## Step 3: Route Ops Through Per-Device `DeviceOps`

### Current Design

Today, `bind_native()` directly replaces a `DeviceOps` method with a native function. Once bound, the original `DeviceOps` method is bypassed.

An op can therefore only use one implementation: native ops or Torch ops.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Before["Before: function replacement"]
        A["DeviceOps.op()"] -->|"bind_native() overwrites op"| B["native_op()"]
        C["DeviceOps.op()"] -->|"no native binding"| D["torch_op()"]
    end
```

### Proposed Design

After this change, `DeviceOps` methods are always retained. Each device-specific `DeviceOps` subclass intercepts the call, performs necessary device-specific handling, and forwards the call to native ops or Torch ops dynamically.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph After["After: DeviceOps interception and forwarding"]
        E["DeviceOps.op()"] --> F{"platform / device routing"}
        F --> G["native_op()"]
        F --> H["torch_op()"]
    end
```

### Motivation

1. **Use Tensor as the unified upper-layer interface**

   Upper-layer code should always pass Tensors and should not need to know whether the selected backend is native ops or Torch ops.

   If native ops are selected, the device-specific `DeviceOps` subclass can convert Tensors to pointers as needed. If Torch ops are selected, it forwards Tensors directly.

2. **Route based on KV format**

   A device vendor may support only a subset of KV formats in its native ops, while Torch ops provide complete functional coverage.

   The device-specific `DeviceOps` subclass can select native ops for supported formats and fall back to Torch ops for unsupported formats.

   For example, the vLLM path can use the optimized native path when supported. The SGLang path may prioritize functional coverage and fall back to Torch ops when a native implementation does not support the requested KV format.

3. **Simplify the current code structure**

   There is currently a significant amount of logic under `platform` that exists because upper layers pass pointers and need to reconstruct Tensors.

   Moving backend-specific conversion and routing into the device-specific `DeviceOps` subclass will simplify the platform code structure.

4. **Make multi-op composition easier**

   The device-specific `DeviceOps` subclass can combine multiple low-level ops into a single API for upper layers.

   For example, `multi_block_transfer` and `memcpy_async` can be composed behind one API, while the upper layer does not need to know the composition details.

5. **Support multiple backends per device**

   This design allows a device to select among multiple backends, such as native ops, Torch ops, TorchMUSA, Triton, or other vendor-specific implementations.

   For example, MUSA can dynamically select between its `torchmusa` and native backends. The same structure can support additional backends in the future.
