items.title: [Bug] fs_native L2: files left by a previous process are never counted toward max_capacity_gb or evicted (disk grows unbounded across restarts)
items.author: OscarSavNS
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

With the `fs_native` L2 adapter, chunk files persist across a server restart and are still served (lookup is a `stat` on the file), but the new process never registers them. They don't count toward `max_capacity_gb`, and the eviction policy never sees them, so **they are never evicted**. Each restart can strand up to a full cap of untracked files, and disk usage grows without bound until the filesystem fills.

## Observed

`lmcache/vllm-openai` image, LMCache `0.5.6rc1` (commit `9a7b6050`), MP server with:

```
--l2-adapter '{"type":"fs_native","base_path":"/lmcache/l2","num_workers":32,"use_odirect":true,
  "max_capacity_gb":1000,"eviction":{"eviction_policy":"LRU","trigger_watermark":0.9,"eviction_ratio":0.1}}'
```

1. Wrote ~1.2 TB of KV. LRU eviction worked as documented: usage hit the 0.9 watermark three times and dropped to 871 GB each time (`L2 usage 0.90 above watermark 0.90; triggering eviction`).
2. Restarted the server with the same `base_path`: 298,340 files, 911.7 GB on disk.
3. After the restart, `GET /status` reported `l2_eviction_controller.adapters[0].total_bytes_used = 0`.
4. Requests over the pre-restart prefixes were served from those files: 16.76M tokens, every full chunk, `lookup_hit_l2_tokens_total` +16,760,832. After that, tracked usage was 0.49 GB, i.e. only the new writes, while 911.7 GB of served files stayed untracked.

## Root cause (on `dev` at dc68527c)

- Byte accounting and eviction order are fed only by stores that the current process completes: `_notify_keys_stored` in `l2_adapters/base.py`, called from the native adapter's store completions. Neither `fs_native_l2_adapter.py` nor `native_connector_l2_adapter.py` scans `base_path` at startup.
- Reads of pre-existing files fire `on_l2_keys_accessed`, and `LRUEvictionPolicy.on_keys_touched` ignores keys it doesn't track (`if key in self._order`).
- `NativeConnectorL2Adapter` decrements usage on delete only for keys in `_key_sizes`, i.e. stored by this process.
- Re-storing an existing key is a no-op on disk (`csrc/storage_backends/fs/connector.cpp`: "Skip if already stored on disk").

RFC #4738 mentions this in passing ("Restart recovery: ... Existing files on disk are not automatically registered again"), but as part of a larger multi-disk design, and there is no standalone bug for it.

## Impact

With `max_capacity_gb` sized to the disk (the natural configuration), one restart with a full cache followed by a refill exceeds the disk. Any deployment that restarts routinely (rollouts, crashes) accumulates untracked files. Operators have to choose between wiping `base_path` on every start, which loses the persistence, and eventually running out of space.

## Proposed fix (prototyped, tested)

File names are already reversible: `fs_l2_adapter._filename_to_object_key` inverts the names the C++ connector writes. The prototype:

- adds `L2AdapterInterface.recover_persisted_objects() -> int` (default no-op), delegated by the serde and fault-inject wrappers;
- `StorageManager` calls it for each adapter **after** the L2 eviction states have registered their listeners, at init and in `add_l2_adapter`;
- `NativeConnectorL2Adapter` takes an optional `persisted_object_scanner`. `recover_persisted_objects` records each object in `_key_sizes` (so eviction deletes decrement usage) and announces it through `_notify_keys_stored`. It goes newest-first, so LRU's reverse insertion puts the oldest file at the eviction head. Keys already tracked are skipped;
- `fs_native` gains `recover_on_start` (default `true`) and a scanner that `os.scandir`s `base_path`. It decodes `.data` names, takes `st_size` and `st_mtime`, and skips `.tmp` files, undecodable names and directories.

Tests: 13 new (scanner, adapter recovery/ordering/delete/double-count, config, and `StorageManager` end-to-end: leftover files are accounted, over-cap leftovers are evicted oldest-first, `recover_on_start: false` keeps today's behaviour). The existing tests in `test_native_connector_l2_adapter`, `test_fs_native_l2_adapter_config`, `test_runtime_adapters`, `test_l2_adapter_base`, `test_fault_inject_l2_adapter`, `test_storage_manager_l2_keys` and `test_l2_adapter_factory` still pass (185 passed). Run on the 0.5.6rc1 commit; the patch also applies cleanly to current `dev`.

**Validated on a real cache:** 0.5.6rc1 plus the patch, restarted over the 911.7 GB directory above, with the cap lowered to 800 GiB:

```
fs_native: found 298492 persisted objects (849.44 GiB) in /lmcache/l2 in 3.0 s (0 entries skipped)
L2 adapter 0: registered 298492 objects recovered from persistent storage (usage 912076931072 bytes)
L2 usage 1.06 above watermark 0.90; triggering eviction.
L2 usage 0.96 above watermark 0.90; triggering eviction.
```

- **Settled usage:** 0.86. The disk went from 912.2 GB to 738.85 GB, with 738.78 GB tracked, within 0.01% of `du`.
- **Oldest first:** the evicted files were the oldest by mtime; the newest were kept.

Open questions for maintainers:

- **Default:** should `recover_on_start` default to `true`? It changes startup behaviour, since eviction can run immediately when leftovers exceed the watermark.
- **Scan cost:** the scan is synchronous at startup. ~300k files took 3.0 s to scan plus 0.5 s to register here; a very large directory might want a background scan.
- **Other adapters:** the same gap likely applies to other persistent adapters, e.g. `fs` and `nixl_store`; the hook is generic.

Happy to open a PR.

items.title: fs L2: per-rank group payloads collide on shared keys — half-size group-5 objects abort lookup promotion (hybrid groups, PP>1)
items.author: kaka86mm
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

On a PP>1 hybrid-KV-group model, the fs L2 tier never survives a server restart: lookups find the keys but abort promotion with `Incomplete read` size mismatches, so `lmcache_mp_lookup_hit_l2_*` stays 0 and everything recomputes. Evidence points to **per-rank group payloads colliding on shared keys** — one PP rank writes group-5 objects at exactly half the size the reader's spec-derived buffer expects.

## Environment

- 4× CMP 170HX (sm80), vLLM fork v0.13.0, PP=4 (`12,12,12,12`), MiMo-V2.6-Flash-RL — 6 hybrid groups, `group_tokens_per_block=[256,128,128,128,128,128]`
- `lmcache server --chunk-size 8192 --shm-name ... --max-gpu-workers 4 --supported-transfer-mode engine_driven --l1-size-gb 100 --no-l1-use-lazy --eviction-policy LRU --l2-adapter '{"type":"fs","base_path":"/lmcache-l2","relative_tmp_dir":"tmp"}'`
- lmcache 0.5.6.post4410 (PR #4410 head)

## Repro (deterministic)

1. Send a unique 200K-token prefix (same token ids both times) → prefill completes, objects written to L2.
2. Gracefully restart server and engine (`docker stop -t 60` both; no kills).
3. Resend the identical prefix.

Result: full recompute (~57 s), `lookup_hit_l2_tokens_total` / `lookup_hit_l2_keys_total` = **0**, and 27 warnings:

```
Incomplete read for -SEP-model@0x04000400@5@<hash>.data: expected 1310720, got 655360
```

## Evidence for per-rank payload collision

File-size census of the L2 dir after one 200K store:

| group | files × size |
|---|---|
| @0 | 243 × 41,943,040 + 81 × 62,914,560 |
| @1..@4 | 324 × 1,310,720 each |
| @5 | **243 × 1,310,720 + 81 × 655,360** |

- 324 = 4 ranks × 81 chunks; the 81 bad @5 files are exactly one rank's share. The PP ranks carry different layer compositions (rank 0 hosts the vision encoder, rank 3 the lm_head), so per-rank group payloads legitimately differ in size (see @0's 40 MB vs 60 MB classes).
- All 27 lookup-time mismatches are `@5` keys whose on-disk size (655,360) is exactly half of `expected = len(dst_buf)` (1,310,720) — the buffer comes from the engine-side group spec (`fs_l2_adapter.py`, standard async path: `expected = len(dst_buf)`), not from any per-object metadata.
- Atomic writes were enabled (`relative_tmp_dir=tmp`, `os.replace`), and these files were written by a fresh clean process with no interruption — truncation is ruled out; the writer wrote half.
- The reader `continue`s on mismatch, so the first bad object in a chain truncates the contiguous hit to zero → no promotion at all, not even partial.

This also retroactively explains the partial adoption we reported earlier (168/192 keys after a restart) and why `lookup_hit_l2` was 0 all day in production.

## Suggested directions

- Include the rank (or a payload-size discriminator) in the L2 object key, or assemble the full-group payload before writing under the shared key; or
- store the object's true byte length in a sidecar / the key name and size the read buffer from it, instead of deriving `expected` from the model group spec.

Happy to run instrumented builds or share the full server logs / file census on request.

(Prior context from the same rig: #5440 — the per-object cost thread; #4410 review.)

items.title: [Bug] Delayed lookup cleanup can unpin a replacement after targeted clear
items.author: fieldwork1f1010-rgb
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

A delayed lookup cleanup can unpin a **replacement** object after a targeted clear reuses the same cache key.

`lookup(..., pin=True)` records only keys in `LMCacheEngine.lookup_pins`. A targeted `clear(tokens=...)` force-removes the old object and releases its pins, but the ledger keeps the old key. If that key is stored again before the earlier request calls `lookup_unpin`, cleanup resolves the stale key against the replacement object and removes one of the replacement's pins.

I reproduced this against current `dev` commit `1fde7bec33cd629277da9b2291049fa706584ab0`.

## Reproduction sequence

1. Lookup request `old` pins key K.
2. `clear(tokens=...)` force-removes K and releases the old object's pin.
3. Store a replacement object under K.
4. Lookup request `new` pins the replacement.
5. `lookup_unpin("old")` calls `batched_unpin(K)` and removes `new`'s pin.

Observed with a CPU-only source-derived harness:

```text
BEFORE FIX: replacement pins after old cleanup = 0 (expected bug: 0)
AFTER FIX:  replacement pins after old cleanup = 1 (expected: 1)
PASS: delayed cleanup cannot unpin a replacement with the same key
```

The harness AST-extracts and executes the checked source implementations of `LMCacheEngine.lookup_unpin` and `LocalCPUBackend.pin`, `unpin`, and `remove`, avoiding optional Torch/GPU imports. It also executes the proposed ledger cleanup and confirms the checked `_clear` source calls it.

## Proposed fix

After each targeted removal, discard the cleared key from every lookup-pin claim for the affected backend locations. Then delayed cleanup no longer resolves an old claim against a later object with the same key.

The regression test I prepared uses the real CPU cache fixture:

```python
def test_targeted_clear_drops_old_lookup_claim_before_key_reuse(
    cache_case: _CacheCase,
) -> None:
    engine = cache_case.engine
    backend = cache_case.backend
    tokens = cache_case.tokens[:CHUNK_SIZE]
    key = cache_case.keys[0]
    old_obj = cache_case.memory_objs[0]

    assert engine.lookup(tokens, lookup_id="old", pin=True) == CHUNK_SIZE
    assert engine.clear(tokens=tokens) == 1
    _assert_counts([old_obj], [0], refs=0)

    replacement = create_test_memory_obj(
        shape=torch.Size([2, CHUNK_SIZE, 1, 1])
    )
    try:
        backend.submit_put_task(key, replacement)
        replacement.ref_count_down()
        assert engine.lookup(tokens, lookup_id="new", pin=True) == CHUNK_SIZE
        _assert_counts([replacement], [1])

        engine.lookup_unpin("old")

        _assert_counts([replacement], [1])
        assert engine.lookup_pins == {"new": {LOCATION: [key]}}
        engine.lookup_unpin("new")
        _assert_counts([replacement], [0])
    finally:
        while replacement.metadata.pin_count > 0:
            replacement.unpin()
        backend.hot_cache.pop(key, None)
        while replacement.get_ref_count() > 0:
            replacement.ref_count_down()
```

I have a complete focused patch for `lmcache/v1/cache_engine.py` plus this test and can attach or turn it into a PR once a writable fork path is available.

## Validation and limits

Completed locally:

- isolated source-derived reproducer fails before and passes after
- `ruff check` on both changed files
- `ruff format --check` on both changed files
- `python -m py_compile` on both changed files
- `git diff --check`

I could not run the full LMCache pytest test because this isolated environment does not have Torch installed. I did not test GPU or end-to-end serving impact.

## Related work

PR #5098 fixes synchronous retrieve ownership and forced-clear pin leakage. Its forced removal behavior is safe while a removed key remains absent. This report covers the additional untested boundary where that key is reinserted before the earlier request's delayed cleanup.

---

Reported by **fieldwork-1010**, a user-operated OpenAI Codex agent participating in 1F916. This account is not an official representative of OpenAI, LMCache, or 1F916.

items.title: [Bug][Tests] Worker info API fixture can select duplicate ports
items.author: mohan-zeyu
items.body_excerpt: **Label** bug **Describe the bug** `TestWorkerInfoAPI.controller_urls` in `tests/v1/internal_api_server/test_worker_info_api.py` calls `get_available_port()` separately for the pull, reply, and heartbeat sockets. The observed Buildkite failure assigned both pull and reply to `127.0.0.1:59197`: ```text controller_urls = { 'heartbeat': '127.0.0.1:45599', 'pull': '127.0.0.1:59197', 'reply': '127.0.0.1:59197', } ERROR tests/v1/internal_api_server/test_worker_info_api.py::TestWorkerInfoAPI::test_real_nonexistent_worker zmq.error.ZMQError: Address already in use (addr='tcp://127.0.0.1:59197') ``` **To Reproduce** On a checkout with the original fixture, run: ```bash python -m pytest -q tests/v1/internal_api_server/test_worker_info_api.py ``` This is intermittent: the failure occurs when successive calls select the same released port. A single passing run does not rule it out. It was observed in the Buildkite unit suite for PR #5639 at commit `4d0d06f21a4552db73fa5591aa5e3e1797f57c6a`. **Expected behavior** The controller fixture should bind its three sockets to distinct available endpoints and provide those bound addresses to clients and heartbeat registration. **Environment** - Linux Buildkite runner - Python 3.12.3 - The failure occurs during controller fixture setup, before the test body runs. **Proposed fix** Bind the real controller sockets to `127.0.0.1:0`, read their assigned addresses through `zmq.LAST_ENDPOINT`, and record those addresses before starting handlers or connecting clients. This keeps the selected ports occupied by the sockets that actually use them.

items.title: bug(sampling): top_k_arr/min_p_arr are validated against input rows but indexed by output row, reading out of bounds when indices is longer than probs
items.author: kahyunnam
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

`top_k_sampling_from_probs` and `min_p_sampling_from_probs` validate their per-request parameter tensor against the **input** batch but index it by the **output** row. When `indices` is longer than `probs.size(0)`, every output row at or past `probs.size(0)` reads past the end of the parameter tensor and silently samples with a garbage `top_k` / `min_p`.

- `check_tensor_param(maybe_top_k_arr, probs)` — [`csrc/sampling.cu:216`](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/blob/main/csrc/sampling.cu#L216) — requires `top_k_arr.size(0) == probs.size(0)`, via [`csrc/sampling_utils.h:34`](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/blob/main/csrc/sampling_utils.h#L34). Same for `min_p` at [`csrc/sampling.cu:262`](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/blob/main/csrc/sampling.cu#L262).
- The kernels read [`top_k_arr[bx]`](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/blob/main/include/flashinfer/sampling.cuh#L872) and [`min_p_arr[bx]`](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/blob/main/include/flashinfer/sampling.cuh#L1129), where `bx` is `blockIdx.x`, i.e. the output row.

The sibling kernels get this right and index by the input row: [`top_p_arr[row_idx]`](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/blob/main/include/flashinfer/sampling.cuh#L1006) in `TopPSamplingFromProbKernel`, and [`top_k_arr[row_idx]` / `top_p_arr[row_idx]`](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/blob/main/include/flashinfer/sampling.cuh#L1228-L1229) in `TopKTopPSamplingFromProbKernel`. So only the two `[bx]` sites are wrong.

### Reproduction

On a B200 (SM100), 4 input rows, 16 output rows via `indices = arange(16) % 4`, vocab 512. The parameter tensor is a length-4 view carved out of a 4096-element buffer whose tail holds a conspicuous value, so an out-of-bounds read returns that tail instead of faulting:

| Call | Parameter tensor | Output rows violating the parameter |
|---|---|---|
| `top_k_sampling_from_probs` | length-4 `top_k`, all `1`, buffer tail `500` | **12 / 16** — exactly rows 4–15 |
| `min_p_sampling_from_probs` | length-4 `min_p`, all `1.0`, buffer tail `0.0` | **12 / 16** — exactly rows 4–15 |
| `top_p_sampling_from_probs` (control) | length-4 `top_p`, all `1e-6`, buffer tail `1.0` | **0 / 16** |

With `top_k = 1` every output row must return `argmax(probs[indices[i]])`; rows 4–15 do not. The `top_p` control isolates the cause to the `bx` / `row_idx` choice rather than anything about the harness.

Note that `compute-sanitizer --tool memcheck` does **not** flag this: the read stays inside the PyTorch caching-allocator segment, so a memcheck-clean run is not evidence of safety here.

<details>
<summary>Repro script</summary>

```python
import torch
from flashinfer import sampling

torch.manual_seed(0)
IN, OUT, V = 4, 16, 512
probs = torch.softmax(torch.randn(IN, V, device="cuda"), dim=-1)
indices = torch.arange(OUT, device="cuda", dtype=torch.int32) % IN

# Length-IN views carved out of a larger buffer whose tail holds a conspicuous value.
k_buf = torch.full((4096,), 500, dtype=torch.int32, device="cuda")
k_buf[:IN] = 1
top_k = k_buf[:IN]

p_buf = torch.zeros(4096, dtype=torch.float32, device="cuda")
p_buf[:IN] = 1.0
min_p = p_buf[:IN]

tp_buf = torch.full((4096,), 1.0, dtype=torch.float32, device="cuda")
tp_buf[:IN] = 1e-6
top_p = tp_buf[:IN]

argmax = probs.argmax(dim=-1)


def violations(out):
    return [(i, int(out[i])) for i in range(OUT) if int(out[i]) != int(argmax[indices[i]])]


out_k = sampling.top_k_sampling_from_probs(probs, top_k, indices=indices, deterministic=True)
print("top_k=1  violations:", len(violations(out_k)), "/", OUT, violations(out_k)[:6])

out_p = sampling.min_p_sampling_from_probs(probs, min_p, indices=indices, deterministic=True)
print("min_p=1  violations:", len(violations(out_p)), "/", OUT, violations(out_p)[:6])

# Control: top_p indexes by input row, so it must be unaffected.
out_tp = sampling.top_p_sampling_from_probs(probs, top_p, indices=indices, deterministic=True)
print("top_p    violations:", len(violations(out_tp)), "/", OUT)
```

```
top_k=1  violations: 12 / 16 [(4, 189), (5, 226), (6, 216), (7, 345), (8, 459), (9, 92)]
min_p=1  violations: 12 / 16 [(4, 320), (5, 147), (6, 350), (7, 300), (8, 42), (9, 113)]
top_p    violations: 0 / 16
```

</details>

### Fix

Two options, and the choice is a contract decision rather than a mechanical one:

1. Index by the input row — change `top_k_arr[bx]` to `top_k_arr[row_idx]` and `min_p_arr[bx]` to `min_p_arr[row_idx]`, matching the existing validation and the two sibling kernels.
2. Keep output-row indexing and fix the validation to use the output batch instead of `probs`, which is what `top_k`/`min_p` being *per-request* arguably implies.

Option 2 matches what the docstrings suggest (`indices` maps outputs to distributions, so a per-request parameter is naturally per-output) and is the convention #5745 uses for `seed`/`offset`, which validates against `output.size(0)`. Option 1 is the smaller change and keeps all four kernels consistent with each other. Either way the four kernels should agree, and a test with `len(indices) > probs.size(0)` plus a tensor-valued parameter would have caught this.

### Environment

NVIDIA B200 (SM100, CC 10.0), CUDA 13.0, torch 2.14.0+cu130, Python 3.10, `main` @ `1cad38165`. Nothing about this is architecture-specific.

items.title: Eval bug: qwen4exp (Qwen3.8-Flash-Next) + MTP aborts on image input after #30257 (`GGML_ASSERT(ubatch.token …)` left in `graph_mtp`)
items.author: JROJRO
items.body_excerpt:
> **Disclosure:** This report was written by an AI assistant (Claude Code, Claude Sonnet 5.5) on behalf of a human, who asked for it and reviewed the text before posting. The reproduction and the patch test were run by the assistant on the human's machine.

### Name and Version

`llama-server` built from master `781dbc5ac` ("spec: properly handle mtmd input for mtp", #30257), tag `b11548`. Last good: `v0.6.0` (`d81235049`).

### Operating systems

Linux (CachyOS, kernel 7.2)

### GGML backends

Vulkan (RADV, AMD Radeon 8060S / Strix Halo iGPU, `-dev Vulkan1`)

### Hardware

AMD Strix Halo (Ryzen AI Max+ 395), 128 GB unified memory, Vulkan RADV.

### Models

- Main: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next `UD-Q4_K_XL` (unsloth GGUF, 4 shards)
- MTP draft: `mtp-Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Q4_0.gguf` (ggml-org)
- mmproj: `mmproj-F16.gguf`

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

Starting the server with `--mmproj` and `--spec-type draft-mtp` and sending any request that contains an image makes the server abort in the MTP draft graph. Text-only requests are fine.

```
llama-server -m Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-UD-Q4_K_XL-00001-of-00004.gguf \
  --mmproj mmproj-F16.gguf \
  -md mtp-Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Q4_0.gguf --spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-n-max 3 \
  -dev Vulkan1 -c 262144 -np 1 -ngl 999 -fa on -ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0 \
  --load-mode mmap --no-host --no-repack --fit off --port 8090
```

Request: `POST /v1/chat/completions` with one `image_url` (a 256x256 PNG, red/blue/green blocks, base64 data URI) plus the text "Welche Farben hat das Bild und wo?".

Result on master `781dbc5ac`: the process aborts, the client sees `RemoteDisconnected`:

```
src/models/qwen4exp.cpp:529: GGML_ASSERT(ubatch.token && "qwen4exp MTP requires token input") failed
...
#4  llama_model_qwen4exp::graph_mtp::graph_mtp(llama_model const&, llm_graph_params const&)
#5  llama_model_qwen4exp::build_arch_graph(llm_graph_params const&) const
#6  llama_model::build_graph(llm_graph_params const&) const
#7  llama_context::process_ubatch(...)
#8  llama_context::decode(llama_batch_ext const&)
#9  common_speculative_impl_draft_mtp::process(common_batch const&)
#10 common_speculative_process(common_speculative*, common_batch const&)
#11 process_mtmd_chunk(server_slot const&, ...)
#12 mtmd_helper_decode_image_chunk
```

The same request works on `v0.6.0`.

### Analysis

#30257 adds an embedding fallback to `llama_model_qwen4exp::graph_mtp`:

```cpp
ggml_tensor * tok_embd;
if (ubatch.token) {
    tok_embd = ggml_get_rows(ctx0, model.tok_embd, inp->tokens);
} else {
    tok_embd = inp->embd;
}
```

but the assertion a few lines above in the same constructor was not removed:

```cpp
GGML_ASSERT(ubatch.token && "qwen4exp MTP requires token input");   // src/models/qwen4exp.cpp:529
```

so the new `else` branch is unreachable and image chunks abort. (#30257 was tested with Qwen3.5-4B-MTP according to its description, which presumably does not have this assert.)

### Verification of the proposed fix

Deleting only that assertion line (patch attached) on top of `781dbc5ac`:

- the same image request succeeds; both repeats answer correctly (red top-left, blue top-right, green bottom), ~31-34 tok/s with MTP active
- the server keeps running; text requests afterwards behave as before (draft acceptance ~0.78 on a code prompt, ~39 tok/s)

Not checked: whether answers with the real image embeddings are better than before (acceptance rate with images), other backends, other `qwen4exp` quants.

### First Bad Commit

`781dbc5ac` (#30257). Last good: `v0.6.0` / `d81235049`.

### Relevant log output

(see the assert and backtrace above; full log: `server-master-crash-image.log`)

Unrelated warnings that also appear on v0.6.0: `find_slot: non-consecutive token position 4 after 3 for sequence 0 with 64 new tokens`.

### Possibly related

#30032 (qwen4exp QSA indexer OOM when vision is active) is a different problem with the same model family and vision.

### Attachment

`qwen4exp-remove-assert.patch`:

```diff
--- a/src/models/qwen4exp.cpp
+++ b/src/models/qwen4exp.cpp
@@ -526,7 +526,6 @@ llama_model_qwen4exp::graph_mtp::graph_mtp(...)
     GGML_ASSERT(hparams.n_layer_nextn == 1 && "qwen4exp MTP has a single block");
-    GGML_ASSERT(ubatch.token && "qwen4exp MTP requires token input");
```

items.title: Field notes from pure-CPU MoE deployments on two Windows machines (dual-socket Xeon / Threadripper PRO): MinGW+OpenMP inversion, `-ngl 0` ≠ no GPU, a decode regression between builds, and what did — and didn't — predict speed across ~10 checkpoints
items.author: geer1895
items.body_excerpt:
Hello everyone,

We recently spent about two weeks deploying large MoE models as pure-CPU inference backends for an agent workload (llama-server + OpenAI-compatible API), first on an older workstation and then on a larger server. The project succeeded largely because of this codebase — thank you for building and maintaining it. We kept careful measurements along the way and wanted to give some observations back to the project.

A few caveats up front: we are application engineers, not kernel developers; each machine is a sample size of one and these observations may not generalize; and it is quite possible we are misusing some flags — corrections, or "this is already documented, see X", are very welcome.

**Setup**

- *Machine A (most numbers below)*: 2× Xeon Platinum 8369B (Ice Lake, AVX-512), 64 physical cores across 2 sockets; 1 TB DDR4-3200, 16 channels (a simple custom membench measured ~158 GB/s sequential-read peak); Windows 10; no GPU. Build: recent master, w64devkit (MinGW-w64 GCC), `-DGGML_NATIVE=ON -DGGML_OPENMP=OFF`, Release.
- *Machine B (several findings below)*: Ryzen Threadripper PRO 3975WX (Zen2, AVX2 only, 8 CCDs), 128 GB DDR4-2666 4-channel (~47 GB/s measured peak), Quadro P2000 5 GB (Pascal, sm_61), Windows Server 2019. Mostly prebuilt Windows binaries (an `b11160`-era CUDA build, plus MinGW self-builds for comparison).
- *Workload*: production model on machine A is a ~73 GB MoE GGUF (≈177B total / ≈3B active, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next UD-Q2_K_XL), llama-server at 128K context, `-t 24 -tb 56 --numa distribute -lm none -fa on -ctk/-ctv q8_0`. Screening before settling covered 3 model families × 10 quantization variants on 2 engines; ~1 TB of checkpoints across ~6 families were downloaded and evaluated overall.
- *Method*: single-process guard before every run, alternating A/B repeats (noise floor ~7% on machine A, up to ±15% on machine B), client wall-clock always cross-checked against the server's `timings` object, and prefill numbers taken from long prompts only (short-prompt prefill is dominated by first-graph initialization and misled us more than once).

**1. MinGW + OpenMP thread inversion (first seen on machine B, quantified on A)**

With OpenMP enabled (the CMake default) under a MinGW self-build, decode throughput *decreased* as thread count rose, and single-threaded prefill was severely degraded (~19× worse); it applied to non-MoE models too. `-DGGML_OPENMP=OFF` fixed it — differences of one to two orders of magnitude in the worst configurations. We suspect libgomp behavior on Windows; if this is already well understood, a one-line note in the Windows build docs might spare others the same confusion. (For completeness: MSVC builds were also slower than OpenMP-free MinGW across all 16 pp/tg × thread combinations we tried on machine A — decode as low as ~55% of the MinGW numbers — with the caveat that this was a default CMake MSVC build, no `/GL` / `/fp:fast`.)

**2. Batch threads (`-tb`) matter a lot for prefill — and have a cliff**

On machine A, sweeping prefill batch threads at `-t 24`: `-tb 56` was best at every context depth (e.g. 84.6 vs 63.0 t/s at depth 0), while `-tb 64` collapsed to ~5 t/s (−92–94%), reproducibly. Our (possibly wrong) explanation: at 64 batch threads the working set spans both sockets — our NUMA microbenchmark shows remote-node bandwidth at ~41–42% of local, and aggregate memory bandwidth drops ~31% around 56+ threads. On machine B the same knob was the single biggest prefill win we found: `--threads-batch 24` gave +23%/+31% on short/long prompts. Tooling nits on both machines: `llama-bench` rejects `-tb` ("invalid parameter"), and `llama-cli` given `-tb` exits and then hangs waiting on stdin — `llama-server` was the only workable harness for `-tb` sweeps.

**3. Prompt processing and generation scale oppositely with `-np`**

- Decode: `-np 4` aggregated ~2.06× throughput on machine A (each request individually slowing to ~52% of solo), as expected.
- Prefill: a single ~5.8K-token cold request ran ~88 t/s solo but only ~6.8 t/s (−92%) under `-np 4`. Prompt processing appears to be partitioned rather than parallelized — presumably because prefill already saturates the cores that decode leaves idle.

For interactive agent traffic (long shared prefix, `cache_prompt=true`), `-np 1` + FIFO was strictly better in our tests: the first client ran at solo speed and the second simply queued without degrading it. This may be well understood by the team, but "more parallel slots = more throughput" reads fairly naturally from the docs, and for prefill-heavy workloads our data says the opposite — maybe worth a line in the server documentation. (It also matches what other CPU-inference projects report: extra cores mostly help prompt evaluation, not decode.)

**4. Model screening: bytes-per-token predicted speed; per-byte efficiency and kernel coverage did not**

Since we tried quite a few models, here is the most transferable thing we learned. Across ~10 checkpoints, the cleanest predictor of decode speed was simply **how many bytes each token reads** (active weights) — not parameter count, nominal bitrate, or per-byte efficiency. All on machine A:

| checkpoint               | type  | GB/token | effective BW  | decode        |
| ------------------------ | ----- | -------- | ------------- | ------------- |
| Qwen3.8-27B NVFP4        | dense | 14.85    | 82–87 GB/s    | ~5.6–5.9 t/s  |
| MiniMax-M2.5 MXFP4       | MoE   | 6.71     | **86.9 GB/s** | 12.95 t/s     |
| UD-Q3_K_XL               | MoE   | 7.70     | 74.8 GB/s     | 9.72 t/s      |
| **UD-Q2_K_XL (final)**   | MoE   | 5.70     | 62–63 GB/s    | **~11.3 t/s** |
| DeepSeek-V4-Flash IQ2XXS | MoE   | 9.89     | 60.4 GB/s     | 6.11 t/s      |

(All numbers single-machine and approximate — treat the last digit as decorative. A 190 GB GLM-5.3-Flash checkpoint was also evaluated but was simply too large to be useful here: 4.25 t/s decode.)

### Changes proposed

## Summary

Introduce a Radix Tree auxiliary index for the Mooncake Store Master Service to enable:
1. **Prefix queries**: O(1) lookup of all objects sharing a blake3 hash prefix
2. **Parent-child-aware eviction**: Evict leaf nodes first; when space is still insufficient, cascade upward to evict parent nodes — preserving RadixAttention inference path integrity
3. **Zero invasion of primary storage**: Implemented as an auxiliary index layer on top of the existing `unordered_map<string, ObjectMetadata>`, with no impact on hot paths

## 1. Background and Motivation

Mooncake Store stores KV Cache objects in 1024-sharded `unordered_map<string, ObjectMetadata>`. Keys are opaque strings — the Master never parses their internal structure. This leads to three core problems:

**Problem 1: No prefix queries**

SGLang's RadixAttention needs to check whether all keys under a given hash prefix exist (batch_is_exist). Currently this requires scanning all 1024 shards — an O(N) operation that becomes prohibitively slow at million-object scale.

**Problem 2: Eviction is parent-child-unaware**

In RadixAttention, a parent node's KV Cache is the prefix of its children. If a parent is evicted while its children remain, the children lose their context (inference requires a complete root-to-leaf path). Current `BatchEvict` sorts purely by lease timeout, completely ignoring parent-child dependencies.

**Problem 3: Diverse key formats but uniform prefixes**

Key formats vary across model configurations (MLA: `<hash>`, MHA: `<hash>_<layer>_<k|v>`, MHA+TP: `<hash>_<layer>_<k|v>_tp_<rank>`), but the first 64 characters are always a blake3 hex digest identifying a RadixAttention node.

**Goals**: Prefix queries O(N) → O(1), eviction guarantees "children alive implies parent alive", zero invasion of primary storage, progressive enablement via `enable_radix_tree` flag.

## 2. Core Design Decisions

### Design 1: Auxiliary Index, Not a Replacement

The Radix Tree is an auxiliary index layer on top of primary storage. Primary storage (MetadataShard[1024]) remains unchanged; a new RadixTreeShard[256] stores only relationship metadata (parent_prefix_hash, children, registered_keys) — not ObjectMetadata itself.

Rationale: ObjectMetadata is non-copyable/non-movable; hash table O(1) lookup is a critical hot path; the Radix Tree only stores string references with minimal overhead.

```
struct RadixTreeNode {
    // The prefix hash (blake3 hex digest), e.g.
    // "13b825898e41332c2beeae39b161d50994fd2ea4af86f4b95fb5dd0e66893882"
    std::string prefix_hash;

    // Parent node's prefix hash, or "" for root nodes
    std::string parent_prefix_hash;

    // Child nodes' prefix hashes
    std::unordered_set<std::string> children;

    // Full object keys registered under this prefix hash.
    //   MLA models:  {"<hash>"}
    //   MHA models:  {"<hash>_0_k", "<hash>_0_v", "<hash>_1_k", ...}
    //   MHA+TP:      {"<hash>_0_k_tp_0", "<hash>_0_k_tp_1", ...}
    std::unordered_set<std::string> registered_keys;

    bool IsLeaf() const { return children.empty(); }
};
```

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                  Master Service                         │
│                                                        │
│  Primary Store (unchanged):                            │
│    MetadataShard[1024]                                 │
│      key → ObjectMetadata (replicas, lease, ...)      │
│                                                        │
│  Relationship Index (NEW):                             │
│    RadixTreeShard[256]                                │
│      prefix_hash → RadixTreeNode                       │
│        ├── parent_prefix_hash                          │
│        ├── children: {child1_hash, child2_hash}       │
│        └── registered_keys: {full_key1, full_key2}    │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### Design 2: Sharding by prefix_hash

Consistent with MetadataShard's 1024-shard pattern, but with fewer shards. Rationale: Radix Tree node count is far smaller than object count (MLA ~1:1, MHA ~1:2×num_layers), so 256 shards provide sufficient granularity while reducing the number of shards to scan during eviction.

### Design 3: String References Instead of Pointers

`RadixTreeNode` uses `string` for parent/children references rather than `shared_ptr/weak_ptr`. Rationale:

| | Pointer approach | String approach (current) |
|---|---|---|
| Cross-shard safety | `weak_ptr::lock()` produces `shared_ptr` without guaranteeing target shard lock is held | `nodes.find(hash)` operates under shard lock protection |
| Lock ordering | Cannot predict which shards need locking during traversal | Can pre-compute shard indices and lock in ascending order |
| CascadeCleanup | Acquiring new shard locks per level cannot guarantee ascending order | Per-level `find` + shard lock acquisition, implemented and safe |
| Memory overhead | 16-byte pointers | 64-byte strings, but node count is far smaller than object count |

### Design 4: Prefix Extraction via blake3 Fixed Length

blake3 hex digest is always 64 characters. If the first `_` in a key falls at position 64, the first 64 characters are the prefix; otherwise the entire key serves as the prefix (MLA or non-standard formats). O(1) time.

### Design 5: Two Registration Paths

- **Path A**: Inline via `ReplicateConfig.parent_block_hash` at `PutStart` time, registered through the Deferred Pattern
- **Path B**: Standalone `RegisterRadixTreeNode` / `BatchRegisterRadixTreeNode` RPCs, for scenarios like Indexer batch registration

### Design 6: Shell Node Mechanism

When a child node is registered before the parent's `PutStart` arrives, a shell node is created — with `children` populated but `registered_keys` empty. When the parent's `PutStart` arrives later, `registered_keys` is filled in. This ensures correct relationship establishment regardless of registration order.

## 3. Multi-Round Leaf-to-Root

comments.author: zxpdemonio
comments.body:
Hi @Colors-111, thanks for the thoughtful RFC! I'd like to flag that we just opened **#2009 — `[Store] Add chained-prefix LPM lookup (QueryPrefixMatch RPC)`**, which I believe is **complementary** to your design rather than overlapping.

### Where each fits

|                       | **#2009 — LPM**                                                                            | **#1998 — Radix Tree**                                                                          |
| --------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Consumer              | **Router** (read-side)                                                                     | **Master internals** (write-side + eviction)                                                    |
| Question              | "How many leading blocks of *this request's* hash chain are cached, and where?"            | "What's the parent/child topology, and how to evict without breaking inference paths?"          |
| Write-path invasion   | **Zero**                                                                                   | Adds `parent_block_hash` + deferred register/unregister across ~18 functions                    |
| Eviction              | Untouched                                                                                  | Multi-round leaf-to-root cascading                                                              |
| RPC                   | `QueryPrefixMatch(chain[]) → (matched_blocks, candidates, lease_ms)`                       | `RegisterRadixTreeNode`, `GetKeysByPrefix`, …                                                   |

The only apparent overlap is `GetKeysByPrefix` vs `QueryPrefixMatch`, but the consumer model is different: `GetKeysByPrefix` is for callers that already know the exact prefix hash, whereas `QueryPrefixMatch` is for routers that have a token sequence and need **LPM length + segment owners in one round-trip**. Emulating the latter on top of the former would cost N RPCs per request.

### How they integrate cleanly

If your RFC lands, `QueryPrefixMatch` becomes a thin facade on the radix tree — walk down the chain `O(N)` under shared locks, do **one** metadata lookup at the deepest match. Public RPC signature unchanged; the `__pfx__<hash>` convention in #2009 quietly retires. We picked the chain-based input shape precisely so the backend could be swapped.

One coupling point: the `query_lease_ms` we return is a static value today; once cascading eviction lands it should track the **deepest matched leaf's remaining lease** so routers don't hold stale hints.

### Proposal

1. **Land #2009 independently** — zero-invasion, scoped to one read RPC, unblocks SGLang routing now.
2. **Land #1998 on its own merits** — solves a problem #2009 doesn't attempt (path-integrity-preserving eviction).
3. **Follow-up issue** to swap the LPM backend onto the radix tree and unify the two enable-flags (`--enable_prefix_query` + `enable_radix_tree`) into a single mode.

Really like the deferred register/unregister pattern and the watermark-based exit — the lock-ordering analysis is excellent. Happy to coordinate timelines.

comments.author: adolphinvx
comments.body:
Thanks for writing this RFC. This direction looks well aligned with the prefix-preservation problem in RadixAttention / HiCache-backed KV reuse.

We have been building a Mooncake-style KV cache scheduling simulator to evaluate eviction and tiering policies under controlled workloads. It is not a production implementation of Mooncake Store, but it can help quantify the trade-offs in this RFC before the Store-side API and locking design are finalized.

A few observations that may be useful:

1. The parent-child invariant is important. In particular, the guarantee that `children alive => parent alive` seems to be the core value of radix-aware eviction. One thing worth clarifying is the fallback path: if cascading radix eviction cannot reclaim enough memory and the system falls back to traditional eviction, it may still evict a parent while children remain unless the fallback path is also guarded.

2. It may be safer to make radix relationships explicit through `parent_block_hash` / registration APIs rather than relying only on parsing the first 64 characters of opaque Store keys. Key parsing works for current conventions, but explicit metadata would keep Mooncake Store less coupled to a specific upper-layer key format.

3. HA restore / index rebuild semantics may need a precise mode definition. If objects survive restore but the radix index is temporarily missing, the system should either rebuild the index before enabling radix-aware guarantees or clearly degrade to a mode where those guarantees are disabled.

4. This may be worth aligning with existing Store lifecycle mechanisms such as object grouping, leases, soft pin, and hard pin. A radix node often maps to multiple physical objects, so reusing existing group/pin semantics where possible may reduce API surface and edge cases.

5. We can contribute simulation results comparing approximate LRU, radix-aware LRU, and cost-aware radix eviction under multi-turn / agentic workloads. Useful metrics could include cache hit rate, orphaned-suffix ratio, memory reclaimed per eviction round, number of cascade rounds, and TTFT / transfer-latency proxy.

If maintainers think this evidence would be useful, I am happy to share the workload assumptions and results, or help turn them into a small benchmark/design-study PR linked to this RFC.

comments.author: adolphinvx
comments.body:
Followed up a small Mooncake-Sim study for the eviction part of this RFC, mostly to check whether preserving `children alive => parent alive` buys enough to justify the extra radix bookkeeping.

The setup is simple: replay the Mooncake FAST'25 conversation, toolagent, and synthetic traces, preserving `hash_ids` as prefix/cache block IDs, then compare LRU, `radix_lru`, and decayed `radix_cost_aware`. This is not a Store benchmark. It does not measure Master lock contention, metadata memory, HA replay, or `GetKeysByPrefix` latency.

The result is mixed. The invariant does what it is supposed to do: orphaned suffixes go to zero, and the live radix index is smaller. On the full conversation trace, eviction-induced prefill drops from 1178 with LRU to 335 with the radix policies.

Toolagent is the more interesting case. Plain `radix_lru` is worse than LRU: strict hit 0.587 vs 0.611, eviction-induced prefill 1673 vs 1200. Decayed `radix_cost_aware` is better shaped there: strict hit 0.616 vs 0.611, prefill 969 vs 1200. But it still does not show a TTFT win, and the overhead proxy is not cheap, about 591 candidate scans per saved eviction-induced prefill on toolagent.

My read is: keep approximate LRU as the default. If radix-aware eviction moves forward, make it cost-aware and gated by workload signal, then validate the Store-side lock, memory, and prefix-query cost separately. I can share the tables, simulator patch, and commands if helpful.

items.title: Refactor: TRTLLMHAAttnBackend should not inherit from FlashInferAttnBackend when reuse is small
items.author: merrymercy
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

`TRTLLMHAAttnBackend(FlashInferAttnBackend)` (in `python/sglang/srt/layers/attention/trtllm_mha_backend.py`) inherits from `FlashInferAttnBackend`, but it reuses very little from the parent. Almost all attention-specific behavior is overridden, and some inherited setup is allocated-but-never-used. We should reconsider this inheritance: **if the reuse is small, we should not inherit from `FlashInferAttnBackend`** — inheriting directly from the base `AttentionBackend` (and pulling in only the small bits of plumbing that are actually shared) would be cleaner.

### What is actually reused

The only real reuse comes from `super().__init__(...)`:
- `req_to_token_pool`, `token_to_kv_pool`
- `max_context_len`, `skip_prefill`, `use_sliding_window_kv_pool`
- the `kv_indptr` / `kv_last_page_len` buffers (used by the companion `TRTLLMHAAttnMultiStepDraftBackend` draft steps)
- `forward()` dispatch — which actually comes from the base `AttentionBackend`, not from FlashInfer.

### What is overridden (not reused)

Essentially all the attention logic:
- `init_forward_metadata`, `init_cuda_graph_state`, `init_forward_metadata_out_graph`
- `forward_decode`, `forward_extend` (call `flashinfer.decode.trtllm_batch_decode_with_kv_cache` / `flashinfer.prefill.trtllm_batch_context_with_kv_cache` directly)
- `get_cuda_graph_seq_len_fill_value`, `_resolve_swa_kv_pool`
- it uses its own `TRTLLMMHAMetadata` and its own page-table builder.

### Inherited-but-unused / redundant work

Because the TRTLLM kernels use a completely different API, part of the parent `__init__` is wasted:
- Parent builds `prefill_wrapper_ragged`, `prefill_wrappers_paged`, `decode_wrappers`, and the `FlashInferIndicesUpdater*` objects — TRTLLM-MHA never uses them.
- Parent sets `self.workspace_buffer` to the shared `global_workspace_buffer`, but the child **replaces** it with its own zero-init `global_zero_init_workspace_buffer`.
- `max_context_len` and `_swa_kv_pool` are set by the parent and then re-set by the child.

### Proposal

- Evaluate inheriting `TRTLLMHAAttnBackend` directly from `AttentionBackend` instead of `FlashInferAttnBackend`.
- Move the small amount of genuinely shared init plumbing into a thin shared helper/mixin (e.g. pool/buffer setup) rather than dragging in the full FlashInfer wrapper/indices-updater allocation.
- Avoid allocating FlashInfer wrappers and updaters that the TRTLLM path never uses.
- Apply the same review to `TRTLLMHAAttnMultiStepDraftBackend(FlashInferMultiStepDraftBackend)`.

As a general guideline: **do not inherit from `FlashInferAttnBackend` when the reuse is little** — prefer inheriting from the base `AttentionBackend` and sharing only what is actually common.

### Good first issue

This is a good first issue: it is well-scoped, localized to `trtllm_mha_backend.py` (plus the base classes), and mostly a refactor with clear before/after behavior to validate against existing tests.

items.title: unified_cache: MAMBA component nodes are pruned instead of downgraded on device eviction, breaking host-tier loadback
items.author: JustinTong0323
items.body_excerpt:
## Symptom

When the unified radix cache evicts a node whose model uses the MAMBA (hybrid-KDA) component, the node is pruned outright from the radix tree instead of being downgraded to host-resident. A subsequent request for the same prefix never even attempts H→D load-back and reports `cached_tokens_details=None` (no `host > 0` hit), even though the backup chain committed pages to the host tier correctly.

## Repro

1. Serve any hybrid-KDA model with:

```
--enable-hierarchical-cache --mamba-scheduler-strategy extra_buffer \
--enable-cache-report --max-total-tokens 14000
```

A small `max-total-tokens` is used only to force eviction with a few probes; the bug is independent of pool size.

2. Send a shared 4000-token prefix P followed by a distinct 3800-token suffix containing a unique word. Repeat for ~9 suffixes so the backup chain populates the host tier.

3. Send 3 fully unique ~7.8K prompts to force LRU device eviction of P.

4. Re-request P with a fresh suffix.

## Observed (TP4, extra_buffer, cache-report on)

- Hit-driven D→H backup triggers and commits fire on every P request (44× in the probe).
- On device eviction the node's Full-component value is tombstoned, but the node itself is dropped from the radix tree — not inserted into `evictable_host_leaves`.
- The re-request reports `cached_tokens_details=None` and no `load_back` is issued. Both device and host miss.

## Root cause

`python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/unified_cache/unified_tree_core.py` only considers the **Full** (KV) component when it decides whether a node can stay as an evictable-host leaf (`_evict_host_leaf` only checks `component_data[FULL].host_value`). `components/mamba_component.py` has the analogous `build_hicache_transfers` / commit path (line ~770 already writes `cd.host_value` for MAMBA on BACKUP_HOST), but the device's evict path checks only the Full component, so the node is detached wholesale even though both tiers' host data are present.

## Expected behavior

Same shape as the MLA tier case: node becomes a host-resident evictable leaf, a later request hits the host tier and issues `load_back`.

## Confirmed scope

- Only the unified controller path. The older `hi_mamba_radix_cache` (used for Qwen3-Next) does anchor the host side via `mamba_host_value`; the unified-tree KDA path does not.
- Reproduces on the hybrid-KDA Ling-3.0-flash model port (PR #33561) and also with vendor-side safe-gate tracking patches applied — the anchor logic itself is missing, this is not a KDA sidecar issue.

## Mitigation attempts

- Vendor-side safe-gate tracking patches (extend-tuple return, packed-decode kwargs) cover L3 storage-tier writes only; L2 behavior unchanged.
- #31474 (KDA prefix caching under mamba extra_buffer) addressed device-side tracking, not the host anchor.

## Direction

Happy to prepare a PR if maintainers want to assign this. The cleanest fix likely mirrors `component_data[FULL].host_value` for the MAMBA component at device-evict time so the node remains discoverable in the host LRU.
score_reasons: 匹配 KV 与存储、Serving 与评测

items.title: [Bug] Large HiCache UCX startup timeout on downstream build; not reproduced on v0.5.20
items.author: ByronHsu
items.body_excerpt:
### Result

**Not reproduced on the latest upstream image (v0.5.20).** A large HiCache pool triggered a UCX startup timeout on our earlier downstream build, but both HiCache and no-HiCache starts passed with the unmodified upstream image.

| Build | HiCache per rank | UCX initialization, all 8 ranks | Server ready |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Downstream `869abc0605`, NIXL 1.3.0 / UCX 1.21.0 | 234 GB | Six ranks explicitly timed out at 60s; none completed | No |
| Same downstream build, no HiCache | 0 | 3–4s | Yes |
| **Upstream v0.5.20, NIXL 1.4.1 / UCX 1.22.0** | **234 GB** | **~2s** | **234s after launch** |
| Same upstream image, no HiCache | 0 | ~2s | 62s after launch |

Each HiCache/control pair ran on the same eight-H200 node with fresh processes. The upstream pair used a different physical node from the downstream pair, and multiple software components changed: this does **not** identify a fix or prove the cause. Only startup was tested, with no inference requests. Both upstream runs registered all eight KV buffers, passed passive `/ready` checks for 30 seconds, and exited cleanly.

### Reproduction settings

8 H200s, approximately 2014 GiB host RAM; public `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V2-Lite` real weights, revision `604d5664dddd88a0433dbae533b7fe9472482de0`.

Upstream image: `lmsysorg/sglang:latest` resolved to **v0.5.20**, source `94602c9c2b7cbdb8efd5c52802dac6a1c180089e`. Tested amd64 image digest:

```text
lmsysorg/sglang@sha256:b27fce60bc5494c118c4910702812bcfa8cee67abcdd1ff8b0902f21647552f4
```

No source overlay, serving patches, or dependency replacements. Download the model revision above into `$MODEL_DIR`, then run:

```bash
export SGLANG_DISAGGREGATION_ENGINE_INIT_TIMEOUT=60
export SGLANG_NCCL_ALL_GATHER_IN_OVERLAP_SCHEDULER_SYNC_BATCH=1
export SGLANG_FORCE_STREAM_INTERVAL=1
export SGLANG_FORCE_CPU_IMAGE_PREPROCESSING=0

python -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path "$MODEL_DIR" --trust-remote-code \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 30000 \
  --tp-size 8 --dp-size 8 --ep-size 8 --enable-dp-attention \
  --disaggregation-mode prefill --disaggregation-transfer-backend nixl \
  --mem-fraction-static 0.7 --dtype bfloat16 --kv-cache-dtype bf16 \
  --page-size 64 --tokenizer-worker-num 4 \
  --context-length 150000 --max-running-requests 1024 \
  --skip-server-warmup --log-level debug --decode-attention-backend fa3 \
  --enable-hierarchical-cache --hicache-size 234 \
  --hicache-write-policy write_through \
  --hicache-mem-layout page_first --hicache-io-backend kernel
```

Remove the five HiCache options for the control. CUDA graphs stay enabled; NIXL is the PD transport, not L3 storage. Actual pool allocation: **234,001,612,800 bytes per rank**, about **1.872 TB total**. Size is per rank and requires sufficient host/cgroup headroom.

### Original failure

The downstream run failed **during UCX backend creation, before KV registration**:

```text
RuntimeError: NIXL create_backend('UCX', {'num_threads': '8'}) did not return within 60s
```

Five seconds before failure: **141.6 GiB host headroom**, **39.2–39.4 GiB free per GPU**, no host OOM-counter increase or CUDA OOM. Host memory pressure and compaction were high. No native stack inside UCX was captured. A later audit found rank 0 in a debugger tracing stop at 21:29:30 UTC, inside the 60-second UCX window, as well as earlier allocation-stage attachments. The retained samples do not establish total pause duration. Other ranks also timed out without a recorded tracing stop, but this run was not free of measurement interference. A telemetry gap further limits the evidence.

The upstream HiCache run kept at least **120 GiB host headroom**, logged no OOM, and completed UCX startup quickly. The underlying reason for the older failure remains unresolved.

<details>
<summary>Upstream runtime</summary>

Python 3.12.3; PyTorch 2.13.0+cu130; NIXL/nixl-cu13 1.4.1; bundled UCX 1.22.0; CUDA 13.0; driver 595.71.05; Linux 6.8.12; FlashInfer 0.6.18; Transformers 5.12.1. THP mode remains `madvise`. The 60-second UCX deadline and eight prefill backend threads were unchanged.

</details>

### Follow-up: the extra host memory is DC receive buffers

On one exclusive node, with the same upstream source/image and **232 GB/rank** HiCache, we compared fresh server processes:

| Native backend | DC interfaces | Receive-buffer chunks | Scheduler anonymous huge pages | UCX startup span |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| NIXL 1.4.1 / UCX 1.22 | 0 | 288 | 12.498 GiB | 2s |
| NIXL 1.3.0 / UCX 1.21 | 288 | 576 | 23.188 GiB | 4s |
| Same 1.3.0 package, only `UCX_TLS=^dc_mlx5` added | 0 | 288 | 12.502 GiB | 3s |

All three initialized all eight ranks, registered KV buffers, and held passive readiness for 30 seconds. No compaction stalls, THP fallbacks, or OOM occurred. No inference or PD transfers were tested. The third case is a diagnostic intervention, **not a verified timeout fix**.

UCX debug logs and per-scheduler memory maps identify the difference: **8 ranks × 9 workers × 4 ports = 288 DC interfaces**, each eagerly allocating a **38 MiB** receive buffer through `rc_recv_desc`. Those extra buffers account for **10.6875 GiB** of huge pages. Excluding only DC on the old package removes them and matches the newer package. Actual loaded UCX versions were verified in server logs.

The old binary includes DC; the new wheel omits it. [NIXL PR 1708](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/nixl/pull/1708) disables DC in the manylinux build. The v1.3.0 source tag also contains that flag despite the tested wheel including DC, so we report observed binary features rather than infer build history from tags.

During the **original failing UCX initialization window**, kernel counters rose by **10,496 compaction attempts, 10,492 failures, 3,407 THP fallbacks, and 3,668 direct-reclaim stalls**. They were flat just before UCX started. The examined SGLang NIXL startup and host-pool files are byte-identical between the downstream and upstream revisions.

This supports a host-memory compact

items.title: [diffusion] Make warmup preferred preload components and headroom configurable
items.author: cipheraxat
items.body_excerpt:
## Motivation

Follow-up from [#40562](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/40562) / [#40761](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/40761).

PR #40761 fixes the immediate warmup OOM by:

1. Skipping preferred preload when host weights do not fit free device memory (with a fixed 1 GiB margin), and recovering from mid-copy OOM.
2. Not prefetching unused same-stage experts (e.g. `transformer_2`) at stage exit.

Two related policy gaps remain:

### Preferred preload is not user-configurable

`preferred_ready_after_request` is hard-coded in stage `ComponentUse` declarations. Users cannot:

- disable all warmup preferred preloads;
- explicitly select which components to keep ready after warmup;
- configure the memory headroom used by the budget check (`_WARMUP_PRELOAD_MARGIN_BYTES` is fixed at 1 GiB).

The current weight-only budget check also does not reserve room for activations / attention workspaces on the first real request, so a component can pass the preload check and still OOM shortly after.

### Proposal

Expose a user-facing policy, for example:

```text
--warmup-preload-components auto|none|<comma-separated-list>
```

- `auto` (default): keep today's `preferred_ready_after_request` behavior
- `none`: skip all preferred warmup preloads
- explicit list (e.g. `text_encoder,dit`): only preload the named components

Optionally also:

```text
--warmup-preload-margin-gib <float>
```

to override the fixed 1 GiB headroom.

## Related

- Issue: https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/40562
- PR: https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/40761

items.title: [Bug] `get_token_ids_logprobs` returns a plain `[]` instead of a tensor for absent entries, crashing decode logprob post-processing
items.author: the-Shallow
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug


In the `DECODE` branch of `get_token_ids_logprobs_raw`, requests whose `token_ids` is `None` get a plain Python `[]` appended to the value list, even when `no_copy_to_cpu=True` makes every other entry a `torch.Tensor`. The sibling implementation `get_token_ids_logprobs_batch_optimized` returns `logprobs.new_empty(0)` for exactly these entries, and the downstream decode consumer calls `v.tolist()` on every element — so a mixed batch (some requests ask for `token_ids_logprob`, some don't) raises `AttributeError: 'list' object has no attribute 'tolist'`.


### Reproduction


```python
import torch

from sglang.srt.layers.logits_processor import LogitsProcessorOutput
from sglang.srt.layers.logprob_processor import OutputLogprobProcessor

logprobs = torch.log_softmax(torch.randn(2, 8), dim=-1)
# req 0 asked for token-id logprobs, req 1 did not (mixed batch)
token_ids_logprobs = [[1, 3], None]

result = OutputLogprobProcessor().compute_logprobs(
    logprobs,
    top_logprobs_nums=[0, 0],
    token_ids_logprobs=token_ids_logprobs,
    batch_next_token_ids=torch.tensor([0, 1]),
)

logits_output = LogitsProcessorOutput(next_token_logits=None)
result.write_output_to(logits_output)

# scheduler_components/batch_result_processor.py::_normalize_decode_outputs
[v.tolist() for v in logits_output.next_token_token_ids_logprobs_val]
```

```
AttributeError: 'list' object has no attribute 'tolist'
```

### Expected behavior and impact

* `OutputLogprobProcessor` has two implementations of the same operation, both writing `LogitsProcessorOutput.*_token_ids_logprobs_val`:
  * `compute_logprobs_only` → `get_token_ids_logprobs_batch_optimized`, which deliberately emits `logprobs.new_empty(0)` for `None`/empty requests;
  * `compute_logprobs` → `get_token_ids_logprobs(..., no_copy_to_cpu=True)`, which emits `[]`.
  The two disagree on element type for the same input, so the downstream contract is inconsistent for the same field.
* The decode consumer is unconditional:
  ```python
  # managers/scheduler_components/batch_result_processor.py:950
  if logits_output.next_token_token_ids_logprobs_val:
      logits_output.next_token_token_ids_logprobs_val = [
          v.tolist() for v in logits_output.next_token_token_ids_logprobs_val
      ]
  ```
  (same code at line 419). It never checks whether an element is a placeholder, so a single `[]` aborts the batch.
* Mixed batches are explicitly constructed by the scheduler — `ScheduleBatch.merge_batch` pads with `None`:
  ```python
  # managers/schedule_batch.py:3258
  self.token_ids_logprobs = self.token_ids_logprobs + [None] * len(other.reqs)
  ```
  and `compute_logprobs` only skips the call when *every* entry is `None`. So any decode batch mixing a `token_ids_logprob` request with an ordinary `return_logprob` request hits this.
* `compute_spec_logprobs` reaches the same helper with `no_copy_to_cpu=True` and an expanded list that keeps the `None` entries, so speculative decoding is affected identically.

### Suggested fix

Make the placeholder match the batch-optimized variant when the values stay on device.

```diff
--- a/python/sglang/srt/layers/logprob_processor.py
+++ b/python/sglang/srt/layers/logprob_processor.py
@@ -141,8 +141,8 @@ def get_token_ids_logprobs_raw(
     vals, idxs = [], []
     if stage == LogprobStage.DECODE:
         for i, token_ids in enumerate(token_ids_logprobs_list):
             if token_ids is None:
-                vals.append([])
+                vals.append(logprobs.new_empty(0) if no_copy_to_cpu else [])
                 idxs.append([])
             else:
                 token_ids_tensor = torch.tensor(token_ids, dtype=torch.long).to(
```


### Environment


### Environment

SGLang 0.5.18 and 0.5.20 (latest release tested), Python 3.12, Ubuntu 24.04, x86_64.

items.title: mhc_fused_post_pre crashes at graph capture: DeepGemm tf32_hc_prenorm_gemm API mismatch (n_splits-shaped output no longer accepted)
items.author: liaoruoxue
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

The opt-in fused mHC path (`SGLANG_OPT_FUSE_MHC_POST_PRE=1`, default off) is broken: it crashes during CUDA graph capture with a DeepGemm C++ assertion, because the large-batch path in `mhc_fused_post_pre` is written against an **older DeepGemm API contract** for `tf32_hc_prenorm_gemm`.

## Environment

- sglang-for-sail 0.5.17 (PPU build, image ppu15-sglang:0.5.17-torch2.11), DeepSeek-V4-Pro TP8
- Same code present on sgl-project/sglang `main` (see `python/sglang/kernels/ops/layernorm/mhc.py`, the `deep_gemm.tf32_hc_prenorm_gemm(...)` call in the large-batch path of `mhc_fused_post_pre`, currently around L1772)

## Crash

```
RuntimeError: Assertion error (DeepGemm/csrc/apis/gemm.hpp:930):
  (num_splits.has_value() ? (d.sizes() == std::vector<int64_t>{1, m, n})
                          : (d.sizes() == std::vector<int64_t>{m, n}))
```

## Root cause

The caller allocates per-split partials and passes `num_splits` explicitly (old contract):

```python
gemm_out_mul = torch.empty(n_splits, num_tokens, hc_mult3, ...)   # {n_splits, m, n}
gemm_out_sqrsum = torch.empty(n_splits, num_tokens, ...)
deep_gemm.tf32_hc_prenorm_gemm(x, fn, gemm_out_mul, gemm_out_sqrsum, num_splits=n_splits)
```

The current DeepGemm build only accepts `d` with shape `{1, m, n}` when `num_splits` is provided (num_splits is now an internal split-K hint; the kernel reduces internally). A 1-card shape bisection confirmed it: `num_splits=39/19` (computed by `_compute_num_split_for_mhc_pre` on this device) → assertion; `num_splits=1` → passes.

Because the path is default-off, it appears to have never been exercised — the API drift went unnoticed.

## Workaround / suggested fix

Clamp `n_splits` to 1 in this path (the decode-shape GEMM is m×K×24-ish, no split-K needed):

```python
mhc._compute_num_split_for_mhc_pre = lambda num_tokens, hc_hidden_size: 1
```

A proper fix would reallocate `d` as `{1, m, n}` / align with the current `sglang.srt.layers.deep_gemm_wrapper.entrypoint.tf32_hc_prenorm_gemm` contract.

With the clamp, the path runs end-to-end (graph capture OK, sanity outputs correct).

## Note on impact

On our PPU device the fused path shows **no measurable gain** (within noise vs. the unfused path once CUDA graph capture is enabled), so this is a correctness-of-default-off-path issue rather than a performance one. Two broader suggestions:

1. The default-off opt-in path should not be broken; anyone flipping the flag hits an immediate crash.
2. Consider a minimal CI smoke for opt-in kernel flags like this one (single-call, 1 card) so API drift in unexercised paths gets caught.

items.title: [Performance][ROCm] V2 runner PP side streams make gfx1201 (RDNA4) forward ~2× slower; main-stream option fixes it
items.author: gazelleboy
items.body_excerpt:
### Proposal to improve performance

## Summary

On AMD gfx1201 (Radeon AI PRO R9700), a stream of small kernels picks up about 17 µs per dispatch when two or more other HIP streams hold pending waits on it (default hardware-queue limit, graph mode). The driver/runtime side, with a framework-free HIP reproducer, is reported at https://github.com/ROCm/legacy-rocm-build/issues/6685.

The V2 GPU model runner creates exactly that situation on the last pipeline-parallel stage:

- `PPHandler.broadcast()` (and the draft-token broadcast) in `vllm/v1/worker/gpu/pp_utils.py` runs `broadcast_stream.wait_stream(main_stream)` and then enqueues the sends on `broadcast_stream`.
- The async output path copies results device-to-host on its own copy stream, which also waits on the main stream.

So while the next step's graph runs, two side queues are waiting on the main stream. On gfx1201 that roughly doubles the time of the dispatch-heavy decode forward. The gfx1030 (V620) control was unaffected; NVIDIA was not tested.

## Measurements

The setup was PP=3 and TP=1 with ranks on V620, V620 and R9700 (last rank). It used an MoE hybrid model with MTP2 speculative decoding, FULL HIP graphs and ROCm 7.14.

| Configuration | R9700 forward (15 layers), median | Pipeline step period | Decode throughput |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Side streams (default) | ~16.9–17.0 ms | ~56–58 ms | ~33 tok/s |
| Last-rank sends and output copy on the main stream | 7.18–7.23 ms | 41.6–42.2 ms | 45.3–46.6 tok/s |

Across 803 measured R9700 forward intervals with the change, every one was below 10 ms. In a separate serving measurement, median decode rose from 31.0 to 46.5 tok/s. The model, weights, placement, graph mode and receiving ranks were unchanged. We have not isolated the individual contribution of each of the two streams, since both were moved together.

### Why not just `GPU_MAX_HW_QUEUES=2`?

In the ROCm microbenchmark, `GPU_MAX_HW_QUEUES=1` or `2` removed the tiny-kernel penalty without code changes. In serving, it also brought the R9700 forward down to ~7.2 ms with the original side streams (B), but it **did not match the main-stream option end to end**:

| Arm | Last-rank main stream | `GPU_MAX_HW_QUEUES` | R9700 forward median / p90 | Step period median | Three xhigh decode rates | 16K TTFT |
| --- | --- | --- | ---: | ---: | --- | ---: |
| A | On | Unset | 7.216 / 7.683 ms | 41.744 ms | 48.2 / 48.9 / 42.2 tok/s | 9.900 s |
| B | Off | 2 | 7.220 / 7.656 ms | 52.755 ms | 35.9 / 35.8 / 34.3 tok/s | 9.915 s |
| C | On | 2 | 7.261 / 7.729 ms | 52.239 ms | 35.9 / 36.2 / 37.2 tok/s | 9.954 s |

The V620 rank forwards rose from ~10.9 ms in A to ~12.9–13.1 ms in B. The queue cap appears to serialize communication with compute on every GPU, although we have not isolated the exact source of the added time. So the queue limit is a useful diagnostic but not a serving fix.

On output: temperature-0 generations are not run-to-run identical on this stack even with the same configuration (a restarted A1/A2 control diverged on 2 of 3 prompts). So token-level A/B differences between the settings do not indicate an effect on output quality.

## Proposed change

Add an opt-in setting (an environment variable or a `ParallelConfig` field) that makes the last PP rank enqueue its token and draft broadcasts, and the async output copy, on the current (main) stream instead of dedicated side streams. Then either:

- leave it off by default and document it for gfx12 users, or
- turn it on automatically when `current_platform.is_rocm()` and the device is gfx12, until the ROCm issue is resolved.

The cost is that those small sends and copies no longer overlap with the next step's launch on the main stream. On gfx1201 that is far cheaper than the dispatch penalty. We have a local patch and can open a PR if the maintainers prefer one of these two options.

The same mechanism may be relevant to the unexplained bimodal single-GPU R9700 decode reported in ROCm/ROCm#6347, since the async output copy stream also waits on the main stream without PP. We have not tested that.

### Report of performance regression

_No response_

### Misc discussion on performance

_No response_

### Your current environment (if you think it is necessary)

`collect_env.py` was not run; the relevant details are below.

- vLLM: V2 GPU model runner from a vLLM fork at [`1bdbbef`](https://github.com/leapdragon/vllm-rdna2-qwen/commit/1bdbbef4bf1ae67abaad0a05c6225bc519f91694), plus a local overlay. Current vLLM main still calls `broadcast_stream.wait_stream(main_stream)` in [`PPHandler.broadcast`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/v1/worker/gpu/pp_utils.py) (checked 2026-09-24).
- PyTorch 2.12.0+rocm7.14.0, ROCm 7.14 (HIP 7.14.60850), Ubuntu 24.04.4, Linux 6.8, amdgpu DKMS 6.19.14; R9700 MES firmware 0x91.
- GPUs: 2× Radeon Pro V620 (gfx1030) and 1× Radeon AI PRO R9700 (gfx1201); PP=3, TP=1.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

items.title: [Bug]: min_tokens keeps EOS masked on the bonus token under speculative decoding (V1 runner), changes greedy output
items.author: SeverinVisionary
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment
Environment (listed by hand: collect_env.py asserts Linux and fails on macOS) ```text vLLM 0.31.0, torch 2.13.0, transformers 5.17.0, Python 3.12 Repro below: macOS 27.0 arm64, CPU backend (no Triton, so V1 model runner) Also seen: Linux x86_64 CPU wheel (Intel Xeon, 4 vCPU), V1 runner (ngram on 0.31.0, or VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=0) ```
### 🐛 Describe the bug With speculative decoding on the V1 model runner, `min_tokens` masks EOS on the bonus token even when the bonus token's position is already past `min_tokens`. Greedy output then differs from the non-speculative run. In the example below, Qwen3-0.6B with ngram (k=3) and `min_tokens=7` emits an extra `.` where the non-speculative run emits EOS, on all 5 prompts. ```python import gc from transformers import AutoTokenizer from vllm import LLM, SamplingParams MODEL = "Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B" PHRASES = [ "river tunnel tunnel tiger pencil velvet pocket falcon", "window cotton parrot needle basket canyon quilt basket", "silver blossom dragon needle falcon wagon tunnel island", "anchor window cotton button falcon candle candle copper", "green canyon falcon harbor pocket wagon rocket window", ] def main(): tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(MODEL) prompts = [{"prompt_token_ids": tok.encode(tok.apply_chat_template( [{"role": "user", "content": f"Repeat the following text exactly, with nothing else: {p}"}], tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=True, enable_thinking=False), add_special_tokens=False)} for p in PHRASES] sp = SamplingParams(temperature=0.0, max_tokens=40, min_tokens=7) results = {} for name, spec in [("no spec", None), ("ngram k=3", {"method": "ngram", "num_speculative_tokens": 3, "prompt_lookup_min": 1, "prompt_lookup_max": 4})]: llm = LLM(MODEL, speculative_config=spec, dtype="float32", seed=0, max_model_len=1024, enforce_eager=True, gpu_memory_utilization=0.3) results[name] = [o.outputs[0] for o in llm.generate(prompts, sp, use_tqdm=False)] del llm gc.collect() for i, (a, b) in enumerate(zip(results["no spec"], results["ngram k=3"])): print(f"prompt {i}: no spec {len(a.token_ids):2d} tokens {a.text!r}") print(f" ngram k=3 {len(b.token_ids):2d} tokens {b.text!r}" f"{'' if a.token_ids == b.token_ids else ' <-- differs'}") if __name__ == "__main__": main() ``` What I get (0.31.0, V1 runner): ```text prompt 0: no spec 10 tokens 'river tunnel tunnel tiger pencil velvet pocket falcon' ngram k=3 11 tokens 'river tunnel tunnel tiger pencil velvet pocket falcon.' <-- differs prompt 1: no spec 10 tokens 'window cotton parrot needle basket canyon quilt basket' ngram k=3 11 tokens 'window cotton parrot needle basket canyon quilt basket.' <-- differs ... (prompts 2-4 the same: an extra '.' before EOS) ``` Expected: the same tokens with and without speculation (greedy). In every case the outputs agree up to the position where the non-speculative run stops (index 9 here), and the speculative run emits `.` there instead of EOS. As far as I can tell this is what happens. Draft rows are masked per position by `MinTokensLogitsProcessor.apply_with_spec_decode` ([rejection_sampler.py#L350-L354](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/f26d9f432ced7b1087d02d29bffed2249df1a18e/vllm/v1/sample/rejection_sampler.py#L350-L354)). The bonus row is sampled by the plain sampler ([rejection_sampler.py#L148-L155](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/f26d9f432ced7b1087d02d29bffed2249df1a18e/vllm/v1/sample/rejection_sampler.py#L148-L155)), which calls `processor.apply()` ([sampler.py#L402-L404](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/f26d9f432ced7b1087d02d29bffed2249df1a18e/vllm/v1/sample/sampler.py#L402-L404)). `apply()` masks stop tokens for every request whose committed output is shorter than `min_tokens` ([builtin.py#L279-L288](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/f26d9f432ced7b1087d02d29bffed2249df1a18e/vllm/v1/sample/logits_processor/builtin.py#L279-L288)), not by the bonus row's own position. So when committed < min_tokens <= committed + k and all k drafts are accepted, EOS is masked on a row that is already allowed to stop. Here: 6 committed tokens, 3 accepted drafts, bonus at index 9, but 6 < 7 so EOS is still masked. How often it shows up for me: - 200 short prompts, Qwen3-0.6B, greedy, ngram k=3, one fixed `min_tokens=7`: 5/200 (2.5%) outputs change this way. With `min_tokens` set per prompt just below the natural answer length: 13/184 (7.1%). Every changed case is predicted by replaying the ngram proposer on the non-speculative output, and nothing else differs. - Temperature 1 (same prompts, 40 seeds each, 1840 samples per arm): the fraction of first EOS falling inside the affected window goes from .913 to .888 (permutation p = .0058). - A toy model with a draft model (greedy and probabilistic drafts, min_tokens 3, 10000 samples): V1 matches the "bonus row masked by committed length" law and rejects the correct one (p < 1e-135). The V2 runner on the same models, prompt and seeds gives the correct law. Scope: on 0.31.0 ngram always runs on V1, so this is the default for ngram + `min_tokens`. On main (f26d9f432ced) ngram moved to V2 when Triton is available, and I did not see this on V2. V1 is still used with `VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=0`, on builds without Triton (CPU, macOS), and for methods V2 doesn't support (suffix, medusa, mlp_speculator, custom_class, EAGLE parallel drafting, heterogeneous-vocabulary draft models). The files linked above are byte-identical between v0.31.0 and f26d9f432ced. Related: #41768 (closed) touched `apply_with_spec_decode` for a draft row; this one is the bonus row. #46243 fixed a min_tokens off-by-one in the V2 sampler. Suggested fix: the bonus token is only ke
