items.title: [Bug]: Timed-out put is revoked while its queued slices are still pending; they later overwrite the next object at that address
items.author: yubofredwang
items.body_excerpt:
### Bug Report

#### Summary

When a Store put times out (60 s, hardcoded), the client returns `TRANSFER_FAIL (-800)` and revokes the object. The master frees the replica immediately, and the next put can get the same address. The timed-out transfer is not cancelled: slices still in the transfer engine queue are posted later and overwrite the new object. Nothing reports an error.

#975 / #993 added `discarded_replicas_` for this hazard ("the faulted client ... is still writing data to discarded replicas"). `PutRevoke` doesn't use it.

#### Environment

- `mooncake-transfer-engine-cuda13==0.3.13.post1`; source checked at `e5598b0` (`v0.3.13-rc1`). Same code on current `main`.
- Ubuntu 22.04.5, kernel `6.8.0-1047-nvidia`, `OFED-internal-25.10-1.2.8`, rdma-core `2510.0.10-1`.
- `mlx5_4` (InfiniBand), firmware `28.47.2526`.

#### Reproduce

Single host, RDMA (`MC_STORE_MEMCPY=0`), standalone master with defaults, one 16 MiB segment.

1. Client A: stop its two `transferWorker` threads with ptrace (RPC and heartbeat threads keep running), then put 12 MiB of `0x5C`.
2. After 60 s, A's put returns -800 and the object is revoked.
3. Client B (a separate process): put 12 MiB of `0x33` to a new key, then read it back. It lands at the same address and reads back `0x33`.
4. Resume A's workers. B's key now reads back all `0x5C`, and so does the segment memory.

Result: 8 out of 8 trials, same address every time, no crash. An earlier TCP run with a blackholed port, with no threads stopped, showed the same overwrite once the port came back.

Stopping the workers is artificial. It only stands in for anything that keeps slices queued past the timeout (e.g. a paused rail, `rdma_rail_pause_seconds` = 30, or a blocked worker). We have not reproduced it with a real link failure across two nodes.

#### Expected

A write from a revoked put should never land in memory that has been handed to another object.

#### Why

Links are pinned to `e5598b0`.

1. The timeout only stops waiting ([`transfer_task.cpp#L889-L895`](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/blob/e5598b0992cc258b06d22f24d875480e8931a28e/mooncake-store/src/transfer_task.cpp#L889-L895)). Queued slices aren't removed or marked cancelled.
2. The destructor calls `freeBatchID` ([`transfer_task.h#L226`](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/blob/e5598b0992cc258b06d22f24d875480e8931a28e/mooncake-store/include/transfer_task.h#L226)), which returns `BatchBusy` for unfinished tasks ([`transport.cpp#L42-L50`](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/blob/e5598b0992cc258b06d22f24d875480e8931a28e/mooncake-transfer-engine/src/transport/transport.cpp#L42-L50)). The result is ignored, so the batch is leaked, and the slices stay valid to post later.
3. `PutRevoke` erases the replica right away ([`master_service.cpp#L4869`](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/blob/e5598b0992cc258b06d22f24d875480e8931a28e/mooncake-store/src/master_service.cpp#L4869)). Stale put-start cleanup ([`#L4440-L4450`](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/blob/e5598b0992cc258b06d22f24d875480e8931a28e/mooncake-store/src/master_service.cpp#L4440-L4450)) and upsert preemption ([`#L4944`](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/blob/e5598b0992cc258b06d22f24d875480e8931a28e/mooncake-store/src/master_service.cpp#L4944)) move replicas to `discarded_replicas_` instead.

#### Impact

- The overwritten object belongs to another key whose put succeeded. Reads succeed and return wrong data.
- For a KV cache, every later prefix hit on that key gets the wrong KV until it is evicted.
- Slices read their source at post time. If the caller has reused its source buffer after the -800, the bytes that land aren't even the failed key's data.

#### Questions for maintainers

Before proposing a code change, we'd like your view on:

1. Have we seen other reports related to this issue in production?
2. Can it be prevented without code changes? For example, settings that keep the time a slice can spend queued well under 60 s (rail pause, retry count), or object checksum validation to catch the overwrite on read.

#### Possible fix

If you agree this is a real problem and not just a theoretical one, we'd propose a quarantine: `PutRevoke` moves the replicas to `discarded_replicas_` instead of erasing them, the same way stale put-start cleanup does. Dropping a timed-out batch's unposted slices would make that quarantine time a real upper bound. We can send a PR.

#### Related

#975 / #993 (`discarded_replicas_`), #4247 (same problem in the sync transfer API on Ascend), #3030.

### Before submitting...

- [x] Ensure you searched for relevant issues and read the documentation

items.title: [CI] Multi-rank PG CPU tests flake with ECONNRESET on the WRITE ack read
items.author: he-yufeng
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

The multi-rank CPU transfer tests in `test_pg_p2p` flake on CI with TCP sessions being reset while a WRITE ack is still in flight. Two occurrences within two hours on 2026-10-09:

- main branch run: https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/actions/runs/37930984424
- PR run (unrelated diff): https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/actions/runs/37925444040

Both fail `test-wheel-ubuntu (ubuntu-22.04, 3.12, mooncake-wheel-ci-py312)`, which then fails CI Gate and blocks unrelated PRs.

## Failure signature

```
tcp_transport_session_impl.h:704] ClientSession: failed to read WRITE ack frame. Error: Connection reset by peer (value: 104)
mooncake_worker_thread.cpp:271] Rank N [DATA] transfer to peer 3 (global=3) failed for op 2 status=6 diff_us=23401..41808
```

The reset always arrives at the sender while it is blocked reading the WRITE ack, 20 to 40 ms after the transfer started, and always on a session toward the last global rank. That timing says the receiver side closed or tore down its end of the session mid-transfer rather than the wire dropping.

## Hypothesis

In the split-ranks / multiple-senders patterns the receiver knows how many bytes it expects per peer. If the receiver side of a session is destroyed as soon as its expected receive count is satisfied while the sender still has the final ack outstanding, the socket close lands as ECONNRESET on the sender's ack read. That would make this an ordering bug in session teardown, not test-environment noise, and would also explain why it only flakes under CI host scheduling jitter.

## Impact

Every red occurrence fails CI Gate for the whole matrix, so all open PRs pay the retry cost.

## Next step

I intend to reproduce this locally with the CPU multi-rank tests under `taskset`-style scheduling pressure and pin down the teardown ordering. Filing this so the failure has a tracking home in the meantime; if someone else is already looking at the worker-thread suite, happy to leave it to them.

AI assistance disclosure: this analysis was prepared with AI assistance; the log evidence and the reproduction plan were verified by the human submitter against the linked CI runs.

items.title: [RFC] TENT concurrent registration lifecycle and cleanup retries
items.author: LysanderPhong
items.body_excerpt:
This RFC describes the concurrent-registration extension in [PR #4573](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/pull/4573), implemented in commit `c3ed2fc6365bf71d48ab5de57b3fd55bc6acc54b`. It asks for review of the lifecycle and failure contracts, including the measured performance cost. The original batch-only fix remains a separate commit if maintainers prefer to land it independently.

## Motivation and observed reproduction

The public Python bindings release the GIL around registration. On a frozen
build of the submitted `b63d4ef8bb9667ecdc8e1610267b0f71e75761a5` commit,
four threads mixed single and batch registrations of one live buffer on one
engine. In a local 100-round run, HP_TCP reported 20 overlapping-buffer
registration failures; a corresponding TCP run exposed duplicate metadata in
six rounds. Successful references and backing storage remained alive during
the checks. The Python workflow scripts and raw logs are retained locally and
are not included in the PR diff. The PR includes deterministic C++ regression
tests and real HP_TCP lifecycle tests.

These demonstrate a reachable public API problem, not a measured production
incident or a representative failure rate. We would welcome maintainer input
on integrations that register and unregister dynamically; startup-only users
may see little practical benefit.

The cause is the gap between checking published tracker metadata, entering a
transport, and publishing a newly registered range. Immutable metadata protects
readers but does not make this sequence one lifecycle operation. Final removal
similarly hides metadata before physical cleanup, leaving a gap in which a new
registration can race the previous generation's cleanup.

## Proposed coordination and reference contract

A per-engine `RegistrationCoordinator` reserves every starting address in an
operation together. It sorts and deduplicates the bases, waits until all are
available, then marks them occupied under one mutex. A waiter never owns a
partial batch, so reversed batches cannot introduce ABBA locking. A movable
RAII guard releases the reservation on scope exit; completed reservations leave
no historical address entries behind.

The reservation spans preparation, tracker changes, transport callbacks,
rollback and metadata publication. Callbacks do not hold the coordinator mutex
or the metadata writer mutex. Disjoint bases may enter transports concurrently;
existing metadata publication still has its own serialization. Different
lengths at the same base are coordinated together, including wildcard
unregistration, but are not merged. Arbitrary overlapping ranges with distinct
bases remain subject to transport behavior.

The tracker remains the source of logical references: each successful input
occurrence grants one reference to an exact `(address, length)` pair, including
duplicates within and across calls. Compatible references reuse the generation's
registration in each applicable transport. This does not mean one registration
across all transports, nor does it eliminate temporary RDMA warm-up operations.
Direct internal tracker users retain their existing callback/reentrancy model.

The original six `MemoryOptions` fields are retained locally in an immutable
shared object, excluded from serialized segment metadata. Reusing an exact
range requires equality of `type`, `perm`, `location`, `shm_path`, `shm_offset`
and `internal`. This intentionally compares supplied values, not equivalent
resolved policies; it does not upgrade a registration's permission or transport
coverage implicitly.

## Failure handling and generation boundaries

Registration failure must not grant new local references. If publication fails
after local registration, the engine rolls back this call's input occurrences,
including temporary references to existing ranges. It attempts a compensating
metadata publication. The complete address reservation prevents another call
on those bases from acquiring references during rollback.

Physical cleanup can also fail. A local, non-advertised retired record retains
the original transport keys and only the unfinished transport steps. Successful
steps are removed from that list, and their registered-byte metrics are reduced
once. The retry rule depends on the failed operation:

| Failed operation | Subsequent registration | Retry action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Registration with residual physical cleanup | May attempt cleanup first; must not create a new generation until it succeeds | Retry registration while retaining the backing memory |
| Final unregistration with cleanup or publication pending | Returns `TooManyRequests` at the same base | Retry unregistration; finished physical steps are not repeated |

A final unregistration retains its pending record even when only publication
remains. Allowing registration to consume that record and create a new
generation would let the original unregister retry remove the new owner.

This API has no operation or owner token. It cannot provide exactly-once
semantics for arbitrary delayed, duplicate retries: callers must serialize
retries of a failed unregistration and stop replaying it after success. A
completed unregistration replayed after another owner registers can still
release that later owner's reference.

Metadata compensation is not a distributed transaction. Peers may already have
observed a prior snapshot, and compensation can itself fail. The proposal
guarantees the local reference/cleanup behavior described here; it does not
promise atomic visibility across peers or eliminate existing cache staleness.

## Batch unregistration and publication cost

Batch unregistration processes input occurrences in order. On error, the message
identifies a zero-based failed index: the preceding entries have completed, and
the caller retries only that entry and its suffix.

Publishing once per physical removal would regress a batch into many complete
metadata publications. Instead, under the full address reservation, a lo

items.title: Use atomic_cas inside a loop
items.author: giorgio-arena
items.body_excerpt:
Hi, I'm experimenting with a simple kernel that reduces a rank-3 tensor on its last dimension. The kernel uses atomics to sum across one tensor row (I know it's not efficient, this is just a simple reproducer). I'm using two versions of the atomics, the first using atomic_add, and the second using the lock-like mechanism with atomic_cas and atomic_xchg.

```
@triton.jit
def _sum_kernel(X, Locks, O, width: tl.constexpr, use_atomic_add: tl.constexpr):
  in_off = tl.program_id(0) * width
  out_off = tl.program_id(0)

  for w in range(0, width):
    x = tl.load(X + in_off + w)
    if use_atomic_add:
      tl.atomic_add(O + out_off, x)
    else:
      while tl.atomic_cas(Locks + out_off, 0, 1) == 1:
        pass
      tl.store(O + out_off, tl.load(O + out_off) + x)
      tl.atomic_xchg(Locks + out_off, 0)


def _sum_fn(a, use_atomic_add):
  b, h, w = a.shape
  locks = torch.zeros([b, h], dtype=torch.int32, device='cuda')
  out = torch.zeros([b, h], dtype=a.dtype, device='cuda')
  _sum_kernel[(b * h,)](a, locks, out, width=w, use_atomic_add=use_atomic_add)
  return out

if __name__ == "__main__":
  x = torch.empty((8, 64, 128), dtype=torch.float32, device="cuda").normal_()
  ref = torch.sum(x, axis=-1)
  rtol = 1e-03

  print(torch.allclose(ref, _sum_fn(x, True), rtol=rtol))
  print(torch.allclose(ref, _sum_fn(x, False), rtol=rtol))
```

Unfortunately for the second version I get
```

  File "/usr/local/home/giorgio/triton/python/triton/compiler.py", line 741, in visit_For
    assert for_op_region.size() == 1, "We use SCF, so the loop body should only have one block"
AssertionError: We use SCF, so the loop body should only have one block
```

Any help would be appreciated, thanks.

        triton.Config({'BLOCK_M': 64, 'BLOCK_N': 128, 'BLOCK_K': 32, 'SPLIT_K': 1}, num_stages=4, num_warps=4),
        triton.Config({'BLOCK_M': 128, 'BLOCK_N': 32, 'BLOCK_K': 32, 'SPLIT_K': 1}, num_stages=4, num_warps=4),
        triton.Config({'BLOCK_M': 64, 'BLOCK_N': 32, 'BLOCK_K': 32, 'SPLIT_K': 1}, num_stages=5, num_warps=2),
        # good for int8
        triton.Config({'BLOCK_M': 128, 'BLOCK_N': 256, 'BLOCK_K': 128, 'SPLIT_K': 1}, num_stages=3, num_warps=8),

items.title: [Discussion] Use Isolated MLIR Symbol Namespace and TypeIDs for Out-of-Tree Backends
items.author: hongziqi
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

An out-of-tree plugin that shares the host `MLIRContext` hits one of two link failures. Both come from one MLIR rule: **within a single process, each MLIR C++ type may have only one `TypeIDResolver<T>::id`**.

- **Undefined symbol.** The plugin references a TypeID that `libtriton.so` never defined. `dlopen` fails.
- **Conflicting definition.** The plugin defines a TypeID the host already defined, or a second LLVM/MLIR is loaded beside `libtriton.so`. MLIR then treats one class as two identities.

`PluginInfo` / `TRITON_PLUGIN_API_VERSION` fixes neither case. That version only describes the callback table (`AddPassCallback`, `RegisterDialectCallback`, `AddOpCallback`). It cannot create a TypeID, and it cannot merge two of them.

What `TRITON_EXT_ENABLED=1` does today is re-export the MLIR symbols already linked into `libtriton.so`. On nightly `3.8.0+gitf893845b` that set includes Builtin, Func, Arith, SCF, MemRef, Affine, and LLVM. It does not include `linalg::LinalgDialect` or `tensor::TensorDialect`. A plugin that references those two TypeIDs fails `dlopen` with `undefined symbol`.

This proposal: **an out-of-tree backend compiles its own MLIR in a separate symbol namespace, fully isolated from the host TypeIDs. Dialects the host does not provide are defined by the backend. The host and the backend pass modules as MLIR text and do not share an `MLIRContext`.**

## Problem

`TRITON_EXT_ENABLED=1` only controls symbol visibility. **It does not change the libraries linked into `libtriton.so`.** Visibility and the link line are separate:

- Off: `-fvisibility=hidden` plus a version script. The only exported symbol is `PyInit_libtriton`.
- On: the visibility hide and the version script are removed, so every symbol already linked into `libtriton.so` is exported.
- `TRITON_LIBRARIES` in `CMakeLists.txt` does not change with the option. It contains NVVM, LLVM, GPU, SCF, Math-to-LLVM, and Triton's own libraries. It does not contain `MLIRLinalgDialect` or `MLIRTensorDialect`.

An MLIR TypeID must be unique in the process. A plugin that shares the host `MLIRContext` has only two layouts, and each one fails:

| Layout | What the plugin binary does | Failure |
|---|---|---|
| The host owns TypeID `T` | The symbol is undefined (`U`) in the plugin. `dlopen` binds it to the single global instance in `libtriton.so` | The host binary never linked a definition of `T`. Loading the plugin reports `undefined symbol` (for example the LinalgDialect TypeID) |
| The plugin owns TypeID `T` | The plugin uses `MLIR_DEFINE_EXPLICIT_TYPE_ID`, defines the dialect itself, and registers it | Two TypeIDs exist for one type. MLIR asserts at runtime |

The first failure cannot be fixed inside the plugin alone. If the plugin statically links the missing MLIR dialect archives to fill in the IR dependency, it falls into the second failure.

## Proposal

An out-of-tree backend needs Linalg, Tensor, and whatever dialects come after them. Those dialects are not linked into `libtriton.so` today. The 2026-07-08 meetup listed the following responses to the symbol problem:

| Approach | Conclusion |
|---|---|
| Split LLVM/MLIR into its own library (not recommended) | This only moves symbols. `TRITON_LIBRARIES` does not contain Linalg, so after the split the host still has no TypeID for it. |
| Symbol namespace isolation (recommended) | The backend compiles a private MLIR in its own namespace. Same-named symbols no longer bind to `libtriton.so`, which removes conflicts. Dialects the host lacks are provided by the backend library, which removes undefined symbols. A type in that namespace cannot be inserted into the host `MLIRContext`, so the module crosses the boundary as textual IR. |

The backend defines `TypeIDResolver<T>::id` inside its own namespace. At backend link time those symbols belong to the backend's static libraries. MemRef, Arith, and the other host types stay the host's symbols. The two names stay distinct, so loading both into one process does not merge them. **An op defined in the backend namespace cannot be registered into the host `PassManager`.**

### Recommended boundary

The host serializes the MLIR module to textual IR before handing it to the backend. The backend shared library follows three rules:

- Do not link `libtriton.so`. There is no `DT_NEEDED` on MLIR symbols.
- Compile the private MLIR in its own namespace, so `mlir::detail::TypeIDResolver<...>::id` is a different symbol from the host's.
- Accept and return only textual IR. Do not pass C++ objects such as `mlir::Value` or `PassManager*` across the boundary.

The backend statically links the smallest MLIR subset its lowering needs (Linalg, Tensor, and the transitive dependencies it actually references) and ships that subset in its own wheel. Adding a dialect later means updating the backend's link line, not shipping a new Triton.

```text
# Host: only dialects Triton already has, then serialize.
ttir_text = str(host_module)
# Backend: private MLIRContext, parse the text, lower, return text.
out_text = backend.compile_text(ttir_text)
```

## Questions

1. When an out-of-tree backend needs a dialect the host does not include, is **a separate MLIR symbol namespace, with those dialects defined by the backend, and modules passed as textual IR** the approach upstream recommends?
2. This path does not use `passes.plugin.extend_with` to inject a Linalg pass into the host `PassManager`. Does upstream accept this backend shape, or must every backend share one `MLIRContext`? Is there a better alternative?

items.title: Loop-carry detection skips `prev = cur` when both start as the same value, silently keeping the pre-loop value instead of carrying it
items.author: Hughshine
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug


**TL;DR.** `CodeGenerator._find_carries` decides which variables of a `for` or `while` loop become `iter_args` by comparing IR values after one dry run of the body, instead of asking whether a value can differ between iterations. If `prev` and `cur` are the same IR value before the loop and the loop runs `prev = cur`, `prev` looks unchanged and is not carried, so it keeps its pre-loop value in every iteration and after the loop. Regression from #7200, first in 3.5.0 (3.4.0 is right). Possible fix: also carry every name that is assigned in the loop (as 3.4.0 did), or only those that share their initial IR value with another name.

**Why one dry run misses it.** `_find_carries` ([L485-L524](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/6fe3348e6e907584e07e593ab19a35caee95c37a/python/triton/compiler/code_generator.py#L485-L524), the comparison is [L513](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/6fe3348e6e907584e07e593ab19a35caee95c37a/python/triton/compiler/code_generator.py#L513)) runs the body once with every name bound to its pre-loop value. When `prev = cur` runs there, `cur` is still at its pre-loop value, so `prev` is bound to the value it already had. In the real body `cur` is a block argument, so `prev = cur` is a different value in every iteration. Seeing that takes a second pass that already knows `cur` is carried.

The smallest example. `prev` is `cur`'s value at the start of each iteration; `SAME=False` is the control, where `prev` is equal to `cur` but a different IR value:

```python
import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl


@triton.jit
def kernel(out_ptr, n, SAME: tl.constexpr):
    cur = 0
    if SAME:
        prev = cur          # prev and cur are the same IR value
    else:
        prev = cur + 0      # control: equal to cur, but a different IR value
    for i in range(n):
        prev = cur          # prev is cur's value at the start of the iteration
        cur = cur + 1
    tl.store(out_ptr, prev)      # expected n - 1
    tl.store(out_ptr + 1, cur)   # expected n


n = 5
for same in (True, False):
    out = torch.zeros(2, dtype=torch.int32, device="cuda")
    k = kernel[(1, )](out, n, same)
    print(f"SAME={same!s:5} prev, cur = {out.tolist()}, expected {[n - 1, n]}")
    print("   ", [l.strip() for l in k.asm["ttir"].splitlines() if "scf.for" in l][0].split(" : ")[0])
```
```
SAME=True  prev, cur = [0, 5], expected [4, 5]
    %cur = scf.for %i = %c0_i32 to %n step %c1_i32 iter_args(%cur_0 = %c0_i32) -> (i32)
SAME=False prev, cur = [4, 5], expected [4, 5]
    %prev:2 = scf.for %i = %c0_i32 to %n step %c1_i32 iter_args(%cur = %c0_i32, %prev_0 = %c0_i32) -> (i32, i32)
```
With `SAME=True` only `cur` is an `iter_arg`. 3.4.0 has two `iter_args` in both cases and returns `[4, 5]`. Without an `iter_arg`, `prev` is still bound to its pre-loop value when the body starts, and `enter_sub_region` restores that binding when the loop ends ([L146](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/6fe3348e6e907584e07e593ab19a35caee95c37a/python/triton/compiler/code_generator.py#L146)).

**Why since 3.5.0.** Up to 3.4.0 every name that is assigned in the loop and live before it was carried ([visit_For](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/d4432f6b89ef554007a53ef90f2499d90792d7e7/python/triton/compiler/code_generator.py#L1114-L1115), [visit_While](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/d4432f6b89ef554007a53ef90f2499d90792d7e7/python/triton/compiler/code_generator.py#L1153-L1154)). #7200 (2025-06-23, "Improve detection of loop carries", for builtins that modify their arguments) replaced that with the comparison of IR values; v3.5.0 is the first tag that contains it. The existing tests for shared initial values (`test_loop_carry_shared_initial_value` and its while and tuple variants in test_frontend.py, #11369) update the aliased variables independently (`a = a + 1`, `b = b + 2`), so none has a copy between them.

**Possible fix.** Two variants, both tested as source patches on main @6fe3348e6.

Carry every name that is assigned in the loop, as 3.4.0 did, and keep the comparison:
```diff
--- a/python/triton/compiler/code_generator.py
+++ b/python/triton/compiler/code_generator.py
@@ -493,6 +493,9 @@ class CodeGenerator(ast.NodeVisitor):
         self.scf_stack.pop()
         block.erase()
 
+        # A name that is assigned in the loop may have copied another one, which an unchanged handle doesn't show.
+        assigned = {n.id for n in ast.walk(node) if isinstance(n, ast.Name) and isinstance(n.ctx, ast.Store)}
+
         # If a variable (name) has changed value within the loop, then it's
         # a loop-carried variable. (The new and old value must be of the
         # same type)
@@ -510,7 +513,7 @@ class CodeGenerator(ast.NodeVisitor):
 
                 live_handles = flatten_values_to_ir([live_val])
                 loop_handles = flatten_values_to_ir([loop_val])
-                if live_handles != loop_handles:
+                if name in assigned or live_handles != loop_handles:
                     names.append(name)
                     init_tys.append(live_val.type)
                     init_handles.extend(live_handles)
```
The comparison was added by #7200 for builtins that modify their arguments in place. #8832 (2025-11-25) removed that case ("now that we ban mutations") together with its tests, attribute and item assignment raise, and aggregates cannot be assigned to after construction, so a name whose IR value changes is a name that is assigned. In test_frontend.py and the Gluon frontend tests, 57 of the 181 (name, loop) pairs that `_find_carries` looked at had a changed IR value, and all 57 are assigned in the loop. The set of assigned names comes from the AST, so it does not depend on what the dry run did; that also covers a branch that only the lowering takes (see below). It over-carries assigned names whose value does not change (`x = x`); they become `iter_args` and the canonicalizer in `make_ttir` removes them (the TTIR of t

items.title: Upgrade to Transformers v5
items.author: hmellor
items.body_excerpt:
## What is this issue?

This issue serves as a living tracker for the current issues preventing us from upgrading vLLM to Transformers v5.

We will use sub-issues to track individual failures and PRs should be made against these sub-issues.

The solutions to these issues may need to be applied to either:

- Transformers in the form of:
  - Adding missing backward compatibility (usually for custom code models)
  - General bug fixes/improvements to new features of v5
- vLLM in the form of:
  - Forward compatibility with how something is now done in v5
  - Edge case handling for issues that v4 ignored (such as config validation)

Sometimes, the issue is simply with the model checkpoint itself, for example if it:

- Contains a malformed `config.json` that cannot be used to instantiate the newly input validated `PreTrainedConfig` class
- Custom code* uses deprecated/removed APIs

In these situations, the best solution will likely be to skip these tests in vLLM and open a PR to Transformers to contribute this model. This will be faster and more sustainable than waiting for the model vendor to fix their custom model code, sometimes they nevert do.

Contributing the new model should be done using the new [Modular Transformers](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/modular_transformers) so that the implementation is easy to maintain and will remain maintained by the Transformers team.

_*particularly in the parts of the model implementation that vLLM tries to directly reuse, such as config/tokenizer/multimodal processor_

items.title: [Performance] Measure Transformers backend startup time vs native
items.author: hmellor
items.body_excerpt:
This comes from an old comment and was never backed by measurements, so the first
task is to establish whether the effect is real at all. It may not be.

Runtime throughput was brought in line with native implementations in #47187, but
nobody has measured startup time either before or since.

### Step 1: is there a difference?

Time engine init for a model that has both implementations, e.g.:

    vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B --model-impl transformers
    vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B --model-impl vllm

Compare time-to-ready across a few runs and a couple of model sizes. Warm vs cold
HF cache matters, so control for it.

If there is no meaningful difference, say so and close this issue. That is a
perfectly good outcome and still worth having measured.

### Step 2: only if a delta shows up

The backend does some work at load time that native implementations do not, so
these are plausible starting points rather than known causes:

- `fuser.py` — `get_fuser` traces each module class with `fx` to match it against
  the available fusers. Cached per class, but tracing is not free.
- `base.py` — `recursive_replace` walks the module tree applying fusers per instance.
- Config resolution and `auto_map` handling for remote-code models.

A profile of init (py-spy or cProfile) will be more informative than guessing from
this list.

### Done when

Either the startup delta is quantified and explained, or it is shown that there
isn't a meaningful one and this is closed.

items.title: [Feature] L1/L2/L3 cache hit rate observability — Prometheus metrics, OTel spans & per-request JSONL trace
items.author: grissomsh
items.body_excerpt:
### Motivation

LMCache's current `PrometheusLogger` provides basic metrics (`time_to_retrieve`, `num_retrieve_requests`), but is missing:

1. **Per-tier cache hit rate** — no way to distinguish whether a hit came from L2 (CPU RAM), L3 (NVMe Disk), or a remote backend.
2. **TTFT decomposition** — `frontend_latency` (API server → engine core) and per-request `kv_lookup_time` / `kv_retrieve_time` are not surfaced.
3. **Per-request tracing** — no way to correlate cache-hit details to an individual request for debugging latency spikes.

These gaps make it hard to answer operational questions like: *"Why did TTFT spike — was it a slow disk read, CPU cache contention, or GPU prefix cache eviction?"*

---

### Design Goals

1. **Three-layer observability model**: throughput → latency → cache hit rate
2. **Minimally invasive**: extend existing `LMCStatsMonitor`, `PrometheusLogger`, and `cache_engine` — no breaking API changes
3. **TP-aware**: cross-process bridge via `/dev/shm` for Worker ↔ EngineCore per-request data relay when TP > 1
4. **Self-verifying**: every trace carries token identity equations for automated correctness validation

---

### Proposed Design

#### Layer 1 — Throughput: Token Source Decomposition

```
Tokens/s = local_compute + L1_hit + L2_hit + L3_hit + remote_hit
```

**Approach**: Extend `cache_engine.py`'s `retrieve()` / `retrieve_layer()` to classify hit tokens by storage backend. Add a `_BACKEND_NAME_TO_HIT_TIER` mapping:

| Backend | Tier |
|---------|------|
| `LocalCPUBackend` | L2 |
| `LocalDiskBackend` / `GdsBackend` | L3 |
| `RemoteBackend` | Remote |

**New Prometheus metrics** (6 total):

| Metric | Type |
|--------|------|
| `lmcache:l2_hit_tokens` / `lmcache:num_l2_hit_tokens` | Histogram + Counter |
| `lmcache:l3_hit_tokens` / `lmcache:num_l3_hit_tokens` | Histogram + Counter |
| `lmcache:remote_hit_tokens` / `lmcache:num_remote_hit_tokens` | Histogram + Counter |

#### Layer 2 — Latency: TTFT Decomposition

```
TTFT = frontend_latency + queue_time + prefill_time
prefill_time ⊃ kv_lookup_time + kv_retrieve_time
```

**Approach**: Add `LMCacheKVConnectorStats` (extending vLLM's `KVConnectorStats`) on the vLLM side, and expose per-request timing through `vllm_v1_adapter.py`'s `request_finished()` via `EngineCoreOutput.kv_transfer_params`.

**New Prometheus metrics** (9 bridge metrics + 1 framework metric):

| Metric | Type | Description |
|--------|------|-------------|
| `vllm:lmcache_kv_lookup_seconds` | Histogram | KV lookup latency |
| `vllm:lmcache_kv_retrieve_seconds` | Histogram | KV retrieve latency |
| `vllm:lmcache_retrieve_process_tokens_seconds` | Histogram | Retrieve: process_tokens phase |
| `vllm:lmcache_retrieve_to_gpu_seconds` | Histogram | Retrieve: CPU→GPU DMA phase |
| `vllm:lmcache_num_l2_hit_tokens` | Counter | vLLM-side L2 bridge |
| `vllm:lmcache_num_l3_hit_tokens` | Counter | vLLM-side L3 bridge |
| `vllm:lmcache_num_remote_hit_tokens` | Counter | vLLM-side remote bridge |
| `vllm:request_frontend_latency_seconds` | Histogram | API server → engine core latency |

#### Layer 3 — Cache Hit Rate & Per-Request Trace

One JSONL `[trace]` line emitted per request at completion:

```json
{
  "ts": 1782023561.679,
  "rid": "chatcmpl-xxx",
  "prompt_tokens": 3934,
  "output_tokens": 32,
  "TTFT_ms": 169.2,
  "queue_ms": 0.04,
  "prefill_ms": 130.1,
  "decode_ms": 144.6,
  "e2e_ms": 314.3,
  "frontend_ms": 39.0,
  "input_tokens_cache_hit": 3840,
  "L1_hit": 0,
  "external_kv_hit": 3840,
  "L2_hit": 0,
  "L3_hit": 3840,
  "remote_hit": 0,
  "input_tokens_no_cache_hit": 94,
  "kv_transfer_mode": "non_layerwise",
  "kv_lookup_ms": 1.2,
  "kv_retrieve_ms": 101.5
}
```

**Token identity equations** (verifiable by automated scripts at runtime):

```
prompt_tokens = input_tokens_cache_hit + input_tokens_no_cache_hit
input_tokens_cache_hit = L1_hit + external_kv_hit
external_kv_hit ≈ L2_hit + L3_hit + remote_hit   (≈ due to chunk_size=256 granularity)
```

#### Cross-Process Bridge (TP > 1)

When TP > 1, `retrieve()` runs on Worker_TP0 while `request_finished()` runs on the EngineCore/scheduler process. Per-request data is relayed via file-based bridge in `/dev/shm/lmcache_bridge/` (tmpfs, memory-backed):

- Per-tier counters: file + `fcntl.flock` for atomic cross-process updates
- Timing data: `write-tmp + os.replace` for atomic JSON
- Cleanup: throttled periodic sweep + retry limit (3) to prevent `/dev/shm` exhaustion

#### OTel Span Attributes

8 attributes on the `"llm_request"` span:

| Attribute | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| `gen_ai.latency.time_in_frontend` | API → engine |
| `gen_ai.latency.time_in_kv_lookup` | KV lookup |
| `gen_ai.latency.time_in_kv_transfer` | KV retrieve |
| `gen_ai.usage.l1_hit_tokens` | L1 (GPU prefix cache) |
| `gen_ai.usage.l2_hit_tokens` | L2 (CPU RAM) |
| `gen_ai.usage.l3_hit_tokens` | L3 (NVMe/SSD) |
| `gen_ai.usage.remote_hit_tokens` | Remote backend |
| `gen_ai.latency.kv_transfer_mode` | layerwise / non_layerwise |

---

items.title: Starting a localization (l10n) effort for LMCache
items.author: quaid
items.body_excerpt:
I'd like to propose we start building a localization community around LMCache, beginning with blog posts and expanding to documentation and other parts of the website over time.

tl;dr – 
- localizing content and software is valuable to all of us;
- we can automate the toil of translation but we need human editors who can review the translations and make sure they are properly localized;
- localization means words and phrases are fixed so the final product makes more sense to a native reader;
- we can use RHLF to improve this process and reduce toil over time.

## What is the problem

We already receive blog posts written natively in Mandarin and English. This is a good thing.

But we also need to localize this content without putting a burden on people. Fortunately this content has completed a technical review before being translated, so the focus can be on fixing idioms and grammar for better understanding by the widest audience.

## Why this matters

Ultimately this is about attracting more users to LMCache, some of whom will become intentional contributors over time.

Twenty-five years ago, localization (l10n) projects were one of the main ways Linux distributions and communities like the Fedora Project made headway into new parts of the world. It usually wasn't a corporate initiative. It was people who were enthusiastic about bringing free and open source software to their fellow country members, and who put in the effort to translate strings and make the software make sense locally. That work produced translations AND collaborations. It grew contributors, built regional communities, and carried the free software and open source ethos into places it hadn't reached before.

LMCache has users and watchers all over the world, and there are almost certainly people already adjacent to this project who could help bring information and education about the software to their local communities.

## What I'm proposing

We form loosely as `l10n-sig` out of anyone who wants to be an editor and approver for one or more languages. Languages get added when someone steps forward to take one. Rather than announcing a target list and hoping it fills in, we start with whoever volunteers.

I'm volunteering to be an editor and reviewer for anything translated to English, and I'd love more help with that role. I'm confident we can get Mandarin covered right away. But what else and how?

Japanese and Korean are the obvious early candidates given where our users are, but the principle is that a language becomes active when a person is willing to own it.

It only takes one person to get things started and be the gravity to bring another language.

As I said above, this isn't only English needing localizing. I currently have an original blog post written in Mandarin that I want to bring into English through this same process. I'd like to stop doing one at a time reviews by asking around in Slack to see who might need a break from creating features or fixing bugs. I'd rather offer the opportunity to people who aren't or can't create features or fix bugs.

Therefore, posts written originally in any language are welcome, and translation should flow in whatever direction it needs to.

## This is not a request for volunteer translation labor

LLM translation is pretty good now, and we should lean on it for the first pass. What we need is a human review step, and there are two kinds of people who can do that well.

The first is someone capable in both the source and target language, who can read the machine translation and confirm the meaning carried over and the tone is right. Not necessarily final-polish copy editing — a human or AI copy edit can always be applied later — just confirmation that it makes sense and reads naturally.

The second, and possibly just as valuable, is someone technical who knows their own language well and doesn't necessarily read the source language at all. Because the models are good enough now, a domain expert can look at a translated technical passage and say "ah, I see what this was trying to say" and correct the terminology so it's actually right in their language. Technical accuracy matters as much as idiomatic flow, and that person is well placed to catch it.

So the ask is much closer to "read this and tell us if it sounds right" than "translate three thousand words."

## How the workflow might look

Initially all of this can be manual, while we work out which models produce the best tone for technical writing in each language and we develop any necessary skills.

Longer term this could be automated — a GitHub Action that sends a published post to a translation model, then loads the result into WordPress as a draft where a translation editor reviews and approves it. It could also live partly outside the repo, with approval happening after the fact rather than as a gate. The goal is to distribute this work rather than make it dependent on a paid staffer, and to remove the need to ask permission before contributing.

If anyone already knows of a toolchain or process for this, please say so. I'd much rather adopt something that works than stand up and maintain our own infrastructure.

## What I'm looking for

Ideas or helping hands for:

- Thoughts on the approach
- Pointers to existing tooling
- Anyone in

items.title: llama : integer type consistency in `llama.h`
items.author: MarcusDunn
items.body_excerpt:
# Feature Description

llama.h should prefer to use `sized` (always) + `signed` (mostly) integers.

# Motivation

The integer types in `llama.h` right now are.

| Count | Type            |
|---------|------------------|
| 33      | `int`              |
| 10      | `int32_t`       |
| 24      | `uint32_t`     |
| 2        | `int64_t`       |
| 2        | `uint64_t`    | 

In #4540 there was a discussion around preferences for integer types on new methods. 

Avoiding `int` makes cross platform code simpler at essentially no cost.
Signed makes arithmetic simpler at the cost of some bits if you need something large.

# Possible Implementation

1. Change all `int`'s to `int32_t`
2. As code changes try to prefer signed integers.

We could also do some higher-impact things, but I'd take the lower-impact slower changes over a large find-and-replace.

items.title: [TransferEngine] TcpTransport benchmark note: VRAM-backed transfers pay per-chunk staging; original "2x host-path loss on USE_CUDA" was a benchmark-config artifact
items.author: n-WN
items.body_excerpt:
### Bug Report / Performance

**TcpTransport throughput drops ~2x when the build enables USE_CUDA, even for pure host-memory transfers** — measured on loopback with `transfer_engine_bench` (write, 4 threads × batch 32, duration 3–4 s, same box, same commit `f1f5e40`, only the build flag differs):

| block size | build without CUDA | build with `-DUSE_CUDA=ON` |
|---|---|---|
| 64 KB | 0.99 GB/s | 0.84–0.88 GB/s |
| 256 KB | 2.10 GB/s | 1.09–1.28 GB/s |
| 1 MB | **3.41 GB/s** | **1.53–1.64 GB/s** |

All buffers are plain DRAM (`numa_alloc`/`malloc`); no GPU memory is involved in the transfer.

### Root cause (from reading `tcp_transport.cpp`)

Under `USE_CUDA` (and the other accelerator macros), both `ClientSession::writeBody`/`readBody` and `ServerSession::writeBody`/`readBody` call `getCudaDeviceId(addr)` → `cudaPointerGetAttributes()` **once per 64 KB chunk** (not once per request), on both ends of the connection. For a 1 MB transfer that is 16 chunks × 2 sides = 32 CUDA runtime calls per request; `cudaPointerGetAttributes` costs on the order of a microsecond and serializes on CUDA runtime internals, which is enough to halve throughput at these block sizes. The result of the lookup cannot change between chunks of one request — the address range is fixed at submit time.

### Suggested fix

Resolve the memory type **once per request** (at header processing / `initiate`) and carry `cuda_device` through the chunk loop, instead of re-querying per chunk. That is a small, behavior-preserving change; a further step could consult the registered-buffer metadata (the engine already knows the location string of registered memory) and skip the CUDA query entirely for buffers registered as `cpu:*`.

Happy to pick this up as a follow-up to my in-flight TCP work if nobody else wants it — the benchmark setup above reproduces it in a couple of minutes on any CUDA-build machine.

### Environment
- main @ `f1f5e40`; x86_64 Linux with a recent GCC/CUDA toolchain; loopback P2PHANDSHAKE metadata.

comments.author: he-yufeng
comments.body:
Confirmed the root cause from a read of `tcp_transport.cpp`. In the server read path, `getCudaDeviceId(addr)` is called inside the per-chunk block (around line 261) — and `addr` is the constant buffer base, only `total_transferred_bytes_` advances between chunks. So every 64 KB chunk re-runs `cudaPointerGetAttributes` on the same pointer, which is exactly the overhead you measured; a CUDA build pays it once per chunk instead of once per transfer.

The fix is to resolve the device id once when the transfer starts and reuse it for every chunk. The same per-chunk `getCudaDeviceId(addr)` pattern appears at the other transfer sites (~192, ~399, ~503), so they'd want the same treatment.

I verified this by reading, not benchmarking (no GPU on hand), so the throughput numbers are yours — but the redundant call is clearly on the hot path. Happy to review a PR that hoists it.

comments.author: n-WN
comments.body:
**Correction: I re-ran the attribution today and the original report does not hold up. The ~2x delta was a benchmark-configuration artifact, not a host-path regression.** @he-yufeng — the code fact you confirmed (the query really is per-chunk and redundant) is true, but measurements show it cannot be the cause; details below.

**1. The per-chunk call is ~0.3%, not ~50%.** Microbenchmark on the same H100 box (context initialized, 200k iters):

| pointer class | `cudaPointerGetAttributes` per call |
|---|---|
| plain `malloc` (unregistered host — the class the TCP path queries) | 0.125 µs |
| `cudaMallocHost` / `cudaHostRegister` / `cudaMalloc` | 0.07–0.10 µs |
| unregistered host, different page every call (defeats driver caching) | 0.126 µs |

At 64 KB per chunk that is ~0.3% of chunk wire time even counting both ends — two orders of magnitude short of explaining 2x.

**2. The original A/B compared VRAM buffers against host buffers without knowing it.** `transfer_engine_bench` defines `use_vram` **only under the accelerator macros, with default `true`** — the flag does not even exist in a non-CUDA build (passing it errors out). So with the flag omitted from both command lines, the CUDA build silently benchmarked **`cudaMalloc` VRAM buffers** (per-chunk staging: `new` + synchronous `cudaMemcpy` + `delete` on every 64 KB), while the non-CUDA build used `numa_alloc` host memory. My "all buffers are plain DRAM" claim in the report was wrong for the CUDA column. Same binary, same box today: VRAM 1.32–1.66 GB/s vs `--use_vram=false` 1.73–2.13 GB/s @ 1 MB.

**3. With the configuration fixed, there is no USE_CUDA host-path regression.** Equal-flags rebuild (only `-DUSE_CUDA` flipped, same commit), host memory both sides, interleaved runs on the same box:

| block | non-CUDA build | CUDA build, `--use_vram=false` |
|---|---|---|
| 1 MB | 2.44–2.83 GB/s | 1.95–2.32 GB/s |
| 256 KB | 1.92–2.09 GB/s | 1.77–2.16 GB/s |

Overlapping ranges, within run-to-run variance (absolute numbers differ from the original report — different day/load on a shared box — but the interleaved comparison is internally controlled).

**Consequence:** given these numbers, the hoist I offered in the description would be measurable-benefit-free churn, so I won't send one. The honest disposition is to close this as not-a-bug (mislabeled benchmark configuration), or retitle it as a note that VRAM-backed TCP transfers pay a per-chunk staging cost — which is the real (and expected) difference the numbers were showing. Maintainers' call; apologies for the noise, and thanks @he-yufeng for engaging — the reading was right, the magnitude was not.

items.title: [RFC]: Adaptive prefill token budget based on scheduling pressure
items.author: TimoSaemann
items.body_excerpt:
### Motivation.

vLLM exposes `max_num_batched_tokens` (MBT) as a static scheduling configuration. For long-context workloads, however, we observe that the latency-optimal token budget depends on the current scheduling pressure.

Under low scheduling pressure, a large MBT can improve prefill execution efficiency and reduce end-to-end latency. As concurrent prefill and decode work increases, a smaller prefill budget can become preferable by limiting prefill interference with active decoding.

This means that no single static MBT is optimal across changing load regimes.

We investigated this behavior across multiple models, workloads, and NVIDIA GPUs (RTX 5090, A100, and H100), including kernel-level profiling with Nsight Systems and Nsight Compute. Based on these observations, we developed Prefill-Pressure Adaptive Scheduling (P-PAS), a lightweight policy that adapts the amount of prefill work admitted by the scheduler.

Across the main load sweep, P-PAS reduced average end-to-end latency by 8.5% relative to fixed MBT 2k and by 11.3% relative to fixed MBT 16k.

Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15171

Implementation, benchmarks, raw results, and profiling traces:
https://github.com/TimoSaemann/ppas-vllm

### Proposed Change.

Add an optional adaptive prefill-budget policy to the V1 scheduler.

The evaluated P-PAS policy uses scheduler state that is already available.
Let:

- `N_p` be the number of running and waiting prefill requests
- `N_d` be the number of running decode requests
- `N_th` be a prefill-pressure threshold
- `B_max` be the normal prefill token budget
- `B_cap` be the reduced prefill token budget

The policy is:

```text
if N_p >= N_th and N_d > 0:
    prefill_budget = B_cap
else:
    prefill_budget = B_max
```

For the experiments in the paper:

```text
N_th  = 2
B_max = 16384
B_cap = 2048
```

The global scheduler token budget remains unchanged. The adaptive budget only limits the aggregate amount of prefill work admitted within a scheduler iteration.

The current implementation is a small modification of the vLLM V1 scheduler and can be enabled or disabled without changing the standard scheduling behavior when disabled.

I would be happy to adapt the implementation to the current vLLM scheduler and make the policy/configuration interface consistent with the maintainers' preferred design.

### Feedback Period.

Two weeks.

### CC List.

_No response_

### Any Other Things.

A working implementation for vLLM 0.22.1 is available in the repository linked above. If there is interest in this direction, I would be happy to adapt the implementation to the current vLLM scheduler and prepare a PR.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

items.title: [Bug] ~11% long-prefill regression on SM120 (RTX 5090) between 0.6.12 and 0.6.13, hybrid GDN model via vLLM
items.author: jhsmith409
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

Upgrading FlashInfer **0.6.12 → 0.6.13** costs **~8–11% long-context prefill throughput** on **SM120 (RTX 5090)** with a hybrid GDN + attention MoE model served by vLLM. Decode is unaffected. The regression is isolated to the FlashInfer wheels: swapping *only* `flashinfer-python` / `flashinfer-cubin` / `flashinfer-jit-cache` between 0.6.12 and 0.6.13, with vLLM/torch/cutlass-dsl held constant, reproduces it in **both directions**.

The penalty scales with context length (≈0% at 4K, −8% at 64K, −11% at 131K), which points at the prefill attention path rather than kernel/backend selection.

### Environment

- GPU: **NVIDIA RTX 5090, 32 GB, SM120** (compute cap 12.0), driver 610.43.02, CUDA 13.0
- vLLM: `v0.24.0` (ships FI 0.6.12) and `v0.25.0` (ships FI 0.6.13), official `vllm/vllm-openai` images
- torch 2.11.0+cu130, nvidia-cutlass-dsl 4.5.2 — **identical across all runs**
- Model: `unsloth/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-NVFP4-Fast` — MoE (256 experts, top-8), **hybrid: 30 GDN/linear-attn + 10 attention layers**, 256K context. compressed-tensors NVFP4 (W4A4) experts + FP8 attention.
- Attention backend: **FLASHINFER** (auto-selected). MoE: FLASHINFER_CUTLASS. GDN prefill: Triton/FLA.
- Env: `FLASHINFER_CUDA_ARCH_LIST=12.0f`, `FLASHINFER_FORCE_SM=120f`

Serving flags: `--kv-cache-dtype=fp8 --max-model-len=262144 --max-num-batched-tokens=4096 --gpu-memory-utilization=0.92 --max-num-seqs=16 --enable-prefix-caching --moe-backend=auto`

### Reproduction

Measured with `vllm bench serve` (concurrency 1, `--random-output-len 128` so prefill dominates, 3 prompts). **prefill tok/s = prompt_tokens / mean_TTFT.**

**Stock images:**

| vLLM | FlashInfer | 4K | 16K | 64K | 131K |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| v0.24.0 | 0.6.12 | 27,248 | 31,856 | **18,303** | **12,672** |
| v0.25.0 | 0.6.13 | 26,766 | 31,147 | **16,767** | **11,345** |
| nightly `0.25.1.dev37` | 0.6.13 | 26,742 | 31,428 | 16,844 | 11,369 |

**Isolating FlashInfer** — only the flashinfer wheels swapped (`pip install --no-deps --force-reinstall flashinfer-python==X flashinfer-cubin==X flashinfer-jit-cache==X`), everything else byte-identical:

| build | FlashInfer | prefill@131K | verdict |
|---|---|---:|---|
| vLLM 0.24.0 (stock) | 0.6.12 | **12,658** | good |
| vLLM 0.24.0 | **0.6.13** | **11,271** | **regressed** ← only FI changed |
| vLLM nightly 06-30 (stock) | 0.6.13 | **11,224** | regressed |
| vLLM nightly 06-30 | **0.6.12** | **12,581** | **recovered** ← only FI changed |
| vLLM 0.25.0 | **0.6.12** | **12,724** | recovered |

Decode is unaffected (aggregate output tok/s at 16 concurrent: 2,235 on 0.6.12 vs 2,198 on 0.6.13 — within noise).

### Ruled out

- **Not backend selection.** Both versions log the identical choices: `FLASHINFER` attention backend, `FLASHINFER_CUTLASS` NvFp4 MoE backend, `Triton/FLA GDN prefill kernel (requested=auto, head_k_dim=128)`, and `attention block size 2096`. The vLLM engine-config diff between the two versions is three cosmetic lines.
- **Not the FP8-KV prefill repack** (#3485, `perf(attention): Speed up FP8 KV-cache prefill (FA2 BatchPrefill) by repacking K/V to BF16 in shared memory`). This was my first suspect since the config uses `--kv-cache-dtype=fp8`, but the regression **persists with BF16 KV** (`--kv-cache-dtype=auto`): 12,695 → 11,319, the same ~11%.
- **Not prefix caching.** Gap persists with `--no-enable-prefix-caching`: 12,658 → 11,013 (0.6.12) vs 11,224 → 10,005 (0.6.13).

### Possible culprits

I have not bisected inside the 0.6.12…0.6.13 range. From the [compare](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/compare/v0.6.12rc3...v0.6.13), the autotuner changes look like the most plausible candidates for a context-scaling prefill slowdown via worse tactic selection:

- #3367 `fix(autotuner): differentiate file cache entries by runner specific kernel parameters`
- #3396 `feat(autotuner): enable per-op autotune bypass for faster framework warmup`
- #3373 `Extend autotuner delay kernel length`

Happy to run further probes on this SM120 box (including a wheel-level bisect inside the range) if that's useful — I have the harness set up.

### Workaround

Pinning `flashinfer-python==0.6.12 flashinfer-cubin==0.6.12 flashinfer-jit-cache==0.6.12` on top of vLLM 0.25.0 fully restores prefill throughput (12,724 tok/s @131K) with no other regressions (needle-in-haystack 8/8, no OOM under load).

items.title: [Feature]: FP16/BF16 paged KV append by slot mapping
items.author: animeshsri14
items.body_excerpt:
### Before submitting

- [x] I have searched existing issues and this request has not been filed yet.

### Problem

FlashInfer can write K/V into a paged cache from a flat `slot_mapping` (`slot = page_id * page_size + entry_idx`), but only through the NVFP4 path: `nvfp4_quantize_append_paged_kv_cache_with_slot_mapping` (#3740). The ordinary FP16/BF16 cache has no equivalent. `append_paged_kv_cache` takes `batch_indices` / `positions` plus page-table metadata (`kv_indices`, `kv_indptr`, `kv_last_page_len`).

Slot mapping can be emulated today with a single "request" whose page table is the identity. This writes bit-exact results for both NHD and HND (checked on an L4, bf16, page_size 16, 2 KV heads, head_dim 128):

```python
# Preconditions: slots are unique, non-negative, in range, and fit int32.
zeros = torch.zeros(nnz, dtype=torch.int32, device=dev)
flashinfer.append_paged_kv_cache(
    k, v, zeros, slots, paged_kv_cache,
    torch.arange(num_pages, dtype=torch.int32, device=dev),  # identity page table
    torch.tensor([0, num_pages], dtype=torch.int32, device=dev),
    torch.tensor([page_size], dtype=torch.int32, device=dev),
    kv_layout,
)
```
The workaround has three gaps:

1. **Padding.** Runtimes mark padded tokens with negative slots (for example CUDA-graph padding). `append_paged_kv_cache` does not skip negative positions; passing them through can cause invalid memory accesses. Callers must compact the inputs or send padding to a reserved dummy page.
2. **Index conversion.** Runtimes usually keep `slot_mapping` as int64. The existing wrapper accepts int64 positions but converts them to int32 internally. A direct writer avoids that conversion.
3. **Extra metadata.** The identity page table represents one logical request, but callers must build and retain batch indices and page-table metadata even though the physical slots already identify every destination.

### Requested outcome

An FP16/BF16 counterpart to the NVFP4 slot-mapping writer, following its argument conventions:

```python
flashinfer.append_paged_kv_cache_with_slot_mapping(
    append_key,      # [num_rows, num_kv_heads, head_dim], fp16/bf16
    append_value,    # same shape and dtype
    slot_mapping,    # [nnz], int32 or int64; num_rows >= nnz
    paged_kv_cache,  # existing tuple / stacked-5D formats; same dtype as inputs
    kv_layout="NHD", # "NHD" | "HND"
) -> None
```

- Only the first `nnz` input rows are considered.
- Negative slots and slots `>= max_num_pages * page_size` are skipped, matching the current NVFP4 slot-mapping kernel. This gives direct physical-slot writes a defined contract for padded rows.
- Valid destination slots must be unique; duplicate-destination ordering is outside this proposal.
- The operation supports CUDA graph capture and replay without host synchronization.
- The existing `append_paged_kv_cache` behavior is unchanged. Quantization, RoPE fusion, and attention changes are outside the scope.

### Target hardware

Hardware-independent, SM89 (L4, L40S, RTX 40-series)

### Inference engine

Custom / other

### Affected model or model family

_No response_

### Workload and configuration

- FP16 / BF16 inputs and KV cache; no quantization.
- NHD and HND layouts.
- Hardware: general CUDA. Validation hardware: SM89 (L4). The check above validates the workaround (does not validate the proposed operation).
- Callers: runtimes that already allocate physical cache slots. No downstream integration is included in this proposal.
- Initial validation: head_dim 64/128/256, page_size 1 and 16, and multiple KV-head counts. Intended shape coverage follows the existing append operation, subject to maintainer guidance.

### Current workaround

The identity page table shown above, with filtering or safe dummy destinations for padded rows.


### Impact

API usability or integration complexity

### Acceptance criteria

- Bit-exact against a PyTorch scatter reference for FP16/BF16, NHD/HND, int32/int64 slots, page_size 1 and >1, and tuple/stacked caches, using unique valid destination slots.
- Support strided K/V inputs within the existing append operation's layout and alignment requirements, including a contiguous final dimension.
- Negative and out-of-range slots leave the cache untouched; all-invalid slots and `nnz=0` are no-ops.
- Works under CUDA graph capture and replay, including changes to slot values in the same device buffer.
- Report L4 latency and throughput against the identity-page-table path across representative decode and prefill token counts. Aim for no material regression; no speedup claim is made yet.

### Related work, dependencies, or suggested scope

- #3740: NVFP4 slot-mapping paged KV append, the API and semantics precedent.
- #3647: GPT-OSS FP8 reshape-cache operation for SM100; related but different output dtype and architecture scope.
- #6204 (open): proposes removing host synchronization from the NVFP4 slot-mapping append path; relevant to the graph-safe requirement.
- Suggested implementation: a vectorized CUDA copy kernel and launcher in `include/flashinfer/page.cuh`, C++ bindings, a Python wrapper, API exports/documentation/trace support, and focused correctness and graph-replay tests.

Happy to implement this after confirming the preferred direction:

1. Is a direct slot-mapping API useful here, or would you prefer extending the existing append API to cover padding and index handling?
2. If a new entry point is preferred, is the proposed name and signature appropriate?

### Timing or release need

_No response_

items.title: Eval bug: CUDA graphs hang the GPU channel (RC watchdog + Xid 8) on RTX 5090 Laptop / sm_120; GGML_CUDA_DISABLE_GRAPHS=1 is a complete workaround
items.author: bozdemir
items.body_excerpt:
### Name and Version

```
version: 0.1.0-dev (build 1, commit 9f0d017)
built with GNU 13.3.0 for Linux x86_64
```

Full commit: `9f0d017efb4a388bd5c60a27a575c90f20868e51` (2026-08-17)

### Operating systems

Linux

### GGML backends

CUDA

### Hardware

| | |
|---|---|
| GPU | NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090 Laptop GPU (GB203M), 24463 MiB, compute capability 12.0 |
| CPU | Intel Core Ultra 9 275HX |
| Laptop | HP OMEN MAX 16 (board 8D41) |
| Driver | 595.84 |
| CUDA runtime | 13.2 |
| CUDA toolkit used to build | 13.3, V13.3.73 |
| OS | Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS, kernel 7.0.0-29-generic |

Build configuration:

```
CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE          = Release
CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES  = 120
GGML_CUDA                 = ON
GGML_CUDA_GRAPHS          = ON
GGML_CUDA_FA              = ON
GGML_CUDA_FORCE_CUBLAS    = OFF
GGML_CUDA_FORCE_MMQ       = OFF
GGML_SCHED_MAX_COPIES     = 1
```

### Models

Qwen3.8-27B Q4_K_M GGUF (arch `qwen35`, 27.32B params, 15.65 GiB, hybrid attention + SSM, 64 layers, `n_embd_head_k/v = 256`), loaded together with the F16 mmproj for vision.

The hang reproduces with two different Q4_K_M builds of this architecture: the stock unsloth `Qwen3.8-27B-Q4_K_M.gguf` and a third party abliterated build of the same model. So it is not specific to one quantization run or one finetune.

### Problem description and steps to reproduce

Under sustained inference load, the GPU stops servicing a command channel. The NVIDIA kernel driver's Robust Channel watchdog declares the GPU locked after a 7 second notify timeout, raises Xid 8, and `llama-server` aborts inside `ggml_abort` with a CUDA error.

Setting `GGML_CUDA_DISABLE_GRAPHS=1` eliminates the failure completely. Nothing else needs to change.

Command line that reproduces the hang:

```bash
llama-server \
  --model Qwen3.8-27B-Q4_K_M.gguf \
  --mmproj mmproj-F16.gguf \
  --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 \
  -b 2048 -ub 512 -fitt 0 \
  --cache-type-k q8_0 --cache-type-v q8_0 \
  --cache-ram 32768 --ctx-checkpoints 32 \
  --threads 12 --threads-batch 12 \
  -ngl 999 --no-mmap --mlock \
  --reasoning-preserve \
  --temp 1.0 --top-p 0.95 --top-k 20 --min-p 0.0 \
  --presence-penalty 0.0 --repeat-penalty 1.0 \
  -np 1 -lv 4
```

The exact same command line prefixed with `GGML_CUDA_DISABLE_GRAPHS=1` does not hang.

Steps:

1. Start `llama-server` with the command above.
2. Drive it with a real coding agent workload (I used OpenCode) so the slot stays busy with long prompts and long generations.
3. Wait. The hang is stochastic, not deterministic. It never happens on the first request.

#### Failure rate

Across 11 observed hangs, time from server start to hang was:

```
min      4 minutes
mean   8.6 minutes
max     15 minutes
```

With `GGML_CUDA_DISABLE_GRAPHS=1` the same workload has run 50 minutes and then 32+ minutes without a single hang, on the same boot, same GPU, same model, same client. Assuming the failure rate is unchanged, the probability of surviving 32 minutes by chance is under 3 percent.

#### A/B evidence, same boot, same hour, same model

| PID | `GGML_CUDA_DISABLE_GRAPHS` | fusion | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4555 | not set | enabled | hang at 16:27:41 |
| 10643 | not set | enabled | hang at 16:37:15 |
| 3568 | `=1` | disabled | 50 minutes clean, stopped manually |
| 40527 | `=1` | **enabled** | 32+ minutes clean and still running |

PID 40527 is the important row. It has kernel fusion enabled and only CUDA graphs disabled, and it is stable. So this is not the fusion path, it is the graph path.

#### Collateral damage

While `llama-server` holds the GPU, the X server hits Xid 8 on its own channel too:

```
NVRM: Xid (PCI:0000:02:00): 8, pid=2434, name=Xorg, channel 0x00000002
```

This is consistent with a single long running or non terminating kernel blocking the GPU for more than the 7 second watchdog window, starving other channels.

#### What I ruled out

- **Power / TGP.** Hangs occur identically at the stock 95 W limit and at the full 175 W (150 W base + 25 W Dynamic Boost). Not a power delivery problem.
- **Thermal.** `HW Thermal Slowdown` counter is 0. Temperatures ranged 67 to 82 C against a 87 C target, 89 C slowdown, 92 C shutdown. No thermal event.
- **Hardware fault.** No Xid 79, no Xid 63/64, no ECC errors. A clean reboot does not prevent the hang, it recurs 16 minutes into a fresh boot.
- **MTP / speculative decoding.** Hangs with and without `--spec-type draft-mtp`.
- **Kernel fusion.** `GGML_CUDA_DISABLE_FUSION=1` is not required. With fusion enabled and only graphs disabled the server is stable.
- **KV cache quantization.** `q8_0` K and V are used in both the hanging and the stable configuration.

### First Bad Commit

Not bisected. Present in `9f0d017`.

This looks distinct from the two existing Blackwell reports:

- #21564 reports Xid 43 (illegal memory access) traced to `flash_attn_stream_k_fixup`.
- #24399 reports a device exception from an out of range shared memory store in `mul_mat_q<Q8_0,128>`.

Both of those are illegal accesses. What I am seeing is a **hang**, not an illegal access: the RC watchdog fires on a 7 second timeout and the hardware exception counters stay at zero. Different failure mode, and the workaround is different as well.

### Relevant log output

#### Kernel log

Every hang is preceded by the watchdog line:

```
kernel: NVRM: krcWatchdog_IMPL: RC watchdog: GPU is probably locked!  Notify Timeout Seconds: 7
```

items.title: [Bug] DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash + DSPARK: unbounded SparsePrefillWorkspace allocation OOM-crashes the whole TP group
items.author: hasan-emre-dinc
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

Serving **DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash** with **DSPARK speculative decoding** (`--speculative-algorithm DSPARK`) and **fp8_e4m3 KV cache** on **TP2, 2×B300 (288GB)**, the server passes startup and serves normal traffic fine, but a deep queue of long-context requests (170k–212k prompt tokens each) draining into a single prefill step reliably OOM-crashes the whole TP group:

```
torch.OutOfMemoryError: CUDA out of memory. Tried to allocate 27.20 GiB.
GPU 0 has a total capacity of 267.68 GiB of which 26.77 GiB is free. Including
non-PyTorch memory, this process has 240.52 GiB memory in use. Of the allocated
memory 235.23 GiB is allocated by PyTorch, with 5.54 GiB allocated in private
pools (e.g., CUDA Graphs), and 1.43 GiB is reserved by PyTorch but unallocated.
```

Both TP ranks hit the same error at the same time. The scheduler raises, and the whole server process exits (`kill_process_tree`). Every in-flight request drops. A second replica took over the failover traffic and hit the same crash 12 minutes later, at a smaller allocation size (15.40 GiB tried, 12.74 GiB free). So this is not a one-off. It reproduces whenever the queue depth and context length are large enough compared to whatever memory happens to be free at the time.

Traceback (identical shape on both occurrences, both ranks):
```
Scheduler hit an exception: Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "sglang/srt/managers/scheduler.py", line 5696, in run_scheduler_process
    scheduler.run_event_loop()
  File "sglang/srt/managers/scheduler.py", line 1839, in run_event_loop
    ... dispatch_event_loop -> forward
  File "sglang/srt/layers/attention/deepseek_v4_backend.py", line 3904, in _forward_prefill_sparse
    workspace = self.sparse_prefill_workspace.get(
                ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File "sglang/srt/layers/attention/dsv4/sparse_prefill_utils.py", line 100, in get
    self._buffer = torch.empty(
                   ^^^^^^^^^^^^
torch.OutOfMemoryError: CUDA out of memory. Tried to allocate 27.20 GiB. ...
```

Batch state at the moment of the first crash: `#running-req: 0, #queue-req: 73, #pending-token: 337719` (a 73-request queue draining at once). Second occurrence: `#running-req: 4, #queue-req: 16, #pending-token: 388518`.

**Analysis.** `SparsePrefillWorkspace.get()` in `sparse_prefill_utils.py` reallocates its buffer with a plain `torch.empty(...)` call whenever the requested size is bigger than the current buffer. There is no check before this call:

```python
def get(self, num_tokens, dtype=torch.bfloat16):
    assert num_tokens > 0
    current_capacity = self._buffer.shape[0] if self._buffer is not None else 0
    current_dtype = self._buffer.dtype if self._buffer is not None else None
    if num_tokens > current_capacity or dtype != current_dtype:
        self._buffer = torch.empty(
            (num_tokens, 1, WORKSPACE_DIM), dtype=dtype, device=self.device,
        )
    return self._buffer[:num_tokens]
```

It is called from `_forward_prefill_sparse` with `num_tokens = n_compressed + cache.swa_token_ids.shape[0]`. That is the size of the compressed-region gather plus the SWA-region gather for every request in that prefill step. There is no `mem_get_info` check and no chunking anywhere in this path.

This is not bounded by `--max-prefill-tokens`. That flag only caps new tokens admitted per step. The crashing batch shows `#new-token: 16384`, right at that cap, so the throttle was respected and it still was not enough. It is also not bounded by `--chunked-prefill-size`. Grepping the file shows this flag is never read or enforced against this workspace. So a deep queue of long-context requests can push `n_compressed + swa_token_ids` well past what the new-token cap limits, and the allocation just tries for whatever that adds up to. There is no fallback.

This looks like the same bug class as #30505 (unbudgeted prefill transients in DSA's `flash_mla_with_kvcache` on GLM-5.2) and the budget-check gap we already fixed in the DSV4 indexer's MQA-logits path (related to #34155 and #33246). But this is a different call site, `SparsePrefillWorkspace`, and it has no budget or chunking guard at all.

**Suggestion.** Add the same kind of guard used for the DSV4 indexer's MQA-logits budget check. Read `torch.cuda.mem_get_info()` before the `torch.empty(...)` call in `SparsePrefillWorkspace.get()`. Then either chunk the prefill batch to fit, or raise an error that can be retried, instead of letting an oversized allocation take down the whole TP group. A single request failing is a much better outcome than the whole server crashing on one bad batch.

items.title: [Bug] DFlash2/DSpark + prefix caching corrupt output after a cache hit on Qwen3.8-27B (TP=1) on 0.30/0.31; 0.29 and MTP are fine
items.author: sinmkd
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment

- vLLM 0.31.0 (also reproduced on 0.30.0). vLLM 0.29.0 passes the same test.
- torch 2.13.0+cu130, flashinfer-python/cubin 0.7.0.post1 (0.6.18.post1 on 0.30.0), CUDA 13.3, driver 610.57.04
- 1× RTX PRO 5000 Blackwell 48 GB (sm_120), Ubuntu 24.04, kernel 7.0.0-34
- Target: `Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B` NVFP4 checkpoint, compressed-tensors mixed precision (NVFP4 on the MLP projections, FP8 W8A8 on attention / GDN projections / lm_head, `linear_attn.{in_proj_a,in_proj_b,norm}` and `mtp.*` unquantized via `ignore`)
- Drafter: `z-lab/Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2` (`DFlash2DraftModel`, sliding_window 2048), `num_speculative_tokens: 7`

### 🐛 Describe the bug

Since 0.30.0, serving Qwen3.8-27B NVFP4 with the DFlash2 drafter and prefix caching enabled produces garbage after a prefix-cache hit. The first requests of a conversation are fine. From the third request on, once the prompt resumes from cached blocks, the model emits a single repeated token (`duct`, over and over) with no coherent content, and the drafter accepts nothing (`SpecDecoding metrics: Mean acceptance length: 1.00, Accepted: 0 tokens`). The same five requests against 0.29.0 come back coherent every time. I have run the comparison twice on each version.

The test is a replay of a real agent conversation: five consecutive chat-completions requests from one session (31,776 / 45,606 / 52,737 / 65,364 / 67,502 prompt tokens, 25 tool schemas, seed 17), sent in order to a fresh engine so each request hits the previous one's prefix. The conversation itself is private, but I can build a synthetic equivalent if that helps.

Serve command (production flags):

```
vllm serve /models/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4 --max-model-len 250000 --kv-cache-memory-bytes 17379961324 \
  --max-num-seqs 32 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.92 --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \
  --speculative-config '{"method":"dflash","model":"/models/Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2","num_speculative_tokens":7}' \
  --enable-auto-tool-choice --tool-call-parser qwen3_coder --reasoning-parser qwen3 \
  --override-generation-config '{"temperature":1.0,"top_p":0.95,"top_k":20,"min_p":0.0}' --scheduling-policy priority
```

env: `VLLM_USE_DEEP_GEMM=0 VLLM_ENFORCE_STRICT_TOOL_CALLING=false`. Prefix caching on (default), `mamba_cache_mode` resolves to `align`.

### What I tried, to narrow it down

All on 0.31.0, same five requests, fresh engine each time:

| Change | Result |
|---|---|
| nothing (command above) | fails at request 3 |
| PR #57128 applied (the `MambaManager.find_longest_cache_hit` / `drop_eagle_block` fix) | fails |
| `--gdn-prefill-backend triton` instead of FlashInfer | fails |
| `--linear-backend cutlass` (in-tree CUTLASS NVFP4 GEMM) | fails |
| `--linear-backend marlin` (weight-only W4A16, no activation quant) | fails |
| smaller KV pool / 180K window / util 0.94 (copied from my FP8 route) | fails |
| `"disable_eagle_block_drop": true` in the speculative config | worse: garbage from request 1, even cold |
| **no speculative config at all** | **passes 5/5** |
| **`{"method":"mtp","num_speculative_tokens":3}` (checkpoint's own MTP head)** | **passes 5/5** |
| **`{"method":"dspark","model":"RedHatAI/Qwen3.8-27B-speculator.dspark","num_speculative_tokens":7}`** | **fails at request 3** |
| **FP8 target (`Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B-FP8`, `quant_method: fp8`) with the same DFlash2 config** | **passes 5/5, twice** |

A unique `cache_salt` per request on 0.30.0 also makes requests 3–5 pass, so the failure needs an actual cache hit.

So the NVFP4 GEMM kernels are not involved (three different kernels, including weight-only, all fail), the GDN prefill kernel is not involved, and the KV pool size is not involved. What it needs is: a hidden-state drafter (DFlash2 or DSpark; MTP is fine) + a prefix-cache hit + this compressed-tensors NVFP4 target, on 0.30 or later. The FP8 checkpoint with the identical drafter config is fine. Turning off the EAGLE trailing-block drop makes it strictly worse, which reads to me like the drafter is leaving bad Mamba/GDN state in the cached tail block and the drop normally hides it inside a request but not across requests.

The compressed-tensors checkpoint is the obvious difference from the FP8 one: it has an `ignore` list covering `linear_attn` sub-modules (the bf16 `in_proj_a` / `in_proj_b` / `norm`) alongside `config_groups` that target `linear_attn.{in_proj_qkv,in_proj_z,out_proj}` at FP8. If the drafter path resolves those layers differently from the plain `fp8` loader, that would be where I'd look first, but I haven't gone further than the table above.

Related: #53912 and #55766 describe neighbouring hybrid-GDN prefix-cache corruption with speculative decoding.

### What I can provide

Per-request replay output (prompt token counts, finish reasons, draft metrics), engine logs for every ablation above, and a synthetic reproducer on request.
