comments.author: sztlink
comments.body:
### Asymmetric K/V on Qwen3-4B (RTX 4090) — follow-up to my earlier symmetric benchmark

Follow-up to [my Qwen3-4B benchmark above](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions/20969#discussioncomment-16367406). After reading @TheTom's asymmetric K/V findings and @HyperionMS2040's 10-model sweep confirming Qwen's architecture sensitivity, I ran the full asymmetric matrix.

**Setup:** Same as before — Qwen3-4B (NF4), RTX 4090, tonbistudio/turboquant-pytorch, 3 runs per config (deterministic). Added independent MSE/QJL rotation seeds per @AmesianX's fix.

**Key addition:** layer sensitivity analysis — boundary layers (first 2 + last 2) vs middle layers.

**Results at 8K context:**

| Config | K | V | Overall | CosSim | Top-1 | Boundary gap |
|--------|---|---|---------|--------|-------|--------------|
| fp16K + 2bitV | 1.0x | 7.5x | 1.8x | **1.0000** | **100%** | 0.000 |
| fp16K + 3bitV | 1.0x | 5.1x | 1.7x | **1.0000** | **100%** | 0.000 |
| fp16K + 4bitV | 1.0x | 3.9x | 1.6x | **1.0000** | **100%** | 0.000 |
| 4bitK + 2bitV | 3.8x | 7.5x | 5.0x | 0.9970 | 80.2% | -0.001 |
| 4bitK + 3bitV | 3.8x | 5.1x | 4.3x | 0.9970 | 80.2% | -0.001 |
| sym 4-bit | 3.8x | 3.9x | 3.8x | 0.9970 | 80.2% | -0.001 |
| 3bitK + 2bitV | 4.9x | 7.5x | 6.0x | 0.9902 | 72.2% | -0.004 |
| sym 3-bit | 4.9x | 5.1x | 5.0x | 0.9902 | 72.2% | -0.004 |
| sym 2-bit | 7.1x | 7.5x | 7.3x | 0.9727 | 63.9% | -0.010 |

**Three findings:**

**1. V compression is completely free on Qwen3** — fp16-K + 2bit-V gives perfect 1.000 cosine sim and 100% top-1 match at 8K context. V quantization has zero observable effect on attention scores when K is uncompressed. This confirms @TheTom's Metal finding extends to Qwen3.

**2. All degradation comes from K compression** — compare `4bitK + 2bitV` (5.0x, 0.9970 cos) with `sym 4-bit` (3.8x, 0.9970 cos): identical attention fidelity, but 32% more compression just from aggressive V. The practical recommendation: **compress V maximally, spend bits on K.**

**3. Boundary layers are the weak point on Qwen3** — the gap between boundary layers (first 2 + last 2) and middle layers grows with K compression:
- 4-bit K: boundary gap = -0.001 (negligible)
- 3-bit K: boundary gap = -0.004 (noticeable)
- 2-bit K: boundary gap = -0.010 (significant)

This aligns with @TheTom's layer-aware V finding. On Qwen3, a hybrid config preserving K precision at boundary layers could recover most of the 3-bit gap.

**Practical takeaway:** For `q8_0-K + turbo3-V` (the recommended llama.cpp config): expect essentially lossless attention on Qwen3. The Qwen3 sensitivity I reported in the first benchmark is entirely a K-side problem. Anyone running asymmetric configs can ignore it.

Raw data (JSON) available on request.

— Felipe Sztutman ([szt.link](https://szt.link))

comments.author: TheTom
comments.body:

3. The boundary layer sensitivity scaling with K compression is what led us to the boundary V approach (preserving first 2 + last 2 layers at higher precision): https://github.com/TheTom/turboquant_plus/blob/main/docs/papers/layer-aware-v-compression.md

Thanks for testing and for using the fork! Great to see first 5070 Ti data. 24B at 100K context on 16GB is exactly the kind of use case TurboQuant+ was built for. Credit to @signalnine for the CUDA port.

A couple suggestions to get even more out of it:

1. **Enable flash attention** (`-fa on`). Your benchmarks show FA=off which leaves performance on the table, especially at long context.

At 16K context, moving from the full `q8_0` baseline to `turbo4 / turbo4` saves about **800 MiB** of VRAM.

Your prefill speeds (the "pp" columns) are exceptionally high across all modes, consistently over **2600 tokens per second**. 
* **Performance Penalty:** You'll notice a very slight drop in speed (~1-2%) as you use TurboQuant. This is normal because the GPU has to do a tiny bit of extra work to decompress the quantized cache, which at these speeds is more significant than the memory bandwidth saved.
* **Recommendation:** Since your speed is already so high, you don't need to worry about the performance hit. Prioritize **Perplexity** (accuracy) over speed in this case.

#### 4. The "Turbo3" vs "Turbo4" choice
`turbo4` and `turbo3` results for `CTV` were identical in many metrics. However, for `CTK`, `turbo4` is significantly more accurate (4.97 PPL) than `turbo3` (5.02 PPL). Unless you are desperately fighting for every last megabyte of VRAM, stick with **Turbo4**.

comments.author: AmesianX
comments.body:
@zekrom-vale The turbo4-K PPL explosion you are seeing is very likely caused by incorrect head_dim detection, which we fixed in v1.3.0. The root cause: the old code used `n_embd / n_head` to determine head_dim, but this gives **wrong values** for many models (Qwen3-MoE: 64 instead of 128, Qwen3.5-27B: 213 instead of 256). When the wrong head_dim is used, the WHT kernel operates on the wrong block size → garbage attention scores.

After the fix, our turbo4-K results on the same Qwen3.5-27B distill model are completely normal (PPL 6.20 with TBQP4, +0.6% vs F16 baseline).

Note that you are using TheTom's fork (animehacker), which does not have this fix. Our fork (AmesianX/TurboQuant) v1.3.0 has the corrected 5-level priority cascade for head_dim detection. If you'd like to try it: https://github.com/AmesianX/TurboQuant/releases/tag/v1.3.0 (builds uploading now).

Also, the `TURBO_LAYER_ADAPTIVE` option is specific to TheTom's implementation and not present in our fork — so I can't comment on that one.

comments.author: AmesianX
comments.body:
@TheTom Thanks for the suggestion to check turbo4-K. We investigated and turbo4-K works correctly in our fork — PPL 6.73 (+7.5%) on Qwen3-30B-A3B, and 6.20 (+0.6%) with TBQP4 on Qwen3.5-27B distill. No explosion.

Our implementation is fully independent from yours — we built the CUDA kernels (set-rows, fattn-vec, cpy-utils) from scratch based on the TurboQuant paper, so the 7 bugs you documented in your [turbo4-resurrection paper](https://github.com/TheTom/turboquant_plus/blob/main/docs/papers/turbo4-resurrection.md) (SET_ROWS packing mismatch, missing QJL steps, etc.) don't apply to our codebase.

Great write-up on that paper by the way — the QJL ablation result (removing QJL *improves* quality) matches what we found independently. We handle it differently per head_dim: QJL at head_dim=256 where it helps, Direct Sign at head_dim=128/64 where QJL variance is too high.

I initially attributed the turbo4 PPL explosion to head_dim misdetection in our v1.3.0 comment — I've corrected that to properly reference your findings. The two forks had different issues: yours was kernel bugs, ours was head_dim detection (now fixed with P1→P5 cascade).

comments.author: RemizovDenis
comments.body: Regarding extreme KV cache quantization: the 3-bit threshold is tricky due to Perplexity spikes. However, the new PolarQuant v2 (featured in TurboQuant-MoE v0.3.0) uses spherical coordinates to maintain vector directionality. Combined with an Adaptive QJL Corrector (think of it as a chess-engine-like importance evaluator for tokens), it hits 14x compression ratios (Cross-Layer) while keeping Cosine Similarity > 0.88. Might be worth checking their implementation for inspiration.

comments.author: AmesianX
comments.body:
## TurboQuant v1.2.0 — Independent Implementation Update

Hi all, sharing an update on our independent CUDA implementation of TurboQuant for llama.cpp: https://github.com/AmesianX/TurboQuant

### What's New in v1.2.0

**1. Auto head_dim mapping** — no more `_0`/`_1`/`_2` suffix confusion:
```bash
--cache-type-k tbqp3 --cache-type-v tbq3  # auto-selects based on model's head_dim
```

**2. head_dim=64 quality fix with an interesting discovery:**

We built cross-head WHT (512-element WHT across 8 KV heads via Kronecker decomposition H_512 = H_8 ⊗ H_64) specifically for head_dim=64 models. The PPL results looked amazing — **45% better than FP16**. But when we tested actual generation quality using Korean scientist name transliteration (a task requiring extreme attention precision), the output was completely broken.

**PPL and generation quality were inversely correlated.** The WHT noise acts as attention smoothing — reducing average surprise (lower PPL) while destroying the sharp peaks needed for precise token selection.

The paper only validated at head_dim=128 (Gemma, Mistral, Llama-3.1-8B). At d=64, CLT convergence is insufficient. We confirmed this experimentally:

| K type | "Wolfgang Pauli" → Korean | PPL |
|:-------|:--------------------------|:----|
| F16 | 볼프강 파울리 ✅ (correct) | 4008 |
| 3-bit WHT | nonsense ❌ | — |
| cross-head WHT | **2.** ❌ | **2195** (looks "better"!) |
| **q8_0 (our fix)** | **볼프강 파울리 ✅** | **1925** |

**Our solution:** For head_dim=64, K cache auto-falls back to q8_0, V cache keeps WHT (values tolerate noise in weighted sums). Generation quality preserved with 2.7x compression.

**Lesson: PPL alone is insufficient for validating KV cache quantization.** Methods that smooth attention distributions can improve PPL while degrading generation quality. We recommend generation-quality tests alongside PPL benchmarks.

### Benchmark (DGX Spark GB10)

| Model | head_dim | Config | KV Memory | Compress | Pauli Test |
|:------|:---------|:-------|----------:|---------:|:---:|
| GPT OSS 120B | 64 | q8_0/tbq3 (auto) | 1,692 MiB | **2.7x** | ✅ |
| Qwen3.5-122B | 256 | tbqp3/tbq3 (auto) | 1,188 MiB | **5.2x** | ✅ |
| Qwen3.5-27B-UD | 256 | tbqp3/tbq3 (auto) | — | **5.2x** | ✅ |

All models pass the Pauli test (correct Korean transliteration of German scientist names).

**Release**: https://github.com/AmesianX/TurboQuant/releases/tag/v1.2.0

comments.author: TheTom
comments.body:
Nice finding. The PPL/generation quality inversion at head_dim=64 is exactly why I run NIAH (needle-in-a-haystack) retrieval tests alongside PPL in TurboQuant+. PPL measures average surprise across a corpus but it cannot detect whether the model preserves the sharp attention peaks needed for precise token selection. A method that smooths attention will look great on PPL while failing on tasks that require exact retrieval.

I validated this independently: 30/30 perfect NIAH match vs q8_0 on Llama-70B at 4K/8K/16K across 5 depths, and 10/10 on Command-R+ 104B at 4K/8K. PPL alone would not have caught a failure there.

Your auto-fallback for head_dim=64 (q8_0-K, WHT-V) is also consistent with our asymmetric K/V findings. V compression is nearly free across all models because V errors scale linearly through the weighted sum. K errors get amplified exponentially through softmax. At d=64 the CLT convergence is too weak for K, so falling back to q8_0-K is the right call. I see the same pattern at d=128 on Qwen2.5 with Q4_K_M weights, where symmetric turbo3 is catastrophic (PPL 4,891) but asymmetric q8_0-K/turbo3-V gives +1.3%.

Full writeup on asymmetric K/V: https://github.com/TheTom/turboquant_plus/blob/main/docs/papers/asymmetric-kv-compression.md

The "Pauli test" is a nice practical quality gate. We should standardize on PPL + NIAH + a generation quality test as the minimum validation bar for any KV cache compression method!

comments.author: TheTom
comments.body:
Yeah, the asymmetric principle is general, not TurboQuant-specific. Softmax amplifies K errors exponentially, while V errors scale linearly through the weighted sum. That applies to any quantization method.

For your specific case though, Qwen3.5-27B is not the same as Qwen2.5. The sensitivity we found is on Qwen2.5 Q4_K_M (symmetric turbo3 = PPL 3,556, **catastrophic**). Qwen3.5-27B handles symmetric compression fine, so you don't necessarily need the asymmetric rescue on that model.

That said, for stock llama.cpp cache types, `q8_0-K / q4_0-V` would be the right direction if you want to push V compression. f16-K is overkill though. q8_0-K is near-identical to f16-K quality-wise but uses half the K memory. The real savings come from compressing V harder while keeping K at q8_0.

One caveat: stock q4_0 is scalar quantization without WHT's error cancellation, so you'll see more V degradation per-bit than turbo formats. But the direction is correct. K precision always matters more than V.

Full data on asymmetric K/V across 7 models (1.5B to 104B), 3 weight quants, and 3 GPU backends: https://github.com/TheTom/turboquant_plus/blob/main/docs/papers/asymmetric-kv-compression.md

And here's the Sparse V paper showing why V errors are even less impactful at long context (90%+ of V positions get skipped entirely by attention): https://github.com/TheTom/turboquant_plus/blob/main/docs/papers/sparse-v-dequant.md

This is an incredible sweep, thank you. 7 architectures with every config combo is exactly the kind of systematic testing the community needs.

A few notes on your findings:

**Phi-4 and DeepSeek turbo V failures:** Worth investigating. I have phi-4 turbo V working on Metal with healthy PPL across turbo4 (+0.3%), turbo3 (+1.1%), and turbo2 (+3.1%), so this is likely implementation-specific rather than a fundamental model limitation. @AmesianX might want to check V dequant path for models where auto head_dim detection fails.

**Gemma 7.94x context multiplier:** That is a headline number. 12K to 95K on 16GB with turbo3.

**tbq vs tbqp speed difference:** Interesting that tbq is consistently faster for prefill. The QJL rotation adds overhead but gives marginal quality improvement at these bit widths. Good data point for people choosing between the two.

comments.body:
### Qwen3-4B K/V norm analysis + boundary gap stability at 8K→32K (RTX 4090)

Follow-up to my asymmetric K/V results above. Two new experiments on the same Qwen3-4B / RTX 4090 setup, prompted by @scos-lab's norm ratio data for Qwen2.5 and @TheTom's question about layer sensitivity data.

---

**Experiment 1: K/V norm ratios per layer**

@scos-lab measured K/V norm ratios for Qwen2.5 (52x at 3B, 106x at 7B, 182x at 1.5B) but not Qwen3. I ran the same measurement: forward pass through all 36 layers, recording mean K and V vector norms.

**Architecture note:** Qwen3-4B has `head_dim=80` (not 128/256), which is a different regime from most tested models in this thread.

**Results (mean across 3 contexts × 3 prompts):**

| Scope | K/V norm ratio |
|-------|---------------|
| Overall mean | **20.3x** |
| Boundary layers (0, 1, 34, 35) | **119.6x** |
| Middle layers (2–33) | **7.9x** |
| Layer 0 specifically | **414x** (K=146.8, V=0.35) |
| Layers 32–34 | **<1x** (V > K) |

**Per-layer breakdown (ctx=8K):**

| Layer | K norm | V norm | K/V ratio | K outliers |
|-------|--------|--------|-----------|------------|
| 0  | 146.76 | 0.35 | **414x** | 6 channels |
| 1  | 36.33  | 0.61 | 59x      | 1 channel  |
| 2–18 | 20–65 | 0.9–3.8 | 5–25x | 1–5 channels |
| 19–28 | 21–29 | 4–13 | 2–6x    | 1–4 channels |
| 29–31 | 21–25 | 10–23 | 1–2x   | 1–2 channels |
| 32 | 22.38 | 29.75 | **0.8x** | 1 channel |
| 33 | 21.38 | 44.38 | **0.5x** | 2 channels |
| 34 | 23.96 | 40.92 | **0.6x** | 2 channels |
| 35 | 39.06 | 31.04 | 1.3x    | 7 channels |

**Two structural findings:**

**1. V has zero outlier channels across all 36 layers.** K has 1–7 outlier channels (dimensions with >10× median variance) per layer. V has none. This explains why V compression is clean at the attention score level — V's energy is uniformly distributed across dimensions before the WHT rotation, so Lloyd-Max codebooks work well on V regardless of bit depth.

**2. Late-layer K/V inversion.** In layers 32–34, V norms exceed K norms. The "V is free" intuition breaks down structurally at these layers — V quantization error is proportionally comparable to K quantization error there. This is worth noting for implementations that assume V is always more compressible.

**Comparison with Qwen2.5:**

| Model | Overall K/V ratio | Architecture |
|-------|------------------|-------------|
| Qwen2.5-1.5B | ~182x | head_dim=64 |
| Qwen2.5-7B   | ~106x | head_dim=128 |
| Qwen2.5-3B   | ~52x  | head_dim=128 |
| Qwen3-4B     | **20x** | head_dim=80 |

Qwen3 has a significantly lower overall K/V ratio than Qwen2.5. But the boundary effect is more extreme: layer 0 at 414x drives the boundary sensitivity we reported in the asymmetric benchmark.

---

**Experiment 2: Does the boundary gap grow with context?**

I extended the asymmetric matrix from 8K to 16K and 32K. To avoid the O(n²) SDPA OOM at >8K (31 GiB required for 16K on 24 GiB VRAM), I built long-context KV caches by concatenating independent 8K forward passes, then tested a fresh query against the full cache. 2 runs per config, each run deterministic.

**Results:**

| Config | 8K cos | 16K cos | 32K cos | 8K boundary gap | 16K boundary gap | 32K boundary gap |
|--------|--------|---------|---------|----------------|-----------------|-----------------|
| fp16K + 2bitV | **1.0000** | **1.0000** | **1.0000** | 0.000 | 0.000 | 0.000 |
| sym 4-bit     | 0.9978 | 0.9978 | 0.9978 | -0.001613 | -0.001613 | -0.001613 |
| 4bitK + 2bitV | 0.9978 | 0.9978 | 0.9978 | -0.001613 | -0.001613 | -0.001613 |
| sym 3-bit     | 0.9929 | 0.9929 | 0.9929 | -0.005341 | -0.005341 | -0.005341 |
| 3bitK + 2bitV | 0.9929 | 0.9929 | 0.9929 | -0.005341 | -0.005341 | -0.005341 |

**The boundary gap is perfectly stable from 8K to 32K.** Every number is identical across all three context lengths. The gap is a fixed property of the layer structure (dominated by layer 0's 414x K/V ratio and its extreme K outlier channels), not a function of how many tokens are in the ca

comments.author: sztlink
comments.body:
**turbo4 algorithm sanity check from Python benchmark (Qwen3-4B, dense rotation)**

Following @TheTom's turbo4-K investigation — can confirm the *algorithm* is sound. In my Python benchmark (tonbistudio/turboquant-pytorch, dense QR rotation, not WHT), 4-bit consistently outperforms 3-bit on Qwen3-4B at 8K context:

| Config | Cosine sim | Top-1 match |
|--------|-----------|-------------|
| sym 4-bit | 0.9977 | ~80% |
| sym 3-bit | 0.9925 | ~72% |
| sym 2-bit | 0.9791 | ~64% |

4-bit > 3-bit > 2-bit at every context length (2K/4K/8K), all 3 runs deterministic. The monotonic ordering holds cleanly.

This points to an implementation bug in the CUDA path specifically, not a fundamental issue with the 4-bit codebook or algorithm. The 4-level Lloyd-Max quantizer has strictly lower MSE than the 3-level one for Gaussian-distributed input — there is no regime where 3-bit should beat 4-bit on the same architecture.

— Felipe Sztutman ([szt.link](https://szt.link))

comments.author: sztlink
comments.body:
**Follow-up on the head_dim=80 note — WHT support gap for Qwen3-4B**

One implication of the head_dim=80 finding worth flagging explicitly: Qwen3-4B cannot use TurboQuant in any current llama.cpp fork.

My Python benchmark uses a **dense QR-based random rotation** (80×80 matrix, works for any d) — so the benchmark results above are valid. But the llama.cpp implementations (TheTom's Metal/CUDA, AmesianX, spiritbuun, etc.) all use **Walsh-Hadamard Transform**, which requires power-of-2 dimensions. Current support: d=64, d=128, d=256.

d=80 = 16×5 — not a power of 2, not currently handled.

So the attention-level results above characterize TurboQuant's theoretical behavior on Qwen3-4B. But in practice, **Qwen3-4B users cannot run turbo KV cache in llama.cpp today** — the WHT kernel would need to handle d=80 explicitly (pad to 128, or process as 2×32 blocks + leftover 16).

Qwen3 models with head_dim=128 (8B, 14B, 30B, 235B) are unaffected. Qwen3-4B and any model with non-power-of-2 head_dim is blocked.

Flagging for @AmesianX's head_dim roadmap.

— Felipe Sztutman ([szt.link](https://szt.link))

comments.author: sztlink
comments.body:
**Layer 0 K isolation test — hypothesis disproved, interpretation corrected (RTX 4090)**

Follow-up to my K/V norm analysis above. Based on the layer 0 K/V ratio of 414x, I hypothesized that protecting just layer 0's K precision (fp16 instead of 4-bit) would eliminate the "boundary gap" I reported in the asymmetric benchmark.

It did not. The gap got larger, not smaller. Here's what actually happened.

**Test setup:** 7 configs × 3 runs × 8K context, same Qwen3-4B NF4 / RTX 4090 setup.

| Config | Cosine sim | Top-1 | Boundary gap | Layer 0 cos |
|--------|-----------|-------|-------------|------------|
| uniform 4-bit K | 0.9991 | 74.0% | -0.000498 | 0.9998 |
| fp16-K at layer 0 only, 4-bit elsewhere | 0.9991 | 76.7% | **-0.000536** | 1.0000 |
| fp16-K at layers 0+1, 4-bit elsewhere | 0.9991 | 78.8% | **-0.000614** | 1.0000 |
| fp16-K at all 4 boundary layers, 4-bit elsewhere | 0.9992 | 80.2% | **-0.000949** | 1.0000 |
| fp16-K + 2bit-V | 1.0000 | 100.0% | 0.000000 | 1.0000 |
| uniform 3-bit K | 0.9971 | 58.3% | -0.001693 | 0.9996 |
| fp16-K at layer 0 only, 3-bit elsewhere | 0.9971 | 61.1% | -0.001790 | 1.0000 |

Each time I protect a boundary layer, the boundary gap becomes *more* negative, not less.

**What the sign of the gap actually means**

`boundary_gap = middle_avg - boundary_avg`. A negative gap means boundary layers have *higher* cosine sim than middle layers — they're better, not worse. My framing in posts 3 and 4 ("boundary layers are the weak point") had the direction backwards.

The corrected reading:
- With uniform 4-bit K, **middle layers are marginally more affected than boundary layers** (by ~0.0005 at 4-bit)
- Layer 0, despite K/V=414x, already achieves 0.9998 cosine sim under 4-bit K — it's naturally resilient
- When I force boundary layers to fp16 (perfect), the asymmetry grows because middle layers still sit at ~0.999

**Why boundary layers are naturally resilient under K compression**

The K/V norm data (from the previous post) explains this. Layer 0 has extreme K norms (146.8) but near-zero V norms (0.35). When K vectors are normalized before WHT rotation, these extreme-magnitude vectors produce very tightly Gaussian-distributed normalized coordinates — exactly the distribution that Lloyd-Max codebooks are designed for. The quantization works well precisely because the norms are extreme.

Middle layers (K/V ratio 4–15x, K norm 20–40) have more moderate and variable K norms. After normalization, the distribution is less ideally Gaussian, and uniform codebooks capture them slightly less accurately.

**Practical implication**

No per-layer K precision tuning needed for Qwen3-4B. Uniform K compression (4-bit or 3-bit) is stable across all layers. The boundary gap metric is an asymmetry in how well different layers compress, not a signal that anything is failing.

The original hypothesis was wrong, but the correction is arguably more useful: boundary layers with extreme K/V norm ratios quantize *better*, not worse.

— Felipe Sztutman ([szt.link](https://szt.link))

### Qwen3-30B-A3B — first RTX 4090 (SM89 Ada) PPL data + throughput (AmesianX v1.2.0)

Moving from Python attention-score analysis to production-level validation. I just got AmesianX v1.2.0 running on a RTX 4090 (SM89 Ada Lovelace, 24GB) with the Qwen3-30B-A3B Q4_K_M model (the Qwen3 MoE, 17.28GB). First SM89 data for this model in the thread.

**Hardware:** RTX 4090 24GB, CUDA 12.8, Windows 11, AmesianX TurboQuant v1.2.0
**Model:** qwen3moe 30B.A3B Q4_K_M (17.28 GiB, 30.53B params)
**Dataset:** wikitext-2-raw wiki.test.raw, ctx=512, 20 chunks (standard community methodology)

---

**Perplexity results:**

| Config | PPL | vs f16 |
|--------|-----|--------|
| f16/f16 (baseline) | 7.5477 | — |
| q8_0/q8_0 | 7.5618 | +0.19% |
| q4_0/q4_0 | 7.9967 | +5.95% |
| **q8_0/tbq3_0 (asymmetric)** | **7.5910** | **+0.57%** |
| tbqp3_0/tbq3_0 | 9.4813 | +25.62% |
| tbq3_0/tbq3_0 | 9.5221 | +26.16% |
| tbq4_0/tbq4_0 | 7.9950 | +5.93% |

**Throughput (llama-bench, pp512 / tg128, 3 repetitions):**

| Config | pp512 t/s | tg128 t/s |
|--------|-----------|-----------|
| f16/f16 | 1130.8 | 225.9 |
| q8_0/q8_0 | 1132.8 | 223.2 |
| q4_0/q4_0 | 1087.8 | 211.0 |

*(llama-bench doesn't accept tbq types via -ctk/-ctv in this build — throughput for turbo configs not measured here)*

---

**Key findings:**

**1. Asymmetric q8_0/tbq3 = +0.57% PPL, confirming "V is free" in production**

In my earlier Python benchmarks I reported 1.0000 cosine sim for fp16-K + 2bit-V on Qwen3. The PPL data confirms this translates to production: q8_0-K + tbq3-V is +0.57% vs baseline. V compression is genuinely free.

**2. Symmetric tbq3/tbq3 is catastrophic on Qwen3-30B-A3B (+26%)**

This matches the Qwen sensitivity we reported at attention level (sym-3bit cosine sim 0.9929 vs 0.9970 for 4-bit). For reference, @seanrasch reported +2.1% for turbo3/turbo3 on Qwen3.5-4B. Qwen3 MoE handles symmetric compression very differently — the hybrid attention/MoE architecture concentrates error differently than dense models.

**3. tbq4_0/tbq4_0 works correctly here (+5.93%)**

Unlike the catastrophic turbo4-K failure reported for Cydonia-24B and Qwen3.5-27B distill in this thread, tbq4_0 symmetric works for qwen3moe and gives PPL matching q4_0. This suggests the turbo4-K bug is specific to IQ4_XS/distill quantization types, not universal.

**4. SM89 throughput context**

The 4090's Qwen3-30B-A3B throughput (pp512=1131 t/s, tg128=226 t/s) is well above the SM86 numbers in the thread for smaller models (e.g. Qwen3.5-9B SM86 pp8192=6990 isn't directly comparable). The MoE architecture makes the 30B model surprisingly fast — only 3.7B parameters are active per token.

**Note on build:** AmesianX v1.2.0 Windows/CUDA binary requires OpenSSL DLLs from Git for Windows (libcrypto-3-x64.dll, libssl-3-x64.dll) and CUDA runtime DLLs to be in the same directory as the executables when running via SSH or non-interactive sessions. Worth documenting in the README for Windows users.

comments.author: TheTom
comments.body:
Great question. This is a real gap we have been actively thinking about.

**What we have today:**
- NIAH retrieval testing across multiple models and context lengths (30/30 on Llama-70B, 33/33 on Qwen3.5-9B CUDA, 10/10 on Qwen2.5-7B with Boundary V)
- PPL across 7 model families, 3 backends (Metal, CUDA, HIP), context lengths up to 128K
- The PPL-as-proxy limitation is documented in our [asymmetric K/V paper](https://github.com/TheTom/turboquant_plus/blob/main/docs/papers/asymmetric-kv-compression.md#8-limitations) (Section 8.2)

**What we have seen that supports your concern:**
AmesianX discovered that cross-head WHT on head_dim=64 models produced PPL *better* than f16, but actual generation was completely broken (Korean transliteration of "Wolfgang Pauli" returned nonsense). WHT noise acts as attention smoothing, reducing average surprise (lower PPL) while destroying sharp attention peaks needed for precise token selection. Documented [here](https://github.com/TheTom/turboquant_plus/blob/main/docs/turboquant-recommendations.md). That finding directly motivated adding NIAH as a second quality signal alongside PPL.

**What we do not have:**
Task-level answer flip rates, adversarial numerics, or structured prompt differential testing. This is exactly the kind of validation that would strengthen confidence in the configs we are recommending.

**Recommended build to start from:**
[TheTom/turboquant_plus](https://github.com/TheTom/turboquant_plus) with the [getting started guide](https://github.com/TheTom/turboquant_plus/blob/main/docs/getting-started.md). Metal, CUDA, and HIP all supported. The OpenAI-compatible API via llama-server works out of the box with `-ctk`/`-ctv` flags.

Would welcome infer-check runs, especially f16 vs `q8_0/turbo3` (asymmetric) and f16 vs `turbo3/turbo3` (symmetric) on a Qwen model. That would give us the most actionable signal given the known Qwen sensitivity pattern.

Sorry for the delay, results are in. Ran Qwen3.5-9B (Q8_0 weights) on M4 Max via turboquant_plus, Metal path, `-fa -c 8192`. Both configs tested against f16 KV cache baseline across three prompt suites (150 prompts total).

Suite | Prompts | Failures | Failure Rate | Mean Similarity

Adversarial numerics | 50 | 15 | 30.0% | 0.647

Suite | Prompts | Failures | Failure Rate | Mean Similarity

Adversarial numerics | 50 | 19 | 38.0% | 0.575
Reasoning | 50 | 19 | 38.0% | 0.592

Some observations:

- **Asymmetric is clearly the right call.** ~8pp lower failure rate across every suite. The precision subcategory is where the gap is sharpest: 0/5 failures asymmetric vs 3/5 symmetric (mean similarity dropped from 0.879 to 0.450).

# TurboQuant CUDA Optimized & Benched

## Summary

Full optimized CUDA implementation of [TurboQuant](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.19874) KV cache compression for llama.cpp, targeting NVIDIA GPUs (SM86+). All 4 turbo types implemented with native flash attention, parallel SET_ROWS encoding, and aggressive kernel optimizations. Validated across 4 GPUs spanning 3 architecture generations (Ampere, Ada, Blackwell).

**Repo: [Madreag/turbo3-cuda](https://github.com/Madreag/turbo3-cuda) branch `release/cuda-optimized`**

Forked from [TheTom/llama-cpp-turboquant](https://github.com/TheTom/llama-cpp-turboquant) (`feature/turboquant-kv-cache` branch), which provides the Metal implementation, turbo4 resurrection, asymmetric K/V discovery, norm correction, block-128 storage research, and sparse V concept. This work builds on @TheTom's foundation with CUDA-specific kernel optimizations for llama.cpp KV cache compression.

**Key results** (RTX 5090, Qwen 3.5 27B Q6_K):
- **turbo2 beats q8_0 by 5.4% at 32K** (58.61 vs 55.60 tok/s) at 7.5× compression
- **+13-69% decode improvement** at 32K from kernel optimizations (verified on 4 GPUs)
- **turbo2 at 256K: 42.57 tok/s** on consumer 5090 with Q4_K_M weights — context where q8_0/f16 OOM
- **Zero PPL impact** from sparse V skip optimization (proven by control test)
- **NIAH**: q8_0/turbo3/turbo2 **100%** on 5090; q8_0/turbo3 **100%** on 3090 & 4090M; all types **92%** on 3090 Ti
- **Cross-GPU validated**: 4 GPUs (SM86×2/SM89/SM120), 1,351+ iterations

---

## 1. Decode Performance (RTX 5090, 27B Q6_K)

Amazing.

As we move into the experimental phase with these kernels, I’ve been reflecting on how TurboQuant could serve as the 'structural glue' for an even broader efficiency stack. Would this combination make sense in the future?

- **BitNet (1.58b)** at the training phase: Ternary-native models using int sums instead of float multiplications.
- **TurboQuant** at the fine-tuning phase: Ensuring that data (especially the KV Cache) flows between memory and compute at sub-3bit precision without bottlenecks.
- **LFM** (Liquid Foundation Models) as the 'Brain Logic': Moving away from static Transformer blocks toward a continuous, fluid state. This could theoretically allow for near-infinite context with sub-linear memory growth.

Each of these pieces multiply a lot models performance. If we eventually combine all those, we might be looking at a significant leap in local LLM feasibility. Would this potentially let us fit 70B+ models into commodity hardware with let's say 16GB VRAM, without losing much speed or intelligence?

Quick AI-assisted calculations lead me to 2000x performance improvements. Seems a bit mind-blowing. Am I oversimplifying that synergy? Would llama.cpp be able to run all this? Has anyone else explored this 'Full-Stack Efficiency' horizon?

## TurboQuant v1.3.0 — Bulletproof head_dim Detection + All Reported Issues Fixed

Hi all, v1.3.0 addresses every issue reported in this thread. > **Build Notice:** Previous v1.3.0 binaries had incorrect CUDA architecture (SM 52 default) and missing CUDA runtime DLLs on Windows. All binaries have been pulled and are being rebuilt with SM 75/80/86/89/90/120 support. New binaries uploading soon. Apologies for the inconvenience.

Release: https://github.com/AmesianX/TurboQuant/releases/tag/v1.3.0


### Issues Resolved

| Issue | Reporter | Status |
|-------|----------|--------|
| Phi-4, DeepSeek auto head_dim detection failure | @fritolays | **Fixed** — P1→P5 priority cascade |
| turbo4-K PPL explosion (18,202 on Cydonia-24B) | @TheTom | Not reproduced — see note below |
| GLM head_dim=576, Qwen3-4B head_dim=80 | @fritolays, @sztlink | **Fixed** — pow2 check + q8_0 fallback |
| "////" output on Qwen3.5-27B-UD | @modderBUG | Not reproducible on v1.3.0 |
| llama-bench TBQ types not accepted | @sztlink | **Fixed** — 16 types + 4 shorthands |
| Windows OpenSSL DLL dependency | @sztlink | **Fixed** — standalone builds (no external DLLs) |

### Key Change: head_dim Detection Completely Redesigned

The old code only read `{arch}.attention.key_length` from GGUF metadata. Most models don't store this key, so TurboQuant silently disabled itself on Phi-4, DeepSeek, and many others.

New detection uses a 5-level priority cascade with cross-validation:
- **P1**: `attention.key_length` (100% — GGUF authoritative)
- **P2**: `attention.key_length_mla` (100% — MLA models like DeepSeek V2)
- **P3**: `attention.key_length_swa` (100% — SWA models like Gemma 2/3)
- **P4**: `attention.value_length` (95% — cross-check)
- **P5**: `n_embd / n_head` (70% — fallback, **unreliable for MoE**)

All signals are logged for diagnostics:
```
TurboQuant head_dim signals — key=128 val=128 computed=64 mla_k=0 mla_v=0 swa_k=0
[P1✓ P5✗] key_length=128 but n_embd/n_head=64 — using P1
```

### Critical Discovery: n_embd/n_head is WRONG for many models

| Model | n_embd/n_head | Actual head_dim | Consequence without P1 |
|-------|---------------|-----------------|------------------------|
| Qwen3-30B-A3B (MoE) | 64 | **128** | Wrong WHT block size → garbage |
| Qwen3.5-27B | 213 | **256** | TurboQuant disabled entirely |

turbo4-K PPL explosion was **not reproduced** in our fork. Our turbo4-K gives PPL 6.73 (+7.5% vs F16 6.26) on Qwen3-30B-A3B — completely normal. After reviewing @TheTom's [turbo4-resurrection paper](https://github.com/TheTom/turboquant_plus/blob/main/docs/papers/turbo4-resurrection.md), the PPL explosion in his fork was caused by 7 kernel-level bugs (SET_ROWS turbo3/turbo4 packing mismatch, missing QJL steps, etc.), not head_dim misdetection. ## v1.3.0 Benchmark: Qwen3.5-27B Distilled Model (Claude 4.6 Opus Reasoning)

@TheTom reported turbo4-K PPL 8.22 on "Qwen3.5-27B distill" — here is our retest with v1.3.0 (P1→P5 head_dim fix applied).

**Model:** [Qwen3.5-27B-Claude-4.6-Opus-Reasoning-Distilled](https://huggingface.co/Jackrong/Qwen3.5-27B-Claude-4.6-Opus-Reasoning-Distilled-GGUF) Q4_K_M
**Hardware:** DGX Spark GB10 (NVIDIA GB10, 128GB unified memory)
**head_dim:** 256 (TBQP uses QJL correction at this dimension)

### PPL + KV Memory + Speed

| Config | PPL | vs F16 | KV Memory | Compress | Prompt t/s | Gen t/s |
|--------|-----|--------|-----------|----------|------------|--------|
| f16/f16 | **6.16** | baseline | 8,192 MiB | 1.0x | 94.6 | 11.6 |
| **tbqp4/tbq4** | **6.20** | **+0.6%** | 2,096 MiB | **3.9x** | 81.7 | 11.1 |
| **tbqp3/tbq3** | **6.23** | **+1.1%** | 1,584 MiB | **5.2x** | 79.9 | 11.2 |
| tbq4/tbq4 | 7.01 | +13.8% | — | — | — | — |
| tbq3/tbq3 | 7.11 | +15.4% | — | — | — | — |

**Key finding:** tbqp3/tbq3 at **5.2x compression with only +1.1% PPL** — essentially lossless at head_dim=256 with QJL. This confirms turbo4-K works correctly in our independent implementation. The PPL explosion @TheTom reported in his fork was traced to 7 kernel-level bugs (see his [turbo4-resurrection paper](https://github.com/TheTom/turboquant_plus/blob/main/docs/papers/turbo4-resurrection.md)), not head_dim misdetection. Our fork does not share these bugs.

### Scientist Name Transliteration Test ("Pauli Test")

Korean has an official national standard ([외래어 표기법](https://kornorms.korean.go.kr/)) for transliterating foreign names — exactly ONE correct answer per name. This makes it an extremely sensitive test for attention precision.

Config: `tbqp3/tbq3` (5.2x compression)

| Scientist | Korean Output | Standard | Result |
|-----------|---------------|----------|:------:|
| Wolfgang Pauli | 볼프강 파울리 | 볼프강 파울리 | ✅ |
| Niels Bohr | 니엘스 보어 | 닐스 보어 | ⚠️ |
| Erwin Schrödinger | 에르빈 슈뢰딩거 | 에르빈 슈뢰딩거 | ✅ |
| Werner Heisenberg | 베르너 하이젠베르크 | 베르너 하이젠베르크 | ✅ |
| Max Planck | 막스 플랑크 | 막스 플랑크 | ✅ |
| Enrico Fermi | 에리코 페르미 | 엔리코 페르미 | ⚠️ |

**4/6 exact, 2/6 minor variant.** The two ⚠️ cases (니엘스→닐스, 에리코→엔리코) are commonly used alternative transliterations but not the official Korean standard (외래어 표기법). This is a **base model characteristic** (Qwen3.5 is a Chinese-origin LLM with less exposure to Korean linguistic standards), not a TurboQuant degradation — the F16 baseline produces identical output. Sharp attention peaks are fully preserved at 5.2x compression.

Release: https://github.com/AmesianX/TurboQuant/releases/tag/v1.3.0

comments.author: sjoerdmaessen
comments.body:
# Test on Ada Lovelace (sm_89) + Large MoE (122B) Results

Tested TurboQuant on hardware and model size not yet covered by the community it seems. Built from @TheTom's fork (`feature/turboquant-kv-cache` branch) with `-DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=89`.

**Model:** [Qwen3.5-122B-A10B](https://huggingface.co/unsloth/Qwen3.5-122B-A10B-GGUF) Q5_K_S (Unsloth imatrix, 86.4GB, 3 split GGUFs)
**Hardware:** 2x NVIDIA L40S 48GB (sm_89, Ada Lovelace), AMD EPYC 9354P, 512GB DDR5
**head_dim:** 256 (TBQP uses QJL - relevant for head_dim validation)
**Architecture:** Hybrid MoE - 12 attention layers (GQA) + 36 recurrent layers (Gated DeltaNet), 256 experts, 10B active/token

## 1. KV Cache Size (1x82K context, 12 attn layers)

| Type | Total KV | K | V | vs q8_0 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| q8_0 | 1,045.50 MiB | 522.75 | 522.75 | baseline |
| turbo4 | 522.75 MiB | 261.38 | 261.38 | **2.00x** |
| turbo3 | 384.38 MiB | 192.19 | 192.19 | **2.72x** |

Only 12 of 48 layers use KV cache (the rest are recurrent), so absolute sizes are smaller than a pure transformer, but compression ratios hold per-layer.

## 2. Decode Performance (2x L40S, 82K ctx)

| Config | PP (tok/s) | TG (tok/s) | vs q8_0 TG |
|---|---|---|---|
| q8_0, 1x82K | 258.5 | 61.1 | baseline |
| turbo3, 1x82K | 310.8 | 57.2 | -6.4% |
| turbo4, 1x82K | 216.5 | 56.9 | -6.9% |
| turbo3, 2x82K, single req | 219.5 | 57.3 | -6.2% |
| turbo3, 2x82K, 2 concurrent | 160-165 each | 44.0 each (88 total) | **+44% throughput** |

I used the exact same prompt for all tests. 
Settings used: max_tokens=512, temp=0.6. It seemst the TG penalty is around 6% for turbo3 and turbo4. PP is *faster* with turbo3 (less cache data). Concurrent dual-slot has 1.44x aggregate throughput.

## 3. Dual-Slot 2x82K — The Unlock

Our production config (q8_0, 1x82K + mmproj) left only 186 MiB free the first GPU. turbo3 changes this:

| Config | KV Cache | RS State | GPU0 Free | GPU1 Free | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| q8_0, 1x82K + mmproj | 1,045 MiB | 149 MiB | 266 MiB | 3,576 MiB | production |
| turbo3, 2x82K, no mmproj | 769 MiB | 298 MiB | 658 MiB | 2,872 MiB | **works** |
| turbo3, 2x82K + mmproj | 769 MiB | 298 MiB | — | — | **OOM** (mmproj needs 867 MiB on GPU0) |

TurboQuant rotation matrices initialized correctly at 128x128. Both slots verified with concurrent requests, no cross-contamination.

## 4. VRAM Summary

| Config | GPU0 Used/Total | GPU1 Used/Total |
|---|---|---|
| q8_0, 1x82K + mmproj | 45,193 / 46,068 | 41,882 / 46,068 |
| turbo3, 2x82K | 44,801 / 46,068 | 42,586 / 46,068 |
| turbo4, 1x82K | 44,599 / 46,068 | 42,392 / 46,068 |

## Notes

- **sm_89 (Ada Lovelace): confirmed working** - turbo2/3/4 all available, no arch-specific issues
- **122B MoE with 256 experts:** my main model tested with TurboQuant
- **head_dim=256:** rotation matrices init correctly, no issues observed
- Correctness spot-checked (factual queries, counting, primes) - all correct
- Did not run `llama-perplexity` - I couldnt run this, the model is too large for quick PPL runs alongside production workload
- Cross-GPU validated: KV buffers split correctly across both L40S GPUs (384.50 + 384.38 MiB for turbo3 2x82K)

- Special note on multimodal: dual-slot 2x82K + mmproj (vision projector, ~867 mb) fails with OOM on the first GPU, only 658 MiB free after KV+RS allocation. The mmproj always allocates on GPU0. Our production  baseline (q8_0, 1x82K + mmproj) works fine. The OOM only occurs when combining  dual-slot turbo3 with mmproj.

Happy to run additional tests if useful, jsut let me know, for example specific context lengths, turbo2 results or other stuff.

comments.author: TheTom
comments.body:
This is fantastic data. First L40S validation, first 122B model, and the dual-slot unlock is exactly the kind of production use case that shows why KV compression matters beyond benchmarks. +44% aggregate throughput from freeing VRAM for a second slot is a real win.

A few observations and requests if you have time:

1. **turbo3 prefill beating q8_0 by 20%** (310.8 vs 258.5) at 82K context is consistent with what we see on Metal at 32K+ on large models. Less KV cache data = less memory bandwidth pressure during prefill. Great to see this confirmed on multi-GPU CUDA.

2. **Asymmetric test:** Would be interested to see `-ctk q8_0 -ctv turbo3` on your setup. This keeps K at full precision while compressing V. On sensitive models this is the safest config, and on your 122B MoE it might recover some of that 6% decode penalty since the K-side dequant cost would be eliminated.

3. **turbo2 if you get a chance.** On our MoE testing (Qwen3.5-35B), turbo2 actually beats q8_0 at 32K+ decode due to the smaller cache footprint. Curious if the same crossover happens on L40S at 82K. Boundary V auto-enables with turbo2.

4. **The mmproj OOM** is interesting. If turbo2 frees enough additional VRAM over turbo3, dual-slot + mmproj might become viable.

Thank you for testing this on production hardware. Multi-GPU split + concurrent slots is territory we have not validated before. Really valuable data.

comments.author: TheTom
comments.body:
This is outstanding. The asymmetric result is the strongest production validation we have seen for the core thesis.

**The headline number:** q8_0/turbo3 at 61.1 t/s matching q8_0 baseline exactly, with 31% KV savings. The entire 6.4% symmetric penalty is K-side dequant. This is exactly what the asymmetric paper predicts, but seeing it hold at 122B on dual L40S at 82K context with zero decode loss is a different level of confidence than our original testing on Apple Silicon.

**The turbo2 no-crossover finding is equally valuable.** On our Qwen3.5-35B (Metal, 32K), turbo2 beats q8_0 by 5.4%. Your 122B hybrid MoE with only 12 attention layers does not show the same crossover at 82K. This suggests the mechanism is architecture-dependent: models with fewer KV attention layers relative to total compute may not generate enough cache bandwidth savings for turbo2 to win. That is a real limitation worth documenting and your data is the first to show it.

**The 19 MiB mmproj miss is painful.** If llama.cpp ever supports cross-GPU mmproj placement, your turbo2 dual-slot + mmproj config would unlock immediately.

If you have time for one more test that would be very useful for the papers: **asymmetric q8_0/turbo2 single-slot at 82K.** We have q8_0/turbo3 (100% TG recovery) and symmetric turbo2 (-5.6% TG). The asymmetric turbo2 number would tell us if V can be pushed all the way to 2-bit without any decode penalty on this architecture, and whether Boundary V (auto-enabled on turbo2) helps or hurts on a hybrid MoE with only 12 attention layers.

Thank you for running all of this on production hardware. This is exactly the kind of data the project needs.

comments.author: sjoerdmaessen
comments.body:
Ran the asymmetric q8_0/turbo2 test. Here are the results alongside the q8_0/turbo3 from earlier for comparison.

## Asymmetric V compression: turbo3 vs turbo2

| Config | KV Size | K | V | PP (t/s) | TG (t/s) | vs q8_0 TG |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| q8_0 / q8_0 (baseline) | 1,046 MiB | 522.75 | 522.75 | 258.5 | 61.1 | — |
| q8_0 / turbo3 | 715 MiB | 522.75 | 192.19 | 294.5 | **61.1** | **0.0%** |
| q8_0 / turbo2 | 686 MiB | 522.75 | 163.36 | 295.9 | **61.3** | **+0.3%** |

The answer to your question: **V can be pushed all the way to 2-bit without any decode penalty on this architecture.** The entire symmetric turbo2 penalty (-5.6%) is K-side, same as with turbo3. The V-side dequant cost is negligible regardless of bit-width.

| turbo3 / turbo3 | 384 MiB | 57.2 | -6.4% |

| q8_0 / turbo3 | 715 MiB | 61.1 | 0.0% |
| q8_0 / turbo2 | 686 MiB | 61.3 | +0.3% |

comments.author: sjoerdmaessen
comments.body:
**Correction: asymmetric q8_0-K / turbo3-V produces corrupt output**

When deploying the asymmetric config to production (Charles, our Matrix chatbot), we noticed empty/garbled responses. Investigation revealed the model outputs literal U+003F (`?`) characters, not a rendering issue, actual ASCII question marks. This affects both direct llama-server requests and requests through LiteLLM.

The speed measurements I reported earlier are accurate (61.1 t/s, zero TG penalty) the model generates tokens at full speed, they're just wrong tokens. I only caught this when checking actual content in production because my latest benchmarks were speed-only and maybe a bit rushed because of excitement.

**Symmetric turbo3/turbo3 works correctly.** Same fork, same binary, switching from `-ctk q8_0 -ctv turbo3` to `-ctk turbo3 -ctv turbo3` immediately produces coherent output. Verified with factual queries, counting, reasoning in Dutch, all correct actual content.

This suggests the K and V turbo3 quantization paths need to be paired, mixing q8_0 K with turbo3 V breaks the attention computation, possibly because the rotation matrices are only applied to turbo3-quantized tensors.

## What we're running now (production, verified working)

| Config | Ctx/slot | Slots | Vision | TG | Content |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ~~q8_0-K / turbo3-V~~ | — | — | — | 61.1 | **CORRUPT** |
| ~~q8_0-K / turbo2-V~~ | — | — | — | 61.3 | **not verified, likely same issue** |
| **turbo3-K / turbo3-V** | **104K** | **2** | **yes** | **58** | **correct** |

The asymmetric config also has a much larger compute buffer on GPU0 for turbo3-K (2074 MiB vs 858 MiB for q8_0-K), which limits max context with symmetric turbo3 compared to asymmetric. The max / sweet spot now is 2x104K with `MTMD_BACKEND_DEVICE=CUDA1` for the mmproj.

## Updated production config

```
--cache-type-k turbo3 --cache-type-v turbo3
--ctx-size 212992 (2x104K)
--parallel 2
MTMD_BACKEND_DEVICE=CUDA1
```

2x104K dual-slot, vision on GPU1, cron jobs verified, interactive chat verified. 58 t/s single, ~6% slower than q8_0 baseline. Very happy with this as a production config nonetheless.

Sorry for the incorrect asymmetric data, lesson learned to always verify output content, not just generation speed.

comments.author: TheTom
comments.body:
Thank you for catching this.

I have been investigating this tonight and opened [issue #47](https://github.com/TheTom/llama-cpp-turboquant/issues/47) to track it. After tracing through the code paths, I found two concrete bugs that affect asymmetric configs:

**1. Rotation matrix initialization (llama-kv-cache.cpp:332)** — The turbo rotation matrices and InnerQ scale tensors were only allocated when K is a turbo type. With `-ctk q8_0 -ctv turbo3`, these tensors were never created. Fixed to check both K and V types.

**2. V unpad gated on K type (llama-graph.cpp, 3 instances)** — Three V unpad blocks that extract the original head_dim after inverse WHT were checking `k->type` instead of `v->type`. With asymmetric q8_0-K, these blocks were skipped even when V is turbo and needs processing. This affects MHA, MLA, and ISWA attention paths.

Honest assessment: your model has head_dim=256 which is already 128-aligned, so the unpad is a no-op and bug #2 alone would not explain the corruption. Bug #1 ensures the rotation infrastructure exists, which may be the missing piece. Every other successful asymmetric test to date has been on head_dim=128 models, so yours is the first to exercise this combination. There may be additional issues I have not found yet.

I also added diagnostic logging to the fix so we can see exactly what code paths are being taken. When you run with the fix branch you should see lines like:

```
[DIAG #47] turbo rotation matrices allocated (K=q8_0, V=turbo3_0, asymmetric=YES)
[DIAG #47] build_attn il=0: K=q8_0 V=turbo3_0 asymmetric=YES Q_prerot=SKIP innerq_scale=allocated head_dim_v=256
```

Fix branch: [`fix/asymmetric-rotation-init`](https://github.com/TheTom/llama-cpp-turboquant/tree/fix/asymmetric-rotation-init)

```bash
git fetch origin fix/asymmetric-rotation-init
git checkout fix/asymmetric-rotation-init
```

If it does not resolve the corruption, please paste back the `[DIAG #47]` log lines and any other startup output — that will tell me which paths are active and help narrow down where the issue is.

It is late here so I may not respond until morning, but wanted to get this in your hands as soon as possible.

@fritolays Thank you for this incredible 17-model sweep — 17 models across 11 architectures is exactly the kind of systematic validation we need. Gemma 7.94x, DeepSeek 5.09x on 16GB are great numbers, and confirming P1→P5 fixes Phi-4/DeepSeek detection is very valuable. Your `tbq4_0/q8_0` best-balance recommendation is a great finding — will add to README.

**Quick question:** Did you build from source or use the release binaries? We discovered the release binaries had incorrect CUDA architectures (SM 52 default instead of SM 75-120). We've pulled those and are rebuilding now.

**On the Qwen3.5 turbo V "???" issue:**

We downloaded the exact same model (`Qwen3.5-27B-heretic-v3.i1-Q3_K_M.gguf`) and ran with the exact same options (`--cache-type-k tbq3_0 --cache-type-v tbq3_0 -ngl 99 --flash-attn on`). Output is completely normal on our local build (SM 121 native, DGX Spark GB10):

```
Hello! I'm doing well, thanks for asking. How about you?
```

No question marks. This strongly suggests the issue is **build-related** (SM 52 release binary running on SM 89 via JIT emulation), not a code bug.

**On the 50–75% prompt processing drop:** Also likely build-related. On our SM 121 native build, tbqp3/tbq3 prompt processing drops only ~15% vs f16 (94→80 t/s). SM 52 JIT emulation causes massive degradation on compute-heavy WHT kernels.

The corrected builds (SM 75/80/86/89/90/120 native) are compiling now — 6 architectures take significantly longer than the previous single-arch build. Will update when ready. Apologies for the build issue.

## Ampere (RTX 3080 Ti) Benchmark Data — Mixed KV Parity, PR #36 Validation, PR #43 turbo4 Fix

@TheTom — you mentioned wanting CUDA mixed `q8_0 × turbo` parity data. Here's a full matrix from an RTX 3080 Ti (SM 86, Ampere, 12GB).

**Model**: Qwen3.5 9B Q4_K_M (bartowski)
**Build**: seanrasch/llama-cpp-turboquant master @ `e99452f` (upstream HEAD + V unpad gate fix)
**Config**: FA on, ngl=99, single GPU, 10s cooling between runs

### Mixed q8_0 × turbo — Speed (t/s)

| Cache (K / V) | pp512 | pp2048 | pp8192 | pp16384 | tg128 |
|---------------|-------|--------|--------|---------|-------|
| f16 / f16 | 4108 | 4198 | 4081 | 3888 | 106.2 |
| q8_0 / q8_0 | 4063 | 4101 | 3984 | 3803 | 104.8 |
| q8_0 / turbo3 | 3988 | 4027 | 3915 | 3746 | 103.6 |
| q8_0 / turbo2 | 3988 | 4025 | 3915 | 3748 | 103.9 |
| turbo3 / turbo3 | 3984 | 4020 | 3909 | 3739 | 102.7 |
| turbo2 / turbo2 | 3978 | 4013 | 3904 | 3739 | 103.3 |

### Mixed q8_0 × turbo — PPL (wikitext-2, 16K context)

| Cache (K / V) | PPL |
|---------------|-----|
| f16 / f16 | 6.5706 |
| turbo3 / turbo3 | 6.6245 |
| q8_0 / turbo3 | 6.6478 |

**Takeaway**: On Ampere, mixed `q8_0-K + turbo3-V` is within noise of symmetric `turbo3/turbo3` for both speed and PPL. The K type doesn't meaningfully affect decode speed on this hardware — turbo K costs ~1% decode vs q8_0 K. Prefill is similarly flat across all turbo configs (~97% of f16). The asymmetric recommendation holds on SM 86.

### PR #36 (signalnine FA optimizations) — Ampere A/B

Tested `test/pr36-signalnine-fa-opt` @ `a75045b` against master. Same model, same hardware.

| Cache (K / V) | tg128 master | tg128 PR #36 | Delta |
|---------------|-------------|-------------|-------|
| f16 / f16 | 106.2 | 105.5 | -0.7% |
| q8_0 / q8_0 | 104.8 | 104.6 | -0.2% |
| turbo3 / turbo3 | 102.7 | 103.7 | **+1.0%** |
| turbo2 / turbo2 | 103.3 | 104.0 | **+0.7%** |

PPL: symmetric turbo3 shifted from 6.6245 to 6.6478 — consistent with auto-asymmetric overriding to q8_0 K (matches the q8_0/turbo3 baseline exactly). Auto-asymmetric is working correctly.

**Takeaway**: PR #36 gives +35% decode on RTX 5090 but only +1% on Ampere. No regression on any config. The shmem LUT and occupancy tuning are Blackwell-optimized — Ampere's smaller shared memory doesn't benefit as much. Safe to merge from an Ampere perspective.

### PR #43 (Dubascudes turbo4 WHT dequant fix) — Validated

We previously reported turbo4 K+V producing PPL 6952 on Llama arch (NeuralDaredevil 8B). Tested PR #43 @ `033742c` on Qwen3.5 9B:

| Cache (K / V) | PPL (2K) | Status |
|---------------|----------|--------|
| turbo4 / turbo4 | 7.3859 | **Fixed** |
| turbo4 K / turbo3 V | 7.4075 | Sane |
| turbo3 K / turbo4 V | 7.3648 | Sane |

turbo4/turbo4 speed: pp512=3970, pp16384=3707, tg128=101.8

The WHT/dense rotation mismatch in the C reference was indeed the root cause. turbo4 K+V is now functional on CUDA.

### Hardware Note

RTX 3080 Ti (12GB, SM 86, Ampere, PCIe Gen 3 x16). This is representative of the 30-series/40-series consumer cards that most people are actually running. Happy to run additional configs if useful.

comments.author: primoco
comments.body:
Hi, sharing task-accuracy benchmarks as a complement to PPL — since as @TheTom noted, PPL and generation quality can diverge.

We ran a KV cache recall benchmark on Qwen3-14b (no-think mode) using the spiritbuun CUDA fork, testing whether quantization corrupts recall of information stored earlier in context. The method: place a math problem at position 0, fill with N tokens of unrelated text, ask the model to recall and solve.

52 tests: 2×2 matrix mult, 3×3 matrix mult, scalar arithmetic — at 0/200/500/1000 token filler distances.

Cache config | Accuracy | Tok/s | KV VRAM -- | -- | -- | -- F16 / F16 | 52/52 — 100% | 73.1 | 100% q8_0-K / tq4_0-V | 52/52 — 100% | 73.5 | ~62% tq4_0-K / tq4_0-V | 49/52 — 94.2% | 56.0 | ~53% tq3_0-K / tq3_0-V | 47/52 — 90.4% | 56.4 | ~44%

Key findings:

  1. Asymmetric q8_0-K / tq4_0-V matches F16 exactly — same accuracy, same throughput, 38% less KV VRAM. This directly confirms @scos-lab's K/V magnitude disparity finding and @TheTom's "V is free" observation.

  2. The throughput paradox is caused by quantized K. Symmetric TQ drops from 73 to 56 tok/s (-23%). Keeping K at q8_0 eliminates the FWHT overhead penalty entirely. This explains why some people see TQ slower than baseline without Flash Attention fully compensating.

  3. Degradation only appears under context pressure with quantized K. Direct recall (no filler) is 100% across all configs. 3×3 matrix recall at 1000t filler: TQ3_0 drops to 1/3, q8k/tq4v stays 3/3.

  4. Scalar arithmetic is completely immune at all distances and all quantization levels.

The benchmark script is open source: https://github.com/eullm/eullm/blob/main/bench/turboquant_math_accuracy.py

Tested on EULLM Engine (Ollama-compatible Rust inference server) wrapping the spiritbuun CUDA fork. ctx=16384, temperature=0, num_predict=2048.

### Results

| # | Category | Score | Detail |
|---|----------|-------|--------|
| 1 | Large tool response synthesis | **PASS** | 6-item order list (~3K token JSON). f16@16K: 1/6 items, wrong total. turbo2@32K: 6/6 items, correct math. |
| 2 | Multi-turn context retention | **PASS** | 3-turn diagnostic. Context retained across all turns, KV cache reuse confirmed. |
| 3 | Multi-tool dependency chain | **PASS** | 9 tools available, 6 needed. Correct dependency ordering, parameter extraction from nested JSON. Cache reuse 99.7% (1330/1334 tokens). |
| 4 | Cross-platform data reconciliation | **PASS** | 8 SKUs across 2 platforms. 5/5 discrepancies found, 3/3 matches confirmed, all quantities and directions correct. |
| 5 | 4-turn diagnostic escalation | **PARTIAL** | Flawless diagnostic reasoning (metrics → DB → locks → runaway query). Final tool call emitted as XML in thinking block instead of tool_calls JSON — Qwen3.5 format fallback, not compression artifact. |
| 6 | Multi-currency financial calculation | **PARTIAL** | 15 transactions, 3 currencies. 11/12 values correct. One EUR fee sum off by $2.00 (mental arithmetic error on 5-addend sum). Correct methodology throughout. |
| 7 | Dense entity/relationship extraction | **PASS** | ~500 words, 6 people, 4 orgs, 10 relationships, 3 conflicts. All entities found. All relationships correct. 5 conflicts identified (3 required + 2 bonus). One minor label inconsistency. |
| 8 | Contradictory information handling | **PASS** | Status check says healthy, logs show 93% failure rate. Model explicitly flagged contradiction, assessed source reliability, investigated upstream. |
| 9 | Esoteric knowledge (Banach-Tarski) | **PASS** | Zero factual errors. Correct group-theoretic argument (SO(3) free subgroup vs SO(2) abelian). Missing historical attribution (model knowledge gap, not compression). |

### Key Finding: Test 001

This is the most important result. Same model, same hardware, same prompt:

| Backend | Items Reported | Total Calculated | Result |
|---------|---------------|-----------------|--------|
| f16 KV @ 16K context | 1/6 | $140 (hallucinated) | **FAIL** |
| turbo2 KV @ 32K context | 6/6 | $2,157.69 (correct) | **PASS** |

The f16 backend couldn't fit system prompt + conversation history + 6-order JSON tool response in 16K. It anchored on numbers from earlier in the conversation and hallucinated the total. turbo2 at 32K fit everything with headroom.

**This isn't a compression benchmark — it's a context window benchmark.** turbo2 gives you more context in the same VRAM, and more context means the agent can actually read its own tool responses.

### The Two Partial Passes

Both failures are Qwen3.5 model behaviors, not compression artifacts:
- **Test 005**: Model emitted tool call as XML inside reasoning block instead of OpenAI tool_calls format. Known Qwen3.5 fallback behavior — happens on any backend.
- **Test 006**: EUR fee sum off by $2.00 on a 5-addend mental arithmetic problem. This is a 9B model arithmetic limitation — would fail the same way on f16.

### Throughput

Decode speed across all tests: **95-100 t/s** on turbo2 KV. No measurable throughput difference from f16 at these context lengths.

Hi Everyone,
thank you all for your excellent work, absolutely fantastic and incredibly exicting to follow the progress.

# Ada Lovelace (RTX 4090) Benchmark Data — FA Flag Impact, Asymmetric Matrix, turbo3 vs turbo4

Sharing Ada Lovelace (SM 89) data since I don't see any RTX 4090 results in this thread yet. Two findings that might be useful for people building from @spiritbuun's fork.

**Hardware:** RTX 4090 24GB, i9-14900K, CUDA 12.4, Windows, VS 2022  
**Build:** spiritbuun `feature/turboquant-kv-cache` @ `5047b3e9a`  
**Model:** Llama 3.1 8B Instruct Q4_K_M (4.58 GiB)

---

## Finding 1: FA Build Flags — Free 7.4% Prefill

Comparing the same binary with and without `-DGGML_CUDA_FA=ON -DGGML_CUDA_FA_ALL_QUANTS=ON`:

| Build | pp512 (t/s) | tg128 (t/s) |
|-------|-------------|-------------|
| Without FA flags | 9,365 | 150.4 |
| With FA flags | 10,060 | 149.3 |
| **Delta** | **+7.4%** | ~0% |

The spiritbuun README doesn't prominently mention these flags. Without them, turbo cache types compile fine but the fused FA kernels are missing — and turbo requires FA at runtime (FWHT-rotated KV space). Easy to miss, significant impact.

Full cmake line that works:
```
cmake -B build -DGGML_CUDA=ON -DGGML_NATIVE=ON -DGGML_CUDA_FA=ON -DGGML_CUDA_FA_ALL_QUANTS=ON -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=89 -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
```

---

## Finding 2: Full KV-Cache Config Matrix on Ada (SM 89)

All results with FA flags enabled:

| KV-Cache (K / V) | pp512 (t/s) | tg128 (t/s) | Δ Prefill | Δ Decode |
|-------------------|-------------|-------------|-----------|----------|
| f16 / f16 | 10,060 ± 352 | 149.3 ± 0.5 | baseline | baseline |
| **q8_0 / turbo4** | **10,903 ± 545** | **140.0 ± 0.2** | **+8.4%** | **−6.2%** |
| q8_0 / turbo3 | 10,925 ± 503 | 138.4 ± 0.2 | +8.6% | −7.3% |
| turbo3 / turbo3 (adaptive=1) | 10,476 ± 432 | 128.3 ± 0.2 | +4.1% | −14.1% |
| turbo4 / turbo4 | 10,405 ± 496 | 124.3 ± 0.1 | +3.4% | −16.8% |

Confirms @TheTom's asymmetric recommendation on Ada: **q8_0-K + turbo4-V is the best config for Q4_K_M** — fastest prefill of any config tested (+8.4% vs f16!) with only 6.2% decode cost.

Interesting: **symmetric turbo3 beats turbo4 at decode** (128.3 vs 124.3 t/s). This makes sense — turbo3 can use the dequant+MMA tensor-core path for prefill, while turbo4's QJL correction loses precision in the fp16 round-trip, so it falls back to the slower path.

Also confirms @primoco's finding: all turbo configs show **equal or better prefill than f16**. The FWHT inverse during prefill plays well with tensor cores on Ada too.

---

## Qwen3.5-9B UD Q4_K_XL (pre-FA build, for reference)

| KV-Cache | pp512 (t/s) | tg128 (t/s) | Δ Decode |
|----------|-------------|-------------|----------|
| f16 | 9,149 | 119.6 | baseline |
| turbo4/turbo4 | 8,927 | 113.6 | −5.0% |

Planning to re-run Qwen with FA flags + asymmetric config.

---

## Dual-GPU Note

System has RTX 4090 + RTX 5090. Build is sm_89 only — `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0` is mandatory, otherwise the 5090 (sm_120) receives layers it can't execute and falls back to CPU-speed inference (~6 t/s instead of 150 t/s). Blackwell validation on this codebase would require CUDA 12.8+ with `-DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES="89;120a"`. Happy to run that if there's interest.

---

*Running local inference for document processing workflows. Sharing to fill the Ada Lovelace gap in the benchmark data.*

@nenkoru : try asymmetric K/V instead of symmetric. Use `-ctk q8_0 -ctv tbq3` (or `-ctk q8_0 -ctv turbo3` on our fork). Symmetric compresses both K and V with WHT which doubles the transform overhead and uses more VRAM for the rotation matrices. Keeping K at q8_0 is lighter on memory, and on Q4_K models it's actually better for quality too. We've documented cases where symmetric turbo on K produces catastrophic PPL on sensitive models while asymmetric q8_0-K/turbo-V stays clean.

On 40GB split across two V100s, VRAM is tight enough that the difference between symmetric and asymmetric K could be what's pushing you past the allocation limit. That's likely why our fork was fitting at contexts that AmesianX's doesn't - the default configs differ.

# Vilenkin-Hartley Transform for KV Cache Compression — Findings

Research and implementation report. Branch: `feature/vilenkin-hartley`

## Summary

We implemented the Vilenkin-Hartley Transform (VHT) — a mixed-radix generalization
of Walsh-Hadamard — as both a replacement rotation for TurboQuant and a basis for
a new sparse coefficient KV cache format. The work produced one clear win, one niche
win, and one negative result.

**Clear win:** VHT enables TurboQuant for non-power-of-2 head dimensions (Phi-2
head_dim=80, Pythia-2.8B head_dim=80, DeepSeek V3 head_dim=56). Previously impossible
with WHT, which requires power-of-2. For power-of-2 dims, VHT reduces exactly to
WHT with zero regression.

**Niche win:** Sparse Vilenkin coefficient encoding achieves 3-4× compression on
large head_dim models (GPT-J head_dim=256, Pythia-1B head_dim=256) where per-vector
index storage overhead is manageable. Multi-pass progressive refinement improves
quality by 4-5% cosine over single-pass.

**Negative result:** The coefficient cache doesn't outperform turbo3 (fixed-centroid
quantization) on mainstream head_dim=128 models. The KV vectors are near-Gaussian
in the VHT basis — energy is uniformly distributed, shared masks don't concentrate,
and per-vector index storage eats the compression budget.

## 1. Vilenkin-Hartley Transform

### What it is

WHT factors dimensions as 2^n and uses binary butterflies. VHT factors any dimension
into its primes and uses mixed-radix butterflies — binary for p=2, p-point Hartley
(cas kernel: cos+sin) for p>2. Self-inverse, norm-preserving, O(d log d).

### Implementation

| Component | Location |
|-----------|----------|
| Python prototype | `turboquant_plus/turboquant/vilenkin.py` |
| C implementation | `llama-cpp-turboquant/ggml/src/ggml-turbo-quant.c` |
| CUDA kernel | `llama-cpp-turboquant/ggml/src/ggml-cuda/turbo-wht.cu` |
| Graph integration | `llama-cpp-turboquant/src/llama-graph.cpp` |

### Results: VHT vs zero-padded WHT

Quantization MSE on synthetic data, PolarQuant 4-bit:

| head_dim | WHT (padded to 128) | VHT (native) | VHT/WHT |
|----------|---------------------|-------------|---------|
| 64 | 0.00908 | 0.00908 | 1.00 (identical) |
| 80 | 0.25390 | 0.00945 | **0.04 (27× better)** |
| 96 | 0.19118 | 0.00952 | **0.05 (20× better)** |
| 128 | 0.00965 | 0.00965 | 1.00 (identical) |
| 192 | 0.19292 | 0.00929 | **0.05 (21× better)** |
| 256 | 0.00927 | 0.00927 | 1.00 (identical) |

Zero-padding is catastrophic for non-power-of-2 dims: 48 zeros mixed into 80 real
elements corrupt the transform. VHT handles these natively.

### End-to-end validation

Phi-2 (head_dim=80) with turbo3 KV on RTX 5090:

| Config | PP512 | TG128 | vs baseline |
|--------|-------|-------|-------------|
| fp16 KV baseline | 21,225 | 435 | — |
| turbo3 + VHT (head_dim=80) | 21,142 | 342 | 78.6% |

First model with non-power-of-2 head_dim to use TurboQuant in any llama.cpp fork.
The 78.6% decode ratio is from zero-padding the turbo3 block format (QK=128) — a
VHT-native block format would eliminate this waste.

## 2. Sparse Vilenkin Coefficient Cache

### The idea

Instead of storing all elements quantized (turbo3: 3.125 bpv), store only the top-k
VHT coefficients. The hypothesis from the Position_Is_Arithmetic research: KV cache
vectors are sparse in the prime-harmonic basis, with ~10 universal indices per
(layer, head) explaining >90% of energy.

### Block format (GGML_TYPE_VILENKIN_3)

```
block_vilenkin_3 {
    half norm;                    // 2 bytes
    half scale;                   // 2 bytes
    uint8_t coeffs[N_COEFFS/2];  // int4-packed coefficient values
}
```

At 64 coefficients: 36 bytes per 128 elements = 2.25 bpv = 7.1× compression.
The basis mask (which coefficients to store) is set via `ggml_vilenkin_set_basis_mask()`.

comments.author: AmesianX
comments.body:
@nenkoru The `failed to create context` error is caused by the `-ctv tbqp4` option.

**tbqp** (MSE + QJL correction) can only be used for **K cache**, not V cache. QJL correction is not applicable to V — V cache only supports **tbq** (MSE-only) types.

Your command has K and V types swapped:
```bash
# Wrong — tbqp on V will fail
-ctv tbqp4 -ctk tbq4

# Correct — tbqp for K, tbq for V
-ctk tbqp4 -ctv tbq4

# Or 3-bit variant
-ctk tbqp3 -ctv tbq3
```

It looks like the older version allowed specifying tbqp for V without rejecting it at CLI level. In the next update, we'll add explicit validation to block tbqp types on `-ctv` so this kind of mistake is caught early with a clear error message.

## TurboQuant+ Weight Compression Update — TQ4_1S Merged to Main (fork)

Following up on the KV cache compression work. I extended the same WHT rotation + Lloyd-Max centroid approach to model weights. After community validation across 12+ GPUs, 11+ models, and 10+ independent testers, weight compression is now merged to main alongside KV compression.

Special thanks to @signalnine for the CUDA port and load-time conversion. 13 kernel versions tested, shipped overnight. The load-time TQ4_1S to q8_0 conversion gives native q8_0 decode speed at compressed file size.

### What it does

Post-training weight compression. One command, no retraining, no calibration data. Takes a Q8_0 GGUF and produces a 28-42% smaller model.

### Stacking

This is not a replacement for KV cache compression. It stacks on top of it. Weight compression makes the model smaller. KV compression makes conversations longer. Together, a 35B MoE model at 32K context uses 59% of baseline total memory. The model is smaller AND the conversation is longer. One VRAM budget, both compressions, no additional quality penalty from stacking. 4+ independent testers have confirmed this across Metal, CUDA Ada, and dual-GPU setups.

An [independent implementation](https://github.com/dhawalc/turboQuantDC) (662 tests, MIT license) tested TQ4_1S + turbo3 on a single RTX 4090: 100K context in 5.8 GiB for an 8B model. turbo3 was actually faster than f16 at 8K context (86.5 vs 78.4 tok/s) due to reduced VRAM pressure.

### How I got here

I started by compressing every tensor the same way. 47% smaller but 30% slower and +11% PPL. Not good enough.

Through systematic A/B isolation I found that different tensor roles have dramatically different sensitivity:

- Attention tensors tolerate WHT-rotated compression well
- FFN gate/up tensors compress well
- FFN down-projection is quality-critical (feeds the residual stream)
- First 2 + last 2 layers are disproportionately sensitive (same pattern as [Boundary V](https://github.com/TheTom/turboquant_plus/blob/main/docs/papers/layer-aware-v-compression.md) for KV cache)

The result is "Config I": TQ4_1S for attention + FFN gate/up, native Q4_K for ffn_down, boundary 2+2 protection.

### Results by model family

**Qwen/Phi (Config I, full support):**

| Model | Compression | PPL Delta |
|-------|------------|-----------|
| Qwen2.5-1.5B | -27% | +1.7-1.9% |
| Qwen3.5-27B | -28% | +1.3-2.5% |
| Qwen3.5-35B MoE | -37% | +1.4% |
| Qwen2.5-72B | -38% | +3.9% (8 chunks) |
| Phi-4 14B | -32% | +0.76-1.0% |

**Mistral (Hybrid config):**

| Model | Compression | PPL Delta |
|-------|------------|-----------|
| Mistral 7B v0.3 Hybrid | -39% | +1.28% |
| Mistral 7B v0.3 Premium | -24% | +0.41% |

**Llama (Hybrid/Premium, FFN sensitive to WHT):**

| Model | Config | Compression | PPL Delta |
|-------|--------|------------|-----------|
| Llama 3.1 70B | Hybrid | -42% | +16% |
| Llama 3.1 70B | Premium | -29% | +5.8% |
| Llama 3.2-3B | Hybrid | -34% | +1.9% |

Llama amplifies per-layer FFN quantization error 6-8x more than Qwen/Phi. The effect scales with depth. Full investigation in the [paper Section 5.7](https://github.com/TheTom/turboquant_plus/blob/main/docs/papers/weight-compression-tq4.md).

### Decode speed

| Hardware | Decode vs Q8_0 |
|----------|---------------|
| M5 Max (Metal) | 94-102% |
| M4 Max (Metal) | 85-99% |
| RTX 5090 (CUDA, load-time conversion) | **107%** |
| 2x L40S (CUDA Ada) | 81% |
| RTX 4090 (CUDA Ada) | 63-67% (fused), 100% (load-time) |

### Regressions

Zero regressions on uncompressed models across all tested hardware (so far) (Metal, CUDA Ada, CUDA Blackwell, M2 Pro, M5 Max, RTX 4090, L40S, RTX 5090).

### Links

- [Paper](https://github.com/TheTom/turboquant_plus/blob/main/docs/papers/weight-compression-tq4.md) — full methodology, Config I discovery process, Llama investigation
- [Community results](https://github.com/TheTom/turboquant_plus/blob/

## Asymmetric K/V + BitNet Compound Case. Metal Benchmarks (M4 Pro)

Sharing benchmark findings from testing TurboQuant KV cache compression on Apple Silicon (M4 Pro 24GB). Built Metal dequant shaders using Lloyd-Max codebook quantization (block_size=128, head_dim-aligned) with FA integration, tested across 14 configurations.

### Key Finding: Asymmetric K/V is Essential

**Symmetric 4-bit compression destroys quality, but asymmetric q8_0-K / 4-bit-V is near-lossless.** This confirms @TheTom's observations about K sensitivity and @primoco's recall benchmark results.

**7B (Qwen2.5-7B Q4_K_M, wikitext-2-raw c=512):**

| KV Config | PPL | vs f16 | KV Memory | Savings |
|-----------|-----|--------|-----------|---------|
| f16 (baseline) | 8.0348 | — | 112.0 MiB | — |
| q8_0 | 8.0624 | +0.34% | 59.5 MiB | 47% |
| **q8_0-K / 4bit-V (asymmetric)** | **8.0557** | **+0.26%** | **44.2 MiB** | **61%** |
| 4bit symmetric | 4126.7 | +51261% | 28.9 MiB | 74% |
| 3bit symmetric | 16100.2 | +200281% | 21.9 MiB | 80% |

**1.7B (Qwen3-1.7B Q8_0):**

| KV Config | PPL | vs f16 | KV Savings |
|-----------|-----|--------|------------|
| f16 (baseline) | 17.6910 | — | — |
| q8_0-K / 4bit-V | 17.5789 | -0.63% | 61% |
| 4bit symmetric | 51.2758 | +190% | 74% |

The asymmetric config actually *improves* PPL on 1.7B (-0.63%), likely because q8_0 K provides slight regularization.

### BitNet Compound Case

Tested TQ2_0 (BitNet b1.58-2B) with compressed KV, compound extreme quantization (ternary weights + 4-bit KV values). Haven't seen this tested elsewhere:

| KV Config | PPL | vs f16 |
|-----------|-----|--------|
| f16 (baseline) | 1519.89 | — |
| q8_0-K / 4bit-V | 1522.82 | +0.19% |
| 4bit symmetric | 1524.87 | +0.33% |

BitNet is much less K-sensitive than standard decoder models; even symmetric 4-bit works (+0.33%). The compound case (TQ2_0 weights + compressed KV) enables significant memory savings with negligible quality loss.

**Note:** BitNet + TurboQuant KV requires FA enabled. The CPU dequant fallback without FA produces NaN. With Metal FA, it works cleanly.

### NIAH at 32K

All 14 configurations pass needle-in-a-haystack retrieval at 32K context, including the symmetric configs with catastrophic PPL. Retrieval still works even when generation quality is destroyed.

### Generation Speed (Metal, M4 Pro)

| Config | Prompt (tok/s) | Gen (tok/s) |
|--------|---------------|-------------|
| 7B f16 | 43.87 | 46.58 |
| 7B q8_0-K/4bit-V | 43.13 | 44.45 |
| 1.7B f16 | 214.28 | 107.26 |
| 1.7B q8_0-K/4bit-V | 216.03 | 96.77 |

Dequant overhead: ~5% on generation, negligible on prompt eval.

### Takeaways

1. **Asymmetric q8_0-K / 4bit-V should be the default recommendation.** Symmetric 4-bit is only viable with QJL Stage 2 correction on the K channel (or on BitNet where K magnitudes are naturally smaller).

2. **BitNet compound case is a win.** TQ2_0 + compressed KV is a viable on-device configuration with near-zero quality loss. Worth considering as the ecosystem matures.

3. **3-bit is not viable** at any model size without QJL Stage 2. 41x degradation on 1.7B, 2004x on 7B.

4. **NIAH survives everything.** Even configs with catastrophic PPL still retrieve needles at 32K — retrieval and generation quality degrade independently.

Happy to share more details if useful.

*Tested on: Apple M4 Pro 24GB, macOS, built on @tetherto QVAC Fabric fork. AI tools were used in an assistive capacity for benchmarking automation; all measurements verified locally.*

| 2,630 | 39.3 | None | PASS |

No quality degradation at 1500-2500 token generation range. Coherent output throughout.

### What Changed

v1.4.1 used scalar **vec kernels** (WHT-domain dot product per element). v1.4.2 uses **MMA tensor cores** for Q·K and softmax·V matrix multiplication.

Key implementation details:

- **Spatial K/V dequant**: K decoded to spatial f16 (with IWHT in dequant kernel). V = K view = spatial. MMA kernel receives standard f16 tiles.
- **QJL scalar correction**: TBQP 1-bit QJL correction as lightweight scalar: `dq × Σ(Q_wht2[i] × sign[i])`. Reads sign bits directly from raw TBQP blocks via kernel parameters. QJL uses a different sign basis (signs2) than MSE (signs1).
- **Warp shuffle IWHT**: Cooperative IWHT butterfly optimized with `__shfl_xor_sync` for stages 0-4. `__syncthreads` reduced from 8 to 4 per sub-block.
- **Fused Q WHT**: Single kernel reads Q directly, computes Q_wht1 + Q_wht2 for QJL. No cudaMemcpy.

All TBQ/TBQP 3-bit and 4-bit variants benefit.

### Pauli Quality Test

TBQP3 correctly transliterates "Wolfgang Pauli" → "월프강 파울리" (Korean), confirming QJL correction works with MMA path.

comments.author: TheTom
comments.body:
Nice work on the Gemma 4 dk512 implementation and the math accuracy testing — the divergent case analysis across models is genuinely useful data. A few observations and some fresh test results that might help.

**Reproduction: Qwen3.5-35B-A3B Q8_0, head_dim=256, M5 Max 128GB (Metal)**

Ran [primoco's math accuracy benchmark](https://github.com/eullm/eullm/blob/main/bench/turboquant_math_accuracy.py) (patched for llama-server OpenAI API) with temp=0, deterministic, filler 500/1000/1500/2000 tokens.

| Config | Pass/Total | % | KV Memory |
|:---|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| f16 / f16 (baseline) | 17/65 | 26.2% | 160 MiB |
| q8_0 / turbo3 (asymmetric) | 17/65 | 26.2% | 58 MiB |

Identical accuracy. 2.7x KV compression. 4 divergent cases, split 2-2 (f16 wins 2, turbo3 wins 2) — balanced, no systematic bias. No degradation at 1500-2000t context distance.

**Asymmetric K/V matters**

We used `q8_0` K / `turbo3` V — not symmetric. Our [asymmetric KV docs](https://github.com/TheTom/turboquant_plus/blob/main/docs/papers/asymmetric-kv-compression.md) show that on Q4_K_M models, symmetric turbo3 can produce PPL 3,556 vs asymmetric q8_0-K/turbo3-V at PPL 6.71 (same compression budget). K determines attention routing through softmax, which amplifies small perturbations exponentially. Keeping K at q8_0 is cheap insurance.

@primoco  : the 1500-2000t recall degradation you're seeing in [#11](https://github.com/AmesianX/TurboQuant/issues/11) doesn't reproduce on our fork with asymmetric q8_0/turbo3 on Metal. A few things to check:
1. Are you using symmetric compression on both K and V? Try `q8_0` K with turbo V only
2. The block_size mismatch you identified (tbq4_0 on head_dim=128) is a real issue. The Rust bindings bypass auto-detection, so you'd need tbq4_1 (blck_size=128) explicitly
3. Boundary V layer protection (q8_0 on first/last 2 layers) recovers 37-91% of quality gap in our testing, worth trying if recall at distance is the specific concern

**On the dk512 divergence pattern**

Gemma 4 31B shows 10 divergent cases, all f16 wins (zero TBQ wins). Compare to Qwen3-14B head_dim=128 at 9-9 balanced. One-directional divergence isn't random quantization noise... it suggests the 2-pass 256-block WHT decomposition for dk512 may introduce systematic bias. Worth investigating whether a single-pass dk512 WHT produces a more balanced divergence pattern.

**Methodology note**

The response to #11 used `--temp 0.6 --top-k 20 --top-p 0.95` while primoco's original test used temperature=0. Non-deterministic sampling masks precision differences between cache types. For KV recall benchmarks, temp=0 is essential to isolate cache fidelity from sampling noise.

---

Separate note: this discussion has been a great research hub for TurboQuant findings and cross-implementation data. Would be good to keep it focused on that. Release announcements fit better on the respective fork's releases page. Keeps signal-to-noise high for everyone following the research.
