@TheTom thanks for running with temp=0 and the Qwen3.5-35B data — identical F16/turbo3 accuracy with 2.7x compression is exactly what we'd hope to see.

@AmesianX we think we've found the root cause of your F16=30.8% baseline. We tested F16/F16 on Qwen3-14B Q4_K_M with two ctx sizes, identical prompts:

ctx-size 16384 → 82.4% (75/91), 1500-2000t bucket: 27.8% ctx-size 32768 (native) → 100% (91/91), 1500-2000t bucket: 100%

The prompts at 2500t filler are only ~1780 tokens — well within both windows. F16 is lossless so the degradation comes from the attention computation itself, not the cache. Our hypothesis is RoPE frequency scaling applied when ctx_size < model native context (32768 for Qwen3-14B).

Once ctx_size matches native context, all three configs hit 100%:

Config | Accuracy | Tok/s -- | -- | -- f16/f16 | 100% (91/91) | 67.0 f16/tbq4_1 | 100% (91/91) | 63.9 q8_0/tbq4_1 | 100% (91/91) | 62.9

Could you re-run at --ctx-size 32768? We suspect your 30.8% F16 will move to 100%, which would mean zero accuracy cost from TurboQuant on Qwen3-14B with correct setup.

Confirming @TheTom's point: tbq4_1 (blck_size=128) must be specified explicitly for head_dim=128 models via Rust bindings — auto-detection doesn't propagate through the API layer.

We've also filed a separate issue on ggerganov/llama.cpp about the ctx_size/F16 behavior.

Benchmark script: https://github.com/eullm/eullm/blob/main/bench/turboquant_math_accuracy.py

comments.author: AmesianX
comments.body:
## D=512 WHT Research: Pushing TurboQuant Beyond Paper Limits

Sharing detailed findings from our attempt to optimize TBQ quality for Gemma 4's head_dim=512. This goes beyond the TurboQuant paper's validated range (head_dim=128/256).

### The Challenge

Gemma 4 has head_dim=512 (global attention). Our initial 2-pass approach (two independent 256-block WHTs) worked but showed quality gaps. We attempted a 512-point single-pass WHT to improve cross-block decorrelation.

### What We Tried (Exhaustive)

| Approach | Math Accuracy | Notes |
|----------|:---:|-------|
| f16 baseline | 38/65 (58.5%) | Reference |
| 2×256-block WHT (attn_rot ON) | 20/65 (30.8%) | Original approach, matched f16 at earlier run |
| **512-WHT + global norm** | **31/65 (47.7%)** | **Best result** |
| 512-WHT + per-block norm | 9/65 (13.8%) | Cross-block scale mismatch |
| 512-WHT + per-block norm + attn_rot OFF | 5/65 (7.7%) | Worse without attn_rot |
| TBQP3 512 + QJL (gamma RMS, correlated signs) | 28/65 (43.1%) | QJL correction too weak |
| TBQP3 512 + QJL (gamma L2, correlated signs) | 23/65 (35.4%) | QJL overcorrects |
| TBQP3 512 + QJL (gamma L2, independent signs) | 28/65 (43.1%) | Sign independence didn't help |
| 512-WHT + per-block norm (corrected dispatch) | 28/65 (43.1%) | Per-block still worse than global |

### Key Findings

**1. Global norm is essential for 512-WHT.**
When 512-WHT output is split into two 256-blocks, per-block normalization destroys the cross-block scale relationship. Storing the same global norm in both blocks preserves scale consistency. This single insight improved accuracy from 13.8% to 47.7%.

**2. QJL does not help at D=512 — it hurts.**
We tested every combination: RMS vs L2 gamma, correlated vs independent sign patterns, weak vs strong correction. In ALL cases, adding QJL degraded quality (47.7% → 23-43%). At D=256, QJL improves accuracy. At D=512, the 1-bit sign approximation adds more noise than it corrects.

**3. The TurboQuant paper's validated range matters.**
The paper validates at head_dim=128, where our implementation achieves identical accuracy to f16 (7:7 balanced divergence at temp=0). At head_dim=512, 3-bit quantization with 512-WHT achieves 47.7% vs f16's 58.5% — functional but with a measurable gap.

**4. attn_rot (upstream Hadamard) + TBQ WHT = beneficial double rotation.**
Counter-intuitively, the double rotation (attn_rot 512-Hadamard + TBQ 512-WHT) performs well. Both Q and K receive the same transforms, so dot products are preserved. The combined decorrelation is more effective than either alone.

### Bugs Fixed Along the Way

Five genuine bugs were found and fixed for Gemma 4 support:
- SWA cache type auto-remapping (mixed head_dim 512/256)
- Variable GQA attn_rot activation (per-layer head_count_kv)
- D=512 flash attention vec dispatch
- K dot product reading only half the blocks
- set_rows dispatch using tensor dimension instead of head_dim

### What's Next

The 47.7% result with 3-bit global norm is our current best for D=512. Possible future directions:
- 4-bit (TBQ4) at D=512 — more centroids should close the gap significantly
- Model-specific centroid calibration
- Hybrid bit allocation (4-bit for high-energy WHT coefficients, 3-bit for rest)

All benchmarks: Gemma 4 26B-A4B MoE, DGX Spark GB10, temp=0, [turboquant_math_accuracy.py](https://github.com/eullm/eullm/blob/main/bench/turboquant_math_accuracy.py).

## Update: tbq3-K / f16-V = Perfect Match on Gemma 4

Following @andrei-ace's finding that V cache quality is critical, we tested asymmetric K/V on Gemma 4 26B-A4B MoE (CUDA, DGX Spark GB10, temp=0):

| Config | Math Accuracy | K Memory | V Memory | Total KV |
|--------|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| f16/f16 | **38/65 (58.5%)** | 5,120 MiB | 5,120 MiB | 10,240 MiB |
| **tbq3/f16** | **38/65 (58.5%)** | **490 MiB** | 2,560 MiB | **3,050 MiB** |
| tbq3/tbq3 | 31/65 (47.7%) | 490 MiB | 490 MiB | 980 MiB |

**Identical accuracy to f16 with 3.4x KV compression.** K cache reduced 10.4x (5,120 → 490 MiB) with zero quality loss. The entire accuracy gap we observed was from V quantization, not K.

This confirms @andrei-ace and @TheTom's asymmetric K/V finding — keeping V at higher precision is essential for maintaining quality at D=512. The K cache tolerates aggressive 3-bit WHT quantization perfectly.

Note: q4_0 V is not yet supported at D=512 in our CUDA vec kernel dispatch (only f16 and TBQ types). Adding q4_0/q8_0 V dispatch for D=512 would enable further V compression while likely maintaining quality.

**RTX 5090 + RTX 4090 — Full KV × LA Matrix (spiritbuun v2, CUDA 12.8 + 13.2)**

Follow-up to my earlier Ada results. Rebuilt from the new `llama-cpp-turboquant-cuda` repo with CUDA 12.8 (sm_89 + sm_120) and 13.2 (sm_89 + sm_120a) on a dual-GPU setup. Ran every KV config × LA mode on both GPUs.

| KV-Cache          | pp512 (t/s) | tg128 (t/s) | Δ Prefill | Δ Decode |

| q8_0-K + turbo3-V | 10,936.64   | 137.81      | +8.5%     | -8.2%    |

### RTX 5090 (Blackwell, sm_120) — Build CUDA 12.8

| KV-Cache          | pp512 (t/s) | tg128 (t/s) | Δ Prefill | Δ Decode |
|-------------------|-------------|-------------|-----------|----------|
| **LA=off**        |             |             |           |          |
| f16 (default)     | 12,850.64   | 230.70      | —         | —        |
| q8_0-K + turbo4-V | 12,388.47   | 162.95      | -3.6%     | -29.4%   |
| turbo3 / turbo3   | 11,309.70   | 125.44      | -12.0%    | -45.6%   |
| turbo4 / turbo4   | 11,914.27   | 134.12      | -7.3%     | -41.9%   |
| q8_0-K + turbo3-V | 12,369.44   | 153.54      | -3.7%     | -33.4%   |
|                   |             |             |           |          |
| **LA=1**          |             |             |           |          |
| f16 (default)     | 12,761.21   | 231.93      | —         | —        |
| q8_0-K + turbo4-V | 12,352.17   | 173.43      | -3.2%     | -25.2%   |
| turbo3 / turbo3   | 11,799.41   | 139.90      | -7.5%     | -39.7%   |
| turbo4 / turbo4   | 11,739.74   | 144.22      | -8.0%     | -37.8%   |
| q8_0-K + turbo3-V | 12,420.45   | 161.79      | -2.7%     | -30.2%   |

### Key Findings

1. **Ada handles TurboQuant decode far better than Blackwell.** RTX 4090 loses only 7% decode with q8₀+t4 (LA=1), while RTX 5090 loses 25%. This appears structural — Ada's int8 dp4a instructions align well with TurboQuant's dequant path, while Blackwell's tensor cores are optimized for fp8/fp4.

2. **sm_120a (CUDA 13.2) provides no benefit over sm_120 (CUDA 12.8)** for TurboQuant workloads on Blackwell. Tested both — identical results within measurement noise.

3. **LA=1 improves decode speed** — not just quality. The q8_0 layers at first/last 4 positions use faster native int8 decoding. On RTX 4090: q8₀+t4 decode goes from 136.4 t/s (LA=off) to 139.8 t/s (LA=1).

4. **`CUDA_DEVICE_ORDER=PCI_BUS_ID` is required** on mixed-arch systems (Ada + Blackwell). Without it, `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES` silently routes to the wrong GPU. Cost me an afternoon of debugging.

5. **Recommendation:** `q8_0-K + turbo4-V` with `LA=1` — best balance of compression, speed, and quality on Ada.

comments.body:
@WaveboSF you are on fire. RTX 5090 data in the same day, this is incredible.

The Ada vs Blackwell decode gap is the most interesting finding here. -6.9% on 4090 vs -25.2% on 5090 for the same config (q8_0+turbo4 LA=1) points to a real architectural difference. Your dp4a vs fp8/fp4 tensor core theory is compelling. Worth noting this is on spiritbuun's CUDA kernels though, so some of the Blackwell regression may be kernel-specific rather than purely architectural.

We recently merged a fused single-phase TQ mmvq kernel (signalnine's V12) into TurboQuant+ that eliminates the global scratch buffer and shares activations through shmem. This is a fundamentally different CUDA decode path from spiritbuun's and could behave very differently on Blackwell's memory hierarchy. Would be very interesting to see the same matrix on [TurboQuant+](https://github.com/TheTom/turboquant_plus).

The LA=1 speed finding is great new data. We documented boundary V for quality recovery but the decode speed improvement (136.4 -> 139.8 on 4090, 162.9 -> 173.4 on 5090) makes sense: q8_0 boundary layers skip the WHT transform entirely and use native int8 decode which is faster on every architecture.

Also appreciate the dual-GPU debugging note about CUDA_DEVICE_ORDER. That's the kind of thing that saves people hours.

Would you be willing to run the same matrix on our fork? Getting started guide is [here](https://github.com/TheTom/turboquant_plus/blob/main/docs/getting-started.md).

comments.author: sandahltim
comments.body:
Great discussion — we've been running a TurboQuant CUDA fork in production for a couple weeks now and have some findings that might be useful to the community. Our setup: Qwen3.5-27B Q5_K_M on RTX 3090 Ti (24GB), turbo3 KV cache, 65K context, serving a business AI assistant.

### Norm correction makes turbo3 BEAT q8_0

The discussion mentions <2% PPL degradation as the target. We found that with a simple norm correction — storing `original_norm / ||reconstruction||` instead of `original_norm` — turbo3 actually **beats** q8_0 in perplexity:

| Config | PPL (Qwen3.5-27B, 2K/8chunks) | vs q8_0 |
|--------|------|---------|
| q8_0 baseline | 5.8375 | — |
| turbo3 + norm correction | 5.8323 | **-0.09%** |
| turbo4 + norm correction | 5.8186 | **-0.32%** |

The corrected norm ensures the dequantized vector's L2 magnitude exactly matches the original. Zero decode cost — just a different value stored during quantization.

### Layer-adaptive modes: -1.17% better than q8_0

We systematically tested keeping critical layers at q8_0 while turbo3-ing the rest. Best config ("LA-1": first 4 + last 4 of 40 layers at q8_0):

| Config | PPL | vs q8_0 | Compression | Prefill | Decode |
|--------|-----|---------|-------------|---------|--------|
| LA-1 turbo3 | **5.7690** | **-1.17%** | 3.5x | 99.6% of q8_0 | 97.5% |
| LA-5 turbo3 (2+2) | 5.8091 | -0.49% | 4.2x | 98.8% | 96.8% |
| turbo3 uniform | 5.8323 | -0.09% | 4.9x | 99.3% | 96.8% |

Key findings:
- **Last 2 layers dominate** — protecting them gives most of the quality gain
- Both K and V must be promoted together (asymmetric K-only or V-only promotion hurts due to norm correction mismatch)
- LA-1 fits at 65K on 24GB; for 128K, use LA-5 (4 layers q8_0) or uniform

### Values matter more than Keys (contradicts "More Keys Less Values" paper)

We tested all asymmetric K/V combinations. On Qwen3.5-27B:

- turbo3-K + turbo4-V: PPL 5.8212 (-0.28%) — **good**
- turbo4-K + turbo3-V: PPL 5.8653 (+0.48%) — **worst**

Values need higher precision on this model. The paper's prediction was wrong here, possibly because norm correction changes the error dynamics.

### QJL is worth keeping (with norm correction)

There's been discussion about dropping QJL from turbo4. We tested this explicitly:

- turbo4 WITH QJL + norm correction: PPL 5.8186 (-0.32%)
- turbo4 WITHOUT QJL + norm correction: PPL 5.8501 (+0.22%)

Without QJL, turbo4 is worse than turbo3 in quality AND speed. QJL + norm correction is the combo that makes turbo4 beat q8_0. However, QJL has a practical issue: the correction magnitude (~0.001) is at the fp16 precision limit, so the prefill dequant+MMA path loses ~1.3% PPL for turbo4 (turbo3 prefill MMA works perfectly at 98.8% of q8_0 speed).

### Prefill solved: dequant-then-MMA

The discussion mentions prefill as a gap. We implemented bulk dequantization to fp16 temp buffers before MMA (tensor core) dispatch during prefill:

- turbo3: 631 → **1125 tok/s** (1.78x improvement, 98.8% of q8_0)
- turbo4: 586 → **1113 tok/s** (1.9x, but +1.3% PPL due to fp16 QJL precision loss)

Memory overhead is ~16 MB per KV head group (temporary, freed after each attention call).

### 128K context on 24GB RTX 3090

With turbo3 uniform or LA-5, we run 128K context where q8_0 OOMs at ~65K:

| Context | Prefill tok/s | Decode tok/s |
|---------|--------------|-------------|
| 65K | 847 | 29.79 |
| 128K | 671 | 29.89 |

Decode speed is essentially constant across all context lengths. The model's full 128K context window is usable on consumer hardware.

### head_dim=128 quality gap + InnerQ fix

turbo3 quality degrades ~3-4% on head_dim=128 models (Qwen3-14B, Gemma-3-27B) vs <0.3% on head_dim=256. We implemented InnerQ-style per-channel equalization (per-channel scaling before L2 norm + FWHT, with inverse scaling on Q in the FA kernel) that closes ~46% of this gap. Auto-disables on already-balanced head_dim=256 channels.

### Bug reports for impleme

@WaveboSF incredible benchmark work, thank you for running the full matrix. 80 runs across two architectures and two CUDA versions is exactly the kind of rigorous validation we needed.

I want to be clear about attribution here: this is @signalnine's  win. He authored the V12 fused mmvq kernel from scratch. The numbers speak for themselves. Going from a 40% decode penalty to 7% on Blackwell is not an incremental improvement, it is a fundamentally different outcome. The LA mode divergence between forks is interesting and worth investigating further. The fact that turboquant_plus prefers LA=7 for asymmetric configs suggests the fused kernel changes the cost model for boundary layer operations.

## TurboQuant on Gemma4 26B — Metal Implementation Results

Tested on **Gemma4 26B A4B-it Q4_K_M** (iSWA, dk=256 SWA / dk=512 global), Apple M4 Pro 48GB. CPU + Metal, flash attention required. Branch: [`turboquant-gemma`](https://github.com/andrei-ace/llama.cpp/tree/turboquant-gemma) Results [`here`](https://github.com/andrei-ace/llama.cpp/tree/turboquant-gemma/benches/tq-metal).

### QJL matters for K

On this model, **tq2j (2-bit MSE + 1-bit QJL = 3.12 bpv) paired with q4_0 V scores 36/37** — the single miss was an empty response, consistent with token-budget exhaustion rather than an observed wrong answer. At 3.12 bpv for K, that's remarkable.

QJL makes the Q·K inner product estimator unbiased (paper Theorem 2). The 1-bit sign correction is cheap and restores unbiasedness to the inner-product estimator; on low-bpv K it appears worthwhile in practice.

Needle-in-a-haystack test (8 specific facts buried in a 12K-token document padded with 80 filler paragraphs — the model must retrieve exact numbers, names, and details): **8/8 for all viable configs**, including tq2j/q4_0 at 3.12 bpv K. No retrieval degradation was observed in this NIAH setup.

On this model, q4_0 for V gave the best quality and speed among tested configs. TQ V (tq3 at 3.06 bpv) works and saves memory, but adds an inverse FWHT pass on the attention output every token.

### Speed: +34% over q4_0 at 131K context

All layers use the same quant type — no per-layer calibration or mixed precision. tg128 (t/s):

| Config | pp512 | d=512 | d=4K | d=16K | d=32K | d=65K | d=131K | KV bpv |
|:------:|:-----:|:-----:|:----:|:-----:|:-----:|:-----:|:------:|:------:|
| f16/f16 | 770 | 60.8 | 57.0 | 51.9 | 45.8 | 36.0 | 21.1 | 32.00 |
| q4_0/q4_0 | 758 | 57.3 | 50.2 | 38.3 | 29.0 | 19.4 | 11.6 | 9.00 |
| **tq2j/q4_0** | 760 | 57.2 | 52.1 | 42.5 | 34.2 | 24.5 | **15.6** | 7.62 |
| **tq2j/tq3** | 753 | 56.0 | 50.3 | 40.3 | 31.6 | 22.1 | **14.0** | 6.18 |
| tq3j/q4_0 | 750 | 57.6 | 51.8 | 41.1 | 31.9 | 19.0 | 13.7 | 8.62 |

TQ overtakes q4_0 from **d=4096 onward**. f16 remains fastest at all depths because the native half-precision Metal GPU path is highly optimized, while quantized KV paths pay extra dequant/unpack overhead.

### Quality: matches q4_0 for tq3j/q4_0; within one empty miss for tq2j/q4_0

37 tests adapted from [eullm/bench](https://github.com/eullm/eullm/tree/main/bench) (math, 2×2 matrix multiply, factual, logic, code, Korean transliteration, delayed-recall with 500-token filler), `temperature=0`, `max_tokens=4096`:

| Config | Score | KV bpv |
|:------:|:-----:|:------:|
| f16/f16, q4_0/q4_0, **tq3j/q4_0** | 37/37 (100%) | 32.0 / 9.0 / 8.62 |
| tq2j/q4_0, tq3j/tq3, **tq2j/tq3** | 36/37 (97%) | 7.62 / 7.18 / **6.18** |

The 36/37 misses are empty responses, consistent with token-budget exhaustion — no wrong answers were observed. The benchmark uses lenient substring matching (e.g. `파울리` matches `볼프강 파울리`), not strict exact-answer equivalence.

### Metal kernel details

- **K attention (vec FA):** fused dot product reads K directly from device memory — no dequant to shared memory, no barriers. NE=4 (8 threads per K token, 3 shuffle reductions). Centroid lookup from constant memory, branchless sign dot.
- **V attention:** V dequantized in FWHT space, inverse FWHT on accumulated output (`TQ_FWHT_O`) via register + `simd_shuffle_xor`.
- **Q transform:** FWHT on Q once per token in shared memory (register + shuffle, barrier-free).

Supports dk=128/256/512. Mixed K/V types (e.g. tq3j K + q4_0 V) work via separate kernel instantiations.

### Per-layer variance analysis

Calibration on Gemma4 26B (512 tokens PTB) shows variance concentration varies significantly across layers. Top 25% of channels' share of total variance:

| Layer | Type | dk | Top 25% variance |
|:-----:|:----:|:--:|:-----------------:|
| 0 | SWA | 256 | 79.6% |
| 1 | SWA | 256 | 63.2% |
| 5 | Global | 512 | 34.4% |
| 6 | SWA | 256 | 57.9% |
|

## Working C Implementation — quant.cpp

We have implemented the full TurboQuant pipeline in pure C (zero dependencies) as part of [quant.cpp](https://github.com/quantumaikr/quant.cpp):

**Verified results (WikiText-2 PPL, SmolLM2 1.7B):**

| Config | Compression | PPL vs FP32 |
|--------|-------------|-------------|
| TQ 4-bit K + Q4 V | 6.9x | **+0.0%** |
| TQ 3-bit K + Q4 V (delta) | 8.5x | +1.3% |
| llama.cpp Q4_0 KV | 3.8x | +10.6% |

**Implementation includes:**
- PolarQuant (3/4-bit polar coordinate quantization)
- QJL (1-bit sign hash with random projection)
- TurboQuant composite (Polar + QJL hybrid)
- Delta compression (P-frame encoding, I-frame every 64 tokens)
- WHT + QJL + MSE pipeline
- NEON-optimized fused dot product kernels
- 34 unit tests, all passing

**Real hardware numbers (16GB Mac M1 Pro):**
- Llama 3.2 3B: 50K to 350K tokens context (6.9x)
- Gemma 4 26B MoE: 4K to 30K tokens context (6.9x)

The core quantize/dequantize/attention functions are self-contained in ~2K LOC of C and could be adapted for ggml type registration. Happy to collaborate on a PR if there is interest in integrating this approach.

Code: https://github.com/quantumaikr/quant.cpp
Paper reference: Zandieh et al., TurboQuant (ICLR 2026), arXiv:2504.19874

Following up on [@WaveboSF’s Blackwell/Ada matrix](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions/20969#discussioncomment-16449345) and [@dagbdagb’s question](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions/20969#discussioncomment-16450302) about what makes this practical for regular users:

from one **RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Workstation Edition 96 GB** pass, I’d be cautious about claiming a single global TurboQuant default already. My local results pointed more toward **per-family / per-surface defaults** than one universal recommendation.

A few concrete takeaways from my side:

- **Within Qwen3.5-27B**, `Config I + turbo3` stayed the best balanced `llama.cpp` lane in my pass: local PPL was essentially flat vs `Q8_0` (`+0.048%`), working set dropped by `2.49 GiB`, and prompt-side throughput improved.
- **native vLLM 0.18** was clearly the long-prefill specialist, but not the balanced default on this workstation: much higher memory footprint, slower decode.
- **On the Gemma side**, `q8_0/turbo4` validated cleanly at `64K`, `128K`, and `262K`, and was the strongest measured interactive long-context GGUF lane in this tested set on this workstation.
- I would **not** generalize that into “TurboQuant behaves roughly the same everywhere” yet. The thread is already showing the opposite:
  - `@WaveboSF`’s Blackwell vs Ada results
  - `@sandahltim`’s Qwen layer-adaptive findings
  - `@andrei-ace`’s Metal/Gemma4 results
  all point toward hardware- and model-family-specific behavior.

So my current bias would be:

1. conservative **per-family defaults**
2. explicit specialist modes where needed (balanced / throughput / prefill / long-context)
3. heuristics/autodetection only after we have enough hardware-family evidence to avoid encoding the wrong default
4. no cross-family promotion from tokenizer-dependent PPL alone

comments.author: WaveboSF
comments.body:
## Gemma 4 26B Accuracy Matrix — TurboQuant vs f16 (RTX 4090 + 5090)

Ran the math accuracy suite (13 direct + 39 delayed, filler 200/500/1000) against `gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-UD-Q5_K_XL` on the `turboquant_plus` fork build (CUDA 12.8, sm_89 + sm_120). Main question: does `head_dim=512` (outside the paper's validated range ≤256) corrupt recall under KV quantization?

**Short answer: No visible corruption. TurboQuant delta stays within f16's own non-determinism.**

| Config | RTX 4090 | RTX 5090 |
|---|---|---|
| f16 / f16 | **52/52 (100.0%)** | 51/52 (98.1%) |
| q8_0 / q8_0 | 51/52 (98.1%) | 50/52 (96.2%) |
| q8_0 / turbo4 | 51/52 (98.1%) | 51/52 (98.1%) |
| turbo4 / turbo4 | 51/52 (98.1%) | 50/52 (96.2%) |

**Key observations:**

- **The f16 baseline itself is not deterministic across architectures.** Same model, same prompts, `temperature=0.0` — RTX 4090 passes 52/52, RTX 5090 fails 1/52. That puts the noise floor at ~1/52 before TurboQuant enters the picture.
- **Every failure is a 2048-token truncation**, not a wrong answer. The model goes into verbose reasoning and hits the generation cap before emitting the final value. Empty `last_line`, full 2048 `eval_tokens`.
- **The dominant failure (`7*8 + 6*9 + 5*10 = 160`) occurs at `filler=0`** — zero KV pressure. Any KV-corruption hypothesis has to explain a failure that happens before KV is loaded. It doesn't.
- **TurboQuant vs f16 delta: 0–2 tests out of 52**, inside the cross-GPU f16 spread. Decode throughput essentially unchanged across configs (≤5% variance).

**Takeaway:** On Gemma 4 with `head_dim=512`, `turboquant_plus` shows no accuracy regression beyond baseline sampling noise. The failures that exist are a Gemma-4 verbosity/truncation issue, reproducible on f16.

Happy to run extended matrices (longer filler levels, more configs, Llama 3.3 70B head_dim=128 as crosscheck) if useful — [QLauncher](https://github.com/WaveboSF/TurboQuant-QLauncher) makes iteration quick.

Good info, this helps a lot.

**Repetition above 128K:** That tracks with what we see. All-tensor TQ3_1S compresses FFN weights too aggressively and the error compounds at long context. The mixed policy fixes this in our testing.

To requantize with attn-only TQ3_1S (FFN stays q8_0):

```
llama-quantize --allow-requantize \
  --tensor-type attn_q=TQ3_1S \
  --tensor-type attn_k=TQ3_1S \
  --tensor-type attn_v=TQ3_1S \
  --tensor-type attn_output=TQ3_1S \
  your-model-q8_0.gguf output-mixed.gguf q8_0

comments.author: caiovicentino
comments.body:
## Empirical findings from PolarQuant (40+ models quantized)

Following up on our earlier comment — we've now quantized 40+ models with Hadamard + Lloyd-Max and have concrete empirical data to share:

### Weight quantization (PQ5, 5-bit)

**Key finding: PQ5 can BEAT BF16 on benchmarks** (regularization effect):

| Benchmark | BF16 | PQ5 | Δ |
|-----------|------|-----|---|
| HellaSwag (0-shot, n=200) | 64.5% | **67.0%** | +2.5% |
| Winogrande (0-shot, n=200) | 72.5% | **73.0%** | +0.5% |
| ARC-Challenge | 61.0% | 60.0% | -1.0% |
| VRAM | 56.4 GB | **18.7 GB** | -67% |

*(Qwopus3.5-27B, PQ5 weights + torchao INT4 runtime)*

cos_sim consistently >0.998 across all 40+ models (LLMs, diffusion, video).

### KV cache quantization (Q3, 3-bit)

| Model | head_dim | Token match (Q3 vs FP16) | Memory savings |
|-------|----------|--------------------------|----------------|
| Qwen3.5-27B | 128 | 85%+ | 5.3x |
| Gemma-4-31B | 256 | 72% | 5.3x |
| Holo3-35B-A3B | 256 | testing | 5.3x |

Confirms your finding that **Keys need higher precision than Values**. We keep last 128 tokens in FP16 (residual buffer) which helps significantly.

### Video/diffusion models

PQ5 works identically on diffusion transformers:
- **OmniWeaving** (Tencent): 79 GB → 28 GB (-65%), generates video successfully
- **Wan2.2-Animate-14B**: 72 GB → 55 GB, cos_sim >0.999
- **FLUX.2-klein-9B**: 28 GB → 18.8 GB

### What we found about WHT vs alternatives

Agree with @Arclabs001 — WHT substantially outperforms random rotations. We also found:
- **Block size 128** is optimal (matches common head_dim, good Hadamard properties)
- **Lloyd-Max centroids** (iterative, 100 steps) beat uniform quantization by ~0.2 PPL
- **Bit-packing is essential** — 5-bit packed saves 37.5% vs int8 storage

All models available at: https://huggingface.co/caiovicentino1
Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.29078

comments.author: caiovicentino
comments.body:
Great question @TheTom! Here's what we've measured:

### Weight PPL (PQ5 → torchao INT4)

| Model | BF16 PPL | PQ5+INT4 PPL | Delta |
|-------|----------|-------------|-------|
| Qwen3.5-9B (dense) | 6.37 | **6.56** | +0.19 |
| torchao INT4 absmax | — | 6.68 | +0.31 |

PQ5 beats direct INT4 absmax by **0.12 PPL** — Hadamard rotation reduces MSE by 54% vs absmax at same bits.

### KV Cache Q3 — token match rates

You're right that architecture matters a lot:

| Model | Type | head_dim | KV Heads | Token Match |
|-------|------|----------|----------|-------------|
| Qwen3.5-9B | Dense | 128 | 8 | **85%+** |
| Qwen3.5-27B | Hybrid (attn+Mamba) | 128 | 8 | ~80% |
| Gemma-4-31B | Dense | 256 | 16 | **72%** |
| Holo3-35B-A3B | Hybrid (30 linear+10 full) | 256 | 2 | **28%** |

### Key observations:

1. **head_dim=128 → better** than head_dim=256 (more Hadamard blocks per vector, better compression)
2. **Dense → better** than hybrid (hybrid models have fewer KV-cached layers, less data to amortize quantization)
3. **More KV heads → better** (GQA with 2 heads vs 8+ — fewer heads means each head carries more critical info)
4. **Residual buffer helps**: keeping last 128 tokens in FP16 consistently improves match by 10-15%

We haven't measured PPL specifically for KV cache alone (our benchmark uses token match rate). If you have a PPL measurement setup for KV quantization we'd be interested in comparing.

All models: https://huggingface.co/caiovicentino1

comments.author: TheTom
comments.body:
Thanks for the detailed breakdown. I'd strongly recommend adding PPL measurement for the KV cache configs. Token match alone can be misleading. In our testing, we've seen models with reasonable-looking token match produce catastrophic PPL (3,500+) on certain model families. Without perplexity you can't tell if the output is coherent or gibberish, especially at long context where errors compound.


Here's the general validation suite many of us use:

1. **PPL (WikiText-2)**: Run perplexity on a standard corpus with the compressed KV cache active. This is the ground truth for compression quality. Compare delta vs FP16 baseline. Anything under +2% is good, +5% is usable, above that needs investigation.

2. **KLD (KL Divergence)**: Measures how much the output probability distribution shifts vs baseline. Catches cases where the model still picks the right token but confidence is degrading. Below 0.01 is excellent.

3. **NIAH (Needle-in-a-Haystack)**: Insert a known fact at various depths in a long context, ask the model to retrieve it. Tests whether compression preserves retrieval accuracy at different context lengths. We run Kamradt single-needle at 5 depths across 3+ context lengths. 30/30 perfect match = compression is safe for retrieval workloads.

All three matter because they catch different failure modes. PPL catches overall quality degradation, KLD catches subtle distribution shifts before they become visible in PPL, and NIAH catches long-context retrieval failures that PPL on short chunks can miss.

comments.author: caiovicentino
comments.body:
Good point @TheTom — token match rate is a proxy metric, not a direct quality measure. PPL for KV cache is the right thing to measure.

We'll add KV cache PPL to our next benchmark round. The setup would be:
1. Generate text with FP16 KV → compute PPL on continuation
2. Generate same text with Q3 KV → compute PPL on continuation
3. Report delta

For the repetition issue @Xcc313r4n7 saw with TQ3_1S on FFN weights — we see the same pattern. Our approach:
- **PQ5 for all weights** (not PQ3) — 5-bit is the minimum for stable FFN weights
- **PQ3 only for KV cache** — cache is more tolerant since it's regenerated each inference
- cos_sim 0.94 on MLP layers is our observed minimum threshold for coherent generation

This separation (PQ5 weights + PQ3 KV) avoids the compounding error problem at long context.

Re speculative decoding @jschoch — haven't tested that combination yet but it should work since PQ5→INT4 weights are standard torchao tensors. The KV cache compression would need speculative decoding to be KV-cache-aware though.

comments.author: caiovicentino
comments.body:
@jschoch Good question on speculative decoding. We've worked on MoE inference optimization in vLLM and have some observations:

### PQ5 weights + speculative decoding

PQ5 weights are dequanted to BF16 then compressed to torchao INT4 at load time. After that, they're standard `AffineQuantizedTensor` objects — speculative decoding should work out of the box since it only depends on the forward pass being correct. We co-authored the expert offloading commits in vLLM ([commit 1](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/commit/73a7584ae781d3a959ec90e4a8ed680ccfd8444a), [commit 2](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/commit/71ed1fc8086778f086417f62b5a6dcbfe3cb0d56)) and speculative decoding works with those MoE models.

### KV cache compression + speculative decoding

This is where it gets interesting. Speculative decoding generates N draft tokens then verifies them in a single forward pass. The KV cache from the draft model and target model need to be compatible. With PQ3 KV cache:

- **Draft model**: could use FP16 KV (small model, fast)
- **Target model**: PQ3 KV cache (large model, compressed)
- The verification step reads the target's KV cache — PQ3 dequant adds ~0.1ms/layer which shouldn't bottleneck since verification is compute-bound, not memory-bound

Haven't benchmarked the actual tok/s impact yet, but architecturally it should compose cleanly. The LFRU expert cache eviction we built for vLLM (cache=8 LFRU beats cache=16 LRU) could also interact well with speculative decoding for MoE models.

Would be a great experiment to run if anyone has a speculative decoding setup ready.

comments.author: AmesianX
comments.body:
**Gemma 4 26B-A4B-it: Research findings on 3-bit KV cache optimization for hybrid SWA architectures**

We conducted extensive research on achieving f16-equivalent quality with 3-bit KV cache on Gemma 4's hybrid SWA architecture (25 SWA layers + 5 global layers). Key research findings:

**Finding 1: SWA quantization noise dominates quality**
By profiling 2072+ V blocks across the full benchmark, we discovered that the small SWA cache (~300 MiB, 25 layers) was the dominant source of quality degradation. Despite being 5:1 in layer count vs global, its quantization noise masked every optimization attempt. Bypassing SWA to f16 (negligible memory cost) immediately revealed the true effect of all other techniques.

**Finding 2: V distribution characteristics (2072 samples)**

| Metric | Global V (D=512) | SWA V (D=256) |
|--------|-----------------|---------------|
| Kurtosis | 3.35 | 3.05 |
| Adjacent correlation | 0.09 | 0.15 |
| Distribution | Near-Gaussian | Near-Gaussian |

Both are near N(0,1) — standard Lloyd-Max is already near-optimal. Heavy-tail compensation (×1.05~1.25) showed no measurable benefit at this kurtosis level.

**Finding 3: Research journey (what we tried before the breakthrough)**

We spent extensive effort optimizing within the 3-bit scalar quantization framework before discovering the real bottleneck:

1. **Dithering** (Schuchman 1964) — subtractive/additive, scale 0.05~0.20 → no measurable effect
2. **Heavy-tail centroid scaling** (×1.05~1.25) — profiled kurtosis ~3.35, adapted boundaries/centroids → SWA mismatch negated all gains
3. **DPCM** (differential prediction, α=0.5) — measured adj_corr ~0.09, mixed-sign → made quality worse
4. **Sign-bit adaptive centroids** — 1 bit per block for centroid table selection → 0.004 bits/element, unmeasurable
5. **Dense-and-Sparse** (KVQuant-style outlier isolation) — simulated fixing top-3 outliers per block → only 8.5% MSE reduction
6. **Cross-layer delta compression** (XQuant-style) — measured 0% correlation between adjacent global layers → dead end
7. **V 256-WHT** (per-block independent WHT) → worse than nowht
8. **V 512-WHT** (same as K) → appeared equal to nowht... until SWA bypass revealed it was actually better

**The breakthrough:** All these experiments were poisoned by SWA quantization noise. Once SWA K+V was bypassed to f16 (~300 MiB, negligible overhead), the true signal emerged — 512-WHT + QJL restoration immediately achieved f16 parity.

**Finding 4: Double vs triple rotation**
attn_rot (upstream Hadamard) + WHT (TBQ Hadamard) = beneficial double rotation for pure 3-bit (TBQ3). But adding QJL's random projection creates harmful triple rotation. Solution: auto-disable attn_rot for TBQP types.

**Finding 5: 512-WHT for V (matching K)**
Previously V used direct quantization without WHT ("nowht"), which appeared superior. With SWA noise removed, 512-WHT proved better — aligning with the original TurboQuant paper's design where both K and V use the same rotation.

**Benchmark**
Model: [unsloth/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-GGUF](https://huggingface.co/unsloth/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-GGUF) (Q4_K_XL)
Hardware: DGX Spark GB10, 262K ctx, temp=0
Benchmark: [turboquant_math_accuracy.py](https://github.com/eullm/eullm/blob/main/bench/turboquant_math_accuracy.py) (2x2/3x3 matrix multiply + scalar arithmetic, filler 0-2000t, 65 tests, 10 runs each)

| Config | K cache | V cache | attn_rot_k | Global KV | SWA KV | Math Accuracy (10 runs) | Avg | Compression |
|--------|---------|---------|-----------|-----------|--------|------------------------|-----|-------------|
| tbqp3/tbq3 | 2-bit+QJL | 3-bit WHT | OFF | 990 MiB | 300 MiB(f16) | 37,38,40,38,38,36,37,36,37,37 | **37.4** | **4.2x** |
| tbq3/tbq3 | 3-bit WHT | 3-bit WHT | ON | 980 MiB | 300 MiB(f16) | 39,39,37,37,38,35,35,39,35,36 | **37.0** | **4.2x** |
| f16/f16 | f16 | f16 | OFF | 5120 MiB | 300 MiB(f16) | 37,36,36,36,36,38,36,38,37,36 | 36.6 | 1.0x |

comments.author: Stuartemk
comments.body:
Based on the technical discussion threads provided, we can evaluate the current status of **TurboQuant** as follows. The short answer is: **We are at 90-95% of a functional and stable implementation**, but it is not yet considered "100% ready for universal production" due to specific integration and stability challenges.

Here is the detailed breakdown of what is working and what remains to reach 100%:

### ✅ What is Working (The 90% Achieved)

1.  **Basic Functionality:**
    *   Functional implementations exist for **CPU (pure C)**, **Metal (Apple Silicon)**, and **CUDA (NVIDIA RTX 3090/4090/5090)**.
    *   Support for **Flash Attention** is operational in the latest versions of the forks.
    *   KV cache memory compression works as expected (approximately **4x to 5x** compression vs. FP16).

2.  **Quality (Perplexity/PPL):**
    *   In most tested models (Qwen3.5, Llama 3.3), the quality degradation is minimal, generally **<1% PPL delta** compared to FP16 or Q8_0.
    *   Some users report that with norm correction, TurboQuant can even **slightly outperform Q8_0** in quality.
    *   Token matching in "Needle-in-a-Haystack" (NIAH) tasks is high (8/8 in 12K token tests).

3.  **GPU Performance (After Optimizations):**
    *   Initially, there were severe decode penalties on Blackwell GPUs (RTX 5090) of up to 40%.
    *   With the implementation of fused kernels (V12 by @signalnine), the decode penalty dropped to **~7%**, and prefill is now even faster than FP16 in some configurations.
    *   On CPUs, performance is nearly identical to the baseline.

### ⚠️ What is Missing for 100% (Remaining Obstacles)

1.  **Integration into Main `llama.cpp` Repo:**
    *   Currently, it is **not in the main `llama.cpp` repository**. Users must compile from specific forks (like `turboquant_plus`, `spiritbuun`, or `quant.cpp`).
    *   Automated integration tests and official validation in the standard workflow are still pending.

2.  **Stability and Specific Bugs:**
    *   **CUDA:** Segfaults are reported in specific CUDA versions (e.g., 13.1) and memory issues (OOM) in certain commits.
    *   **Hybrid Models:** Models like **Gemma 4** have SWA (Sliding Window Attention) architectures that require special configurations (bypass to FP16 for certain layers) to avoid quality degradation. It is not "plug-and-play" for all architectures yet.
    *   **Weight Compression:** Experimentation with weight quantization (TQ3_1S) shows instability (text repetition >128K context) if applied too aggressively to all layers (including FFN). A mixed policy (Attention TQ, FFN Q8) is recommended.

3.  **Performance Parity:**
    *   Although quality is nearly identical, decode performance still carries a **5-10% penalty** compared to native FP16 on high-end hardware (due to real-time dequantization). To reach "100%" in speed, more optimized kernels would be needed to eliminate this overhead completely.

4.  **Algorithm Debate (QJL vs. MSE):**
    *   There is still community disagreement on whether to include the QJL algorithm (Algorithm 2) or only MSE (Algorithm 1). Some say QJL improves precision at very low bits, while others say it introduces unnecessary variance. This creates confusion regarding default configurations.

### 🚀 Current Recommendation (Advanced Beta Status)

If you want to use it today based on these threads:
*   **Do not use it for critical production** without PPL testing on your specific hardware.
*   **Use Mixed Policies:** Keep FFN layers at Q8_0 and apply TurboQuant only to Attention (K/V cache) to avoid instability.
*   **Hardware:** Works best on **Blackwell (RTX 5090)** with the recent fused kernels, and on **Apple Silicon (M-Series)** with Metal support.
*   **Configuration:** For models like Gemma 4, ensure you use the specific patches for SWA.

### Conclusion
We are **a few weeks or commits away** from having a stable integration in the main repository, once CUDA bugs are resolv

The right approach is to scale norm correction to find KLD optimum, which is what I did for my TCQ implementation. Norm correction also has different effects at different context lengths. What I've done is apply norm correction *at decode* for the exact amount of tokens in the context window at decode with the amount appropriate for that many tokens. You can check my branch for full implementation

comments.body:
@dagbdagb Great questions.

### f16 vs q8 as starting point

We always start from BF16/FP16. Quantizing from q8 compounds error. Our measurements on Qwen3.5-9B:
- BF16 → PQ5: PPL 6.56 (+0.19 from baseline 6.37)
- BF16 → torchao INT4 absmax: PPL 6.68 (+0.31)
- PQ5 produces 54% less MSE than absmax at same bits because Hadamard rotation normalizes the distribution

Starting from q8 would add ~0.1-0.2 PPL on top. Not recommended.

### Extending convert_hf_to_gguf.py for TQ/PQ weights

We have a working GGML integration for PolarQuant:
- GGML_TYPE_PQ3_0 (type 41), 14 files modified, compiles clean
- Block: 128 values → FWHT → Lloyd-Max Q3 → 50 bytes (3.125 bits/value)
- Usage: `--cache-type-k pq3_0 --cache-type-v pq3_0`

Currently KV cache only (runtime quant). For weight quantization in GGUF:
1. Add PQ5 type to GGML (PQ3 already there) ← straightforward
2. Extend convert script with Hadamard + Lloyd-Max ← straightforward
3. CUDA FWHT dequant kernel for inference ← the bottleneck

Right now we dequant to BF16 at load time then use torchao INT4. A native PQ5 kernel in llama.cpp would skip that step.

Happy to collaborate on the CUDA FWHT kernel — the math is identical to TurboQuant KV cache path, just applied to weights.

comments.author: AmesianX
comments.body:
Sharing some research findings on improving PPL for 3-bit KV cache at D=512 (Gemma 4).

We noticed a significant PPL gap (1.21x vs f16) at ctx=2048 that didn't match the math benchmark results. After investigation, we found several issues:

**1. V rotation bug (attn_rot_v)**

attn_rot was being applied to both K and V, but the IWHT decode path for V has no inverse rotation. K is safe because Q gets the same rotation and it cancels in the dot product (orthogonal transform property). Disabling V rotation gave the biggest single improvement.

**2. Attention score sharpening**

Quantization noise in K flattens the softmax distribution. We derived a correction factor α = 1 + 1/(2×SQNR) from MMSE theory — this compensates the flattening without empirical tuning. Different α for TBQ3 vs TBQP3 since their noise profiles differ.

**3. Per-block norm for D=512**

After 512-point WHT, each 256-half gets its own RMS norm instead of sharing a global norm. Exception: TBQP3 keeps global norm because QJL residual uses cross-block 512-WHT.

### Memory & Compression (262K ctx, Gemma 4 26B MoE)

| Config | Global KV | SWA KV | Total KV | Compression |
|--------|-----------|--------|----------|-------------|
| f16/f16 | 5,120 MiB | 300 MiB (f16) | 5,420 MiB | 1.0x |
| tbqp3/tbq3 | 990 MiB (K:500 + V:490) | 300 MiB (f16) | 1,290 MiB | 4.2x |

### PPL (wikitext-2-raw, ctx=2048)

| Config | PPL | ± | vs f16 |
|--------|-----|---|--------|
| f16/f16 | 419.8 | 3.37 | 1.00x |
| tbqp3/tbq3 (before) | 509.9 | — | 1.21x |
| **tbqp3/tbq3 (after)** | **454.7** | 7.27 | **1.08x** |

### Math Accuracy (262K ctx, temp=0, 35 problems × 10 runs)

| Config | 10 runs (/35) | Avg | Peak |
|--------|---------------|-----|------|
| tbqp3/tbq3 | 19,23,18,22,18,20,19,16,19,17 | 19.1 | 23 |
| f16/f16 | 19,20,21,20,20,21,21,19,20,20 | 20.1 | 21 |

The attention sharpening idea might be applicable to other KV quantization schemes (q4_0, q8_0) since the SQNR-based derivation is general. Curious if anyone has seen similar softmax flattening effects with other quant types.

comments.author: domvox
comments.body:
That's expected mainline behavior, not something specific to my port.

`--swa-full` makes the SWA cache full-size instead of window-sized, which increases KV memory substantially. In current HEAD, SWA is created with the same `type_k` / `type_v` as the rest of the KV cache, so `-ctk turbo3 -ctv turbo3` should apply to SWA as well — I don't think SWA is being forced to f16 here.

There was an upstream attempt to keep SWA unquantized (#21277), but it was reverted in #21332, so current HEAD lets SWA follow the configured cache types.

The memory increase you're seeing with `--swa-full` should be from the larger SWA allocation size, not from an f16 override. Without `--swa-full`, the default windowed SWA cache should be much lighter.

Great work on TurboQuant! We've been working on the same WHT + Lloyd-Max approach independently — published as PolarQuant ([arxiv.org/abs/2603.29078](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.29078)).

**What we have working:**

1. **KV cache (Q2/Q3/Q4)** — production-ready in our vLLM plugin ([polarengine-vllm](https://github.com/caiovicentino/polarengine-vllm/tree/main/polarengine_vllm/kv_cache)). Full BitPacker for 2/3/4-bit, Lloyd-Max centroids, WHT rotation. Benchmarked on RTX PRO 6000:
   - Q3 KV: 5.3x compression, **zero speed overhead** (44.1 vs 43.5 tok/s baseline)
   - Code generation: 100% token match vs FP16
   - [Benchmark details](https://huggingface.co/caiovicentino1/Qwopus3.5-9B-v3-PolarQuant-Q5)

2. **Weight quantization (Q5)** — GGML_TYPE_PQ5_0 integrated into llama.cpp fork (14 files, builds clean). Block: 82 bytes / 128 values = 5.125 bpv. Standalone C test: cos_sim 0.998783.
   - CUDA kernel with FWHT in shared memory (718 lines)
   - GGUF converter from HF PQ5 safetensors (866 lines)

3. **49 quantized models on HuggingFace** — text, video (Wan2.2, OmniWeaving), MoE (Gemma 4), multimodal. All use WHT + Lloyd-Max.

**Findings that align with yours:** Lloyd-Max alone (without QJL) is optimal. Hadamard makes the distribution near-Gaussian, and Lloyd-Max centroids are MSE-optimal for Gaussian — adding anything on top is redundant.

**Your finding about K needing more bits than V** is interesting — we'll test asymmetric allocation. Makes sense: K determines attention routing, V is just the payload.

**Bonus — native quantized training:** We're also exploring WHT + Lloyd-Max + STE *during training* (not just inference). PoC at 125M showed Q5 native **beats** BF16 baseline by 15.8% PPL. Currently scaling to 7B. The Hadamard rotation acts as a regularizer (QGen 2024).

Happy to collaborate. GGML patch: [ggml-integration/](https://github.com/caiovicentino/polarengine-vllm/tree/main/ggml-integration)

comments.author: AmesianX
comments.body:
We're exploring applying a dynamic SQNR-based sharpening function to attention scores. The static α (fixed constant per quant type) already improved PPL from 1.21x to 1.08x vs f16, but we think a context-aware function could do better.

### The problem

Quantization noise in K flattens the softmax distribution. More tokens competing → higher chance a noisy score steals softmax mass from the correct token. This worsens with longer context.

### Static formula (current)

```
α = 1 + 1/(2 × SQNR_eff)
```

### Dynamic formula (next step)

```
α(N) = 1 + 1/(2 × SQNR_eff) × √(ln N / ln N₀)
```

- N = current KV token count (actual fill, not max ctx)
- N₀ = 2048 (reference context where static α was validated)
- √(ln N) from Extreme Value Theory — expected max noise among N tokens grows as √(2 ln N)

### Why TBQ3 and TBQP3 need different α

TBQ3 (3-bit Lloyd-Max): clean per-element noise only → effective SQNR ≈ 31.2 → small α

TBQP3 (2-bit MSE + 1-bit QJL): the QJL correction `d_qjl × Σ(Q_wht2[i] × sign[i])` adds a **second noise source** to attention scores. QJL reduces K reconstruction MSE (good), but increases attention score variance (bad for softmax). So TBQP3 needs stronger sharpening despite better reconstruction.

| Type | Structure | Effective SQNR | α coefficient |
|------|-----------|----------------|---------------|
| TBQ3 | 3-bit Lloyd-Max (8 levels) | 31.2 | 0.016 |
| TBQP3 | 2-bit MSE + 1-bit QJL | 13.8 | 0.036 |
| TBQ4 | 4-bit Lloyd-Max (16 levels) | 56.2 | 0.009 |
| TBQP4 | 3-bit MSE + 1-bit QJL | 24.5 | 0.020 |

### Dynamic α by context size

| ctx N | TBQ3 | TBQP3 | TBQ4 | TBQP4 |
|-------|------|-------|------|-------|
| 256 | 1.012 | 1.027 | 1.007 | 1.015 |
| 512 | 1.013 | 1.030 | 1.007 | 1.017 |
| 1024 | 1.015 | 1.033 | 1.008 | 1.018 |
| **2048** | **1.016** | **1.036** | **1.009** | **1.020** |
| 4096 | 1.017 | 1.038 | 1.009 | 1.021 |
| 8192 | 1.018 | 1.041 | 1.010 | 1.023 |
| 32768 | 1.019 | 1.044 | 1.011 | 1.025 |
| 131072 | 1.020 | 1.047 | 1.011 | 1.026 |
| **262144** | **1.021** | **1.048** | **1.012** | **1.027** |

The full range is narrow (1.007–1.048) since √(ln N) grows very slowly — 128× context increase only shifts α by ~0.012. This validates using a fixed constant as a practical first approximation.

Implementation cost: one `logf()` per token in the attention kernel. The dynamic α adapts naturally as KV cache fills up — similar to AGC (Automatic Gain Control) in radio receivers.

@spiritbuun — saw your note on finding alpha scaling curves per context size. Our approach derives α from SQNR theory rather than empirical fitting, and accounts for different noise profiles across quant types (TBQ vs TBQP). Would be interesting to compare curves.

Code: https://github.com/AmesianX/TurboQuant/releases/tag/v1.5.2

comments.author: domvox
comments.body:
**SWA bypass confirmed on HIP/ROCm (gfx1100, RX 7900 XTX)**

@AmesianX — your SWA finding checks out on AMD too. I independently reproduced it on a clean HIP/ROCm TurboQuant port on llama.cpp HEAD. This lines up well with the recent finding in this thread that SWA K/V quantization was masking the true TurboQuant signal.

**What I observed on Gemma 4 26B-A4B-it Q4_K_M (Wikitext-2, 20 chunks, ctx=512):**

| Config | Global KV | SWA KV | Total KV | PPL | ± |
|--------|-----------|--------|----------|-----|---|
| f16 / f16 baseline | 40 MiB | 400 MiB | 440 MiB | **24,882** | 2,647 |
| turbo3 / turbo3 on all layers | 8 MiB | 78 MiB | 86 MiB | **>100,000** | — |
| turbo3 on global + f16 on SWA | 8 MiB | 400 MiB | 408 MiB | **27,706** | 2,975 |

So on this model, quantizing **all** KV layers is catastrophic, but keeping **SWA K/V in f16** while compressing only the global layers restores usable quality and dramatically improves over all-layer turbo3.

I implemented this as separate SWA cache-type overrides:

- `--cache-type-k-swa`
- `--cache-type-v-swa`

The implementation is small and isolated:

- `GGML_TYPE_COUNT` used as sentinel meaning "follow main --cache-type-k/v"
- models without SWA never instantiate `llama_kv_cache_iswa`, so they are unaffected
- current diff is ~59 added lines across 11 files

**Example:**

```bash
llama-perplexity -m gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-Q4_K_M.gguf -ngl 99 \
  --cache-type-k turbo3 --cache-type-v turbo3 \
  --cache-type-k-swa f16 --cache-type-v-swa f16 \
  --chunks 20 -f wiki.test.raw
```

On a non-SWA model (Qwen3.5-27B), I'm not seeing any apparent regression from these changes in my tests.

Hardware: RX 7900 XTX (gfx1100), ROCm 6.4
Branch: `feature/turboquant-hip-port-clean` in [domvox/llama.cpp-turboquant-hip](https://github.com/domvox/llama.cpp-turboquant-hip)

I'd be interested in maintainer feedback on the API shape:

1. Is `GGML_TYPE_COUNT` an acceptable sentinel here?
2. Are separate SWA cache-type flags the right interface, or would you prefer a different configuration mechanism?
3. Any ABI concerns with adding `type_k_swa` / `type_v_swa` to `llama_context_params`?

comments.body:
**Adaptive Alpha Scaling for Turbo Dequant Norms: New Finding**

Inspired by @spiritbuun's [Trellis-Coded Quantization paper](https://huggingface.co/datasets/spiritbuun/turboquant-tcq-kv-cache) and his work on adaptive alpha scaling for KLD optimization, I ran a systematic experiment on norm scaling for turbo3 dequantization.

**Setup:** M5 Max 128GB and M2 Pro 32GB. Three models (phi-4 14B Q8_0, Qwen3.5-35B MoE Q8_0, Mistral-24B Q4_K_M), four context lengths (512, 2048, 8192, 32K), four alpha values (0.99, 1.00, 1.01, 1.02). All tests with q8_0-K / turbo3-V, KLD measured against fp16 baseline logits.

**The idea:** Multiply the stored turbo3 norm by a fixed alpha factor at dequant time. Zero speed overhead (one multiply per block).

**Key finding: Q4_K_M models benefit significantly from alpha=1.02.**

Mistral-24B Q4_K_M (M5 Max), alpha=1.02 vs baseline (alpha=1.00):

| Context | KLD baseline | KLD alpha=1.02 | Improvement | PPL impact |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 512 | 0.00536 | 0.00456 | **-15.0%** | improved |
| 2048 | 0.00558 | 0.00463 | **-16.9%** | improved |
| 8192 | 0.00454 | 0.00378 | **-16.8%** | improved |
| 32K | 0.00356 | 0.00319 | **-10.4%** | within noise |

Alpha=1.02 wins on every metric at every context length: KLD, PPL, RMS delta-p, and Same-top-p.

**M2 Pro results (Qwen2.5-7B Q8_0):**

| Context | Best alpha | KLD baseline | KLD best | Improvement |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 512 | 1.00 | 0.02876 | 0.02876 | no benefit |
| 2048 | 1.01 | 0.02381 | 0.02181 | **-8.4%** |
| 8192 | 1.01 | 0.01303 | 0.01259 | **-3.4%** |

Q8_0 model shows modest benefit at longer context only. Alpha=1.00 is optimal at 512.

**Summary across all models (M5 Max):**

| Model | Weights | Best alpha | KLD gain |
|---|---|---|---|
| phi-4 14B | Q8_0 | 1.01-1.02 | 1-4% |
| Qwen3.5-35B MoE | Q8_0 | varies | mixed |
| **Mistral-24B** | **Q4_K_M** | **1.02** | **10-17%** |

**Root cause:** Q4_K_M weight quantization introduces a systematic norm bias in the attention computation. The WHT-rotated KV vectors interact with quantized-weight Q projections, and the compounded error shifts the optimal dequant scale slightly above 1.0. Alpha=1.02 corrects this. Q8_0 weights are precise enough that the norm is already correct at alpha=1.00.

This is consistent with the asymmetric K/V finding: K quantization stacks with weight quantization. Alpha scaling is another manifestation of the same quantization stacking effect.

**Implementation:** Single env var. Set `TURBO_ALPHA=102` before launch. Applied to Metal and CPU dequant paths.

```bash
TURBO_ALPHA=102 llama-server -m model-Q4_K_M.gguf -ctk q8_0 -ctv turbo3 -fa on
```

PR: [TheTom/llama-cpp-turboquant#60](https://github.com/TheTom/llama-cpp-turboquant/pull/60)

Credit to @spiritbuun for the adaptive alpha scaling concept. His TCQ paper demonstrated that norm correction is a significant lever for KLD optimization. Our experiments found the effect is primarily weight-quant-dependent rather than context-dependent, but his intuition about norm correction was the key insight that motivated this work.

Full experiment writeup with all raw data: [PR #60 comment](https://github.com/TheTom/llama-cpp-turboquant/pull/60#issuecomment-4200293045)

comments.author: unamedkr
comments.body:
Sharing a data point from quant.cpp ([github.com/quantumaikr/quant.cpp](https://github.com/quantumaikr/quant.cpp)), a small single-header C engine that ports the TurboQuant paper structure end-to-end.

After landing a literal port (RHT → Lloyd-Max-Gaussian codebook → 1-bit QJL residual + ‖r‖₂) we ran a Karpathy-loop ablation on Llama 3.2 3B perplexity and got an interesting empirical result that may be relevant to the discussion here:

**The 1-bit QJL residual stage contributed _byte-identical zero_ to attention scores**, regardless of input. Disabling it produced perplexity values bit-for-bit equal to the full pipeline. We believe this is because the constant `√(π/2)/m` in the unbiased estimator is derived for Gaussian projection rows, and on Rademacher (±1) rows the per-key contribution gets dwarfed by the residual norm scaling — which after a good codebook fit is small enough that the entire QJL term rounds away.

Independently, [@Arclabs001 reported](#) similar findings (MSE-only ≥ MSE+QJL on their tests) — so this might be a more general issue with the Rademacher-row variant in practice rather than something specific to our code.

We then took the freed 16 bytes per block and reinvested them in a 2× larger Lloyd-Max codebook (3-bit → 4-bit / 8 → 16 levels at the same block size). Combined with max-abs scaling instead of theoretical √d, the resulting single-stage estimator is structurally simpler than the paper's two-stage and empirically beats both our previous baseline and llama.cpp q4_0 KV at the same 4-bit budget on Llama 3.2 3B:

| KV type | bits/elem | PPL | Δ vs FP32 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| FP32 | 32 | 13.56 | — |
| **quant.cpp turbo_kv_4b (Variant F)** | 4 | **14.28** | **+5.3%** |
| quant.cpp uniform_4b | 4 | 14.41 | +6.3% |
| llama.cpp q4_0 KV (rough comparison) | 4 | ~14.99 | +10.6% |

We're not claiming to reproduce the paper's exact LongBench numbers (those are on Llama 3.1 8B and may also benefit from per-channel outlier handling we don't implement). Just sharing that **dropping the QJL stage and reinvesting in codebook resolution worked better than the literal paper port** in our embedded-targets benchmark.

If anyone is pursuing the literal paper algorithm and seeing the QJL stage actually help, we'd love to know what's different — could be Gaussian rows, larger sketch dim, different data, or a constant we're getting wrong. Full Karpathy-loop history with 6 rounds of variants is in [bench/results/turboquant_reproduction.md](https://github.com/quantumaikr/quant.cpp/blob/main/bench/results/turboquant_reproduction.md), and the ablation commit is [4da6915](https://github.com/quantumaikr/quant.cpp/commit/4da6915).

quant.cpp's angle is the embedded/edge niche (single-header C, runs on iOS / Android / WASM / MSVC / microcontrollers), so we're not pursuing a llama.cpp PR ourselves — but happy to share kernels or details if any of the in-flight ggml integrations want to compare notes.

comments.author: TheTom
comments.body:
@TimDettmers 

Coming back through this after the recent EDEN exchange surfaced a few related "TurboQuant is just X" framings worth addressing in one place.

A few clarifications:

**TurboQuant+ uses scalar Lloyd-Max, not vector quantization.** That's the Google TurboQuant lineage (arXiv:2504.19874 §3 specifies scalar quantizers per coordinate after random rotation). HIGGS contributes vector codebooks (CLVQ) for the weight-quantization setting; TurboQuant+ doesn't use them. Empirical comparison earlier in this thread ([comment 16489646](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions/20969#discussioncomment-16489646)) showed scalar Lloyd-Max beating the vector-grid variant by 11.4× MSE and 51× speed on synthetic post-WHT Gaussian (d=128, b=4). On real KV (across the model families referenced earlier in the thread), the same direction holds, though the gap narrows in practice. Vector codebooks are well-suited for the weight setting HIGGS targets; for rotated KV at b=3–4, scalar is the empirical winner.

If there's a specific vector baseline (codebook construction, training distribution, bit allocation, and rotation setup) you consider canonical for the HIGGS setting, I'm happy to run that directly for a like-for-like comparison.

**On "first to propose VQ + Hadamard":** RaBitQ (SIGMOD May 2024, [arXiv:2405.12497](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.12497)) also combines random rotation with vector quantization prior to HIGGS (Nov 2024), and the rotation + quantization pattern itself goes back further: DRIVE (NeurIPS 2021), EDEN (ICML 2022), RaBitQ (May 2024), HIGGS (Nov 2024), TurboQuant (Apr 2025). HIGGS is one instantiation in that lineage: a particular vector-quantization design within a broader rotation+quantization pattern. HIGGS's genuinely novel contributions on this stack are the linearity theorem (per-layer ℓ₂ MSE → PPL) and dynamic per-layer bit allocation via DP, both of which are real and worth citing. I'll add the full antecedent stack to the README's prior-work section in the next docs pass.

**On the rename:** TurboQuant+ specifically implements and extends the Google TurboQuant algorithm (scalar Lloyd-Max quantization after rotation, with production modifications on top). Renaming to HIGGS would collapse two distinct design choices (scalar vs vector quantization) into one label and, in doing so, misrepresent the lineage in the opposite direction. HIGGS targets weight quantization with vector codebooks; this work targets KV cache with scalar quantization. It would also create downstream confusion given existing usage under the current name.

Happy to compare against a stronger vector baseline on real rotated KV tensors if you have one to run. The empirical question (scalar vs vector for rotated KV at b=3–4 with WHT) is straightforward to test and seems like the cleanest place to settle it empirically.

comments.author: unamedkr
comments.body:
@TimDettmers — thank you for the correction, you're right. We've updated quant.cpp's docs to credit HIGGS.

I went back and read [HIGGS (arXiv:2411.17525)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.17525) carefully. The structural pattern of *Random Hadamard Transform + MSE-optimal grid quantization on the rotated values* was introduced by HIGGS in Nov 2024 for weight quantization, ~5 months before the published TurboQuant. Our shipped Variant F (which we initially developed as a port of TurboQuant) is empirically much closer to HIGGS than to the published TurboQuant — through 9 rounds of Karpathy-loop ablation we found the QJL residual stage contributed *byte-identical zero* to attention scores and removed it, then reinvested the freed bytes into a finer Lloyd-Max scalar codebook. What remained is essentially HIGGS-style scalar grid quantization on RHT-rotated values, applied to KV cache.

| Aspect | HIGGS (Nov 2024) | TurboQuant (Apr 2026) | quant.cpp Variant F |
|---|---|---|---|
| Application | **Weights** | KV cache | KV cache |
| RHT preprocessing | **✓ origin** | ✓ | ✓ |
| Quantizer | Vector grids (CLVQ) | Scalar Lloyd-Max | Scalar Lloyd-Max |
| Outlier channels | — | 32 ch. split | — (4bo variant: 8 ch.) |
| Residual stage | — | 1-bit QJL | — (dropped via ablation) |

Updated commits:
- [9481870](https://github.com/quantumaikr/quant.cpp/commit/9481870) — README + README.ko + reproduction doc credit HIGGS, document the lineage, explicitly state we don't claim our shipped variant is the published TurboQuant algorithm

Also relevant for this discussion: we just published [v0.6.4](https://github.com/quantumaikr/quant.cpp/releases/tag/v0.6.4) which corrects an earlier wrong claim of ours. Our [v0.6.3 release notes](https://github.com/quantumaikr/quant.cpp/releases/tag/v0.6.3) said "turbo_kv beats fp32 KV speed at 7× compression". That was an artifact of our fp32 attention path being unoptimized scalar — once we added NEON to the fp32 path too, the honest gap is `−7%` vs fp32, not `+10%`. We caught and corrected it through validation before it spread further.

| Type | Bytes/block | Compression | tok/s | vs FP32 | PPL Δ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| FP32 KV (NEON) | — | 1× | **14.63** | baseline | — |
| `turbo_kv_4b` (default) | 72 | 7.1× | 13.57 | **−7.2%** | +5.7% |
| `turbo_kv_5b` (quality) | 88 | 5.8× | 12.90 | −11.8% | **+0.7%** |

Reference C implementation: [`integrations/llamacpp/tq_kv_cache.cpp`](https://github.com/quantumaikr/quant.cpp/blob/main/integrations/llamacpp/tq_kv_cache.cpp). Single-header version: [`quant.h`](https://github.com/quantumaikr/quant.cpp/blob/main/quant.h). Full Karpathy loop history with ablations and reverts: [`bench/results/turboquant_reproduction.md`](https://github.com/quantumaikr/quant.cpp/blob/main/bench/results/turboquant_reproduction.md).

quant.cpp's angle remains the embedded niche (single-header C, runs on iOS / Android / WASM / MSVC / microcontrollers), so we're not pursuing a llama.cpp PR ourselves — but happy to share kernels or comparison data if any of the in-flight ggml integrations want to use them. And @TimDettmers, if you have thoughts on whether our scalar Lloyd-Max codebook should instead use HIGGS-style vector grids for KV cache, that's a research direction we'd welcome guidance on.

comments.author: TimDettmers
comments.body:
Thank you @unamedkr, much appreciated! Regarding HIGGS vector grids. There are two things: vector vs scalar (quantization) and Lloyd-Max vs CLVQ (optimization). 

Lloyd-Max optimization yields local optima codebook while CLVQ yield globally optimal ones. But if you do enough random k-means inits and use a very large sample size the relative difference between CLVQ and Lloyd-Max is smaller than 0.5% (essentially identical). 

As for vector vs scalar: this is a very big difference. Definitely use vector optimal codebooks. It is the single largest improvement that you can make. I was assuming that you were already doing this. Scalar + Lloyd-Max is quite weak in terms of quantization performance.

comments.author: TheTom
comments.body:
Ran a quick empirical test on this since the scalar-vs-vector question keeps coming up. On synthetic post-WHT Gaussian data (d=128, 10K vectors, 4-bit budget), a scalar Lloyd-Max codebook outperformed the vector-grid variant I tested by a wide margin in both MSE and inner-product error, and was also much faster:

| Method | MSE | IP Error | Time |
|--------|-----|----------|------|
| Scalar Lloyd-Max | 0.0000740 | 0.0001248 | 22ms |
| TQ-style 3b + 1b residual | 0.0002734 | 0.0004894 | 31ms |
| 2D vector-grid variant | 0.0008453 | 0.0012671 | 1,135ms |
| RaBitQ-style 1-bit binary | 0.0031355 | 0.0057636 | 6ms |

Related papers:
- RaBitQ (May 2024): https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.12497
- HIGGS (Nov 2024): https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.17525
- TurboQuant (Apr 2025 preprint): https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.19874

In this post-rotation setting, scalar Lloyd-Max was 11.4x lower MSE and 51x faster than the vector-grid setup I tested. That matches the intuition that WHT is trying to make coordinates closer to independent and Gaussian, which reduces the amount of cross-coordinate structure available for vector quantizers to exploit. So my current evidence points toward scalar quantization being the stronger choice for rotated KV-cache data in this synthetic setup, though I'd still treat that as an empirical result rather than a universal claim.

At the end of the day we all want this faster and better. Happy to compare against stronger vector-codebook baselines on real rotated KV tensors if anyone has a stronger baseline handy. Appreciate the input, Tim.

comments.author: unamedkr
comments.body:
**Update from quant.cpp**: after our v0.6.4 honest correction (where we walked back the wrong "beats fp32" claim), profile-driven analysis revealed the entire speed gap was in the inner attention loop, not in dispatch or memory bandwidth. We've now landed [v0.7.0](https://github.com/quantumaikr/quant.cpp/releases/tag/v0.7.0) where `turbo_kv_4b` matches fp32 KV speed at 7.1× compression, validated across 3 models.

## What changed (Round 10)

Profile data at long context (Llama 3.2 3B, PPL eval, seq_len ~950, **CPU-only build, no Metal**):

```
                  matmul    attention   other    total
  fp32           38.6 ms    15.7 ms    1.4 ms   55.7 ms
  turbo_kv_4b    38.9 ms    19.8 ms    1.8 ms   60.5 ms   ← 8% gap, all in attention
```

The matmul code path is identical between fp32 and quant (Q/K/V projection over Q4 weights). The 8% speed gap was **entirely** in the attention dot-product loop. **It was compute-bound, not memory-bound** — surprising for a 16-entry LUT lookup.

Root cause: our inner loop was scalar (per-element LUT load + mul + add) while fp32 was 4-way NEON SIMD. About 2× more instructions per element.

## The fix: NEON `vqtbl1q_s8` 16-entry table lookup

Apple Silicon has `vqtbl1q_s8`, a single instruction that does 16 byte-table lookups across 16 lanes. Perfect for a 16-entry codebook.

```c
// Once at startup: quantize 16 Lloyd-Max-Gaussian centroids to int8
static int8_t s_cb_i8[16];
for (int j = 0; j < 16; j++) s_cb_i8[j] = (int8_t)(cb[j] * (127.0f / 2.7326f));
int8x16_t cb_vec = vld1q_s8(s_cb_i8);

// Per attention call, 32 elements per iteration:
for (d = 0; d + 31 < dim; d += 32) {
    uint8x16_t bytes = vld1q_u8(mi + d/2);                    // 16B = 32 nibbles
    uint8x16_t low_nib  = vandq_u8(bytes, vdupq_n_u8(0x0F));
    uint8x16_t high_nib = vshrq_n_u8(bytes, 4);
    int8x16_t low_vals  = vqtbl1q_s8(cb_vec, low_nib);        // 1 instr, 16 gathers
    int8x16_t high_vals = vqtbl1q_s8(cb_vec, high_nib);
    // ... interleave + int8→fp32 + per-block scale + vfmaq_f32
}
```

The int8 quantization of the 16 centroids costs ~1% precision, well below our regression test threshold of `cosine ≥ 0.99`.

## Results across 3 models

| Model | turbo_kv_4b speed gap (R9 → R10) | PPL Δ vs FP32 |
|---|---|---|
| SmolLM2 135M | −14.5% → −3.1% | +5.7% |
| Llama 3.2 1B | −16.3% → −1.3% | +5.4% |
| **Llama 3.2 3B** | **−8.4% → +4.5%** ⬆ | **+3.8%** |

PPL also slightly improved on all three models — the int8 discretization happens to align favorably (or it's regression-to-mean noise; both are within the threshold).

## Honest framing — and a meta point

Our previous comment in this thread had to walk back a "beats fp32" claim because we had benchmarked fp32 in scalar form while quant was NEON. After fixing that, the honest gap was −7%. We then thought the gap might be unfixable on CPU.

The lesson from Round 10: **the answer existed; we just hadn't profiled to find it**. Nine rounds of guessing at local fusions missed what the `--profile` flag would have revealed in 30 seconds. The actual bottleneck wasn't memory bandwidth or LUT access — it was scalar vs SIMD instruction count.

For others in this thread implementing TurboQuant-class compression on Apple Silicon: if your KV path is slower than fp32, profile first. If the gap is in attention rather than dispatch, the answer is probably `vqtbl1q_s8`.

## quant.cpp position

Same as before: we ship a single-header C reference engine for embedded targets (iOS, Android, WASM, MSVC, microcontrollers). Not pursuing a llama.cpp PR ourselves. v0.7.0 release: https://github.com/quantumaikr/quant.cpp/releases/tag/v0.7.0

Reference impl: [`integrations/llamacpp/tq_kv_cache.cpp`](https://github.com/quantumaikr/quant.cpp/blob/main/integrations/llamacpp/tq_kv_cache.cpp). The Round 10 attention kernel is in [`src/core/tq_turbo_kv.c`](https://github.com/quantumaikr/quant.cpp/blob/main/src/core/tq_turbo_kv.c#L460).

Cross-impl benchmarking welcome. We measure CPU-only on Apple

## HIP/ROCm TurboQuant update — full benchmarks (2026-04-10)

Posting here since this is where the TurboQuant community lives. Full writeup in [Discussion #21526](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions/21526).

**TL;DR:** Symmetric turbo3 K+V on AMD (RX 7900 XTX) with K-side sharpening:
- GSM8K: **72.0%** on full 1319 problems (vs 71.9% f16) — Qwen3.5-27B
- NIAH: **20/20** at 2K–16K
- Tool calling: **15/15**
- PPL: +0.02% at 4K, **-0.9% at 16K** (turbo3 matches or beats f16)
- Speed: 1-2% overhead
- Gemma 4 26B: -1.5% GSM8K drop with SWA bypass config

**Findings relevant to this thread:**

1. **K-side vs V-side sharpening depends on K/V symmetry.** spiritbuun's "alpha only on V" is correct for asymmetric q8_0-K + turbo3-V. For symmetric turbo3-K + turbo3-V, K-side sharpening is critical (83% vs 74% without).

2. **Boundary V hybrid fix.** TheTom's LA-V7 boundary detection uses raw layer index, which mis-targets hybrid architectures (Qwen3.5: 64 layers, 16 KV). Fixed to use KV layer ordinal.

3. **Gemma 4 D=512 FA dispatch on HIP.** Global attention layers (head_dim=512) fall through to TILE FA kernel which has no turbo3 dequant. Proper VEC dequant made accuracy worse (68% vs 81%). Hypothesis: TILE fallback acts as effective layer dropout, less harmful than structured quantization noise.

Repo: https://github.com/domvox/llama.cpp-turboquant-hip

comments.author: TheTom
comments.body:
I validated TriAttention with TurboQuant+ across three model families (Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen3.5-27B, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B) at 32K and 64K context. Paper-faithful scoring breaks needle-in-a-haystack retrieval at 90% retention (10% eviction). At 75% pruning the retrieval damage will be significantly worse.

Concrete test to verify: insert a random needle (e.g. "PURPLE ELEPHANT 7742") at character positions 400, 65000, and 120000 in a 32K wikitext prompt. Generate with `--no-display-prompt` and check if the model retrieves the exact string. If it fails at the end position, the eviction policy is dropping semantically important tokens.

I found that a minimal hybrid policy (prefix protection for the first 128 tokens plus per-segment eviction quota) moves to a strictly better Pareto point: +0.31% PPL at 90% retention with clean NIAH at all three positions on standard transformers. At 64K context the PPL delta drops to effectively zero. The implementation self-calibrates during inference from the model's own Q projections. No training, no offline calibration files, no external dependencies. One CLI flag.

Full methodology, strict NIAH results, speed optimization details, and documented negative results (hybrid Mamba+Attention architectures do not transfer on retrieval) are published here:

https://github.com/TheTom/turboquant_plus/blob/main/docs/papers/triattention-v3.md

comments.author: TheTom
comments.body:
I documented this empirically across seven model families in March. Boundary layers need higher bit budgets because they handle the input/output translation while interior layers do the coupled representation work. It is built into the TurboQuant+ stack as a protection rule.

Sharpe 2026 gives the physics derivation (driven lattice nodes under different dynamics than interior oscillators). I also tested whether boundary layers should be excluded from eviction scoring and got a clean negative result, which refined the understanding further.

Asymmetric KV paper (boundary sensitivity + why V compresses freely but K does not): github.com/thetom/turboquant_plus/blob/main/docs/papers/asymmetric-kv-compression.md

TriAttention V3 paper (boundary skip experiment, Section 4.8): github.com/thetom/turboquant_plus/blob/main/docs/papers/triattention-v3.md

comments.body:
**TurboQuant validation: GLM-4.5-Air (106B MoE) on 3x RTX 3090 (Ampere sm_86)**

Filling the CUDA / 100B+ gap flagged earlier in this thread. Build: `TheTom/llama-cpp-turboquant` `feature/turboquant-kv-cache` @ `8590cbf`, `-DGGML_CUDA=ON -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=86`.

**Model:** `huihui-ai/Huihui-GLM-4.5-Air-abliterated-GGUF` Q4_K_M (110.47B params, 106B.A12B MoE, 46 layers)

**Hardware:** 3x RTX 3090 (72 GB VRAM total), 125 GB system RAM

**Config:**
```
--n-gpu-layers 999 --n-cpu-moe 8 --split-mode layer --tensor-split 20,13,13
--flash-attn on --ctx-size <varies> -ctk <varies> -ctv <varies>
```

With `--tensor-split 20,13,13` compensating for the first 8 layers' experts being CPU-resident (those land on CUDA0, so CUDA0 gets more layer count to balance VRAM).

### KV cache comparison (the headline number)

| Config | Context | KV total | K | V |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `q8_0 / q8_0` baseline | 32,768 | 3128 MiB | 1564 | 1564 |
| **`turbo3 / turbo3`** | **131,072** | **4600 MiB** | 2300 | 2300 |

**4x the context for 1.47x the KV cache.** Per-token KV dropped from ~95 KiB/tok (q8_0) to ~36 KiB/tok (turbo3) — roughly 2.6x effective compression ratio.

Projected q8_0 cost at 128K would have been ~12.5 GB, which does not fit our per-card budget. Turbo3 at 128K fits comfortably.

### Per-card VRAM @ 128K turbo3/turbo3

| GPU | Weights | KV | Compute | Total / 24 GB |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| CUDA0 | 19.2 | 2.1 | 1.2 | 22.5 |
| CUDA1 | 20.2 | 1.4 | 0.3 | 21.9 |
| CUDA2 | 17.2 | 1.1 | 0.3 | 18.6 |

### Performance

| Config | Prompt tok/s | Decode tok/s |
|---|---|---|
| q8_0 / q8_0 @ 32K | 58.74 | 35.96 |
| **turbo3 / turbo3 @ 128K** | **50.65** | **28.86** |

~14% prompt, ~20% decode slowdown — cost of the WHT rotation + 3-bit dequant kernels. In exchange for 4x usable context, that's a good trade.

### Quality

Identical 26-token coding prompt produced semantically equivalent outputs across both configs. Reasoning, instruction-following, and refusal behavior all preserved. No NaN blowups, no coherence degradation in informal testing.

### Notes

- `llama_kv_cache: upstream attention rotation disabled (TurboQuant uses kernel-level WHT)` — confirms the fused kernel path is active. `attn_rot_k = 0`, `attn_rot_v = 0` in both q8_0 and turbo3 modes.
- `blk.46` (MTP layer) correctly flagged as unused on load.
- `--cache-type-k` / `--cache-type-v` CLI surface exposes `turbo2/turbo3/turbo4` — TCQ variants (`turbo3_tcq`, `turbo2_tcq`) mentioned elsewhere in docs don't appear here. Not blocking, just a note for anyone expecting them.
- CUDA mixed `q8_0` × `turbo3` also loads cleanly — just didn't capture numbers in this run.

Happy to run turbo2 (2-bit), a long-context NIAH sweep, or a different MoE if it'd fill another gap in the test data.
