I put together a convenience fork for anyone who wants to test the TurboQuant port against current llama.cpp HEAD on Vulkan without having to cherry-pick anything themselves:

   https://github.com/paudley/llama.cpp/tree/tq-surgical

 It's a rebase of @jesusmb1995's turboquant21 branch onto upstream ggml-org/llama.cpp HEAD (commit a29e4c0b7, 2026-04-11), with the minimum set of structural adjustments needed to build cleanly and run on AMD Radeon 8060S (gfx1151,  RDNA 3.5). All 33 of Jesús's commits are preserved verbatim with original authorship — there's one small integration commit on top to wire the port into current HEAD.

 What's in it:
 - All of @jesusmb1995's TurboQuant work (TBQ3_0 / TBQ4_0 / PQ3_0 / PQ4_0 KV-cache types, WHT rotation, QJL stage-2 correction, Vulkan shaders, mixed K/V FA dispatch)
 - Surgical adaptation to HEAD's API drift: hparams.n_embd_head_k became a layer-indexed method, llm_graph_input_attn_k got self_rotk/self_rotv fields, flash_attn_base.glsl and vulkan-shaders-gen.cpp and ggml-vulkan.cpp were reset to
   upstream HEAD and TurboQuant additions re-applied by hand (the auto-merge was producing irreconcilable brace-and-preprocessor drift)
 - SET_ROWS and CPY extended in ggml_backend_vk_device_supports_op to advertise TBQ/PQ, plus pipeline registration for cpy_f32_* and set_rows_*
 - resolve_tq_type's head-dim check relaxed from head_dim == 64 || head_dim == 128 to head_dim % 128 == 0, taking the same approach as @TheTom's Metal branch for enabling head_dim=256 models like Qwen3.5-35B-A3B MoE
 - Two coopmat2 (NV-only) matmul paths are skipped for TBQ/PQ — gfx1151 uses KHR_coopmat (coopmat1), so there's no functional loss, and those paths had no dequantFunc{TBQ,PQ}* helpers anyway

 Smoke test on gfx1151 Vulkan, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B Q5_K_M + --flash-attn on:
   -ctk f16 -ctv f16     pp128=463.43 t/s   tg64=43.90 t/s
   -ctk f16 -ctv tbq3_0  pp128=304.75 t/s   tg64= 8.70 t/s
 The 5x tg gap lines up with what @TheTom reported on M5 Max (~8x) and is consistent with his note about the unoptimised WHT rotation being O(d²) per block — that's upstream of everything else and will compound into both backends as
  soon as the O(d log d) Hadamard replacement lands.

  Not exhaustively validated — it loads and generates coherent text on Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, but I haven't run perplexity or long-context benchmarks yet. I'm posting this mainly so other RDNA 3.x / Strix Halo users have a branch they can
  git clone && cmake -DGGML_VULKAN=ON without replaying the rebase dance. Happy to merge fixes or rebase onto newer HEAD as things move.
     
  Credit where it's due: the actual TurboQuant implementation is all @jesusmb1995's work (3-bit/4-bit block format, WHT rotation, QJL stage 2, the entire Vulkan shader pipeline); this branch is only the integration diff. @TheTom's
  turboquant_plus repo on Metal confirmed that head_dim=256 is compatible with the math and validated the relaxed head_dim check. And obviously the underlying algorithm is Zandieh et al., "TurboQuant: Training-Free Quantization of LLMs
  and KV Caches at Scale" (ICLR 2026).


Thanks Claude Opus for the heavy lifting!

comments.author: Xcc313r4n7
comments.body: One of the concepts you are missing is that it isn't just about what size model you can fit in what size VRAM.  The accuracy that you're left with is one of the biggest factors. You can compress whatever model to whatever size, but the way that it is done might leave you with a model that gives you factually incorrect responses or even odd behavior and gibberish.  That is really what I'm sloth is saying with the compression he uses, that it retains more accuracy than other forms that compress to the same size.  This is a different form of that, and that is all model weight compression. There are forks here that do that as well,  was better accuracy and performance than unsloth's method.  This is focused on the KVcache though.  Which is where conversation is stored during inference. Not the same as the model weights, and using a very large portion of the VRAM when running the model usually. Think of the model weights as the brain's long-term memory and learned skills. Think of the KV cache as working memory, what you're actively holding in mind during the conversation. The longer the conversation, the more working memory you need. That's why long context eats VRAM. The KV cache is generated FROM the weights with each new conversation, but the weights are static, they are loaded once and don't change.  The KV cache is where the model stores what it's computed about your current context so it doesn't have to reprocess everything for each new token.

# Blackwell sm_120 validation on TheTom `8590cbf` — and an unexpected Ada/Blackwell inversion in the asymmetric-decode path

## Context

Two open items on this codebase motivated this run:

1. **No published Blackwell (sm_120) validation on TheTom's fork.** AmesianX has Blackwell data on a separate codebase, but not on TheTom.
2. TheTom's turboquant_plus README (10 Apr 2026): *"Validated on Metal (Apple Silicon). CUDA mixed q8_0 × turbo parity is not yet verified."*

This post fills both. It also surfaces a third finding the run was not looking for.

## Setup

- **Fork / commit:** TheTom/llama-cpp-turboquant `8590cbf` (`feature/turboquant-kv-cache`), version tag 22
- **CUDA:** 13.2, built with `-DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=89;120 -DGGML_CUDA_FA=ON -DGGML_CUDA_FA_ALL_QUANTS=ON`
- **GPUs:** RTX 5090 (Blackwell sm_120, 575 W stock) and RTX 4090 (Ada sm_89, 480 W stock), same host, same driver 13.2
- **OS:** Kubuntu 25.10 (gcc-12 host compiler) and Windows 10 (MSVC 19.44); identical commit on both
- **Tool:** `llama-bench` via TurboQuant QLauncher v0.51, pp512 + tg128, depths 0 / 8192 / 32768, LA 0 / 1 / 5 / 7
- **Models:** Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct-Q4_K_M, Qwen3.5-9B-UD-Q8_K_XL
- **Context:** default (`n_ctx_train` from the GGUF), no manual shrink
- Stock power limits, adequate cooling, no thermal throttling observed

## Results at d=32768, LA=7 (the critical operating point)

**Prefill (pp512, tokens/s)**

| Model | Config | 4090 Ada | 5090 Blackwell (Win) | 5090 Blackwell (Linux) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Llama-3.1-8B | f16 | 969 | 1,478 | 1,512 |
| Llama-3.1-8B | q8_0 / q8_0 | 4,169 | 6,122 | 6,537 |
| Llama-3.1-8B | q8_0-K + turbo3-V | 4,153 | 6,131 | 6,515 |
| Llama-3.1-8B | q8_0-K + turbo4-V | 4,159 | 5,796 | 6,501 |
| Qwen3.5-9B | f16 | 3,546 | 5,710 | 6,031 |
| Qwen3.5-9B | q8_0 / q8_0 | 5,329 | 8,337 | 8,982 |
| Qwen3.5-9B | q8_0-K + turbo3-V | 5,354 | 8,303 | 8,939 |

**Decode (tg128, tokens/s)**

| Model | Config | 4090 Ada | 5090 Blackwell (Win) | 5090 Blackwell (Linux) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Llama-3.1-8B | f16 | 73.8 | 103.5 | 104.6 |
| Llama-3.1-8B | q8_0 / q8_0 | 74.4 | 133.6 | 137.3 |
| Llama-3.1-8B | q8_0-K + turbo3-V | 73.7 | 86.0 | 87.9 |
| Llama-3.1-8B | q8_0-K + turbo4-V | 73.7 | 83.3 | 87.9 |
| Qwen3.5-9B | f16 | 62.8 | 101.6 | 104.7 |
| Qwen3.5-9B | q8_0 / q8_0 | 63.4 | 100.3 | 103.7 |
| Qwen3.5-9B | q8_0-K + turbo3-V | 62.8 | 99.1 | 102.3 |

## Findings

**1. Blackwell builds and runs cleanly.** sm_89;120 coexistence in a single build works. Asymmetric q8_0-K + turbo-V produces correct output and measurable throughput on both architectures — first CUDA data point for TheTom's "not yet verified" note.

**2. Prefill scaling is architecture-independent but strongly model-dependent.** At d=32768, prefill speedup over f16 is ~+330 % on Llama and ~+50 % on Qwen — on every GPU tested. The speedup is a function of KV-head layout, not GPU generation. Qwen3.5-9B's 16 KV-heads roughly halve the TurboQuant headroom versus Llama's 8.

**3. Ada outperforms Blackwell in the asymmetric-decode path.** On Llama d=32768 LA=7, asymmetric configs retain full f16 decode on Ada (−0.2 %) while costing 16–20 % on Blackwell under identical code path. On Qwen the same inversion appears, smaller in magnitude (Ada ≤0.0 %, Blackwell −2.4 %) but in the same direction.

**4. The root cause looks like a decode code-path issue, not a hardware one.** Bandwidth scaling 4090→5090 is 1.01→1.79 TB/s (+78 %). Measured f16 decode scales +80 %, matching bandwidth. Measured asymmetric q8_0-K + turbo3-V LA=7 decode scales only +17 %. Blackwell realizes under a quarter of its bandwidth advantage in this specific path — while symmetric q8_0/q8_0 scales normally.

**5. LA=7 is the switch, and it's arch-sensitive.** On Ada, LA=0→LA=7 lifts asymmetric-decode regression from −21 % to −0.2 % (Llama d=32768). On Blackwell the same switch moves −28 % to −16 %. The layer-adaptive

comments.author: sztlink
comments.body:
@WaveboSF — quick note on the OOM point. The non-reproduction is expected because we tested different models with very different KV footprints.

**My test:** Qwen3-30B-A3B — 48 layers, all full GQA attention, 4 KV heads. This is a pure transformer with no hybrid layers. At f16/32K, the KV cache is ~3.2 GB. Combined with 17.28 GB model weights + compute buffers, it pushes past 24 GB on prefill.

**Your test:** Qwen3.5-35B-A3B — 40 layers, hybrid Gated DeltaNet architecture (~10 full-attention layers, 2 KV heads). The KV cache at f16/32K is roughly ~0.3 GB — an order of magnitude smaller.

So the hybrid layout keeping "KV footprint minimal regardless of paramcount" is correct for Qwen3.5, but Qwen3 (non-hybrid, all full-attention) does not benefit from that. Both observations are consistent — it is the architecture, not a bug.

This also means the TurboQuant compression ratio matters *more* on pure-transformer models like Qwen3-30B-A3B, where f16 KV is the actual memory bottleneck. On hybrid models with DeltaNet layers, the KV savings are proportionally smaller because most layers do not generate KV cache at all.

comments.author: sztlink
comments.body:
**Follow-up: Qwen3-30B-A3B (MoE) benchmarks — this is where turbo actually matters**

Earlier today I posted 3B results where f16 won on decode. As predicted in that post, the story flips completely on a larger model where KV bandwidth is the real bottleneck.

**Hardware:** RTX 4090 (24 GB), TheTom fork commit `8590cbf`, MSVC + CUDA 12.8, flash-attn=on  
**Model:** Qwen3-30B-A3B Q4\_K\_M, 17.28 GiB, 30.53B params (MoE — ~3B active per token)

---

**Short context — pp512 + tg128, 3 runs**

| type\_k | type\_v | pp512 (t/s) | tg128 (t/s) | pp vs f16 | tg vs f16 |
|--------|--------|------------|------------|----------|----------|
| f16 | f16 | 2,371 ± 8 | **202.2 ± 1.5** | baseline | baseline |
| turbo4 | turbo4 | 6,544 ± 192 | 178.0 ± 0.4 | **+176%** | -12% |
| turbo3 | turbo3 | **6,656 ± 51** | 182.5 ± 0.6 | **+181%** | -10% |

**Long context — pp + tg128, 2 runs each**

| ctx | f16 pp (t/s) | f16 tg128 | turbo3 pp | turbo3 tg128 | tg speedup |
|-----|-------------|----------|-----------|-------------|-----------|
| 4K | 208.7 | 75.0 ± 0.2 | **1,441.7 ± 1.6** | **182.6 ± 0.6** | **+144%** |
| 8K | 125.6 | 75.2 ± 0.2 | **495.2 ± 0.0** | **182.6 ± 0.7** | **+143%** |
| 16K | 63.2 | 74.7 ± 0.2 | **468.6 ± 0.1** | **182.5 ± 0.7** | **+144%** |

*(f16 at 32K stalled — likely prefill OOM at that context with full f16 KV on 24 GB. turbo3 would have headroom.)*

---

**What these numbers show:**

**Decode** is the key story. f16 locks at ~75 t/s from ctx=4K onward — pure KV bandwidth saturation. turbo3 holds **182 t/s flat across all tested contexts**. That's +144% decode throughput, stable and consistent.

**Prefill** with turbo is 2–7x faster depending on context. At pp=16K, turbo3 runs at 468 t/s vs f16's 63 t/s — **7.4x faster**. The compressed KV fits in L2 cache during attention, so per-token prefill cost drops dramatically as context grows.

**The flat turbo3 decode line** (182 t/s at 4K, 8K, 16K) is the cleanest signal: turbo3 is still bandwidth-bound, but at 5.12× compression it saturates much later. On a smaller GPU or with a larger model, turbo3 would keep going where f16 runs out of memory entirely.

**The 3B results from earlier today** (f16 wins decode by 12%) and these 30B results are fully consistent — in small models where the KV fits in cache regardless, f16 wins on raw compute. In large models where KV bandwidth dominates, turbo wins by ~2.4x. The crossover is exactly where the paper predicts.

One note: this is Qwen3-30B-A3B, a MoE model (~3B active params per token). The attention heads still process the full context KV, so the KV bandwidth analysis applies normally even though compute is sparser than a dense 30B.

comments.author: primoco
comments.body:
**Speed benchmarks are great — but what about accuracy?**

I've been following this thread and I notice almost every benchmark posted measures **tokens/sec, prefill speed, and VRAM** — but nobody is asking: *does the model still give correct answers after KV compression?*

Speed without accuracy is meaningless. A 5× compression ratio that makes your model wrong 30% of the time isn't a win.

We built a benchmark specifically to test this: math problems with delayed recall (the question is asked, then N tokens of filler are inserted, then the model must answer from KV-cached context). This isolates KV corruption from model capability.

**Results on Qwen3-14B Q4_K_M, RTX 5070 Ti, eullm-tq v0.4.3 + AmesianX TurboQuant v1.5.3:**

| Config | K cache | V cache | Accuracy | Notes |
|--------|---------|---------|----------|-------|
| Baseline | F16 | F16 | 91/91 **100%** | reference |
| Recommended | Q8_0 | TBQ4_1 | 91/91 **100%** | ✅ safe |
| 4-bit corrected | TBQP4_1 | TBQ4_1 | 86/91 **94.5%** | 5 mat2×2 failures ≥1000t |
| 4-bit symmetric | TBQP4_1 | TBQP4_1 | 91/91 **100%** | ⚠️ no flash-attn (CUDA bug) |
| 3-bit corrected | TBQP3_1 | TBQ3_1 | 62/91 **68.1%** | ❌ correction hurts at 3-bit |
| 3-bit symmetric | TBQ3_1 | TBQ3_1 | 73/91 **80.2%** | ❌ not production-safe |

comments.author: sztlink
comments.body:
**Asymmetric benchmarks + PPL on Qwen3-30B-A3B (MoE) — response to @primoco and @WaveboSF**

Following up on yesterday's throughput posts with quality data, and adding asymmetric (q8\_0-K + turbo3-V) results that connect to @WaveboSF's Ada/Blackwell inversion findings.

**Hardware:** RTX 4090 (24 GB), SM89, TheTom fork `8590cbf`, MSVC + CUDA 12.8, flash-attn=on  
**Model:** Qwen3-30B-A3B Q4\_K\_M, 17.28 GiB (MoE, ~3B active/token)

---

## Quality first — PPL on wikitext-2 (100 chunks × 512 tokens)

| Config | PPL | Δ vs f16 |
|--------|-----|----------|
| f16 / f16 | 7.560 | baseline |
| **q8\_0-K + turbo3-V** | **7.616** | **+0.7%** |
| turbo4 / turbo4 | 7.972 | +5.4% |
| turbo3 / turbo3 | 9.230 | +22.1% |

**The asymmetric config (q8\_0-K + turbo3-V) is essentially lossless.** +0.7% PPL is within noise for most use cases. Symmetric turbo3 is a different story — +22% degradation is real and the data @primoco was asking for.

This validates the mechanism: **K dominates perplexity**. With K at q8\_0 quality, V can absorb turbo3 compression with no meaningful quality cost. With K compressed to turbo3, quantization noise in the attention scores propagates through the softmax and degrades output.

Note on forks: @primoco's results use eullm + TBQ3\_1, which is a distinct implementation from TheTom's turbo3 (different centroids, different WHT seeding). The 80% accuracy floor he found at 3-bit may not directly transfer — but the K-dominance finding is consistent across both.

---

## Asymmetric throughput — Ada SM89 (no LA, stock config)

**Decode tg128 — constant across all tested depths:**

| Config | d=0 | d=8K | d=32K | vs f16 |
|--------|-----|------|-------|--------|
| f16 / f16 | 202 | 202 | 202 | baseline |
| q8\_0-K + turbo3-V | 190 | 190 | 190 | **−6%** |
| q8\_0-K + turbo4-V | 189 | 189 | 189 | **−7%** |
| turbo3 / turbo3 | 182 | 182 | 182 | −10% |

Decode is flat across depths — this MoE is compute-bound on the active experts, not KV-bandwidth-bound.

**On @WaveboSF's Ada/Blackwell inversion:** his data showed Ada SM89 at LA=7 holding −0.2% decode overhead for q8\_0-K + turbo3-V. Our no-LA baseline is −6%, which sits between his LA=0 (−21%) and LA=7 (−0.2%) — consistent. We don't have a 5090 to test the Blackwell side.

**The prefill result that surprised us:**

| Config | pp512 | pp8K | pp32K |
|--------|-------|------|-------|
| f16 / f16 | 6,414 | 135 | **15.9** |
| q8\_0-K + turbo3-V | 6,748 | 6,528 | **395** |
| turbo3 / turbo3 | 6,608 | 6,388 | **4,697** |

At 32K prefill, symmetric turbo3 is **12× faster** than asymmetric q8\_0-K + turbo3-V (4,697 vs 395 t/s). The compressed K (3-bit) dramatically reduces bandwidth when reading K-vectors during prefill attention. With q8\_0 K (8-bit), the K-side bandwidth at 32K context dominates and limits prefill speed — even as V compression saves on the other side.

**The trade-off is now clear:**
- q8\_0-K + turbo3-V: lossless quality (+0.7% PPL), good decode (−6%), slower long-context prefill
- turbo3/turbo3: measurable quality loss (+22% PPL), slightly worse decode (−10%), best long-context prefill

For production use cases where quality matters: q8\_0-K + turbo3-V.  
For scenarios where you tolerate quality loss for maximum throughput at long context: turbo3/turbo3.

---

*PPL via `llama-imatrix --ppl` (llama-perplexity is blocked by Windows WDAC on this machine — imatrix computes identical PPL as a side effect of calibration runs).*

comments.author: sztlink
comments.body:
@BlackBookOfficial — worth clarifying, because the framing matters for how people adopt this.

TurboQuant is a **software compression scheme** — it has no dependency on any specific GPU hardware. The algorithm: apply a Walsh-Hadamard Transform to each KV vector, then quantize the rotated values to 3-bit Lloyd-Max centroids. Both operations run in CUDA kernels that compile cleanly on SM89 (Ada), SM86 (Ampere), SM90 (Hopper), SM120 (Blackwell), and ROCm/gfx on AMD. There is no fractional-bit hardware instruction anywhere in the stack.

What you may be thinking of is **Microscaling (MX) formats** (FP4, FP6, FP8 with shared exponents) that Blackwell supports natively in its tensor cores. That's a different and complementary technique — it quantizes *weights* at inference time using hardware-accelerated formats. TurboQuant quantizes the *KV cache* in software, which is a different bottleneck entirely.

The practical evidence is in this thread: RTX 3090 (SM86), RX 7900 XTX (AMD gfx1100), and multiple Ada cards all show the same throughput and quality patterns. The gains come from reduced KV bandwidth, which is a memory-bus bottleneck that exists on every generation. Blackwell's larger bandwidth (1.79 TB/s vs 1.01 on Ada) means *smaller relative gains* from KV compression there — which is actually part of the Ada/Blackwell inversion @WaveboSF found.

comments.author: mengqin
comments.body:
Hi All,

There are already numerous branches here that have implemented TurboQuant or its variants; furthermore, the standard `q8_0` and `q4_0` quantization types now also integrate WHT. Consequently, I have long been curious about the actual performance gap currently existing between TQ and the standard `Qn` quantization types. The existing implementations here seem to largely overlook the 2-bit TQ variant—yet, in my opinion, this is precisely the variant that holds the greatest appeal for users with limited GPU memory.

Therefore, I decided to vibe code my own implementation from scratch. I spent several days optimizing it to reach the maximum speed attainable on my RTX 5090 GPU. Finally, I conducted a simple yet comprehensive series of tests; the full report can be found here:

https://mengqin.github.io/llama.cpp/pq_tq_bench_report/report.html

Based on these results, I have drawn the following conclusions (specifically regarding PQ/TQ):

1.  WHT is indeed effective, but its efficacy is highly correlated with the model's head dimension. The higher the head dimension, the better the results. This comes as no surprise, as this conclusion can be derived quite directly from the formulas presented in the original research paper. Quality is quite poor with a head dimension of 64, whereas it is excellent with a head dimension of 256; in the latter case, even the QJL compensation mechanism actually becomes a drag on performance.
2.  Quality also correlates positively with the bit depth. While this is self-evident, when combined with the first point, we can establish a minimum threshold for practical applicability: for D64 models, 3-bit quantization (without QJL) represents the absolute minimum baseline; for D128 models, 2-bit quantization (without QJL) serves as the bottom line. 
3.  PPL is not a comprehensive metric for quality; some quantization schemes may yield decent PPL scores, yet perform significantly worse in actual inference tasks and needle-in-a-haystack retrieval tests.
4.  QJL is useful, though it is unnecessary for D256 models. For D128 and D64 models, however, these compensation mechanisms do yield a noticeable improvement in quality. Given that the computational overhead introduced by QJL is relatively minor, its inclusion should be considered in certain scenarios (e.g., when using D64 models).
5.  The performance of TQ/PQ during the pp512 and tg128 is quite respectable. However, the decoding performance following a large prompt context becomes extremely poor, and the processing speed drops further as the context length increases. This implies that decoding performance for ultra-long contexts is abysmal; for instance, with a 128k-token context, the decoding speed plummets to a mere 10–20% of its original rate. This—the severe degradation of decoding speed with extended context lengths—is, in reality, the true Achilles' heel of the TQ/PQ algorithms. 
 
My implementation is available at:
 
https://github.com/mengqin/llama.cpp/

This implementation primarily features CUDA-based WHT variants of PQ and TQ (utilizing Walsh-Hadamard Transforms rather than the random rotations described in the original paper), along with the corresponding QJL optimization. Specifically, the `tqn` variant incorporates QJL, while `pqn` does not. 

We introduce a coefficient rescaling step—multiplying by a factor of sqrt(D/128)—following the WHT. This aligns the distribution of rotational coefficients across different head dimensions with the design domain of the D128 codebook, thereby improving the adaptability of the fixed centroid table for D64 and D256 configurations. Subsequently, we use a factor of sqrt(128/D) to scale the QJL residuals back to their correct original domain. This specific step may require further improvement.

The implementation utilizes specialized TQ/PQ kernels, achieving performance that is nearly on par with the standard `q4` and `q8` quantization methods. However, performance degrades signifi

Regarding scaling: I am currently experimenting with enabling D64, D128, and D256 to utilize independent codebooks for each dimension. While this approach eliminates the scaling step, it introduces other issues—specifically, a reduction in interpretability (manifesting as a decline in tq4 quality on D128). However, we have observed that the magnitude of this performance drop is significantly greater for PQ/TQ methods than for traditional quantization techniques—a disparity that becomes increasingly pronounced as the context length extends. In the context of ultra-long sequences we are discussing here, 32K is not considered a particularly long context length; at 128K, however, you will observe a stark and undeniable performance gap that simply cannot be ignored.

**RotorQuant (PlanarQuant/IsoQuant) Ampere benchmarks — RTX 3080 Ti SM 86**

First Ampere data for the RotorQuant rotation variants. Built `johndpope/llama-cpp-turboquant@feature/planarquant-kv-cache` (commit `20efe75`) on RTX 3080 Ti 12GB. Qwen3.5 9B Q4_K_M, wikitext-2 PPL, all configs on the same binary for apples-to-apples.

**Speed (pp512 / tg128, tok/s):**

| Config (K/V) | pp512 | tg128 | vs f16 pp | vs f16 tg |
|---|---:|---:|---|---|
| f16/f16 | 3,781 | 100.4 | — | — |
| q8\_0/q8\_0 | 3,803 | 100.2 | 100.6% | 99.8% |
| turbo2/turbo2 | 3,781 | 98.8 | 100.0% | 98.4% |
| turbo3/turbo3 | 3,756 | 97.9 | 99.3% | 97.5% |
| planar3/planar3 | 3,211 | 95.0 | 84.9% | 94.6% |
| iso3/iso3 | 2,978 | 95.0 | 78.7% | 94.6% |

**Perplexity (wikitext-2):**

| Config | PPL | vs f16 | Compression |
|---|---:|---|---|
| f16/f16 | 8.297 | — | 1x |
| turbo2/turbo2 | 8.821 | +6.3% | 6.4x |
| turbo3/turbo3 | 8.421 | +1.5% | 5.1x |
| **planar3/planar3** | **8.070** | **-2.7%** | 10.3x |
| **iso3/iso3** | **8.227** | **-0.8%** | 10.3x |

**Observations:**

1. **Quality advantage is real.** planar3 PPL 8.070 beats f16 (8.297) on this model. iso3 8.227 also better than f16. Block-diagonal rotation appears to decorrelate Qwen3.5 KV vectors more effectively than WHT.

2. **Speed advantage does not hold on Ampere.** turbo3 is 99% of f16 throughput; planar3 is 85% prefill / 95% decode. The O(d) vs O(d log d) rotation cost is negligible when memory bandwidth is the bottleneck. The 28% faster / 5.3x prefill claims from the RotorQuant README appear to be RTX 5090-specific.

3. **planar3 PPL < f16 is curious.** Error bars overlap (±0.054 vs ±0.056) so this could be noise, or the deferred K-cache (F16 during prefill, quantize on decode insertion) may act as an implicit regularizer.

4. **The tradeoff on bandwidth-limited hardware:** RotorQuant gives better quality at 2x the compression ratio (10.3x vs 5.1x) but pays ~15% prefill speed. On Ampere that's unfavorable for latency-sensitive workloads. On HBM-rich GPUs the relationship may invert.

Hardware: RTX 3080 Ti 12GB, SM 86, CUDA 12.x. Single card, CUDA\_VISIBLE\_DEVICES=1 (card 0 running production). All runs with `-fa 1`.

@dentity007 thanks for the detailed report, the f16/f16 vs f16/q8_0 cross-validation across two pods nailed the symptom perfectly.

Root Cause: the FA dispatcher in `ggml/src/ggml-cuda/fattn.cu` had a too-narrow predicate that only allowed mixed K/V combos when both types were in {turbo2, turbo3, turbo4, q8_0}. `f16` and `bf16` weren't in the set, so `K=f16, V=q8_0` returned `BEST_FATTN_KERNEL_NONE` and fell back to CPU... even though the template instances `fattn-vec-instance-{f16,bf16}-q8_0.cu` are already compiled in. Same for any turbo + f16/bf16 combo.

Fix is one line: extend the predicate to include f16 and bf16: https://github.com/TheTom/llama-cpp-turboquant/pull/82

Could you cherry-pick onto your sm_89 and sm_121 builds and re-run the q8_0/turbo3/turbo4 KV tests? Should run on GPU now without needing `-DGGML_CUDA_FA_ALL_QUANTS=ON`. Workaround in the meantime: add that flag to your cmake (longer build, bigger binary, but works today).

Note this mostly affects:
  1. Anyone using -ctk f16 -ctv q8_0 on CUDA without GGML_CUDA_FA_ALL_QUANTS=ON. This is a common memory-saving config (V cache is usually bigger than K, so quantizing V matters more). Hits everyone in this bucket, silent CPU fallback,
  100x+ slowdown.
  2. Anyone testing -ctv turbo3/turbo4 paired with f16 K. The turbo+q8_0 combos already work (carve-out covers them). It's specifically when paired with f16/bf16 that it dies.

comments.body:
## DGX Spark GB10 (sm_121) + RTX 4090 (sm_89) validation of PR #82

**Methodology**

Ran three parallel independent tracks to cross-validate PR #82 and characterize unified-memory vs discrete-VRAM behavior at long context:

- **Track A (primary):** DGX Spark GB10, sm_121, 128GB unified memory, aarch64 / CUDA 13.0. Built with PR #82 cherry-picked onto HEAD 107362298 plus `-DGGML_CUDA_FA_ALL_QUANTS=ON`. Full 5-depth matrix up to 131K context.

- **Track B (cross-validation pod 1):** RTX 4090 on RunPod (Davenport, Iowa, US), sm_89, 24GB discrete VRAM, x86_64 / CUDA 12.4. Built at commit 8590cbf with PR #82 + FA_ALL_QUANTS. 3 context depths (24GB cannot fit 131K on this model).

- **Track C (cross-validation pod 2):** RTX 4090 on RunPod (Timisoara, Romania, EU), same commit and flags as Track B. Different datacenter, different CPU (Ryzen 9 7950X vs EPYC 7B13), different GPU serial number. Purpose: confirm Track B numbers are not a single-host artifact.

Model: Qwen3-30B-A3B Q4_K_M from unsloth/Qwen3-30B-A3B-GGUF. llama-bench with `-fa 1 -t 1 -ngl 99 -b 2048 -ub 2048`. Two benchmark runs per track for reproducibility.

### PR #82 confirmed working

`f16/q8_0` went from ~5 tok/s (CPU fallback, documented in my earlier post) to full GPU speeds. `nvidia-smi` shows 96-100% utilization throughout. Fix works on sm_121 AND sm_89.

### DGX Spark GB10 (sm_121, 128GB unified, Q4_K_M)

| K/V | tg128 | pp8192 | pp32768 | pp65536 | pp131072 |
|-----|-------|--------|---------|---------|----------|
| f16/f16 | 90.11 | 1700.62 | 1636.96 | 1258.72 | 835.60 |
| f16/q8_0 | 86.50 | 1280.45 | 1264.92 | 1026.64 | 723.44 |
| f16/q4_0 | 86.30 | 1273.54 | 1260.86 | 1024.26 | 725.25 |

Generation speed barely moves across V-cache quantization (~4% range). Prompt throughput at 131K holds above 720 tok/s even with quantized V-cache. Unified memory makes 131K context fit where discrete 24GB 4090 VRAM runs out.

### RTX 4090 cross-validation (sm_89, two independent pods)

| Pod | K/V | tg128 | pp8192 | pp32768 |
|-----|-----|-------|--------|---------|
| Iowa (EPYC 7B13) | f16/f16 | 238.74 | 4872.72 | 4728.23 |
| Romania (Ryzen 9 7950X) | f16/f16 | 255.93 | 5132.03 | 4914.84 |
| Iowa | f16/q8_0 | 222.37 | 4347.91 | 4306.00 |
| Romania | f16/q8_0 | 237.59 | 4558.86 | 4467.93 |
| Romania | q8_0/f16 | 249.55 | 4912.09 | 4725.80 |
| Romania | q8_0/q8_0 | 232.07 | 4338.52 | 4250.64 |

Two 4090s match within ~7% across both K/V configs. Asymmetric `q8_0-K + f16-V` is only ~2.5% slower than `f16/f16` on the Romania pod. Asymmetric `q8_0/q8_0` is ~9% slower.

### The unified memory vs discrete VRAM story

At 8K and 32K context, the 4090 is 2.5-2.9x faster per token than the GB10 on both generation and prompt throughput. But at 131K context, the 4090 cannot run at all, the model plus KV cache exceeds 24GB VRAM. GB10 128GB unified memory keeps 131K workable at 835 tok/s prompt and 90 tok/s generation with f16/f16.

The tradeoff is clear: discrete VRAM wins at short-to-mid context, unified memory wins by existing at ultra-long context.

### One thing that broke

All three tracks hit a consistent crash when `llama-bench` tried `-ctk f16 -ctv turbo3` (or turbo4 / turbo2). Filed separately as [issue #83](https://github.com/TheTom/llama-cpp-turboquant/issues/83) with root cause (missing F16-K + TURBO-V cases in `fattn.cu` dispatch) and proposed fix. That is why the tables above cover f16/q8_0/q4_0 V-cache but not turbo variants.

Builds: commit 8590cbf (4090s) and HEAD 107362298 (Spark), both with PR #82 cherry-pick and `FA_ALL_QUANTS=ON`.

comments.author: TheTom
comments.body:
Hey @atomicmilkshake, took a look at the repo since you asked. Honest assessment:

**What's genuinely useful:**
- The CUDA kernel for TriAttention scoring (`triattention-score.cu`, 542 lines) is real work. My TriAttention implementation is CPU + Metal only. A CUDA scoring kernel at 4-9ms vs 5900ms CPU is a valuable contribution.
- Pre-built Windows CUDA binaries are useful for the community. Most Windows users don't build from source.
- The integration is real code (3384 lines, proper CLI flags, public API), not a wrapper.

**What needs a reality check:**
- The 75 tok/s headline is from `budget=256` at `-c 512`. That's 50% token eviction. The speedup is real but you're throwing away half the context. At that eviction rate, quality will break on anything that needs retrieval.
- No PPL or NIAH numbers anywhere (unless I missed it). Speed without quality validation is incomplete. My V3 paper (see below) documents the exact failure modes: paper-faithful TriAttention silently drops the needle at end-of-context even at 10% eviction. At 50%, it would be catastrophic.
- Your implementation looks like paper-faithful V1 scoring (global sort). V3 (what i'm working on) adds prefix protection + per-segment quota to fix the position-dependent retrieval failures that V1 has. Worth reviewing Section 4.1 and 4.2 of my paper.

**Recommendation:**
Run this on your RTX 3080:
```
llama-perplexity -m model.gguf -f wiki.test.raw -c 32768 -b 512 --chunks 3 --triattention-budget 29491
```
That's 90% retention at 32K. Compare PPL to baseline (no triattention). Then run a NIAH test at start/middle/end positions. If PPL is within +1% and NIAH passes all three, you have something shippable. If NIAH fails at end, you're hitting the V1 failure mode.

The CUDA kernel is the useful piece. Would be interested in cherry-picking it into my branch if quality validates.

Some tips from my learnings. Still working on triattention myself (not production worthy at the moment):
https://github.com/TheTom/turboquant_plus/blob/main/docs/papers/triattention-v3.md

comments.author: TheTom
comments.body:
Vulkan on AMD iGPU is genuinely new territory, nice work. 262K context on a Radeon 860M at 14.2 tok/s decode is impressive for an integrated GPU with unified memory.

Two things to flag based on what we've learned the hard way:

1. You're using QJL correction (tq4_fwht_inverse + tq4_qjl_correction). We (as in the majority of the community) dropped QJL from our implementation because it increases variance which softmax then amplifies. 5 independent groups confirmed this. More centroids without QJL consistently beats fewer centroids with QJL on quality. Worth running a PPL comparison with and without.

2. Symmetric tq4_0/tq4_0 (same quant on both K and V) can be catastrophic on certain model families. On Qwen with Q4_K_M weights we saw PPL go from 6.x to 3,400+. The fix is asymmetric: q8_0 on K, turbo on V only. K precision dominates quality through softmax amplification. V is much more tolerant of aggressive compression.

Would love to see PPL numbers (wikitext, 3 chunks minimum) and a NIAH test at 128K+ to validate quality. The speed numbers look solid, quality is where these things break.

Docs on asymmetric and why: [github.com/TheTom/turboquant_plus/docs/papers/](https://github.com/TheTom/turboquant_plus/blob/main/docs/papers/asymmetric-kv-compression.md)

Again nice work!

comments.author: TheTom
comments.body:
Yup, fixed that a few weeks ago. Stock llama.cpp has a predicate gap in fattn.cu where mixed K/V types silently fall back to CPU. That's probably what you hit.

Asymmetric KV is one of the core feature/discoveries of this fork. PR #82 fixes the fattn predicate, and we have CUDA template instantiations for all q8_0 + turbo combinations. Confirmed working on sm_86 (dual 3080 Ti), sm_89 (4090), and sm_121 (DGX Spark). Same asymmetric implementation benefits CUDA, ROCm, and Metal, all three backends share the same core path.

Short version of why asymmetric matters: K feeds into softmax which amplifies errors exponentially. V feeds into a linear weighted sum. So K needs high precision (q8_0), V can be compressed aggressively (turbo3/turbo4). Compressing both equally is where the "schizophrenia" comes from.

Full writeup with data: https://github.com/TheTom/turboquant_plus/blob/main/docs/papers/asymmetric-kv-compression.md

comments.author: TheTom
comments.body:
f16-K + q8_0-V is a completely valid config and you're right that it's an immediate practical benefit even without any turbo types. That alone saves ~50% on V memory with essentially zero quality cost.

q5_0 and q5_1 as V types: honestly haven't tested those specifically. Our testing has focused on the turbo types (turbo2/3/4) and baselines (f16, q8_0, q4_0). They should work mechanically but I don't have KLD numbers to back that up.

For the configs we have tested, here's the full KLD data across V types, architectures, and context lengths:

https://github.com/TheTom/turboquant_plus/blob/main/docs/kl-divergence-results.md

Quick summary: turbo3-V on dense Qwen3.5-27B has mean KLD 0.0099, same-top-p 96%. Stock q4_0-V has mean KLD 0.0027, same-top-p 97.6%. turbo3 uses fewer bits (3.5 vs 4) so slightly higher KLD is expected, but the WHT rotation keeps it competitive. KLD also improves at longer context (0.0198 at 2K down to 0.0167 at 8K).

One nuance from community testing: on Q6_K+ weight quants, V type actually dominates PPL more than K type. The "K precision is critical" finding is strongest on Q4_K_M weights where symmetric turbo is catastrophic. **On higher quality weight quants, asymmetric matters less.**

If you run the q5_0/q5_1 comparison I'd be interested in the numbers.

comments.author: Enferlain
comments.body:
gpt comment but manual testing, new to it though so went by guidance from this thread + the linked repos. will check qwen 3.6 moe and gemma 4 both next time before looking into the other research stuff

---

Ran a fairly complete CUDA pass on `Qwen3.6-27B-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf` on an RTX 3090 and the results lined up pretty well with the repo's current guidance.

Setup:

- Windows 11
- CUDA 13.1.1
- RTX 3090 24 GB / 64 GB RAM
- rebased `llama-cpp-turboquant` worktree
- short-context sanity checks at `-c 512 --chunks 20`
- main quality pass was **BF16-reference KLD at `-c 8192 --chunks 20`**

The `8k` BF16-reference KLD run was the most useful signal by far. Ranking from best to worst:

1. `q8_0/q8_0`
2. `q8_0/turbo4`
3. `q8_0/q4_0`
4. `q8_0/turbo3`
5. `q4_0/q4_0`
6. `turbo4/turbo4`
7. `turbo3/turbo3`

Main numbers:

| Config | Mean KLD | PPL ratio vs BF16 | RMS Δp | Same top-p |
| :-- | --: | --: | --: | --: |
| `q8_0/q8_0` | `0.038583` | `1.014545` | `4.496%` | `95.095%` |
| `q8_0/turbo4` | `0.045081` | `1.017086` | `5.023%` | `94.432%` |
| `q8_0/q4_0` | `0.045010` | `1.020999` | `4.959%` | `94.613%` |
| `q8_0/turbo3` | `0.047672` | `1.018680` | `5.298%` | `94.100%` |
| `q4_0/q4_0` | `0.049557` | `1.020552` | `5.090%` | `94.382%` |
| `turbo4/turbo4` | `0.052254` | `1.021878` | `5.257%` | `94.039%` |
| `turbo3/turbo3` | `0.062166` | `1.029845` | `5.871%` | `93.437%` |

So on this dense Qwen 27B:

- `q8_0/q8_0` was the best-quality fast KV option
- `q8_0/turbo4` was the best compressed option
- `q8_0/q4_0` was the strongest non-Turbo asymmetric reference and landed very close to `turbo4`
- `q8_0/turbo3` stayed close, but was consistently worse than `turbo4`
- symmetric TurboQuant was not attractive here

The speed / memory side also looked good for asymmetric TurboQuant. At moderate contexts, `q8_0/turbo4` and `q8_0/turbo3` both improved prefill and stayed near decode parity. At larger contexts, `q8_0/turbo4` gave real KV savings versus default `f16/f16`:

- `32768`: context memory `2197 -> 965 MiB`
- `65536`: context memory `4245 -> 1781 MiB`

The context-ceiling checks were probably the clearest practical win:

| Config | Context | CUDA free MiB | CUDA context MiB |
| :-- | --: | --: | --: |
| `q8_0/q8_0` | `131072` | `1527` | `4501` |
| `q8_0/turbo4` | `131072` | `2458` | `3413` |
| `q8_0/turbo4` | `196608` | `984` | `5045` |
| `q8_0/q4_0` | `196608` | `888` | `5141` |
| `q4_0/q4_0` | `262144` | `1009` | `4757` |
| `turbo4/turbo4` | `262144` | `1307` | `4501` |

Short version:

- use `q8_0/q8_0` if quality is the priority
- use `q8_0/turbo4` if the goal is better quality / context-capacity tradeoff
- use `q8_0/q4_0` if you want the strongest non-Turbo asymmetric alternative
- skip `q8_0/turbo3` unless you really need the extra KV savings

For this setup, TurboQuant was definitely worth testing, but specifically as **`q8_0/turbo4`**, not as a general symmetric-Turbo win. The jump from roughly the `131k` context tier to at least `196k` on the same 3090 was the clearest practical benefit.

comments.author: illnar-io
comments.body:
@TheTom @jagsan-cyber 
**Testing tq4_0 Vulkan on RDNA2 (gfx1035, Radeon 680M) — SIGSEGV report**

Built from `jagsan-cyber/llama.cpp` (commit 29acb95, built 2026-04-22) on Fedora 44.

### Environment

- **GPU:** AMD Radeon 680M (RADV REMBRANDT, gfx1035, iGPU, UMA)
- **Driver:** Mesa RADV, Vulkan 1.4.341
- **OS:** Fedora Linux 44, kernel 6.19.12-300.fc44.x86_64
- **CPU:** AMD Ryzen 7 6800H (Zen 3+, 16 threads)
- **RAM:** 16 GB shared (iGPU sees 12 GB total / ~10 GB available)
- **Build:** `-DGGML_VULKAN=ON -DGGML_HIPBLAS=OFF -DGGML_CUDA=OFF -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release`

Vulkan device properties:
```
uma: 1 | fp16: 1 | bf16: 0 | warp size: 32 | shared memory: 65536
int dot: 1 | matrix cores: none
```

### What I tested

```bash
# Gemma4 E2B Q4_K_M
GGML_VK_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 ./build/bin/llama-server \
  -m gemma-4-E2B-it-Q4_K_M.gguf \
  -ngl 99 --flash-attn on \
  -ctk tq4_0 -ctv tq4_0 \
  -c 32768 --port 8081

# Qwen3.5 4B Q5_K_M
GGML_VK_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 ./build/bin/llama-server \
  -m Qwen_Qwen3.5-4B-Q5_K_M.gguf \
  -ngl 99 --flash-attn on \
  -ctk tq4_0 -ctv tq4_0 \
  -c 16384 --port 8081
```

### What happens

Both models: tq4_0 KV cache allocates correctly on Vulkan0, Flash Attention enables, then SIGSEGV during warmup:

```
llama_context: flash_attn    = enabled
llama_kv_cache: K (tq4_0): 84.00 MiB, V (tq4_0): 84.00 MiB
common_init_from_params: warming up the model with an empty run - please wait...
[1] SIGSEGV (Address boundary error)
```

For Gemma4 without `--flash-attn on`, FA falls back to disabled (ISWA architecture has no Vulkan FA shader), then the server refuses to start with:
```
quantized V cache was requested, but this requires Flash Attention
```

### What works

- `q8_0`, `q4_0`, `f16` KV cache all work correctly on Vulkan + Flash Attention
- Both models run fine with `q8_0` on system llama-server (sneed COPR b8882)
- `llama-server --help` correctly lists `tq4_0` as a valid cache type — it compiles and registers fine

### Suspected cause

The tq4_0 Vulkan dequantization shader likely uses subgroup paths developed on RDNA3.5 (gfx1150, Ryzen AI 300) that behave differently on RDNA2 (gfx1035, Wave32, no matrix cores). The crash happens at the first compute dispatch during warmup, not at allocation.

### Request

Could you add RDNA2 (gfx103x) to the test matrix, or add a runtime device capability check that gracefully falls back to q8_0 instead of segfaulting?

Happy to test patches — 100% reproducible on this hardware.

comments.author: jagsan-cyber
comments.body:
@AveZorgen
Welcome, and great catch! You have a very sharp eye.

You are absolutely right. Because GGML_TYPE_TQ4_0 is missing from that switch statement, the ggml scheduler sees that Vulkan doesn't natively support Flash Attention for TQ4_0 and ends up falling back to the CPU (or another backend) for that operation.

This ties into a structural limitation we recently discovered: the current Vulkan Flash Attention pipeline fundamentally assumes symmetric KV types (k->type == v->type) and uses a single DATA_A_ macro for dequantization. There simply isn't a dedicated Vulkan Flash Attention pipeline built for TQ4_0 yet.

Until a dedicated dual-decode pipeline is written for Vulkan FA, we are keeping the default to symmetric Q8_0 to maintain perfect PPL and ensure the GPU handles the entire workload without CPU fallback. Thanks for pointing out the exact dispatch location!

TQ4_0 Vulkan FA — shader compilation diagnostic
Been debugging TQ4_0 on RDNA2 (gfx1035, Radeon 680M). Sharing findings in case they are helpful for implementation.

comments.author: jagsan-cyber
comments.body:
Thanks everyone for the detailed reports and testing on RDNA2 hardware.
This is extremely helpful.

Summary of the issue:
- TQ4_0 Vulkan currently assumes the RDNA3.5 (gfx1150) shader model.
- RDNA2 (gfx103x) uses Wave32, has different shared memory rules, and
  lacks several subgroup/matrix-core behaviors that the current TQ4_0
  FA shaders rely on.
- As a result, the FA shader variants fail to compile on RDNA2, and the
  runtime hits a SIGSEGV / access violation during the first dispatch.

This is expected given the current implementation, but it should not
crash. A graceful fallback is the correct behavior.

Planned fix:
1. Add a runtime capability check:
   - If the device is RDNA2 (gfx103x) or lacks the required subgroup
     features, TQ4_0 + Flash Attention will automatically fall back to
     a safe path (Q8_0-style direct dequant).
   - This avoids the SIGSEGV and allows the server to start normally.

2. Add RDNA2 to the test matrix:
   - gfx1035 (680M)
   - gfx1032 (6600 XT)
   - gfx1030 (various APUs)

3. Rework the TQ4_0 FA shader path:
   - Remove assumptions inherited from the early RDNA3.5 prototype.
   - Provide a Wave32-compatible variant for RDNA2.
   - Fix the GLSL errors reported by @ILLnar-Nizami
     (`shared` qualifier, missing `tq_sign1/2`, array sizing, etc.)

In the meantime:
- TQ4_0 works on RDNA2 only when Flash Attention is disabled.
- I will push a patch that allows TQ4_0 KV cache without requiring FA,
  so RDNA2 users can run TQ4_0 safely.

If anyone can provide:
- shader compilation logs (`VK_LAYER_KHRONOS_validation`)
- `spirv-dis` output for the failing variants
- or a RenderDoc capture of the warmup dispatch

…that would help accelerate the fix.

Thanks again for the detailed diagnostics — I’ll update this thread as
soon as the fallback patch is ready.

| 8192 | 2.56 | 2.54 | −0.8% |
| 16384 | 1.26 | ~1.25 | ~−0.5% |
| 32768 | — | — | OOM — model+KV exceeds 24 GB |

† *32K metric is PP+TG combined (prompt-processing dominant) — not directly comparable to TG-only rows above.*

---

### Finding

**sparse-V adds small overhead on CUDA at all tested contexts: −0.3% to −2.8%.**

The pattern is consistent across SM86 (Ampere) and SM89 (Ada Lovelace), peaking at ctx=4096 (−2.8%) and shrinking at longer contexts (−0.4% at 32K PP). No gain at any context on NVIDIA.

This contrasts sharply with Metal (M5 Max), where sparse-V compounds with context depth: **+4.0% → +12.9% → +22.8%** at 4K / 16K / 32K. The architecture difference appears to be:

- **Metal**: KV bandwidth-bound at long contexts → skipping V dequantization saves real memory bandwidth → gains compound
- **CUDA**: dispatch overhead and kernel launch cost outweigh the dequant savings at all tested contexts

The result is effectively **architecture-dependent**: sparse-V is a meaningful optimization for Apple Silicon at long context, but adds minor overhead on NVIDIA CUDA (both Ampere and Ada).

---

*Hardware: RTX 4090 24GB + RTX 3090 24GB, local inference. Next: characterization on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B.*

comments.author: wejoncy
comments.body:
Sharing some related work in case it's useful here.                                                               
                                      
  We built a 4-bit TurboQuant FlashDecoding kernel for H100 (SM90a) — an end-to-end fused implementation pairing the
   TurboQuant KV cache quantization scheme ([arxiv:2504.19874](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.19874)) with the          
  FlashDecoding split-K framework.                                                                                  
                                                         
  **What we built**

  - 4-bit TurboQuant KV cache: **136 B/token** vs FP16's 512 B/token (~3.8× compression), no calibration / no       
  learned scale
  - Fused decode kernel: in-register dequant + online softmax + WGMMA matmul + split-K reduce                       
  - KV cache physical layout aligned to WGMMA `m64n8k16` RS register mapping → zero shuffle / zero indexing         
  arithmetic at decode time                                                                                         
  - `byte_lut + prmt.b32` 4-bit dequant at **2 instructions per byte** (vs ~5–7 for the naive shf+lop3 path)        
  - Software-pipelined inner loop overlapping LSU / Dequant ALU / Tensor Core                                       
  - V dequant pre-issued across the softmax barrier to overlap LSU with softmax ALU                                 
  - FA4-style conditional O-rescaling skipping most tiles                                                           
                                                                                                                    
  **Performance on H100 80GB HBM3, head_dim=128, GQA G=8**                                                          
                                                         
  vs FlashInfer FP16 (same paged decode interface):                                                                 
                                                                                                                    
  | bs \ sl | 16K | 32K | 64K | 128K |
  |---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|                                                                                        
  | 16 | 2.04× | 2.11× | 2.14× | **2.23×** |             
  | 32 | **2.17×** | 2.16× | **2.26×** | — |                                                                        
   
  vs FlashAttention-3 FP8 (uncompressed-cache SOTA):                                                                
                                                                                                                    
  | bs \ sl | 16K | 32K | 64K |
  |---:|---:|---:|---:|                                                                                             
  | 20 | **2.35×** | **2.34×** | **2.32×** |             
                                                                                                                    
  Peak speedups: **2.45× over FlashInfer FP16** (bs=32, sl=32K) and **2.47× over FA3 FP8** (bs=20, sl=16K).
                                                                                                                    
  At 128K context, bs=1: latency matches FA3 FP8 (148.7 µs vs 143.3 µs) but the KV cache footprint is 1/4 — the same
   80GB GPU fits roughly 4× the batch.

comments.author: Defilan
comments.body:
M5 Max numbers, in case useful for the upstream PR shape:

Ran a 7-hour sweep across f16 / q8_0 / turbo3 / turbo4 at depths 0 to 1M tokens on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B Q8 via this fork (turbo3 sparse-V dequant on by default).

Two findings I haven't seen surfaced explicitly in the thread:

1. **turbo3 matches or beats q8_0 on prompt processing past ~128K.** At 256K depth: turbo3 128 t/s vs q8_0 124 t/s. The bandwidth-bound regime favors the smaller cache once contexts grow.

2. **turbo3 and turbo4 split by phase at long context.** At 256K depth turbo3 wins prefill by +27% over turbo4, but turbo4 wins decode by +11%. The decode gap widens to +20% at 512K. Suggests workload-specific guidance: agentic / coding (deep context, lots of generated tokens) favors turbo4; RAG / batch QA (heavy prefill, short answers) favors turbo3.

Plus: **1M context runs.** turbo3 KV at 1M is ~52 GB, fits with the 37 GB weights in 128 GB unified memory. 30 t/s prefill, 6.5 t/s decode at 1M. Slow but works.

Thanks @TheTom for the Metal port. Built clean on the M5 Max and the sparse-V dequant is doing real work at depth.

Full grid and bench script: https://llmkube.com/blog/turboquant-m5-max-long-context

---

Got the test rig set up this morning and ran the matrix end-to-end on the M5 Max. Writeup with full grid + methodology: https://llmkube.com/blog/vllm-swift-turboquant-m5-max

**Setup**: vllm-swift v0.3.0 from your Homebrew tap, mlx-community/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-8bit (35 GB on disk), 36-cell matrix (fp16 / turbo4v2 / turbo3 × 1K / 8K / 16K / 32K depths × 1 / 8 / 32 concurrency). Subprocess-per-cell, unique prompts, greedy temp=0, 50 generation tokens. 53 minutes wall, no OOMs.

**Phase 0 sanity** reproduced your README short-context numbers within ~5% on Qwen3-4B-4bit (B=8: 480.2 vs published 477; B=32: 1185 vs 1194; B=64: 1482 vs 1518), so I'm confident the rig is sane.

**Per-sequence decode tok/s at B=32** (35B-A3B-MLX-8bit):

| depth | fp16 | turbo4v2 | turbo3 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 1K | 115.4 | 104.0 (-10%) | 93.9 (-19%) |
| 8K | 110.9 | 97.4 (-12%) | 70.8 (-36%) |
| 16K | 105.9 | 91.0 (-14%) | 67.2 (-37%) |
| 32K | 96.2 | 79.7 (-17%) | 58.3 (-39%) |

Aggregate at B=32 d=32K: **fp16 3,078 tok/s**, turbo4v2 2,550, turbo3 1,866.

Three honest takeaways:

1. **fp16 wins decode at every cell we tested up to 32K.** The bandwidth-bound crossover that powered turbo on the llama.cpp fork past 256K doesn't show up in this regime here. Two non-exclusive reasons: (a) we capped at 32K depth following your README's `--max-model-len 40960` example and didn't experiment with pushing past that, and (b) the contiguous `BatchedKVCache` access pattern is different enough from llama.cpp's GGML kernels that the regime where compression wins on bandwidth may not trigger the same way. Can't distinguish those two from this data.

2. **Per-seq decode is essentially flat across concurrency** — fp16 d=8K is 102.2 / 110.6 / 110.9 at B=1 / 8 / 32. Aggregate scales near-linearly. Your `BatchedKVCache` story is real and the data confirms it cleanly.

3. **fp16 d=32K B=32 runs at 3,078 tok/s aggregate on a single MacBook Pro** for a 35B-A3B MoE. The model's `text_config` (`layer_types: 10 × full_attention + 30 × linear_attention`, `head_dim: 256`, `num_key_value_heads: 2`) means full-attention KV is ~20 KB per token, so the working set at this cell is ~55 GB — well within 128 GB UMA. (My initial framing claimed naive math said this should OOM at ~182 GB; that was wrong, I was carrying over Qwen3-4B numbers (36 layers × 8 KV × 128 head_dim) instead of the 35B-A3B's actual architecture. Apologies for the noise. The throughput number stands.)

**One bug worth flagging** (filed as [TheTom/vllm-swift#11](https://github.com/TheTom/vllm-swift/issues/11)): under vllm 0.19.1, `LLM(model="/path/to/local/MLX-dir")` with `additional_config` silently falls back to `Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B` from the HF cache and the SwiftInferenceEngine fails on that path. Worked around by routing through the C bridge directly (`vsm_engine_create` accepts `kv_scheme` + `kv_bits` as direct C API params), which kept the matrix easy to drive. Repro and full log in the issue.

**One observation that might be a feature, not a bug**: turbo4v2 is consistently 5–15% slower decode than turbo4 was on the llama.cpp fork at equivalent depth (different engine, different model file format, so the comparison is apples-to-mangoes — but worth flagging in case the v2 kernel has a Metal-specific tuning gap).

What I'd love to see next: any documented path to push past 40K on this engine. The model itself has `max_position_embeddings: 262144`, so the cap looks like a vllm-swift README convention rather than a model constraint, but I didn't find a knob in the published ex

comments.author: TheTom
comments.body:
thanks for the run + the harness rigor. the phase-0 sanity reproduction and the on-the-fly arch correction both tell me the data is solid.

on the 40k cap: pure readme convention, no code limit. `--max-model-len N` plumbs straight through `worker.py` to the swift engine without any enforcement; accepts whatever the model's max_position_embeddings allows (262144 for qwen3.6-35b-a3b). bump it and the matrix should run unchanged.

the cells worth running, with rough working-set math (20 kb/token kv × depth × batch + ~35 gb weights, using your corrected numbers):

| depth | fp16 (b=32) | turbo4v2 (b=32) | what i'd expect |
|---|---|---|---|
| 64k | ~75 gb | ~50 gb | both fit, fp16 likely still wins per-seq |
| 128k | ~115 gb | ~55 gb | fp16 near 128 gb uma ceiling, probably still fits |
| 192k | ~155 gb | ~65 gb | fp16 oom; compression wins by being the only option |

the 192k cell is where the compression value prop actually lands on this hardware. checking m5 max's ~400 gb/s sustained bandwidth against your per-lane decode rates, we aren't bandwidth-bound at any depth tested, so the bandwidth-bound crossover argument from the llama.cpp side is doing less work here than i'd expected. on this model + b=32, compression is mostly about staying under the memory ceiling, not raw decode throughput.

turbo4v2 vs llama.cpp turbo4 perf gap is a fair observation. different engine, different kernel, and i haven't done a head-to-head perf chase yet. a metal tuning gap on the long-context path is plausible.

TheTom/vllm-swift#11: reproduced + fixed in TheTom/vllm-swift#12. CLI bug was real. `vllm-swift serve <path>` was forwarding the positional path straight through to vllm's argparse, which mapped it to the deprecated `model_tag` slot instead of `--model`, so the path was silently dropped and vllm fell back to its built-in placeholder default. TheTom/vllm-swift#12 rewrites the wrapper to pass `--model "$1"` explicitly. the python `LLM(model=...)` path actually works on an unpatched wrapper, your script needs `if __name__ == '__main__':` around the `LLM(...)` block. without it, macos spawn recursively re-imports the script and the child's vllm config degrades to defaults during the broken handshake. that's why your `bench_throughput.py` workaround worked: it goes through ctypes against the dylib directly and skips multiprocessing entirely. with the main guard your exact `additional_config` + local-path pattern lands clean (verified locally with turbo4v2 on qwen3-0.6b-4bit).

appreciate the work + the writeup. if you want to join a small private group of folks working on llm inference, let me know and i'll send info to your email.

comments.author: TheTom
comments.body:
> is running tests on such old models even a valid comparison?

valid question, three answers:

1. those are the models rotorquant chose to publish against. its readme tested on llama 3.1 8B Q4_K_M and qwen2.5-7B Q3/Q4_K_M. if those models are invalid for comparing TurboQuant, then they're invalid for the original "beats turboquant 6.91 vs 7.07 ppl" claim too. either both work or neither does. you can't pick model coverage based on which way the result lands.

2. kv cache rotation math is architecture-agnostic on standard MHA/GQA. same head_dim, same RoPE, same softmax. the WHT decorrelation argument doesn't get more or less true on a newer model... it's a property of the rotation geometry, not the weights. that's why rotorquant published against qwen2.5-7B in the first place.

3. i did run newer too. qwen3-30B-A3B (MoE, same family) was in the bench set. on hybrid Mamba/GDN models like qwen3.6-35B-A3B the comparison gets weird because both rotations have to argue about how they interact with the linear-attention path, and that hasn't been benchmarked yet. it's not a free win for either side.

the structural point in #34 comment 16 doesn't depend on model year. WHT mixes all 128 dims at once, block-diagonal SO(n) doesn't decorrelate across groups. that gap holds on llama-2-7B and on qwen3.6 hybrid equally. testing on a newer dense model wouldn't change it.

> *Per-sequence decode tok/s at B=32* (35B-A3B-MLX-8bit):
> depth fp16 turbo4v2 turbo3
> 1K 115.4 104.0 (-10%) 93.9 (-19%)
> 8K 110.9 97.4 (-12%) 70.8 (-36%)
> 16K 105.9 91.0 (-14%) 67.2 (-37%)
> 32K 96.2 79.7 (-17%) 58.3 (-39%)
>
> Aggregate at B=32 d=32K: *fp16 3,078 tok/s*, turbo4v2 2,550, turbo3 1,866.
>
> Three honest takeaways:
>
>    1.
>
>    *fp16 wins decode at every cell we tested up to 32K.* The
>    bandwidth-bound crossover that powered turbo on the llama.cpp fork past
>    256K doesn't show up in this regime here. Two non-exclusive reasons: (a) we
>    couldn't push past ~32K cleanly because the published examples cap
>    --max-model-len at 40960 and we didn't experiment with RoPE scaling,
>    and (b) the contiguous BatchedKVCache access pattern is different
>    enough from llama.cpp's GGML kernels that the regime where compression wins
>    on bandwidth may not trigger the same way. Can't distinguish those two from
>    this data.
>    2.
>
>    *Per-seq decode is essentially flat across concurrency* — fp16 d=8K is
>    102.2 / 110.6 / 110.9 at B=1 / 8 / 32. Aggregate scales near-linearly. Your
>    BatchedKVCache story is real and the data confirms it cleanly.
>    3.
>
>    *fp16 d=32K B=32 fits 128 GB UMA and runs at 3,078 tok/s aggregate.*
>    Naive math said it should OOM (~32 × 4.6 GB KV + 35 GB weights ≈ 182 GB).
>    It didn't. Either the 35B-A3B's hybrid DeltaNet shrinks the per-token KV
>    footprint enough that my back-of-envelope is wrong, or your KV management
>    packs more efficiently than the linear estimate. Either way, useful
>    production data point.
>
> *One bug worth flagging* (filed as TheTom/vllm-swift#11
> <https://github.com/TheTom/vllm-swift/issues/11>): under vllm 0.19.1,
> LLM(model="/path/to/local/MLX-dir") with additional_config silently falls
> back to Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B from the HF cache and the SwiftInferenceEngine
> fails on that path. Worked around by routing through the C bridge directly (
> vsm_engine_create accepts kv_scheme + kv_bits as direct C API params),
> which kept the matrix easy to drive. Repro and full log in the issue.
>
> *One observation that might be a feature, not a bug*: turbo4v2 is
> consistently 5–15% slower decode than turbo4 was on the llama.cpp fork at
> equivalent depth (different engine, different model file format, so the
> comparison is apples-to-mangoes — but worth flagging in case the v2 kernel
> has a Metal-specific tuning gap).
>
> What I'd love to see next: any path to push past 32K cleanly on this
> engine. The crossover may live there, and right now we can't tell. If RoPE
> scaling lands or there's a way to relax the max_position_embeddings=40960
> constraint without distillation, I'd happily run a 64K / 128K / 256K
> extension.
>
> Thanks again for shipping this publicly and being open to a head-to-head
> bench. The concurrency story is genuinely good data.
>
> —

> <https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions/20969#discussioncomment-16784459>,
> or unsubscribe
> <https://github.com/notifications/unsubscri

Posting some benchmark data from my testing setup (RTX 4090, SM89) — collected results in a public repo: https://github.com/sztlink/turboquant-cuda-bench

**TurboQuant baseline** (TheTom's branch, q8_0-K + turbo3-V, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B Q4_K_M, 65K ctx):
- NIAH: **25/25** perfect retrieval up to 65K — no degradation from f16/f16
- TG flat across all depths (~180 t/s d0→d32K, MoE is memory-bandwidth bound)
- PPL: q8_0/turbo3 ≈ q8_0/q8_0 with meaningful KV memory reduction

**DFlash** (spiritbuun build 9304, Qwen3.6-27B dense):
- **Bug in build 8909 reproduced and fixed:** dflash.mask_token_id=248070 was registered as a special token in the drafter but absent from the target's special token cache, causing the draft model special tokens must match abort. Fixed in upstream HEAD (b9304).
- **Accept rate: 60%** with --draft 16
- Baseline tg128: 45.0 t/s @ d0, 37.4 t/s @ d32K

Multi-depth DFlash bench (d4096, d16384, d32768) pending — the interesting question is whether there's a crossover at high context depth where the drafter overhead becomes cheaper relative to the baseline degradation.

Drafter architecture note: dflash-draft-3.6-q4_k_m.gguf uses full 27B embedding width (5120) and FF dim (17408), so each of its 5 layers costs roughly as much per token as a target layer. At d0 where the 27B is fast (45 t/s), the drafter doesn't recover that overhead. The 35B-A3B MoE might be a better target pairing.

comments.author: sztlink
comments.body:
Follow-up on the DFlash depth bench.

**TL;DR:** DFlash has an encoder constraint that limits depth benchmarking on consumer hardware.

**Depth results (27B dense, draft=16):**

| depth | accept rate | eff. t/s |
|------:|------------|--------:|
| ~27 tok | 60% | 25.7 t/s |
| ~1500 tok | 37% | 16.9 t/s |

**The blocker for d4096+:** The drafter is non-causal (`causal_attn = false`) and requires `n_ubatch ≥ n_prompt_tokens`. On a 24 GB GPU, n_ubatch > 2048 blows the compute buffer. Benchmarking beyond ~d2K is not feasible on RTX 4090 with current build — would need ≥80 GB VRAM.

**The accept rate drop (60% → 37%)** between d27 and d1500 is notable. Two candidates: (1) repetitive prompt creating a degenerate drafting scenario, (2) KV bandwidth overhead compounding with lower acceptance. The drafter itself runs at constant ~47 t/s across both depths (SWA window = 2048, no depth degradation on drafter side).

Full data: https://github.com/sztlink/turboquant-cuda-bench/blob/main/bench/dflash/results.md

comments.author: sztlink
comments.body:
## RotorQuant (planar3/iso3) vs TurboQuant (turbo3) — Qwen3.6-27B, RTX 4090

Following up with a bench of the RotorQuant fork (`johndpope/llama-cpp-turboquant`, branch `feature/planarquant-kv-cache`) on hardware we have available: Qwen3.6-27B dense Q4_K_M on an RTX 4090.

RotorQuant's published claims are on Llama 3.1 8B (head dim 128, RTX 5090). Qwen3.6 has GQA with `n_embd_head_k = 256` — twice the head dimension.

**Perplexity — wikitext2, 2048 ctx:**

| cache type | PPL | Δ vs q8_0 | KV (2048 ctx, 16 KV layers) | pp t/s |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| q8_0 | 6.1005 | — | 68 MiB | 2789 |
| turbo3 | 6.1507 | +0.82% | 25 MiB | 2748 |
| planar3 | 6.3541 | +4.16% | 76.5 MiB | 1729 |
| iso3 | 6.3701 | +4.42% | 76.5 MiB | 1391 |

**Finding: planar3/iso3 K cache is larger than q8_0 on this model.**

turbo3: K=12.5 MiB, V=12.5 MiB — 63% reduction vs baseline.  
planar3/iso3: K=64 MiB, V=12.5 MiB — K buffer is 88% larger than q8_0's 34 MiB.

The block-diagonal rotation in RotorQuant appears to hit a layout issue with 256-dim heads. At 128 dims (Llama 3.1 8B), the blocks presumably divide cleanly into the quantization grain. At 256 dims on Qwen3.6, they don't — producing an inflated storage representation and 38–50% throughput loss.

turbo3 is the clear winner on this architecture: better PPL, 63% KV reduction, no throughput regression.

Full results: https://github.com/sztlink/turboquant-cuda-bench/blob/main/bench/rotorquant/results.md

Note: `llama-bench.exe` was blocked by Windows Smart App Control on our test machine (same issue we worked around for build-head3). TG speed numbers from `llama-bench` are not available for this run; the pp t/s above come from `llama-perplexity` chunked-batch evaluation and are relative comparisons only.

comments.author: sztlink
comments.body:
**RotorQuant Llama 3.1 8B update** — confirming PPL claim, but K cache and throughput are problematic.

Ran `johndpope/llama-cpp-turboquant` branch `feature/planarquant-kv-cache` (`fc3d1b6`) on **Llama 3.1 8B Instruct Q4_K_M** (head_dim=128, n_kv_heads=8), RTX 4090:

| cache | PPL | K MiB | pp t/s |
|---|---|---|---|
| q8_0 | 6.598 | 68 | 9559 |
| turbo3 | 6.982 | 25 | 9209 |
| planar3 | 6.948 | **128** | 2530 |
| iso3 | **6.822** | **128** | 1734 |

**PPL is confirmed** — iso3 (6.82) beats turbo3 (6.98) on the target model, consistent with the RotorQuant README claim.

**But the K cache is 2× q8_0** (128 MiB vs 68 MiB) despite being nominally 3-bit. And throughput is −82% vs q8_0, not the +28% the README claims. Same K cache anomaly appeared on Qwen3.6-27B (head_dim=256): K was 64 MiB vs 34 MiB for q8_0.

Hypothesis: the K cache is stored at higher precision for deferred rotation at attention time, quantized on-the-fly during dot product — explaining both memory inflation and throughput loss. The PPL gain is real; the memory/speed benefits require a fused write-time quantization path.

Full cross-model data (Llama 8B + Qwen3.6-27B): https://github.com/sztlink/turboquant-cuda-bench/tree/main/bench/rotorquant

@johndpope — issues are disabled on your fork; posting here since the community is active. Is the deferred-rotation hypothesis correct? Is a write-time path planned?

## REFRACT score4 (trajectory v0.1.4) + score3090 — Qwen3-27B & 32B, RTX 4090 & 3090

Following up on my earlier [score3 results](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions/20969#discussioncomment-16810278) (GTM axis, Qwen3.6-27B). Two new datasets tonight.

---

### 1. Axis A: trajectory v0.1.4 vs GTM — Qwen3.6-27B Q4_K_M, RTX 4090 (SM89)

The key finding: **GTM and trajectory disagree significantly on turbo3**.

| candidate | GTM score | GTM band | trajectory | traj band | KLD |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ctk=q8_0, ctv=q8_0 | 95.65 | EXCELLENT | **84.39** | EXCELLENT | 99.61 |
| ctk=q8_0, ctv=turbo3 | 90.99 | EXCELLENT | **57.93** | **DEGRADED** | 98.87 |
| ctk=turbo3, ctv=turbo3 | 89.16 | EXCELLENT | **57.93** | **DEGRADED** | 98.28 |

GTM classifies all three as EXCELLENT. Trajectory v0.1.4 reveals that turbo3 on the V cache degrades generation trajectories by ~33 points — enough to flip the band to DEGRADED. KLD (perplexity on wikitext) stays high regardless, confirming that perplexity alone misses this.

Notable: ctk=q8_0 vs ctk=turbo3 makes **zero difference** to the trajectory score (both 57.93) — the V cache is the critical component.

---

### 2. Cross-model: Qwen3-32B Q4_K_M, RTX 3090 (SM86), GTM axis

First public REFRACT scores for Qwen3-32B dense.

| candidate | GTM | KLD | composite | band |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ctk=q8_0, ctv=q8_0 | 93.87 | 99.44 | **96.58** | EXCELLENT |
| ctk=q8_0, ctv=turbo3 | 88.83 | 97.54 | **92.99** | EXCELLENT |
| ctk=turbo3, ctv=turbo3 | 81.88 | 86.45 | **84.11** | **PASS** |
| ctk=q8_0, ctv=turbo4 | — | — | CRASH | SET_ROWS |
| ctk=turbo4, ctv=turbo4 | — | — | CRASH | SET_ROWS |

Two observations:
- 32B is ~2 pts lower than 27B on GTM (93.87 vs 95.65 for q8/q8) — larger models are not automatically more robust to KV quantization
- turbo3/turbo3 KLD drops to 86.45 on 32B (vs 98.28 on 27B) — the K+V combo hits perplexity harder on this architecture
- turbo4 fails with `ggml-backend.cpp:898: pre-allocated tensor [...] cannot run the operation (SET_ROWS)` on SM86; not yet tested on SM89

---

**Build:** `60fc49547` (turboquant, CUDA), REFRACT v0.3.2.3  
**Models:** `q36_27b_new.gguf` (27B), `Qwen3-32B-Q4_K_M.gguf` (32B)

**Follow-up: REFRACT score5 — Trajectory axis on Qwen3-32B (RTX 3090, SM86)**

Hardware: RTX 3090 (SM86, compute cap 8.6), CUDA 11.8, REFRACT v0.3.2.3
Model: Qwen3-32B Q4\_K\_M

| candidate | traj | KLD | composite | band |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ctk=q8\_0, ctv=q8\_0 | 52.84 | 99.44 | 69.01 | **DEGRADED** |
| ctk=q8\_0, ctv=turbo3 | 23.39 | 97.54 | 37.73 | **FAIL** |
| ctk=turbo3, ctv=turbo3 | 9.97 | 86.45 | 17.87 | **FAIL** |

For reference — 27B trajectory (RTX 4090, SM89, from previous comment):

| candidate | traj | composite | band |
|---|---|---|---|
| q8\_0/q8\_0 | 84.39 | 91.37 | EXCELLENT |
| q8\_0/turbo3 | 57.93 | 73.06 | DEGRADED |
| turbo3/turbo3 | 57.93 | 72.89 | DEGRADED |

**Findings:**

1. **Scale amplifies trajectory divergence dramatically.** 32B shows 3–6× lower trajectory scores than 27B for identical quantization. Even the near-lossless q8\_0/q8\_0 baseline is DEGRADED at 32B scale.

2. **GTM blindspot is much larger for 32B.** Cross-referencing with our previous GTM run (Qwen3-32B, same machine):
   - q8\_0/q8\_0: GTM=93.87 vs traj=52.84 → gap **+41 pts**
   - q8\_0/turbo3: GTM=88.83 vs traj=23.39 → gap **+65 pts**
   - turbo3/turbo3: GTM=81.88 vs traj=9.97 → gap **+72 pts**
   GTM says q8\_0/turbo3 is near-excellent (88.83); trajectory says it has materially broken generation paths (FAIL). The gap grows with model size and quantization aggressiveness.

3. **turbo3 V-cache essentially breaks 32B generation paths.** Trajectory of 9.97 for turbo3/turbo3 means only ~1 in 10 decode steps follows the fp16 reference path. The model generates plausible-looking text (KLD=86.45) while following a completely different reasoning trajectory.

4. **KLD cross-validates previous data.** turbo3/turbo3 KLD=86.45 exactly matches our earlier GTM+KLD run on the same hardware — consistent across test methodologies.

**Technical note:** `llama-completion` compiled natively for SM86 from `tools/completion/completion.cpp` (REFRACT v0.1.4 patch), MSVC 14.41, CUDA 11.8.

### REFRACT attn-fix rerun: 27B + 32B, SM86 + SM89

I reran the REFRACT GTM/Trajectory comparison after the attention fix, using a clean build from the turboquant branch (`69d8e4be4`).

- RTX 4090 / SM89 / CUDA 12.8

- Qwen3-32B Q4_K_M

#### Axis A scores: GTM vs Trajectory

| Model / GPU | Candidate | GTM | Trajectory | KLD in trajectory run |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 27B / 4090 | q8/q8 | 95.65 | 84.39 | 99.61 |
| 27B / 4090 | q8/turbo3 | 90.99 | 57.93 | 98.87 |
| 27B / 4090 | turbo3/turbo3 | 89.16 | 57.93 | 98.28 |
| 27B / 3090 | q8/q8 | 95.96 | 83.49 | 99.58 |
| 27B / 3090 | q8/turbo3 | 91.27 | 57.33 | 99.05 |
| 27B / 3090 | turbo3/turbo3 | 89.68 | 57.33 | 98.29 |
| 32B / 3090 | q8/q8 | 93.87 | 59.32 | 99.44 |
| 32B / 3090 | q8/turbo3 | 88.83 | 24.95 | 97.54 |
| 32B / 3090 | turbo3/turbo3 | 81.88 | 24.95 | 86.45 |

The important part: **ctv=turbo3 preserves high GTM but collapses Trajectory**, and the effect gets much stronger at 32B.

comments.author: seanrasch
comments.body:
**Ampere (RTX 3080 Ti SM 86) — Qwen3.5 9B Hybrid + DeepSeek MoE Update**

Catching up after a few weeks. Two sets of results on the canonical branch tip (`69d8e4be4`), built with `GGML_CUDA_FA_ALL_QUANTS=ON`.

### 1. Qwen3.5 9B Hybrid: turbo beats f16 at long context

Qwen3.5 9B is now a hybrid DeltaNet+attention model (`full_attention_interval=4` — only 8/32 layers have full attention, rest are SSM). `head_dim=256`.

| Config | pp512 | pp2048 | pp8192 | pp32768 | tg128 |
|--------|-------|--------|--------|---------|-------|
| f16/f16 | 3,680 | 3,891 | 3,685 | 2,863 | 101.9 |
| turbo3/turbo3 | 3,842 | 3,904 | **3,807** | **3,380** | 98.8 |
| turbo2/turbo2 | 3,696 | 3,870 | **3,797** | **3,384** | 99.6 |
| turbo4/turbo4 | 3,434 | — | **3,811** | **3,370** | 98.0 |
| q8_0/turbo3 | 3,759 | 3,874 | 3,782 | 3,378 | 99.6 |
| q8_0/turbo2 | 3,723 | 3,853 | 3,785 | 3,383 | 99.2 |

**turbo3 prefill is 103% of f16 at 8K and 118% at 32K.** Same pattern across turbo2 and turbo4. Decode is 96-98% of f16 for all turbo types.

This follows the same dynamic as the MoE 1.76x result from April — when only a fraction of layers use attention, the bandwidth savings from compressed KV cache outweigh dequant overhead. The fewer attention layers a model has, the more turbo helps.

Note: `q8_0/q8_0` fails to create context on this model (filed as TheTom/llama-cpp-turboquant#130). q8_0 K works fine in asymmetric configs.

### 2. DeepSeek MoE: turbo2 advantage inverted

Revisiting the "turbo2 1.76x faster than f16" result from April. On the current canonical:

| Config | pp512 | tg128 |
|--------|-------|-------|
| f16/f16 | 5,328 | **241.5** |
| turbo2/turbo2 | 158 | **108** |

f16 improved **4.28x** (56→242) from upstream llama.cpp MoE optimizations. turbo2 improved 9% (100→108). The turbo2 VEC FA path doesn't benefit from the new optimized MMA-based MoE attention. Result: turbo2 is now **0.45x of f16 on MoE decode**, inverting the April advantage.

Turbo's value on MoE is now purely about memory compression (fitting longer contexts), not decode speed. As upstream improves, turbo types fall behind on models where f16 gets the optimized kernel paths.

**Hardware:** RTX 3080 Ti (SM 8.6, 12GB VRAM), CUDA 12.x
**Model:** Qwen3.5-9B Q4_K_M, DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Lite Q4_K_M

comments.author: X-15
comments.body:
**Disclosure:** follow-up to my [earlier comment](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions/20969#discussioncomment-16845378) — same setup, posted on behalf of @X-15 by Claude (Anthropic's LLM). Data is real; analysis mine.

## Context-length OOM frontier on a single RTX 4090 (Qwen3.6-27B Q4_K_M)

The earlier comment compared decode speed at fixed `-c 65536`. This one probes the other axis: **what's the maximum `-c` that boots without OOM in each config?** Same model file (`froggeric/Qwen3.6-27B-MTP-GGUF` Q4_K_M), same `--parallel 1`, same hardware.

| Config | Max ctx that boots | KV @ max | Total VRAM @ max |
|---|---|---|---|
| Vanilla (`-ctk f16 -ctv f16`, no MTP) | **262 144 (256K, model native max)** | 16.00 GiB | 22.9 GiB |
| TurboQuant only (`-ctk turbo3 -ctv turbo3`, no MTP) | **262 144 (256K, model native max)** | 5.81 GiB | 23.12 GiB |
| **TurboQuant + MTP** (`-ctk turbo3 -ctv turbo3 --spec-type mtp`) | **≈ 136 K** (`-c 139264` boots, `-c 147456` does not) | 3.16 GiB | 24.02 GiB (cliff edge) |

So on a 24 GiB card, with this 27B-class hybrid attention/SSM model:

- Vanilla and TQ-only **both** reach the model-native 256 K ceiling. Vanilla isn't VRAM-limited here at all — only ≈ 16 of 64 main layers carry KV (`qwen35.full_attention_interval = 4`), so 64 KiB/token × 256 K = 16 GiB fits.
- TurboQuant compresses KV by **2.75×** at 256 K (16.00 → 5.81 GiB). The full-bit-rate ratio is ≈ 5×, but the per-block norms in turbo3 push effective bits/element to ≈ 6.
- **MTP roughly halves the practical ceiling on a 4090.** Even with the smaller turbo3 KV (3.16 GiB at 136 K), TQ+MTP at 136 K is already at 24.02 GiB / 24.56 GiB total. The MTP draft branch's own buffers (compute, `n_ubatch`-scaled allocations) eat the headroom that TurboQuant freed up. So MTP delivers its 2× decode-speed win on short outputs at the cost of about half your usable context window on consumer hardware.

## Diagnostic finding worth flagging — misleading error on TQ+MTP OOM

Every TQ+MTP probe past the threshold prints exactly this on stderr:

```
load_tensors: loading model tensors, this can take a while... (mmap = true, direct_io = false)
llama_model_load: error loading model: invalid vector subscript
llama_model_load_from_file_impl: failed to load model
srv    load_model: failed to load MTP head from '...Qwen3.6-27B-Q4_K_M-mtp.gguf'
main: exiting due to model loading error
```

There's no `cudaMalloc failed`, no `out of memory`, no `failed to allocate`. The error surfaces as a C++ STL `invalid vector subscript` exception during the **second-pass MTP head load** (with `override_arch=qwen35_mtp`).

The downstream message — "failed to load MTP head from `<path>`" — strongly implies the GGUF is malformed. **It isn't.** The same GGUF loads cleanly at `-c 65536` and runs all of [the extended battery](https://gist.github.com/X-15/a597ff3b84f15fb32d7434117a9ef160#file-extended_results-md) (NIAH at 5 depths, RULER variable tracking, BFCL irrelevance detection, LoopLLM stress, LongGenBench 50-line generation, greedy `max_diff = 0` MTP-vs-noMTP equivalence — all pass). What changed is the user's `-c` got bigger than the MTP head's compute buffer can fit.

The reason this matters: I had previously seen the **identical** error message on `RDson/Qwen3.6-27B-MTP-Q4_K_M-GGUF`, where the diagnosis was actually a malformed GGUF (no MTP weight tensors). So now `invalid vector subscript` + "failed to load MTP head" is overloaded:

- "Your GGUF doesn't have MTP weights" → real GGUF problem, file an issue with the uploader
- "Your `-c` is too big for VRAM with MTP enabled" → just lower `-c`

A user has no way to tell from the error which one they're hitting. Suggested upstream fix: catch the allocator failure inside the second-pass model load and emit something like `failed to allocate MTP-head buffers; try a smaller -c (got -c=N, last successful at -c=M)` instead of letting an STL exception escape with a misleading file-path reference.
