comments.author: gvillines-hub
comments.body:
Independent data point that lines up with what @sztlink has been finding on the trajectory axis, but from a simpler angle.

I built a benchmark harness comparing KIVI (4-bit and 2-bit) against a norm-direction quantization approach (8-bit norm + 3/4-bit unit direction) across Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-1.5B, Llama-3.1-8B, and Mistral-7B-v0.3. The harness reports per-head minimum cosine similarity alongside average cosine.

The finding that lines up with sztlink's REFRACT work: average-cosine and PPL can both look healthy while worst-case quality has already collapsed.

KIVI 4-bit on Qwen2.5-7B reports avg cos 0.983 — looks fine. Min cos is 0.588, meaning at least one layer/head combination is producing near-random output. Same pattern at Qwen2.5-1.5B (avg 0.983 / min 0.646). On Llama-3.1-8B and Mistral-7B-v0.3, KIVI 4-bit min cos stays at 0.953–0.977. So it's not a universal KIVI failure — it's architecture-dependent, consistent with @scos-lab's K/V norm-ratio data from earlier in the thread.

This isn't the same as what trajectory metrics capture (path divergence over many decode steps), but it's a cheap proxy for one class of the problem — the per-token failures that get averaged away. Easy to compute from the FP16 forward pass without running full generation.

N+D quantization (8-bit norm + low-bit unit direction) stabilizes the Qwen failure: min cos 0.969–0.991 at ~3.9× compression across all four models. It's mechanistically distinct from rotation-based methods — no Hadamard, no codebook. Decomposition primitive overlaps with MiniCache (NeurIPS 2024); the application differs from those. No llama.cpp port; that was paused once it became clear how much serious TurboQuant work was happening here.

Mostly sharing in case the harness is useful: it's pluggable, so dropping in turbo3/turbo4 or any of the rotorquant variants for a direct head-to-head against KIVI and N+D on the same four-model suite is a `Quantizer` subclass in `nd_kv_quant/quantization.py`. PRs welcome.

Repo: https://github.com/gvillines-hub/nd-kv-quant (Apache 2.0)

comments.author: gvillines-hub
comments.body:
Follow-up to my earlier comment. Saturday turned into a longer working session than I expected, so this consolidates two passes of analysis into one post: paper-faithful TurboQuant across four models, then an outlier-aware variant on top of that to test @scos-lab's mixed-precision recipe against the same per-head min cosine probe.
Pass 1: I added paper-faithful TurboQuant to the harness — random rotation (Algorithm 1) and WHT (the variant llama.cpp implementations ship), Lloyd-Max codebook on the Beta distribution from Lemma 1, no QJL residual since the consensus from @arclabs001 and @scos-lab is that QJL hurts attention quality. Implementation verified against the paper's analytical centroid values (page 10) and Lloyd-Max Gaussian distortion reference within 2%.
Pass 2: I then implemented the outlier-aware recipe @scos-lab described in this thread — top-K channels by RMS pulled out and quantized at higher precision, the rest going through the standard TurboQuant rotation + codebook path. Tested three bit allocations.
Per-head minimum cosine across the four models, at compression ratios around 4×:
Method                              Qwen2.5-7B   Qwen2.5-1.5B   Llama-3.1-8B   Mistral-7B-v0.3
KIVI 4-bit (3.9x)                     0.588         0.646          0.977            0.953
N+D N8+D4 (3.9x)                      0.969         0.991          0.990            0.991
TurboQuant uniform 4-bit rand (3.9x)  0.034         0.144          0.974            0.974
TurboQuant uniform 4-bit WHT  (3.9x) -0.051         0.024          0.977            0.977
TQ outlier 3.5b 10%@8+90%@3   (4.4x)  0.132         0.389          0.971            0.978
TQ outlier 3.2b 20%@4+80%@3   (4.8x)  0.595         0.627          0.964            0.977
TQ outlier 2.25b 25%@3+75%@2  (6.7x)  0.320         0.219          0.862            0.914
Three things from this data.

First: paper-faithful TurboQuant matches its published claims on Llama-3.1-8B and Mistral-7B-v0.3 (both around min cos 0.97 at 4-bit, consistent with the paper's Needle-In-A-Haystack result on Llama-3.1-8B), and collapses to near-zero or negative min cosine on both Qwen2.5 models. WHT substitution doesn't help; sometimes makes it slightly worse. This is consistent with what's already in the thread — @scos-lab's K/V norm ratio data predicts exactly this regime, and @sztlink's REFRACT trajectory work is what catches the same kind of failure at long context.

Second: outlier-aware mixed precision rescues TurboQuant partially on Qwen, not fully. The standard recipe (top-10% at 8-bit, rest at 3-bit, ~3.5 effective bits) brings Qwen2.5-7B from -0.05 to 0.13 — better than uniform, still far from deployable. Widening the outlier band to 20% at 4-bit gets Qwen2.5-7B to 0.60 and Qwen2.5-1.5B to 0.63. Better, but still below the 0.95+ threshold where per-head min cosine looks deployment-safe. Worth noting: 20%@4-bit beats 10%@8-bit on Qwen even though the average bit budget is similar — for this architecture the outlier mass appears to be wider than the standard recipe assumes.

Third: on Llama and Mistral, outlier handling makes essentially no difference (0.971-0.978 with vs 0.974-0.977 without). The recipe is a Qwen-class intervention, which is consistent with the same K/V norm ratio data driving the failure in the first place.
What's new here, methodologically, is the cheap proxy. Per-head min cosine on the FP16 forward pass surfaces the failure (and partial-rescue) signature without needing trajectory evaluation, KLD sweeps, or downstream task benchmarks. It runs in seconds and falls out of standard attention math.

Worth being explicit about scope. This tests the paper algorithm plus a recipe layer derived from the thread's findings. It does not test the deployed tq3_0 variants in llama.cpp from @TheTom, @animehacker, or @unixsysdev — those include block-wise handling and engineering specifics the paper doesn't cover. The deployed variants may already address what's shown here,

comments.author: devYRPauli
comments.body:
**Edit (2026-10-05):** some claims below are wrong: the 2K score, the 4x memory figure, the QJL framing, and the speed note. See my correction in the reply to this comment: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions/20969#discussioncomment-18763229

M1 Pro 16 GB datapoint + upstream PRs

Catching this thread late. I ran a full TurboQuant evaluation on Apple M1 Pro 16 GB across two rounds (MLX path via mlx-optiq / turboquant_plus, and CPU+Metal via Aaryan-Kapoor/llama.cpp's turboquant-tq3_0). Stock implementations returned 0% on needle-in-haystack at every context length I tried. After fixing the QJL math and adding the missing Metal kernels, the Hybrid K5/V4 config reached 100% retrieval at 16K tokens.

Five fixes were required. Three were already known or have since been picked up upstream (Hybrid K5/V4, GGML context sizing for the shared rotation tensors — independently fixed by @wxtry in 70e45b7e on llama-cpp-turboquant). Two are new and now upstream PRs:

1. QJL orthogonal projection + sqrt(d) scale factor (the reference Python impl used a Gaussian S and a 1/d scale, both wrong — together they collapse the two-stage design): https://github.com/TheTom/turboquant_plus/pull/93
2. tq3_0 norm correction + zero block handling + full Metal GPU support (the K-path was silently corrupting key magnitudes, and tq3_0 wasn't registered as a supported Metal type): https://github.com/Aaryan-Kapoor/llama.cpp/pull/1

Full benchmarks, logs, patches, and a post-mortem on why every stock implementation degenerated are at: https://github.com/devYRPauli/turboquant-m1pro-evaluation

Headline numbers on Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, M1 Pro 16 GB:
* MLX Hybrid K5/V4 (after QJL fix): 100% needle retrieval at 2K, 4K, 8K, 16K (was 0% at all lengths with stock)
* KV memory at 16K: 562 MB → 140 MB (4x, confirmed)
* Decode: ~1.1 tok/s — heavily Python-bound, unoptimized dequantization is the bottleneck, not the algorithm

Happy to share more detail on any of the fixes if useful.

comments.author: devYRPauli
comments.body:
Correction to my comment above. I reran the MLX numbers from committed code, and some of my claims were wrong.

* **Needle retrieval.** The Hybrid K5/V4 run scored 100% at 4K, 8K, and 16K, and 50% at 2K. It did not score 100% at all four lengths. At 2K the model wrote a corrupted allele name. I had modified the installed mlx-optiq files in place and did not keep them. A rebuild of those changes (`benchmarks/tq_patched.py`) scores 100% at 16K and 50% at 2K, 4K, and 8K on macOS 27.0.1. So 16K is the only Hybrid result that reproduces from the repo.
* **KV memory.** "562 MB -> 140 MB (4x, confirmed)" was a formula figure, not a measurement. mlx-optiq 0.0.1 stores one byte per element and does not pack bits. At 16K the measured cache is 563 MB for FP16 and 436 MB for Hybrid K5/V4, so it is 1.29x smaller. Peak MLX memory is higher with the quantized cache: 3245 MB against 3077 MB for FP16. The cache returns float32 K/V, so attention runs in float32.
* **QJL.** The Gaussian matrix with the 1/d scale is not wrong. It is the paper's construction, and it is unbiased. At head dimension 128 its variance is too high, and generation degenerates. The orthogonal matrix with the sqrt(d) scale is one coupled change that reduces the variance. It does not fix two bugs.
* **Speed.** The 1.1 tok/s figure includes the 16K prefill. The bottleneck is dequantization of the full cache at every step in unfused MLX operations.
* **Metal.** The 16K result is from the MLX path. The Metal kernels in Aaryan-Kapoor/llama.cpp#1 are for the llama.cpp path, which I tested with the needle at 2K and 4K only.

The raw output for each number is in the README results table and in "Reproduction on 2026-10-05" in FINDINGS.md: https://github.com/devYRPauli/turboquant-m1pro-evaluation/blob/main/FINDINGS.md#reproduction-on-2026-10-05

comments.author: Andgihat
comments.body:
Sharing a Windows x64 prebuilt that combines TheTom's TurboQuant kernels
  (cherry-picked into NJannasch's `mtp-turboquant` branch) with `--spec-type draft-mtp`
  from PR #22673. Built natively for `120a-real` (Blackwell consumer sm_120, RTX 5060 Ti
  through 5090), CUDA Toolkit 12.8, MSVC 14.44.

  Targeted at the gap I kept hitting: upstream prebuilts have MTP but no TurboQuant,
  TheTom's `tqp-v0.1.1` has TurboQuant but no MTP and ships CUDA 12.4 with
  `GGML_CUDA_FORCE_CUBLAS=ON` stuck in `CMakeCache.txt` (this disables MMQ on Blackwell —
  ~50% decode loss empirically). AmesianX has Windows sm_120 binaries but no MTP integration.
  NJannasch combined the right pieces in source but hasn't released binaries.

  ### Benchmarks — RTX 5060 Ti 16GB, Qwen3.6-27B-UD-IQ3_XXS (Unsloth MTP variant)

  | Build | pp512 | tg128 | Decode (MTP, prod prompt) |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | TheTom `tqp-v0.1.1` | n/a | 19 | n/a |
  | Upstream b9495 + q8_0, no MTP | 1032 | 34 | n/a |
  | Upstream b9495 + q8_0 + MTP (n_max=5) | 109 | 34 | 54 |
  | **This build (turbo3 + MTP n_max=2)** | **97** | **31** | **47** |

  256K context loads on 16 GB VRAM (~14.7 GB total footprint, ~430 MB free margin).
  Verified end-to-end by downloading my own release zip and re-benchmarking —
  within 3% of source build.

  ### Worth highlighting from the build config

  - `GGML_NATIVE=ON` auto-detects local arch, then `CMakeLists.txt` replaces
    `120-real` → `120a-real` for FP4 tensor cores. Don't pass plain `120` manually
  - `GGML_CUDA_FORCE_MMQ=ON` explicitly (safety against stale caches)
  - `GGML_CCACHE=OFF` (skipped — no ccache installed)
  - **The build dir must be wiped before reconfigure.** `cmake -B build` does NOT
    overwrite cached values, including `FORCE_CUBLAS=ON` from older workflow
    templates. This is the silent root cause of the ~50% TheTom slowdown — if
    anyone else has been mystified by their TurboQuant binary being slow on
    Blackwell, check `build/CMakeCache.txt`

  ### Known limits

  - `--mmproj` + `--spec-type draft-mtp` triggers issue #22867 (slot corruption +
    OOM during mmproj restore) — affects all builds, not specific to this one
  - Running with `-c >small` **without** `--spec-type draft-mtp` triggers
    `llama-memory-recurrent.cpp:173: GGML_ASSERT(rollback >= 1 && rollback <= n_rs_seq)`
    — specific to NJannasch's GDN code path. Workaround: always activate MTP for
    long-context runs, or use upstream for non-MTP
  - CUDA 13.x not tested with TurboQuant kernels (12.8/12.9 confirmed)
  - For RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell (sm_122) and other non-consumer variants, the
    `120a-real` binary won't load — rebuild from source with `GGML_NATIVE=ON`

  ### Links

  - Repo + release v1.0 (zip ~589 MB, all CUDA runtime DLLs bundled):
    https://github.com/Andgihat/llama-cpp-mtp-turboquant-sm120-blackwell-windows
  - `BUILD-NOTES.md` in the repo: full reproducible recipe (~2-3 hours from scratch
    including toolchain install)

  Credits: TheTom for the TurboQuant kernel port that made all of this possible,
  NJannasch for the MTP + TurboQuant cherry-pick base, AmesianX for parallel work
  informing the v1.7.0 Windows sm_120 path. All MIT, this build inherits.

  @NJannasch — your `mtp-turboquant` branch was exactly the cherry-pickable shape
  I needed. If you'd like the link added/removed/cited differently in your repo,
  just say.

items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

There is something very wrong with the float16 implementation in the CPU backend.  It's much slower than the float32 implementation.  I created a very simple matmul test to reproduce the issue, posting results below:

```
PyTorch Version: 2.6.0+cpu
torch.backends.cpu.get_cpu_capability(): AVX512

500x500 matrix multiplication:
fp16: 0.10194063186645508 seconds
fp32: 0.001997709274291992 seconds
fp16 takes x51.0 times


1000x1000 matrix multiplication:
fp16: 0.9695210456848145 seconds
fp32: 0.007059574127197266 seconds
fp16 takes x137.3 times


2000x2000 matrix multiplication:
fp16: 7.783996105194092 seconds
fp32: 0.057384490966796875 seconds
fp16 takes x135.6 times
```

```
PyTorch Version: 2.7.0.dev20250205+cpu
torch.backends.cpu.get_cpu_capability(): AVX512

500x500 matrix multiplication:
fp16: 0.09653520584106445 seconds
fp32: 0.002435922622680664 seconds
fp16 takes x39.6 times


1000x1000 matrix multiplication:
fp16: 0.9120731353759766 seconds
fp32: 0.011063098907470703 seconds
fp16 takes x82.4 times


2000x2000 matrix multiplication:
fp16: 6.930181264877319 seconds
fp32: 0.07475137710571289 seconds
fp16 takes x92.7 times
```

System information: Intel Core i7-1065G7 CPU running on Linux 6.12.11

I am a regular user of llama.cpp, where I use all quants from fp16 to q4, and never observed extreme performance issues of this kind.

The benchmark script is below:

```python
import time
import torch

print(f"PyTorch Version: {torch.__version__}")
print("torch.backends.cpu.get_cpu_capability():", torch.backends.cpu.get_cpu_capability())

items.title: CPU antialiased bilinear and bicubic interpolation repeats the first output row when resizing height with output width 1.
items.author: ethanclawsie
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

In aten/src/ATen/native/cpu/UpSampleKernel.cpp, when the output width is 1, basic_loop_separable_1d_vertical loops over the output rows but calls interpolate_separable_1d_zero_strides with the same index/weight table pointer every iteration, so every output row is computed with row 0's indices and weights.

Repro:

```python
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

x = torch.tensor([0., 1.]).reshape(1, 1, 2, 1)
y = F.interpolate(x, size=(4, 1), mode="bilinear", antialias=True)
y_cuda = F.interpolate(x.cuda(), size=(4, 1), mode="bilinear", antialias=True)
print("cpu: ", y.flatten().tolist())
print("cuda:", y_cuda.flatten().tolist())
```

Output:

```
cpu:  [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0]
cuda: [0.0, 0.25, 0.75, 1.0]
```

## 1. Agentic Cache Scheduling

- Supernode-wide KV Cache Sharing @hzh0425  @Shunkangz
	- Enable sharing of GPU-resident (L1) and host-resident (L2) KV caches across engines within the same NVLink domain.
	- Add cache location awareness to the Router to coordinate request placement and KV transfers based on cache availability and engine load.
	- Extend HiCache linker integration to support GPU-to-GPU KV transfers over NVLink and remote Grace DRAM access through EGM.
	- Optimize small KV-page transfers and NUMA placement; validate correctness, cache hit rate, and TTFT/TPOT on GB200 and GB300/ AMD Rack.
- Build a KV cache orchestrator across the router and engine @ZhaiFeiyue 
	- Identify sessions, sub-agents, and tool calls, and expose `PREFETCH`, `DEMOTE`, and `PIN` hints for global cache scheduling. Align this work with the [[router roadmap](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/25760)](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/25760). 
	- Add session-aware scheduling to the router
- Enhance HiCache Linker Mode @hzh0425 @alphabetc1 @huangtingwei9988 
    - Support fast failover and recovery.
    - Extend support to hybrid models with Mamba and SWA.
    - Improve reliability and observability for production deployment.
    - Refactor `hybrid_pool_assembler.py`：Simplify pool assembly and improve extensibility across model architectures.
- Support a [[unified KV cache layout](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/33651)](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/33651) for host cache and L3 storage: @Shunkangz @huangtingwei9988

    - [[PR #39726](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/39726)](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/39726): Add a JIT kernel to load page-unified host KV back to the device one layer at a time.
    - [[PR #39815](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/39815)](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/39815): Integrate page-unified host pools and storage keys with the HiCache linker.

## 2. Decode Prefix Cache @jojoakm @HZY-Wade

- Support an L2-only `DecodeRadixTree` to increase KV transfer batch sizes and reduce GPU memory pressure ([[PR #38292](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/38292)](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/38292)).

- [[PR #37615](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/37615)](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/37615): Add sharded KV pools that store each rank’s owned pages and assemble the full prefix for prefill attention.

items.title: trtllm-gen 2-CTA FP4 MoE GEMM cubins fault on B300 under per-thread scheduling skew at UTCBAR.2CTA.MULTICAST (0.6.18.post1, 0.7.0.post1, 0.7.1rc5)
items.author: henrylhtsang
items.body_excerpt:
## Before submitting

- [x] I have searched existing issues and did not find a solution or an existing report.

## Environment

```text
GPU: NVIDIA B300 SXM6 AC (SM103, 148 SMs) | Driver 580.159.03 | CUDA 13.0
torch 2.11.0+cu130, python 3.11, Ubuntu 22.04
flashinfer-python / flashinfer-cubin (release wheels): 0.6.18.post1, 0.7.0.post1, 0.7.1rc5
Method: NVBit-based SASS delay injection - per-thread delays inserted before selected
SASS instructions in the running kernel.
```

## Bug description

On B300, the 2-CTA-cluster (`c2x1x1`) trtllm-gen FP4 block-scale routed-MoE GEMM cubins intermittently die with a sticky CUDA error when the cluster-barrier arrivals of one CTA of a 2-CTA pair are delayed relative to their peer by ~1 ms. Without perturbation the kernels are stable: hundreds of clean runs, bitwise-deterministic output, including under heavy external contention - explicitly: 400-iteration output-check runs under SM-saturation and L2-thrash sidecars and a 1,159,193-iteration 20-minute async soak with SM+HBM sidecars, all clean on 0.7.1rc5. Every trial that does not crash produces bitwise-correct output, so no wrong-result behavior is implied.

**What we perturb.** Only SASS sites matching `UTCBAR` in kernels matching `bmm_`. These cubins implement their 2-CTA-pair synchronization with `UTCBAR.2CTA.MULTICAST` instructions, by which each CTA of the pair arrives on the shared cluster mbarrier, alongside `UTCQMMA.2CTA` (paired MMA) and `UTMALDG.3D.MULTICAST.2CTA` (paired TMA loads). Injection evidence on the faulting cubin (28 sites matched, all enabled):

```text
kernel=bmm_MxE4m3_MxE2m1MxE4m3_Fp32_Ab32_Bb32_Cb32_t128x192x256u2_s3_et128x32_m256x192x32_c2x1x1_..._sm100f
  pc=0x50c0  sass='UTCBAR.2CTA.MULTICAST [UR14], URZ, UR19 ;'  delay=1000000
  pc=0x50e0  sass='UTCBAR.2CTA.MULTICAST [UR15], URZ, UR19 ;'  delay=1000000
  pc=0x53b0  sass='UTCBAR.2CTA.MULTICAST [UR14], URZ, UR20 ;'  delay=1000000
  pc=0x53d0  sass='UTCBAR.2CTA.MULTICAST [UR15], URZ, UR20 ;'  delay=1000000
  pc=0x6c90  sass='UTCBAR.2CTA.MULTICAST [UR35], URZ, UR51 ;'  delay=1000000
  ... (28 sites total)
kernel=bmm_Bfloat16_MxE2m1MxE4m3_Fp32_Ab32_Bb32_t128x192x256u2_s3_et128x64_m256x192x32_c2x1x1_..._sm100f
  sass='UTCBAR.2CTA.MULTICAST [UR18], [UR22], UR24 ;'  delay=1000000
```

Delay modes tested: per-thread random (main trigger) and fixed-uniform; magnitudes 100 us (always passes) and 1 ms (crashes); enable probability 1.0. Per-thread random delay at these sites is what skews one CTA's arrivals against its paired peer's.

**What the failure looks like.** The faulted launch raises a sticky CUDA error that surfaces at the next CUDA API call, and the process aborts shortly after the first injected launch, typically within 10-60 s. On the current builds I observe it through the injector's post-launch error check (assertion below); on the September-era build it surfaced directly as CUDA error 719 ("unspecified launch failure") at the sync point. Either way this is not a hang: the grid does not spin; the kernel faults. The GPU itself stays healthy (0 ECC errors, no retired pages, fresh CUDA contexts on the same card work normally afterwards). On an earlier cubin build (0.6.18rc-era, September 2026) the same signature was attributed via node DCGM to Xid 13 (Graphics Engine Exception, an SM-level hardware exception), and a separate experiment showed the cubin's own ptxas-injected tcgen05 breakpoint self-checks did NOT execute before that fault - i.e., the hardware raises the exception, not a software guardrail. That evidence is from a different cubin build and is cited only as corroboration.

Evidence boundary: the sticky error is first observed by the instrumentation hook after the faulted launch, and I cannot exclude an instrumentation interaction at the cluster-barrier instructions. The reason this still looks like a cubin robustness gap: the fault is repeatable across three released versions, tactic-specific (a second 2-CTA tactic at a different geometry passes 9/9 at the same magnitudes), dose-dependent (100 us passes, 1 ms faults), and site-specific (delays at LDTM sites in the same kernels pass).

Affected cubins observed faulting (versions per path listed below):

- `bmm_Bfloat16_MxE2m1MxE4m3_Fp32_Ab32_Bb32_t128x192x256u2_s3_..._c2x1x1_..._sm100f` (MXFP8-activation path)
- `bmm_MxE4m3_MxE2m1MxE4m3_Fp32_Ab32_Bb32_Cb32_t128x192x256u2_s3_..._c2x1x1_..._sm100f`
- `bmm_E2m1_E2m1E2m1_Fp32_Ab16_Bb16_Cb16_t128x192x256u2_s3_et128x64_m256x192x64_c2x1x1_..._sm100f` (NVFP4-activation path - the GLM-5-class production configuration)

Both activation paths fault: MXFP8-activation (MXFP4 weights) crashed 2/3 arms on 0.6.18.post1, 3/3 on 0.7.0.post1, 2/5 on 0.7.1rc5; NVFP4-activation (NVFP4 weights) crashed 1/1 on 0.6.18.post1 and 3/3 on 0.7.1rc5 (not tested on 0.7.0.post1). Async launches, batch 2048. These are per-arm counts from the runs listed, not an estimated rate. Paired enable_pdl on/off arms at 1 ms both crash, so the programmatic dependent-launch setting does not gate the failure.

Expected: stable execution of the 2-CTA cluster tactic under supported scheduling conditions. Whether SASS delay injection preserves those conditions is an open question I cannot fully answer; I am reporting because the fault is repeatable, tactic-specific, and dose-dependent, which looks more like a robustness gap in the cubin than an instrumentation artifact.

## Minimal reproduction

The workload below is self-contained (torch + flashinfer only). Running it plain must print `CLEAN` repeatedly. The failure appears when the same script runs under SASS delay injection targeting `UTCBAR` sites in `bmm_` kernels with ~1 ms per-thread random delays (any NVBit-based injector that can insert per-thread delays before selected SASS instructions works; we used one built for sm_103a).

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""trtllm-gen 2-CTA FP4 MoE GEMM skew repro. Oracle: bitwise determinism + finiteness."""
import sys, torch
from flashinfer.fused_moe import

items.title: [Feature]: DSv4/4.1 Sparse Attention Backend Support (CAKE, NVFP4) for SM100/103/107
items.author: akhilg-nv
items.body_excerpt:
### Before submitting - [x] I have searched existing issues and this request has not been filed yet. ### Problem Requesting NVFP4 sparse-MLA prefill on SM100/SM103 and NVFP4 decode/prefill on SM107 (Rubin) for DSv4/4.1-Flash, plus two `cake` gaps (below). Current support matrix per my understanding (`flashinfer.mla.trtllm_batch_decode_sparse_mla_dsv4`, which handles both decode and prefill): | Arch | BF16 / FP8 KV | NVFP4 KV | |---|---|---| | **SM100 / SM103** (B200, GB200, B300, GB300) | **Decode:** `trtllm-gen` (default), `cake` [1], `cute-dsl` (FP8 only)
**Prefill:** `trtllm-gen`, `cake` [2] | **Decode:** `cake` only (explicit `backend="cake"`, BF16 Q, CUDA >= 13.4, no PDL)
**Prefill:** no dedicated kernel [3] | | **SM107** (Rubin) | **Decode:** `trtllm-gen`
**Prefill:** `trtllm-gen` | none | [1] `cake` has no low-head kernels for the C4A layer: FP8 decode needs >= 64 heads; BF16 needs >= 32 heads in decode and prefill. DSv4-Flash (64 heads) at TP2+ (FP8) / TP4+ (BF16) therefore falls back to `trtllm-gen`, losing `cake`'s mid-batch decode advantage (1.58x at batch 64, B300 FP8 TP1). [2] `cake` prefill is 2.5-5.1x slower than `trtllm-gen` (B300, FP8, 64 heads, full prefill with no prefix cache; prompts 1k-64k at batch 1, up to 32k at batch 2 and 16k at batch 4; largest gap at short prompts). It also hits an illegal memory access above 65,536 query rows at 64 heads (rows x heads x 512 > 2^31). Every other DSv4 path switches to dedicated prefill kernels at large query counts. Notes: - DSv4.1-specific cache formats exist only on SM120/SM121, which already has NVFP4 decode and prefill (`sparse` and `cake` backends). ### Requested outcome 1. Optimized NVFP4 sparse prefill on SM100/SM103 [3]. 2. NVFP4 sparse decode and prefill on SM107 (Rubin). 3. New NVFP4 kernels should match the existing NVFP4 decode head coverage (8/16/32/64/128 heads, i.e. DSv4-Flash TP8 through TP1). 4. `cake` BF16/FP8 low-head kernels for the C4A layer [1]. 5. items.title: b12x W4A16 (BF16) MXFP4: E8M0 scale bias makes weights BF16-subnormal / zero for scale bytes < 121 (rows silently lost, SM12x)
items.author: sjronan
items.body_excerpt:
### Before submitting
- [x] I have searched existing issues and did not find a solution or an existing report.

### Environment
- FlashInfer `main` @ `ee4de7dfd6` (same code in the archived standalone b12x @ `2cc7f66a`)
- GeForce RTX 5080 (SM120), torch 2.12.1+cu130, nvidia-cutlass-dsl 4.7.1, driver 610.88
- Also seen on RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell (SM120), standalone b12x, serving through vLLM

### Bug description

The experimental b12x W4A16 MoE, on the BF16 activation path with MXFP4 weights (`source_format="fp4_e8m0_k32"`), produces wrong output whenever the checkpoint's E8M0 scale bytes are below about 121. Below about 114 small FP4 values are flushed to zero. Rows lose part or all of their expert contribution. There is no NaN or Inf, and the aggregate cosine against the reference can stay at 0.99999, so the existing tests and most accuracy gates do not see it.

**Mechanism** (`flashinfer/experimental/b12x`):

| step | code | value |
|---|---|---|
| FP4 unpack | `_lib/intrinsics.py` `packed_dequant_e2m1x4_to_bfloat2x2` (sign + 3 magnitude bits `>> 6` into a BF16) | `v * 2^-126`. FP4 0.5 is already a BF16 subnormal |
| E8M0 scale | `_lib/intrinsics.py:3378` `packed_dequant_e8m0x4_to_bfloat2x2`: `add.u32 hN, bN, 7; shl 7` (lines 3404-3411) | BF16 exponent field `e + 7`, i.e. `2^(e-120)` |
| MMA weight | `mul.bf16x2` (`_elem2_mul`) | `v * 2^(e-246) = true_weight * 2^-119` |
| epilogue | `moe/_shared/kernels/w4a16/kernel.py:247` `_E8M0_K32_BF16_GLOBAL_COMPENSATION = 2**119`, folded into `global_scale_f32` | restores the true scale |
| clamp | `w4a16/prepare.py:35`, `kernels/reference.py:55`: 247 | keeps the field at 254 or below |

So every nonzero weight is a normal BF16 only for **121 ≤ e ≤ 247**. That window is centred on scales of about 2^57, which no trained checkpoint uses. In real MXFP4 checkpoints the bytes sit at about 100-130:

- **e < 121:** MMA weights are BF16 subnormals. The MMA products `x * w` are carried at 2^-119 of their true value, so for ordinary activations they fall into FP32-subnormal range and lose precision or vanish.
- **e < 114:** FP4 0.5 rounds to zero. At 111, 0.5 to 2 round to zero, and at 110 everything except ±6 does.

Example: MiMo-V2.6-Pro (MXFP4 experts). MoE layers 1-16 have scale bytes 111-117 (dominant 115-117). Layers 17-18 start at 114 (dominant 118-119), and layers 19+ start at 116 (dominant 120). DeepSeek-V4 / V4-Pro sit at 119-122, mostly 120/121. They are at the edge, and in practice we measured no loss there (cosine 0.99999 on the old kernel). The FP16 activation path (`packed_dequant_e8m0x4_to_half2x2` with `_E8M0_K32_FP16_GLOBAL_COMPENSATION = 2**7`) has the same class of problem: weights are normal FP16 only for e ≥ 121, and the scale overflows FP16 above 135. The fix below does not touch it.

### Minimal reproduction

**(a) Bit-level model (NumPy only, no GPU).** It models what the kernel does with one FP4 code and one scale byte. Old constants are `bias=7, clamp=247`.

```python
import math
def bf16(bits):                      # decode a BF16 bit pattern
    s = -1.0 if bits & 0x8000 else 1.0; e = (bits >> 7) & 0xFF; m = bits & 0x7F
    return s * (math.ldexp(m, -133) if e == 0 else math.ldexp(128 + m, e - 134))
def bf16_rn(x):                      # round-to-nearest-even into BF16, subnormals kept
    if x == 0: return 0.0
    q = math.ldexp(1.0, max(math.frexp(abs(x))[1] - 1, -126) - 7)
    return math.copysign(round(abs(x) / q) * q, x)
FP4 = [0, .5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 6]
for e in (110, 113, 116, 120, 121):
    s = bf16(((e + 7) << 7) & 0xFFFF)                                 # the scale the kernel builds
    w = [bf16_rn(bf16(((c << 12) & 0x7000) >> 6) * s) for c in range(8)]  # FP4 unpack x scale
    lost = [FP4[c] for c in range(1, 8) if w[c] == 0]
    sub = [FP4[c] for c in range(1, 8) if 0 < abs(w[c]) < 2**-126]
    print(e, "flushed:", lost, "subnormal:", sub)
# 110 flushed: [0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4] subnormal: [6]
# 113 flushed: [0.5] subnormal: [1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 6]
# 116 flushed: [] subnormal: [0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 6]
# 120 flushed: [] subnormal: [0.5]
# 121 flushed: [] subnormal: []
```

The PR adds a full version as `tests/experimental/b12x/moe/test_w4a16_e8m0_bias_numerics.py`. It sweeps all 255 bytes and 16 codes, and models dot products under both gradual-underflow and flush-to-zero FP32.

**(b) Kernel.** The setup is the public W4A16 API: random FP4 weights, a constant E8M0 byte, all routes valid, and per-row cosine against `moe_reference_w4a16_fp4_e8m0_k32`.

```python

from b12x.moe._shared.kernels.w4a16.prepare import make_w4a16_packed_buffers, prepare_w4a16_packed_weights
from b12x.moe._shared.kernels.reference import moe_reference_w4a16_fp4_e8m0_k32

torch.manual_seed(0)
E, H, I, m, topk = 8, 512, 512, 256, 2
w13 = torch.randint(0, 256, (E, 2 * I, H // 2), dtype=torch.uint8, device="cuda")
w2 = torch.randint(0, 256, (E, H, I // 2), dtype=torch.uint8, device="cuda")
g = torch.ones(E, device="cuda")

w = torch.full((m, topk), 0.5, device="cuda")
LAYERS = os.environ.get("LAYERS", "both")          # both | fc1 | fc2 get the test byte; the other gets 127

items.title: [Bug] FlashInfer autotune cache is discarded every boot under MoE expert parallelism (EP>1): per-rank shapes never agree, so the fused-MoE tactic is re-drawn each start
items.author: ntxf31415
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

`_drop_diverged_autotune_cache()` discards the whole FlashInfer autotune cache — on every boot — whenever the per-rank MoE GEMM shapes differ, which is the normal case with **expert parallelism (EP > 1)**. The cache is then re-tuned from scratch each start, so the fused-MoE tactic is re-drawn every boot. Since the tactic selection is timing-based, end-to-end throughput varies across boots with identical config.

### Environment

- 4× GB10 (DGX Spark), SGLang TP4 / EP2, switchless RoCE ring
- MoE runner backend `flashinfer_mxfp4` (MXFP4 experts), DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash
- `--chunked-prefill-size 4096`, `--mem-fraction-static 0.90`
- FlashInfer 0.6.18, CUDA 13.0, cuDNN 92000

### Root cause

`python/sglang/srt/model_executor/runner/flashinfer_autotune.py`:

```python
def _autotune_cache_digest(cache_path, env):
    ...
    payload = {"file": configs, "env": env}
    return hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(payload, sort_keys=True).encode()).hexdigest()

def _drop_diverged_autotune_cache(cache_path, group, env) -> None:
    digests = [""] * torch.distributed.get_world_size(group)
    torch.distributed.all_gather_object(digests, _autotune_cache_digest(cache_path, env), group=group)
    if len(set(digests)) == 1:
        return
    ...
    cache_path.unlink(missing_ok=True)          # <-- deletes the cache
```

Each rank digests **its own** `rank_tp{N}_pp0_dp0.json` and all four are compared. Under EP sharding each rank owns a different slice of the routed experts, so **the MoE GEMM problem shapes themselves differ per rank** and the files can never be equal. Measured on our four ranks (same boot, same config, caches cleared so all four start from empty):

| rank | distinct shapes in its cache | example expert shape present |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 24 | `(192, 2304, 320)` |
| 1 | 24 | `(64, 2304, 320)` |
| 2 | 24 | `(64, 2304, 320)` / `(192, …)` |
| 3 | 24 | `(16, 5120)`, `(4, 5120)` |

**The intersection of the four shape sets is empty.** So `len(set(digests)) == 1` is never true, the cache is `unlink`ed on every start, and every start re-profiles `trtllm::fused_moe::gemm1` / `gemm2` for all shapes.

Startup log, one boot:

```
Running FlashInfer autotune with cache: /root/.cache/sglang/flashinfer/autotune/0.6.18/sm121/<key>/rank_tp3_pp0_dp0.json
[AutoTuner]: Tuning trtllm::fused_moe::gemm1:   0%|          | 0/8 ...
```

Tuning count is **26–27 profiles per boot** regardless of whether a complete cache file is already present at that path. The shipped image cache contains only `sparse_mla_sm120_decode_dsv4` entries, so the fused-MoE shapes always miss anyway.

Note the digest also includes the environment, so even equal tactics would not be enough — but here the file contents themselves cannot match.

### Impact

The fused-MoE tactic is re-drawn on every start, and it matters a lot. Two consecutive boots of the same configuration, measured with a cold single-stream prefill probe at 8K tokens:

| boot | prefill t/s (8K) |
|---|---|
| A | 3169 |
| B | 2431 |

**−23 % at 8K**, while 100K was essentially unchanged (3266 vs 3164) — i.e. the draw is shape-range dependent, and a bad draw is stable for the whole life of that process. We also saw a full 1.5× swing on longer inputs between boots.

### Workaround we run

We mount a site-patched copy of this file that keeps the digest check and the log line but drops the `unlink`:

```python
    log_info_on_rank0(logger, "[site patch] keeping per-rank autotune caches")
```

With the per-rank caches kept, subsequent boots report **0 tuning profiles** (cache genuinely read and used) and throughput is stable.

⚠️ Caveat we found the hard way: this is only safe if every rank's own cache is **complete**. If some ranks hit and others miss, the missing ranks enter the timing-reduction collective while the others don't — we reproduced that as an NCCL collective timeout at startup with the process hanging, so a partial cache is worse than none.

### Possible fix directions

1. Compare like-for-like per rank (i.e. make the guard per-rank rather than requiring cross-rank equality), given that under EP the shape sets legitimately differ.
2. Or key the digest only on the *tactics for the shapes this rank actually uses*, rather than on the whole file.
3. Or make the reduction group follow the ranks that actually share a shape set.

If the divergence check is load-bearing for a reason we have not understood, it may be worth at least not deleting — logging and continuing — so a partially-cached fleet degrades to slow rather than to a hang.

items.title: [RFC] Composable Kernel with runtime aggregate fields
items.author: sjw36
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

Allow a `@triton.aggregate` to be **constructed on the host** and passed to a
kernel as a single `tl.constexpr` argument. The aggregate's *runtime* data
members (e.g. `tl.tensor`, `tl.tensor_descriptor`, or scalars) are automatically
**lifted to runtime kernel parameters**, while its `tl.constexpr` members are
**baked into the compiled kernel**. Changing a runtime member reuses the already
compiled kernel; changing a compile-time member specializes a new one.

This turns an aggregate into a first-class, composable **kernel-configuration
object** — most naturally, a fused **epilogue** — that a launch site can build,
subclass, and hand to a single kernel body.

## Motivation

Today, customizing a kernel's behavior means threading an ever-growing list of
optional pointers and flags through its signature: a `bias_ptr`, a `has_bias`
flag, a `scale`, an `activation` enum, and so on. Each new fusion variant either
bloats the signature or forces a separate copy of the kernel.

We already have `@triton.aggregate` to bundle values into a struct, and
`@triton.jit` methods to attach behavior. What is missing is the ability to
**build that struct on the host from ordinary runtime data** (a `torch.Tensor`,
a `TensorDescriptor`, a Python scalar) and pass it in as one argument, without
manually splitting it into "the constexpr config" and "the runtime pointers."

The canonical use case is a composable epilogue (see
`python/tutorials/12-composable-kernel.py`):

```python
@triton.aggregate
class BiasAdd:
    bias: tl.tensor        # runtime member  -> lifted to a kernel param
    n_cols: tl.constexpr   # compile-time    -> baked in

    @triton.constexpr_function
    def __init__(self, bias, n_cols):
        self.bias = bias
        self.n_cols = tl.constexpr(n_cols)

    @triton.jit
    def apply(self, acc, offs_n):
        bias = tl.load(self.bias + offs_n, mask=offs_n < self.n_cols, other=0.0)
        return acc + bias[None, :]


@triton.aggregate
class BiasAddScale(BiasAdd):   # inherits fields + apply
    scale: tl.tensor

    @triton.constexpr_function
    def __init__(self, bias, n_cols, scale):
        self.bias = bias
        self.n_cols = tl.constexpr(n_cols)
        self.scale = scale

    @triton.jit
    def apply(self, acc, offs_n):
        return BiasAdd.apply(self, acc, offs_n) * self.scale
```

```python
@triton.jit
def matmul_kernel(a_ptr, b_ptr, c_ptr, ..., epilogue: tl.constexpr, ...):
    ...
    if not epilogue is None:
        acc = epilogue.apply(acc, offs_cn)   # concrete type selects the IR
    ...

# Two launch functions, one kernel body (grid omitted for brevity):
launch(a, b, c, BiasAdd(bias, N))              # base epilogue
launch(a, b, c, BiasAddScale(bias, N, scale))  # derived epilogue
```

Benefits:

- **One clean signature** regardless of how rich the epilogue is.
- **Compile-time polymorphism**: the aggregate's concrete type selects which
  `apply` is emitted — no runtime branching.
- **Cache-friendly**: changing the `bias` tensor or `scale` value reuses the
  compiled kernel; only compile-time members specialize a new one.
- **Composable via inheritance**: derive a richer epilogue from a base one and
  override its `@triton.jit` methods.

## Design

### User-facing contract

An aggregate field is classified by its annotation:

- Annotated `tl.constexpr` → **compile-time member**, baked into the kernel and
  participating in the compilation cache key.
- Any other annotation (`tl.tensor`, `tl.tensor_descriptor`, scalar, …) →
  **runtime member**, lifted to a runtime kernel parameter.

The aggregate is built on the host inside a `@triton.constexpr_function`
`__init__`, and passed to a kernel parameter declared `: tl.constexpr`. Nothing
else in the kernel body changes: `self.bias`, `self.scale`, `self.n_cols` are
accessed exactly as they would be for an in-kernel aggregate.

### Host construction: relaxed field typing (`language/core.py`)

`_aggregate`'s `__setattr__` previously required every assigned value to be an
instance of the field's annotated type. That rejects a raw `torch.Tensor` being
stored into a `tl.tensor` field on the host.

The check is relaxed so that, for **runtime** fields, a raw host value (a
`torch.Tensor`, a host `TensorDescriptor`, a Python scalar) is permitted. Two
guards remain:

- A `tl.constexpr` field still requires a `constexpr` value.
- A *Triton* value (`base_value`) of the wrong type is still rejected.

```python
if ann is constexpr or isinstance(value, base_value):
    raise TypeError(...)
```

This narrowly opens the door for host construction while keeping in-kernel
type-safety intact.

### Runtime lifting (`runtime/jit.py`)

A new `HostConstexprAggregate` wrapper captures, from a host-built aggregate:

- `base_cls`, `field_order`
- `const_bindings` — the compile-time members (by value)
- `runtime_names` / `runtime_values` — the runtime members
- `cache_key` — a **stable, value-based** key computed from the class, the
  compile-time member values, and the runtime member *layout* (names only).
  Runtime member *values* deliberately do **not** enter the key. Tensor members
  are keyed structurally (`tensor(shape, dtype)`), never by contents.

A new `JITFunction._specialize_host_aggregates(backend, bound_args, specialization)`
step runs inside `run()` (and is mirrored in `_filecheck.run_parser`). For each
`constexpr` argument that is a host-built aggregate with runtime members it:

1. Specializes each runtime member via `native_specialize_impl` (obtaining its
   IR type and argument attributes such as divisibility).
2. Rewrites the bound argument to a tuple `(wrapper, *runtime_values)` so the
   members flow through the **existing tuple-argument machinery** (signature,
   launcher, IR) with no new launch path.
3. Records the specialization as `(("constexpr", *member_types), (wrapper, *member_attrs))`
   so the wrapper's identity participates in the cache key and each member's
   attributes are preserved.

A **pure** compile-time

items.title: [RFC][AMD] Reduce steady-state HIP launch overhead with a pre-bound launcher
items.author: adityakankariya
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

Triton's AMD backend already enters C for the final HIP launch through `driver.c::launchKernel`. However, every steady-state invocation still passes through Python `JITFunction.run` / `HIPLauncher` bookkeeping and the generic C launcher repeatedly parses invariant launch metadata and reconstructs the kernel-argument array.

This issue proposes splitting the optimization into two independently reviewable changes:

1. Add a pre-bound HIP launcher that removes repeated launch preparation after a compiled kernel has been selected.
2. Separately evaluate a backend-neutral native specialization-cache proxy that removes the remaining Python specialization/cache lookup on cache hits.

This is host-side dispatch work. It does not change lowering, generated AMDGPU code, or device kernel execution.

A prototype exists in facebookexperimental/triton#3610. That implementation depends on runtime infrastructure specific to that fork, so the intent is to adapt the design to upstream Triton.

## Current path

A steady-state HIP kernel invocation currently follows approximately:

```text
Python JITFunction.run
  -> bind arguments and compiler options
  -> construct specialization/cache key
  -> look up CompiledKernel
  -> Python HIPLauncher
  -> generic C driver.c::launchKernel
  -> HIP launch API
  -> GPU kernel
```

The generic C launcher is fully functional and remains necessary. The opportunity is to avoid repeating work that is invariant for a loaded compiled kernel.

## PR 1: Pre-bound HIP launcher

Introduce a callable C object, tentatively `HIPPreboundLauncher`, for flat pointer/scalar kernel signatures.

Construction would bind invariant state once:

- HIP function handle
- argument type/extractor codes
- `num_warps` and `num_ctas`
- dynamic shared-memory size
- warp size
- cooperative-launch setting
- stable kernel-parameter storage/pointer structure

Each invocation would provide only:

- grid dimensions
- stream
- current pointer and scalar values

The object would use CPython vectorcall and invoke the existing low-level HIP launch helper. This is not a new HIP driver path.

The existing `HIPLauncher` remains the fallback for cases not initially supported, including:

- tensor descriptors
- tuples or structured arguments
- compiler-managed global/profile scratch
- launch hooks or user launch metadata
- unsupported scalar types
- any case where construction or argument extraction cannot be proven safe

The runtime integration should be backend-neutral where practical. In particular, an AMD path should not be controlled through a NVIDIA-specific knob namespace.

### PR 1 validation

Correctness coverage should include:

- device pointers, integer pointer values, and `None`
- signed/unsigned integer and floating-point scalar types
- FP16 and BF16 scalar packing
- rejection of pageable CPU pointers
- constants omitted from the runtime ABI
- zero-sized grids
- dispatcher enabled/disabled behavior
- explicit fallback coverage for descriptors, structured arguments, scratch, hooks, and unsupported signatures

Performance reporting should compare:

```text
upstream generic HIP launch
pre-bound HIP launch
```

using both a minimal short-running Triton kernel and a representative real workload. Measurements should separate complete host/provider latency from device duration (for example, with rocprof) and confirm that the generated GPU kernel is unchanged.

## PR 2: Native specialization-cache proxy

PR 1 begins only after Triton has selected a `CompiledKernel`. Normal `@triton.jit` calls still perform Python argument binding, specialization construction, compiler-option processing, cache-key construction, and Python dictionary lookup.

After measuring PR 1 independently, a second PR can evaluate moving the steady-state cache-hit path into a backend-neutral C vectorcall proxy:

```text
Python kernel call
  -> native specialization-key construction
  -> native cache lookup
  -> HIPPreboundLauncher
  -> HIP launch API
```

This proxy must be fail-safe: cache misses and unsupported objects return to the existing Python path.

Required correctness work includes:

- cache lifecycle and invalidation
- process-fork/deepcopy behavior
- autotuner interaction
- alignment and backend-specific tensor specialization
- optional fast tensor access without making Torch a hard dependency
- fallback through public tensor methods when the optional bridge is unavailable
- complete compiler-option keys

The compiler-option key must represent the effective option set:

```text
options bound by an autotuner/config
+ options supplied at the current call site
= effective compiler options used for lookup
```

Call-time values must override bound values with the same name. Options such as `num_warps` and `waves_per_eu` can change the compiled binary and therefore must not alias in the native cache.

Official Triton's existing Python cache already includes compiler options. This second phase would preserve that behavior in an additional native fast path, not correct the existing Python cache.

## Proposed sequencing

```text
PR 1: AMD pre-bound HIP launcher and conservative fallback
  -> isolate correctness and launch-preparation performance

PR 2: backend-neutral native specialization/cache-hit path
  -> isolate the remaining Python dispatch cost

Future follow-ups: broaden supported ABI features only with tests and measured value
```

## Open design questions

1. Should PR 1 construct the launcher directly from `src.signature` and compiled metadata, or should upstream first introduce a serialized backend launch-ABI schema?

3. Should the native specialization cache be discussed in a separate RFC after PR 1 results are available?

- Triton: current `triton-lang/triton` main
- Backend: HIP/ROCm
- Hardware motivating the investigation: AMD Instinct MI350-class (`gfx950`)

items.title: [WS] getPartitionOutputs assertion in NVWSHoistTmemStore with warp_specialize=True on a pointer-load persistent matmul
items.author: builtin-pb
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

Compiling the kernel below for Blackwell (`cuda:100` or `cuda:103`) stops with an internal assertion when the outer tile loop uses `tl.range(..., warp_specialize=True)`, the inner K loop uses plain pointer loads and `tl.dot`, and C is written with a plain `tl.store`:

```
Partitioning.cpp:24: ... mlir::triton::gpu::getPartitionOutputs(mlir::Operation*): Assertion `op->hasAttr(kPartitionOutputsAttrName)' failed.
... Pipeline failed while executing [`TritonGPUAutomaticWarpSpecialization` on 'builtin.module' operation, `NVWSHoistTmemStore` on 'builtin.module' operation]
RuntimeError: PassManager::run failed
```

This reproduces on Triton 3.8.0 (PyPI wheel; there the assertion is at `Partition.cpp:354`) and on main (`0d4e0a0c`). It is compile-only and needs no GPU; the kernel is never launched (it assumes full tiles and 16-byte-aligned, contiguous fp16 A and B and fp32 C). We are not asking for this loop to be specialized, only for no assertion: `warp_specialize` is documented as an attempt, and loops it cannot partition are otherwise left alone, as with the controls below. Triton's own `test_warp_specialize_tma_matmul_persistent` has the same structure with pointer loads for A and B and expects `ttg.warp_specialize`; it differs only in storing C through a descriptor.

### Reproducer

```python
"""Compile-only reproducer (no GPU needed).

Requesting automatic warp specialization on a persistent tile loop whose body is
an ordinary pointer-load matmul makes Triton hit an internal assertion:
    getPartitionOutputs: Assertion `op->hasAttr(kPartitionOutputsAttrName)' failed.

    python ws_assert_min.py              # warp_specialize=True: assertion
    python ws_assert_min.py --ws 0       # same kernel without it: compiles

--inner 0 drops the inner K loop (one tl.dot per tile); --dot 0 replaces tl.dot
with row/column sums; --cdesc 1 stores C through a TMA tensor descriptor
(as Triton's own persistent warp-specialization test does); --arch picks the target (100 = B200, 103 = B300, 90 = H100);
--warps and --stages set num_warps (default 4) and num_stages (default 3).
"""
import argparse
import inspect

import triton
import triton.language as tl
from triton.backends.compiler import GPUTarget
from triton.compiler import ASTSource


@triton.jit
def ws_min(A, B, C, num_tiles, k_iters,
           BM: tl.constexpr, BN: tl.constexpr, BK: tl.constexpr,
           WS: tl.constexpr, INNER: tl.constexpr, DOT: tl.constexpr, CDESC: tl.constexpr):
    rm = tl.arange(0, BM)
    rn = tl.arange(0, BN)
    rk = tl.arange(0, BK)
    K = k_iters * BK
    if CDESC:
        c_desc = tl.make_tensor_descriptor(C, shape=[num_tiles * BM, BN], strides=[BN, 1], block_shape=[BM, BN])
    for tile in tl.range(tl.program_id(0), num_tiles, tl.num_programs(0), warp_specialize=WS):
        rows = tile * BM + rm
        acc = tl.zeros((BM, BN), tl.float32)
        if INNER:
            for k in range(k_iters):
                a = tl.load(A + rows[:, None] * K + (k * BK + rk)[None, :])
                b = tl.load(B + (k * BK + rk)[:, None] * BN + rn[None, :])
                if DOT:
                    acc = tl.dot(a, b, acc)
                else:
                    acc += tl.sum(a.to(tl.float32), 1)[:, None] + tl.sum(b.to(tl.float32), 0)[None, :]
        else:
            a = tl.load(A + rows[:, None] * K + rk[None, :])
            b = tl.load(B + rk[:, None] * BN + rn[None, :])
            if DOT:
                acc = tl.dot(a, b, acc)
            else:
                acc += tl.sum(a.to(tl.float32), 1)[:, None] + tl.sum(b.to(tl.float32), 0)[None, :]
        if CDESC:
            c_desc.store([tile * BM, 0], acc)
        else:
            tl.store(C + rows[:, None] * BN + rn[None, :], acc)


def main():
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    p.add_argument("--ws", type=int, default=1)
    p.add_argument("--inner", type=int, default=1)
    p.add_argument("--dot", type=int, default=1)
    p.add_argument("--cdesc", type=int, default=0)
    p.add_argument("--arch", type=int, default=100)
    p.add_argument("--warps", type=int, default=4)
    p.add_argument("--stages", type=int, default=3)
    args = p.parse_args()

    constants = dict(BM=128, BN=64, BK=64, WS=bool(args.ws), INNER=bool(args.inner), DOT=bool(args.dot), CDESC=bool(args.cdesc))
    runtime = dict(A="*fp16", B="*fp16", C="*fp32", num_tiles="i32", k_iters="i32")
    names = list(ws_min.arg_names)
    signature = {n: runtime.get(n, "constexpr") for n in names}
    attrs = {(names.index(n),): [["tt.divisibility", 16]] for n in ("A", "B", "C")}
    key = "constexprs" if "constexprs" in inspect.signature(ASTSource).parameters else "constants"
    src = ASTSource(ws_min, signature=signature, attrs=attrs, **{key: constants})
    print(f"triton {triton.__version__}, target cuda:{args.arch}, warps {args.warps}, stages {args.stages}, {constants}", flush=True)
    compiled = triton.compile(src, target=GPUTarget("cuda", args.arch, 32),
                              options=dict(num_warps=args.warps, num_stages=args.stages))
    ttgir = compiled.asm["ttgir"]
    print("COMPILED; ttg.warp_specialize ops in TTGIR:", ttgir.count("ttg.warp_specialize("), flush=True)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

| Command (`--arch 100` or `--arch 103`) | 3.8.0 and main |
|---|---|
| `python ws_assert_min.py` (also with `--stages 1` or `--warps 8`) | assertion |
| `--ws 0` | compiles |
| `--cdesc 1` (C stored through a tensor descriptor) | compiles and emits one `ttg.warp_specialize` |
| `--inner 0` or `--dot 0` | compiles, without specialization |

<details><summary>Full output on main, including the MLIR reproducer</summary>

```
python: triton/lib/Dialect/TritonGPU/IR/Partitioning.cpp:24: llvm::SmallVector<llvm::SetVector<int, llvm::SmallVector<int, 0>, llvm::DenseSet<int, llvm::DenseMapInfo<int, void> >, 0>, 4> mlir::triton::gpu::getPartitionOutputs(mlir::Operation*): Assertion `op->hasAttr(kPartitionOutputsAttrName)' failed.
module {
  tt.func public @ws_min(%ar

items.title: b12x W4A16 MoE: unrouted (-1) top-k ids summed from unwritten FC2 rows -> NaN/garbage (SM12x)
items.author: sjronan
items.body_excerpt:
## Describe the bug

`run_w4a16_moe` (`flashinfer/experimental/b12x`, W4A16 fused MoE) returns NaN or wrong values when some `topk_ids` are negative (unrouted / padded routes) and the call takes the route-packed path (m > 8 with the default route mode, or any m with `route_mode="packed"`).

- With NaN bytes in the per-call scratch, every output element is NaN.
- With zeroed scratch, cosine similarity against the reference falls to about 0.29.
- With all routes valid, the output matches the reference (cos 0.99999).
- The small-m direct-route path is not affected.

**Cause.** The route-pack kernels (`moe/_shared/kernels/w4a16/route_pack.py`) keep only `0 <= id < E`, so a negative id gets no packed row and FC2 never writes its row of `fc2_out` (`intermediate_cache13`). The map-free branch of `W4A16TopKSumKernel.kernel` sets `valid_route = 1` for every slot and checks ids only when `use_expert_map` is set. It therefore adds the unwritten rows to the output. Those rows hold whatever was in the scratch, which can be NaN or FC1 data from the same call. The full-rotation and expert-map sum branches already skip invalid ids. `torch.ops.b12x.w4a16_topk_sum_launch` does not receive the route ids at all.

This is the same "negative id means not routed" contract as #5451 and #5977, but on the experimental b12x W4A16 path.

## Reproduction

Tested at main `a7103ae2`. This is a condensed version of the regression test in the linked PR.

```python
import torch
from b12x.moe._shared.kernels.w4a16.kernel import run_w4a16_moe
from b12x.moe._shared.kernels.w4a16.prepare import (
    make_w4a16_packed_buffers, prepare_w4a16_packed_weights)
from b12x.moe._shared.kernels.reference import moe_reference_w4a16_fp4_e8m0_k32

E, H, I, m, topk = 8, 256, 256, 16, 6
e8m0 = lambda shape, off=0: ((torch.arange(torch.Size(shape).numel(), device="cuda") + off) % 4 + 119
                             ).to(torch.uint8).reshape(shape).view(torch.float8_e8m0fnu)
w13 = torch.randint(0, 256, (E, 2 * I, H // 2), dtype=torch.uint8, device="cuda")
w2 = torch.randint(0, 256, (E, H, I // 2), dtype=torch.uint8, device="cuda")
s13, s2, g = e8m0((E, 2 * I, H // 32)), e8m0((E, H, I // 32), 1), torch.ones(E, device="cuda")
prep = prepare_w4a16_packed_weights(w13, s13, g, w2, s2, g, activation="silu",
                                    params_dtype=torch.bfloat16, source_format="fp4_e8m0_k32")
buf = make_w4a16_packed_buffers(prep, m=m, topk=topk, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device=torch.device("cuda"))

x = torch.randn(m, H, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device="cuda")
ids = torch.full((m, topk), -1, dtype=torch.int32, device="cuda")   # 2 routed + 4 unrouted per token
w = torch.zeros(m, topk, device="cuda")
for r in range(2):
    ids[:, r] = (torch.arange(m, device="cuda") * 3 + r * 5) % E
    w[:, r] = 0.5

buf.intermediate_cache13.view(torch.uint8).fill_(0xFF)              # stale scratch (NaN bytes)
out = run_w4a16_moe(x, prep, w, ids, activation="silu",
    intermediate_cache13=buf.intermediate_cache13, intermediate_cache2=buf.intermediate_cache2,
    output=buf.output, fc1_c_tmp=buf.fc1_c_tmp, fc2_c_tmp=buf.fc2_c_tmp,
    packed_route_indices=buf.packed_route_indices, block_expert_ids=buf.block_expert_ids,
    packed_route_count=buf.packed_route_count, expert_offsets=buf.expert_offsets,
    expert_counts=buf.expert_counts)
ref = moe_reference_w4a16_fp4_e8m0_k32(x, w13, s13, g, w2, s2, g, ids.clamp_min(0), w,
                                       E, H, I, activation="silu", w13_layout="w13")
print(torch.isnan(out).sum().item(), torch.nn.functional.cosine_similarity(
    out.float().nan_to_num().flatten(), ref.float().flatten(), dim=0).item())
# main: 4096 0.0   (zero-filled scratch instead: 0 NaN, cos ~0.29)
```

Results on main for E=8, H=I=256, top-6 with 2 routed and 4 unrouted per token:

| m | route mode | NaN-filled scratch | zeroed scratch |
|---|---|---|---|
| 8 | auto (direct) | cos 0.99999 | cos 0.99999 |
| 8 | packed | all NaN | cos 0.26 |
| 16, 64 | auto or packed | all NaN | cos 0.29 |

The int32 and int64 id dtypes give the same results.

We first hit this with MXFP4 (`fp4_e8m0_k32`) experts at DeepSeek-V4-Pro shapes (hidden 7168, intermediate 3072, top-6) in the standalone b12x package. We were running an expert sidecar that serves a subset of experts on an RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell (SM120) alongside two DGX Stations, and it passes `-1` for every route it does not own. The bug does not depend on shape or scale format; it only needs negative ids on the route-packed path.

## Environment

- FlashInfer main `a7103ae2` (`flashinfer/experimental/b12x`, imported via the `b12x` compat package)
- GeForce RTX 5080 (SM120), driver with CUDA 13.3, torch 2.12.1+cu130, nvidia-cutlass-dsl 4.7.1, Python 3.12
- First observed on RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Max-Q (SM120) with standalone b12x master `2cc7f66a`

## Proposed fix

Pass int32 route ids to the map-free top-k sum and skip ids `< 0`. A PR follows. Positive out-of-range ids are left alone, because with an FC-side expert map they are global ids.

items.title: Feature Request: Generalize per-sequence file payload from tokens to opaque bytes
items.author: CHIPMUNK-T0T
items.body_excerpt:
### Prerequisites

- [x] I am running the latest code. Mention the version if possible as well.
- [x] I carefully followed the [README.md](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/README.md).
- [x] I searched using keywords relevant to my issue to make sure that I am creating a new issue that is not already open (or closed).
- [x] I reviewed the [Discussions](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions), and have a new and useful enhancement to share.

### Feature Description

The per-sequence file API currently represents caller-owned data as a `llama_token[]`, even though that data is separate from the engine-owned sequence state.

This became awkward with multimodal slot persistence in #26640. `llama-server` now serializes its logical slot state into a byte stream containing tokens and multimodal metadata, but `llama_state_seq_save_file()` / `llama_state_seq_load_file()` only accept token arrays.

As a result, the server currently has to pad the serialized byte stream to `sizeof(llama_token)` and reinterpret it as `llama_token[]` before passing it to the sequence-state file API.

I would like to generalize the caller-owned portion of the per-sequence file API so that it can be stored as opaque bytes, while leaving the engine-owned sequence state and the runtime `server_tokens` representation unchanged.

### Motivation

This is an existing API mismatch rather than a hypothetical future use case.

In #26640, the caller-owned slot state is already serialized as bytes, but the public API forces that representation through a token-typed interface. The padding and reinterpretation work around the type mismatch, but libllama does not need to know that caller-owned data represents tokens.

The review discussion in #26640 also suggested generalizing `llama_state_seq_save/load` to support arbitrary user data in a follow-up PR.

Checkpoint persistence and other additional server-owned state are outside the scope of this proposal.

### Possible Implementation

One possible direction would be:

* add a byte-oriented variant of the per-sequence file API rather than changing the existing token API;
* keep the existing token-oriented format supported;
* use a new sequence-state file version to store the exact caller payload byte length;
* preserve the existing query-only load behavior;
* migrate `llama-server` to the new API as its first consumer, removing the token-width padding and reinterpret casts.

Compatibility would target the current token-based sequence-state format; older engine-state formats are outside this proposal.

I would like feedback on whether this API direction and scope are appropriate before preparing the PR.

items.title: vulkan: MUL_MAT_ID loses rows when an expert id appears more than once in a token's row and n > 8
items.author: Anjielon
items.body_excerpt:
If a token's row of ids contains the same expert id more than once, mul_mm_id ends up computing only a portion of the rows assigned to that expert. The problem is that ggml_vk_matmul_id launches ceil(nei1/BN) groups along y for each expert, while count_experts/load_row_ids count individual slots — so a single expert may end up owning as many as nei0*nei1 rows. Any rows beyond the last group are simply never written, and dst is left holding stale data. The n <= 8 case goes through mul_mat_vec_id and is unaffected.

Running test-backend-ops with n_mats=28, n_used=10 and n ranging from 9 to 64 reproduces the issue on Vulkan (RADV gfx1151) when compared against CPU. I already have a fix ready and can open a PR for it.

items.title: [RFC] Review MC_USE_TENT=1 gaps for classic TE callers
items.author: staryxchen
items.body_excerpt:
## How this list was produced

Started as a static pass over:

- the C++ shim (`mooncake-transfer-engine/src/transfer_engine.cpp`, `use_tent_` branches)
- the Python wrapper (`mooncake-integration/transfer_engine/transfer_engine_py.cpp`)
- inference-engine call sites that use `mooncake.engine.TransferEngine`

Local runtime (2026-09-10, installed TENT wheel, 1P1D PD) then confirmed
some items and left others unverified. Status below is as of **2026-09-17**
(`origin/main` `c4d632888b`). Please still reproduce on your tree before
treating a remaining item as confirmed.

## Why the compatibility layer

We are wiring inference engines to TENT's **native** APIs, but that work is
not finished. Until it is, we use the classic TE compatibility layer
(`MC_USE_TENT=1`) to validate TENT **runtime** stability against existing
callers (PD disaggregation and others). This RFC tracks gaps in that layer.
It is not the native-API migration itself.

## Summary

`MC_USE_TENT=1` (and `MC_USE_TEV1=1`) is meant to run existing
`mooncake::TransferEngine` / `mooncake.engine.TransferEngine` code on the TENT
runtime. Register + sync submit/poll are wired up enough for PD KV transfer.

PD happy path **works** under `MC_USE_TENT=1` (local 1P1D Qwen3-4B
`/generate` 200). This RFC is not a claim that PD is broken today.

Most of the original P0/P1/P2 shim holes now have merged PRs. What is still
open is protocol pinning for `efa`/`ascend`, Python sync/poll semantics, and
`installTransport()` returning `nullptr` for classic C/Go/EFA callers.

If you find a **new** compatibility-layer issue, please report it on this
issue. We will add it to the work-item list.

## Non-goals

- Landing inference-engine (or Mooncake Store) native-API migration in this RFC
  (that work is separate and in progress, e.g. #4070).
- Teaching applications to `installTransport` under TENT. Making the shim
  honor the classic `Transport*` contract so existing callers do not treat a
  successful TENT init as failure **is** in scope (`P1-install-transport`).
- Changing TENT runtime scheduling / failover policy.

## Work items

Priority is "if the reading holds, impact is high" — not "already on fire".

| ID | Problem | Difficulty | PR | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| P0-send_probe | Python `send_probe` SIGSEGV (`getMetadata()` is null) | M | #4081, follow-up #4115 | **done** |
| P0-stale-handle | Transfer failure may keep a dead peer's cached handle (`CheckSegmentStatus` was always OK) | M | #4109 | **partial** |
| P0-device-filter | `initialize(device=...)` still opened all HCAs | M | #4028 | **done** |
| P0-force-tcp | `MC_FORCE_TCP=1` / `protocol=tcp` may still select RDMA | M | #4027, follow-up #4113 | **done** |
| P0-efa-ascend | `protocol=efa\|ascend` may no-op or look successful without that transport | H | — | **open** |
| P1-sync-status | Python `transferSync` retry / `CANCELED` handling may not match TENT failover | S–M | — | **open** |
| P1-error-codes | Shim returned TENT `Status::Code` (non-negative); classic callers expect `ERR_*` | M | #4139 | **done** |
| P1-request-options | `priority` / `remote_accessible` were dropped at the shim | M | #4114 | **done** |
| P2-first-buffer | `getFirstBufferAddress` also called `getMetadata()` (same null deref as `send_probe`) | S | #4138 | **done** |
| P1-install-transport | TENT `installTransport()` returns `nullptr`; classic C/Go/EFA callers treat that as install failure | M | — | **open** |

### Residuals on landed items

These do not reopen the row, but they are not "the original hole is gone with no leftover":

- **P0-send_probe.** Python no longer dereferences `getMetadata()`. #4081 closed the segment after probing, which invalidated a handle already stored in Python `handle_map_`; #4115 stopped closing it. C++ `getMetadata()` is still `nullptr` under TENT — any remaining `getMetadata()->sendProbe` caller will still crash.
- **P0-stale-handle.** `CheckSegmentStatus` now probes via `probePeerAliveByID`. Python only calls it when **`submitTransfer` fails**. Peer death that shows up as `getTransferStatus` `FAILED` / `TIMEOUT` still leaves `handle_map_` intact. That leftover belongs with **P1-sync-status**. The unit test covers an never-opened handle, not a still-mapped handle whose RPC probe fails.
- **P0-force-tcp.** #4113 makes `forceTcp()` disable HP TCP so a config with both enabled does not fail init.
- **P1-error-codes.** Integer-returning APIs go through `tentToClassicError()`. `submitTransfer` still wraps TENT failures as `Status::Context(...)`. No in-tree test that failed on main and passed after (#4139 checklist).
- **P1-request-options.** Shim forwards `remote_accessible` → TENT perms and `TransferRequest::priority` on submit. Python `transferSync` does not set `priority` (default MEDIUM). No in-tree red/green test (#4114 checklist).

### Still open

- **P0-efa-ascend.** `init(..., protocol)` is now forwarded, but the TENT branch only special-cases `"tcp"`. `"efa"` / `"ascend"` do not pin those transports. On `USE_EFA` / `USE_CXI` Python builds, `initialize` still calls `installTransport()` after init; under TENT that returns `nullptr` and `initialize` returns `-1`. #4122 is classic TE Ascend Direct selection, not this shim item.
- **P1-sync-status.** `transferSync` still retries `numContexts()+1` times; under TENT `numContexts()` is hardcoded `1`. The poll loop handles `COMPLETED` / `FAILED` / `TIMEOUT` only — not `CANCELED` — and does not evict the cached handle on poll failure.
- **P1-install-transport.** Added from @chlins (2026-09-14). The TENT branch logs `"installTransport not used by TENT"` and returns `nullptr`. Classic contract: `nullptr` means install failed. Store already skips this via `isUsingTent()` (#2596). C / Go (`transfer_engine_c.h`) and EFA/CXI Python do not. Proposed fix A (TENT returns a non-null sentinel; in-tree callers only null-check) is preferred over gating every caller (B) or fixing only the C shim (C). Waiting on TENT owners (@alogfans) before a PR. R

## 🚀 Feature
alias to generate tensor with random uniform distribution.

## Motivation

uniform distribution is one of the most commonly used distributions by users. currently generating tensor distributed uniformly can be done using tensor initializer (`torch.FloatTensor(*size).uniform_(low, high)`), or by definition:
`(high - low) * torch.rand(*size) + low`.

## Pitch

Adding the alias `torch.random.uniform(low, high, size) for initiating a uniformly distributed tensor. 

## Alternatives

described above.

items.title: [inductor] memory_planning: pools exceed peak live bytes when a buffer overlaps two TemporalSplit children
items.author: teerthsharma
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

With `torch._inductor.config.memory_planning = True`, `TemporalSplit._allocate` refuses a block whose live range overlaps two of its children (the `TODO(jansel)` in `torch/_inductor/codegen/memory_planning.py`). `MemoryPlanner` then places that block above the pool, even when the bytes beside those children are free. As a result, pools exceed the peak of simultaneously-live bytes, which is a lower bound for any plan.

Four buffers reproduce it. The pool is 704 bytes, but peak live is 512:

```python
from types import SimpleNamespace

import torch
from torch._inductor.codegen.memory_planning import BufferGroup, LiveRange, MemoryPlanner
from torch._inductor.virtualized import V


def buffer(name, nbytes):
    return SimpleNamespace(
        get_name=lambda: name,
        get_layout=lambda: SimpleNamespace(size=(), storage_size=lambda: nbytes),
        get_dtype=lambda: torch.uint8,
        get_device=lambda: torch.device("cpu"),
    )


planner = MemoryPlanner(wrapper=None)
planner.buffer_groups = []
for name, begin, end, nbytes in [
    ("buf0", 2, 5, 256),
    ("buf1", 5, 6, 256),
    ("buf2", 3, 6, 192),
    ("buf3", 1, 3, 256),
]:
    group = BufferGroup(buffer(name, nbytes))
    group.live_range = LiveRange(begin, end)
    planner.buffer_groups.append(group)

sizevars = SimpleNamespace(optimization_hint=lambda expr, fallback: expr)
with V.set_graph_handler(SimpleNamespace(sizevars=sizevars)):
    planner.allocate_groups()

(pool,) = planner.pools.device_to_pools[torch.device("cpu")]
print(pool.root.get_symbolic_size())  # 704
```

The same pattern shows up on real graphs. These are bytes of one `memory_pool="combined"` pool through `torch.compile`, CPU, random init:

| graph | batch | pool | peak live | over |
|-|-|-|-|-|
| Inception-v3 | 1 | 10,383,744 | 8,214,912 | +26.4% |
| ConvNeXt-tiny | 1 | 8,733,696 | 7,225,344 | +20.9% |
| ConvNeXt-tiny | 8 | 65,052,672 | 57,802,752 | +12.5% |
| GPT-2 | 1 | 27,828,736 | 26,124,800 | +6.5% |

ResNet-50, ViT-B/16, BERT and EfficientNet-B0 already sit at peak live.

### Versions

torch 2.14.0+cu126 wheel with the GPU hidden. `memory_planning.py` is identical at main 44a629b. Windows 11, Python 3.11.

items.title: [Bug] GLM-5.3-Flash (DSA): HiCache host-tier load-back corrupts generation even without speculative decoding — dropped tool calls, degenerate repetition loops (8×H100, TP8)
items.author: d3lavar
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

On GLM-5.3-Flash (packed DSA KV / `DSATokenToKVPool`, `--attention-backend dsa`), enabling HiCache host offload (`--hicache-size` / `--hicache-ratio`) corrupts generation for requests whose prefix round-trips through the host tier (device → host → device). **Speculative decoding is not required — the corruption reproduces with EAGLE/MTP fully disabled; HiCache alone is broken.** Three failure signatures, all appearing only after host load-back:

1. **Tool calls silently dropped** — `finish_reason=stop`, `tool_calls=null`, with a prose "answer" that often hallucinates the tool output, even though the model's reasoning explicitly announces the call.
2. **Degenerate repetition loops / broken token sequences** — output gets stuck repeating filler tokens from the system prompt (or a single phrase) until `max_tokens` truncation.

**Isolation on the same production 8×H100 node, same workload (2026-09-04):**

| HiCache (`--hicache-ratio 2 --hicache-size 140`) | EAGLE/MTP | Result |
|---|---|---|
| ON | ON | **corrupted** — signatures 1–3 |
| ON | **OFF** | **still corrupted** — intermittent: byte-identical warm replays mostly pass, but individual host load-back runs drop tool calls or loop (1 of 6 warm replays broken in one window, 4/4 post-eviction replays broken in another) |
| OFF (device radix only) | ON | clean — 5/5 on the originally broken session |

The corruption is **intermittent** on host load-back: a byte-identical replay succeeds several times in a row, then a later identical replay corrupts (see `warm1/warm2/warm3` below). The fault lives in the **HiCache host-tier load-back path itself**; EAGLE adds its own draft-state sensitivity on top (#28895) but is not required for the bug.

### Setup

- **Hardware:** 8× NVIDIA H100 (single node), TP8 / DP1 / EP8
- **Image:** [`lmsysorg/sglang:glm-5.3-flash`](https://hub.docker.com/r/lmsysorg/sglang) — build of PR #36507 (branch `xinyuan/glm-5.3-flash-support`), with #37925 (`glm53` tool-call parser) and #37534 (packed-DSA HiCache host-row width fix) cherry-picked. The corruption persists with both, so #37534 is not sufficient for the spec-decode combination.
- **Launch (broken config), flags confirmed verbatim from `/server_info`:**

  ```bash
  python -m sglang.launch_server \
    --model-path glm-5.3-flash \
    --tp-size 8 --dp-size 1 --ep-size 8 \
    --attention-backend dsa \
    --page-size 64 \
    --tool-call-parser glm53 --reasoning-parser glm45 \
    --chunked-prefill-size 8192 --max-prefill-tokens 16384 \
    --mem-fraction-static 0.7 --max-running-requests 48 \
    --speculative-algorithm EAGLE \
    --speculative-num-steps 5 --speculative-eagle-topk 1 \
    --speculative-num-draft-tokens 6 --speculative-adaptive \
    --hicache-ratio 2 --hicache-size 140 \
    --hicache-write-policy write_through \
    --hicache-mem-layout page-first-direct \
    --hicache-io-backend direct
  ```

  Removing the `--hicache-*` flags removes the corruption. Disabling EAGLE does **not** — with HiCache on, generation still corrupts without speculative decoding but later, cannot determine the moment yet.
- **Pressure conditions:** device KV pool ~93% used (~601K tokens), host pool LRU ~99.9% full — prefixes actively evict to host and load back between turns.
- **Workload:** agentic client, 47 tools, streaming, OpenAI-style history, 100K–230K-token prompts.

### Evidence (verbatim excerpts from the script above, HiCache ON, glm53 parser + #37534 build; observed with EAGLE both ON and OFF)

Phase 1 (device radix hits) is mostly healthy, but even the first warm window already drops calls intermittently:

```text
cold-180K    dt=27.3s  prompt=225686  cached=128     finish=tool_calls  tools=['bash']
warm1-180K   dt= 1.7s  prompt=225686  cached=225664  finish=tool_calls  tools=['bash']
warm2-180K   dt= 1.1s  prompt=225686  cached=225664  finish=stop        tools=[]      <- BROKEN
warm3-180K   dt= 1.5s  prompt=225686  cached=225664  finish=tool_calls  tools=['bash']
```

`warm2-180K` content — the model hallucinates the tool result instead of calling the tool:

```text
Here's the output from running the command:

```
hello-acceptance
```
```

Phase 3 (same byte-identical prompts after eviction, i.e. served from HiCache host load-back) — tool-call drops plus degenerate repetition loops:

```text
replay1-60K   dt= 0.8s  cached=75328   finish=stop          tools=[]  tail: "echo hello-acceptance"
replay2-60K   dt=33.0s  cached=75328   finish=length(2000)  tools=[]  tail: "oscar oscar oscar oscar oscar oscar 999999999
juliet juliet juliet jul"
replay1-180K  dt=28.0s  cached=225664  finish=length(2000)  tools=[]  tail: "tice the notice the notice the notice the notice ..."
replay2-180K  dt=58.2s  cached=225664  finish=length(2000)  tools=[]
```

`oscar`/`juliet` are random filler words from the system prompt — the model is regurgitating corrupted prefill tokens. Phase 2 (eviction pressure, ~2.2M tokens vs ~601K device pool)

For comparison: with HiCache disabled (device radix only) — clean, including warm replays and post-eviction replays; with EAGLE disabled but HiCache on — corruption is still observed on host load-back (tool-call drops and repetition loops, as above).

### Notes on root cause (hypothesis)

Host-tier backup/load-back corrupts the packed DSA KV rows themselves (`DSATokenToKVPool`): after a device → host → device round-trip the prefill KV no longer matches what the original token sequence produced, so the model "misreads its own history" — no valid tool call, confabulated r
