items.title: [Feature][Training][Rubin] MegaMoE: MXFP8, recomputation, and clamped SwiGLU
items.author: abcdabcd987
items.body_excerpt:
## Problem

We need the MegaMoE training backend in [PR #6053](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/6053) to support activation checkpointing, clamped SwiGLU, and native MXFP8 across Blackwell and Rubin. The target workloads include both 256- and 288-expert models with irregular, unequal per-rank token counts.

The GB200 benchmark at revision `072340e2` also reports 1.4–1.5× slower steps than MoK under uniform routing, and 58.9 GiB of retained output/context per layer at EP32/64 with overflow-safe schedules; the memory figure excludes symmetric workspaces ([benchmark details](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/6053#issuecomment-6026084025)). These are results for that revision, not Rubin measurements or claims about later revisions.

## Requested outcome

- **Recomputation:** Add a context-only recompute API for activation checkpointing, similar to MoK's `recompute_forward_context`. Rebuild the state needed by backward without rerunning unnecessary down projections, combine, and output epilogues; validate that recomputed and saved-context backward agree.

- **GLM-5.3-Flash support:** Support 288 routed experts, including EP8 with 36 local experts and EP32 with 9. Implement clamped SwiGLU for both routed and shared experts: `silu(clamp(gate, max=10)) * clamp(up, min=-10, max=10)`, with matching backward semantics; retain the unclamped option for the GLM-5.2 workload ([GLM-5.3-Flash implementation](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/blob/8073e6dcaea9aa4b42acf2d92ec72148786bbaeb/src/transformers/models/glm5_next/modeling_glm5_next.py#L86-L142)).

- **MXFP8:** Add native MXFP8 routed-expert forward, input gradients, and weight gradients, not fake quantization followed by BF16 GEMMs. Use a MoK-compatible recipe with caller-prequantized weights and fused activation/gradient quantization, including both operand orientations where needed; keep the shared expert in BF16 initially ([MoK reference API](https://github.com/cursor/mixture-of-kittens/blob/caeb2963f855c7ad53bb50c8bbf211086405cb98/README.md)).

- **Memory and speed:** Address the router-gradient backward overhead, capacity-sized saved routed outputs, and computation on padded source rows identified in the [GB200 benchmark comment](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/6053#issuecomment-6026084025). Reduce retained activation memory without trading away numerical quality, and make performance track real work rather than pessimistic reserved capacity.

## Target hardware

Required targets are **`sm_100` (B200/GB200), `sm_103` (B300/GB300), and `sm_107` (Rubin)**. Implement and validate the requested capabilities on all three, rather than treating Blackwell as a comparison-only platform.

Expert-parallel groups must support peers spanning multiple hosts within one NVL72 NVLink domain. An inter-rack transport is not required.

## Inference engine

We use PyTorch native with a custom training integration. This request covers both forward and backward, not an inference-only operator.

## Workload and configuration

- **Data type and quantization:** BF16 baseline and native MXFP8 routed-expert training; BF16 shared expert.
- **Parallelism:** Expert parallelism within one NVLink domain, combined with expert FSDP and activation checkpointing.

`H` is hidden width and `I` is expert intermediate width. Both workloads use top-8 routing and one shared expert of width `I`.

| Workload | H | I | Routed experts | Target EP sizes | Local routed experts |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|---|
| [GLM-5.2-shaped workload](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/6053#issuecomment-6026084025) | 6144 | 2048 | 256 | 4 / 8 / 16 / 32 / 64 | 64 / 32 / 16 / 8 / 4 |
| [GLM-5.3-Flash](https://huggingface.co/zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash/raw/main/config.json) | 4096 | 2048 | 288 | 8 / 32 | 36 / 9 |

**The real input-token count `T_r` is irregular, generally not a power of two, and changes across microbatches and runs.** Ranks in the same EP collective can have different counts, including zero; support this independently of uneven received expert loads, without caller-side activation padding.

Use roughly 8K–32K real tokens per rank as the main benchmark range, including counts such as `8191`, `16172`, `16231`, and `32767`. Token counts and routing must remain runtime inputs.

- **Layouts:** Activations are `[T_r,H]`; routing IDs and coefficients are `[T_r,8]`. Gate and up weights are separate tensors, each `[E_local,I,H]`, used as `gate_e = X_e @ W_gate[e].T` and `up_e = X_e @ W_up[e].T`. Down weights are `[E_local,H,I]`, used as `activation_e @ W_down[e].T`.

## Current workaround

The existing comparison paths are [MoK #17](https://github.com/cursor/mixture-of-kittens/pull/17) and DeepEP HybridEP plus grouped GEMMs, as described in the [benchmark setup](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/6053#issuecomment-6026084025). For the measured adapter revision, activation checkpointing replays the full forward because it lacks a context-only entry point ([recompute comparison](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/6053#issuecomment-6026084025)).

## Acceptance criteria

- **Hardware coverage:** Run correctness and performance qualification on `sm_100`, `sm_103`, and `sm_107` for the listed workloads.
- **Training correctness:** Validate outputs, input gradients, routing-coefficient gradients, and all expert/shared weight gradients against independent references. Include clamp boundaries, uneven/empty ranks, skewed routing, and recomputation; support FP32 weight-gradient accumulation and document the BF16/MXFP8 numerical behavior.
- **Performance:** Compare complete forward/backward and checkpointed execution against MoK and HybridEP plus grouped GEMMs. Include scheduling, quantization, copies, and replay, and report total peak memory with matched ring sizes or an explicit latency-versus-memory comparison.

items.title: [Serve] A batch_size_fn exception stops batching and hangs subsequent valid requests
items.author: ai-yang
items.body_excerpt:
### What happened + What you expected to happen

With `@serve.batch(batch_size_fn=...)`, an ordinary exception from the custom sizing callback terminates the queue's background batching task. The exception is not propagated to the dequeued request futures, and subsequent valid requests to the same batched method also hang. The replica remains alive; the application still reports `RUNNING`.

For example, a string-length sizing callback raises `TypeError` for `None`. The expected behavior is to fail the affected request with that error and continue processing valid strings. Instead, both the invalid request and the next valid request time out. This reproduced on three independently deployed replicas.

### Versions / Dependencies

- Ray `3.0.0.dev0`, `master` commit `be4889928d3a396d7a1476d1bac3288dac72f9ab`.
- Official nightly wheel for that exact commit, with Python sources linked using `setup-dev.py`.
- Linux x86_64, Python 3.11.15; one local Serve replica, no GPU or external service.

### Reproduction script

```python
import asyncio
import ray
from ray import serve

@serve.deployment(num_replicas=1, max_ongoing_requests=8)
class Demo:
    @serve.batch(
        max_batch_size=8,
        batch_wait_timeout_s=0.01,
        batch_size_fn=lambda items: sum(len(item) for item in items),
    )
    async def batched(self, items):
        return items

    async def __call__(self, item):
        try:
            return {"result": await asyncio.wait_for(self.batched(item), 1)}
        except Exception as exc:
            return {"error": type(exc).__name__}

ray.init(address="local", num_cpus=2, include_dashboard=False)
try:
    serve.start(http_options={"location": "NoServer"})
    handle = serve.run(Demo.bind(), route_prefix=None)
    for item in ("ok", None, "ok"):
        print(handle.remote(item).result(timeout_s=30))
finally:
    serve.shutdown()
    ray.shutdown()
```

Expected: `{'result': 'ok'}`, `{'error': 'TypeError'}`, `{'result': 'ok'}`.

Actual: `{'result': 'ok'}`, `{'error': 'TimeoutError'}`, `{'error': 'TimeoutError'}`.

The timeout bounds the reproduction; it is not the cause of the batching task's failure. Without it, the request futures remain unresolved. Inspecting `_is_batching_task_alive()` after the sizing exception returns `False` on the baseline and `True` with exception propagation fixed.

### Root cause

`wait_for_batch()` calls `_compute_batch_size()` while examining the first item and while assembling a batch, without an exception boundary. `_process_batches()` directly awaits it, so the exception ends the only queue consumer. Additionally, `_process_batch_inner()` recomputes sub-batch size before the `try` block that completes request futures on failure; an exception at that stage leaves the corresponding sub-batch unresolved.

### Issue Severity

Medium-high availability impact for deployments using custom batch sizing: one input-related callback exception can make the batched method persistently unavailable to otherwise valid requests. Input validation before enqueueing can avoid the trigger, and restarting an affected replica restores service. The default path without `batch_size_fn` does not have this trigger.

### Duplicate-work check

On 2026-09-13, searched `batch_size_fn`, `batch_size_fn exception`, `batch_size_fn hang`, and Serve batching hang across issues and PRs, and inspected nearby discussions:

- #58956 / #59059 introduced custom sizing. A review comment on #59059 already mentions keyword-argument `IndexError`; this reproduction uses positional arguments and concerns ordinary callback exceptions disabling later valid requests. It does not propose a keyword-argument compatibility fix.
- Closed #50046 concerns an earlier cancellation bug, and closed #42593 concerns earlier batching hangs; both predate custom sizing.
- Open #64595 restructures batching into per-model queues. Its patch adds `CancelledError` handling but does not handle these ordinary sizing exceptions. It touches the same file, so a fix may need rebasing if that work lands first.

No matching in-flight fix was found. AI assistance was used to investigate this issue and prepare the reproduction.

- CPU architecture: x86_64
- GPU: 2× node, 8× NVIDIA H200 each (16 GPUs total), AWS `p5en.48xlarge`
- Networking: AWS EFA (32 NICs/node), EFA 1.50 userspace + aws-ofi-nccl (GIN); Kubernetes StatefulSet with `hostNetwork: true` (pod IP == node IP on a `10.x.0.0/16` primary CIDR), sshd on :2222 for the `mpirun` bootstrap.
- Libraries:
  - Container: `nvcr.io/nvidia/tensorrt-llm/release:1.3.0rc9`
  - TensorRT-LLM: v1.3.0rc9 line (source paths below verified against this line)
  - NCCL 2.30.4, PyTorch as shipped in the container
- OS: Ubuntu 24.04 (container)
- Orchestrator: MPI (`trtllm-llmapi-launch` → `mpirun`), i.e. the `MpiCommSession`/IPC-executor path (not Ray).

### Who can help?

Leaving blank for a core maintainer to route (executor / IPC / multi-node serving).

### The bug

On a **multi-node** `trtllm-serve` launched with the **MPI orchestrator** (ranks spanning two hosts),
startup **hangs at IPC-executor init**. Rank-0's orchestrator creates its ZMQ IPC queues bound to
**loopback** and advertises that `tcp://127.0.0.1:PORT` endpoint to all workers. The 8 worker ranks on
the *second* host try to connect to `127.0.0.1:PORT`, which resolves to *their own* loopback, never
reach rank-0, and exit — so `MpiSession`/IPC init blocks forever waiting for them to connect.

This is specifically an **IPC-executor** problem, not an MPI / NCCL / EFA problem: the `mpirun`
cross-node bootstrap is clean (all 16 ranks start; `orted` launches on the worker node over ssh), and
the hang is **before** NCCL init.

### The hang (reproduced, frozen 8+ minutes, GPUs idle)

`trtllm-serve` freezes right after these lines and never proceeds:

```
[TRT-LLM] [W] Orchestrator is creating IPC executor
rank 0 using MpiCommSession to bind to external MPI processes
[TRT-LLM] [I] Generating a new HMAC key for server proxy_request_queue
[TRT-LLM] [I] Generating a new HMAC key for server worker_init_status_queue
[TRT-LLM] [I] Generating a new HMAC key for server proxy_result_queue
```

Rank-0 waits for the 16 workers to connect to `worker_init_status_queue`; the 8 worker-node ranks
never connect (they start, fail to reach rank-0, exit → `orted` defunct), so init hangs.

### Root cause (source, v1.3.0rc line)

1. `tensorrt_llm/executor/ipc.py:58` — the queue bind address defaults to a hardcoded loopback:
   ```python
   self.address_endpoint = address[
       0] if address is not None else "tcp://127.0.0.1:*"
   ```
2. `tensorrt_llm/executor/proxy.py:494` — `worker_init_status_queue = IpcQueue(is_server=True,
   name="worker_init_status_queue")` is constructed with **no `address`**, so it uses that loopback
   default; `proxy.py:520` then advertises that `tcp://127.0.0.1:PORT` endpoint to the workers.
   Cross-host workers connecting to `127.0.0.1:PORT` hit their **own** loopback → fail.
3. **No routable-IP override exists.** A whole-tree grep of `tensorrt_llm/executor/` for
   `TLLM_*ADDR|*IP|*HOST`, `0.0.0.0`, `get_local_ip`, `use_hostname` finds nothing that sets the
   orchestrator IPC bind address. (`TLLM_SPAWN_PROXY_PROCESS_IPC_ADDR` is an `ipc://` unix socket for
   the RPC-proxy path — even more node-local — and `MASTER_ADDR` is for the Ray backend, not the MPI
   IPC executor.)

So on a single node everything binds and connects on loopback and works; the moment ranks span hosts,
the loopback-bound orchestrator queues are unreachable by the remote workers.

### Expected behavior

A multi-node MPI-orchestrated `trtllm-serve` should let the orchestrator IPC queues bind to a
**routable** address (or `0.0.0.0`) and advertise rank-0's **routable IP** (not `127.0.0.1`) to the
workers, so cross-host workers can connect and `/health` comes up.

### Reproduction

```bash
mpirun -np 16 -H <node0>:8,<node1>:8 \
  --mca plm_rsh_args "-p 2222 -o GSSAPIAuthentication=no" \
  -x TRTLLM_FORCE_COMM_METHOD=... \
  trtllm-llmapi-launch trtllm-serve <a-MoE-model> \
  --tp_size 16 --ep_size 16 --pp_size 1 ...
# hangs at "Orchestrator is creating IPC executor" (see log above); GPUs idle.
```
(`GSSAPIAuthentication=no` is only needed so ssh doesn't stall on GSSAPI KEX against a no-KDC node —
unrelated to the IPC bug.)

### A candidate direction — and why this is filed as an issue, not a "fix" PR

An env-overridable bind address gets *past* the freeze once, but is **not a reliable fix**, so I am
filing this as a defensive-note issue rather than presenting a patch as done:

```diff
--- a/tensorrt_llm/executor/ipc.py
+++ b/tensorrt_llm/executor/ipc.py
-        self.address_endpoint = address[
-            0] if address is not None else "tcp://127.0.0.1:*"
+        self.address_endpoint = address[
+            0] if address is not None else ("tcp://%s:*" % os.environ.get("TLLM_IPC_BIND_IP", "127.0.0.1"))
```
Run with `-x TLLM_IPC_BIND_IP=<rank-0 routable node IP>`.

**Caveat (measured):** with this change + `TLLM_IPC_BIND_IP=<node0 IP>`, **one** attempt advanced all
the way to `launch_server` (past the IPC freeze); a subsequent clean relaunch (stale procs + port
reaped) **re-hung at the same IPC freeze**. So a routable-IP bind is *necessary but not sufficient*.
Unconfirmed which of: (a) the env did not thread to rank-0 on the relaunch (env propagation), (b) a
second worker-connected queue still binds loopback, or (c) an ephemeral-port node↔node reachability
issue. A complete fix should (i) bind the orchestrator IPC to a routable/`0.0.0.0` address, (ii)
advertise the routable IP (not `0.0.0.0`/`127.0.0.1`) to workers, and (iii) ensure **every**
worker-connected queue (not just `worker_init_status_queue`) uses it — then prove a clean multi-host
`trtllm-serve` reaches `/health`.

### Proven workaround

Switching the orchestrator from MPI to **Ray** (`--orchestrator_type ray` / the Ray-backed launch
path, which uses `MASTER_ADDR` for a routable rendezvous) brings multi-node `trtllm-serve` up cleanly
on the same 2-node substrate. So the defect is specific to the **MPI IPC-executor** bind path, and
there is a working alternative

items.title: [Bug]: DSpark cannot load RedHatAI/Kimi-K3-speculator.dspark (speculators config format)
items.author: vsabavat
items.body_excerpt:
### System Info

- TensorRT-LLM main `0970204df7` (also seen on `9bf6b8b9`)
- Kimi K3 (`moonshotai/Kimi-K3`) on 16x GB200
- Drafter: `RedHatAI/Kimi-K3-speculator.dspark` @ `38a88101`

### Who can help?

@juney-nvidia @longlee0622

### Reproduction

```yaml
speculative_config:
  decoding_type: DSpark
  max_draft_len: 7
  speculative_model: RedHatAI/Kimi-K3-speculator.dspark
```

The DSpark drafter path does not read this checkpoint's config.

### Expected behavior

TRT-LLM loads `RedHatAI/Kimi-K3-speculator.dspark` as published.

### Actual behavior

The checkpoint uses the `speculators` config format. TRT-LLM has no support for it; `git grep speculators` on main finds nothing.

- TRT-LLM expects the drafter backbone in a top-level HF config (`model_type: qwen3`), with DSpark fields in `dflash_config` or at top level.
- `speculators` nests the backbone under `transformer_layer_config`.
- It names the capture layers `aux_hidden_state_layer_ids`, in vLLM's convention: a layer's input, so TRT-LLM's id is the value minus 1.

### Additional notes

Workaround: we rewrote `config.json` into TRT-LLM's layout and symlinked the weights. The tensor names already match the GQA DSpark loader. That works, but two gaps remain:

- The GQA path replaces the drafter's `embed_tokens` with the target's. This checkpoint trains its own row for the mask token (163837), so natural acceptance may be lower than intended.
- The checkpoint was trained with a 2048-token sliding window. TRT-LLM's drafter attention rejects it, so we disabled the window. That is exact only while the context stays at or below 2048 tokens.

`Inferact/Kimi-K3-DSpark` loads natively, so this only affects users of the RedHatAI checkpoint.

items.title: [Bug]: [PyTorch backend] Under beam search, logits processors receive per-slot token lists instead of each beam's hypothesis
items.author: lminer
items.body_excerpt:
### System Info

- TensorRT-LLM 1.3.0rc29 (`nvcr.io/nvidia/tensorrt-llm/release:1.3.0rc29`), PyTorch backend
- Also reproduces on `nvcr.io/nvidia/tensorrt-llm/release:1.4.0rc0.dev202610040000`
- GPU: NVIDIA L4
- The code path below is unchanged on `main` at 0970204df7.

### Who can help?

@pranav-nvidia (or whoever owns the PyTorch sampler / beam search)

### Reproduction

`repro_beam_history.py` (below), using `TinyLlama/TinyLlama-1.1B-Chat-v1.0`, `max_beam_width=2`, overlap scheduler off. A logits processor steers the search so that both surviving beams after step 1 come from the second step-0 candidate:

- step 0: allow only `A` (score 0) and `B` (score -1), so slot 0 = `[A]`, slot 1 = `[B]`
- step 1: rows ending in `A` get a flat distribution; rows ending in `B` allow only `C` (0) and `D` (-0.5). Both new beams are children of `B`: `[B, C]` and `[B, D]`.
- step 2: record the `token_ids` passed in and allow only `E`.

```python
"""Logits processors see per-slot token lists, not beam hypotheses, under beam search.

The processor steers a 2-beam search so that, after the second generated token, both surviving
beams descend from the *second* first-step candidate. On the next step it records the token
lists the runtime passes in, then compares them with the beams the request returns.
"""

import os

# Only so this script can read back what the processor recorded; the bug does not depend on it.
os.environ.setdefault("TLLM_WORKER_USE_SINGLE_PROCESS", "1")

from tensorrt_llm import LLM, SamplingParams  # noqa: E402
from tensorrt_llm.sampling_params import LogitsProcessor  # noqa: E402

MODEL = "TinyLlama/TinyLlama-1.1B-Chat-v1.0"
# Arbitrary ordinary token ids.
A, B, C, D, E = 1000, 2000, 3000, 4000, 5000
NAMES = {A: "A", B: "B", C: "C", D: "D", E: "E"}


def allow(row, scores):
    """Mask every token except the given ones."""
    row.fill_(float("-inf"))
    for token, score in scores.items():
        row[token] = score


class SteerBeams(LogitsProcessor):
    def __init__(self, prompt_len):
        self.prompt_len = prompt_len
        self.seen = {}

    def __call__(self, req_id, logits, token_ids, stream_ptr, client_id):
        step = len(token_ids[0]) - self.prompt_len
        self.seen[step] = [[NAMES.get(t, t) for t in ids[self.prompt_len :]] for ids in token_ids]
        print(f"step {step}: token_ids passed to the processor = {self.seen[step]}")
        rows = logits.view(-1, logits.shape[-1])
        for row, ids in zip(rows, token_ids):
            if step == 0:
                # Two candidates; A ranks ahead of B.
                allow(row, {A: 0.0, B: -1.0})
            elif step == 1:
                if ids[-1] == A:
                    # Flat distribution: every continuation of A is unlikely (about -log(vocab)).
                    row.zero_()
                else:
                    # Both continuations of B beat anything that continues A.
                    allow(row, {C: 0.0, D: -0.5})
            else:
                allow(row, {E: 0.0})


def main():
    llm = LLM(model=MODEL, max_beam_width=2, disable_overlap_scheduler=True)
    prompt = llm.tokenizer.encode("The capital of France is")
    processor = SteerBeams(len(prompt))
    params = SamplingParams(
        max_tokens=3,
        use_beam_search=True,
        best_of=2,
        n=2,
        end_id=llm.tokenizer.eos_token_id,
        logits_processor=processor,
        detokenize=False,
    )
    output = llm.generate({"prompt_token_ids": prompt}, params)
    final = [[NAMES.get(t, t) for t in beam.token_ids] for beam in output.outputs]
    print(f"final beams                                  = {final}")

    expected = sorted(beam[:2] for beam in final)  # each live beam's history before step 2
    observed = sorted(processor.seen[2])
    print(f"step 2 histories, expected = {expected}")
    print(f"step 2 histories, observed = {observed}")
    assert observed == expected, "logits processor was given token lists that are not the live beams"


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

```
python repro_beam_history.py
```

### Expected behavior

At step 2, `token_ids` holds the two live hypotheses, `[B, C]` and `[B, D]` (after the prompt), which are also the prefixes of the returned beams `[B, C, E]` and `[B, D, E]`.

### Actual behavior

Same output on 1.3.0rc29 and 1.4.0rc0.dev202610040000:

```
step 0: token_ids passed to the processor = [[]]
step 1: token_ids passed to the processor = [['A'], ['B']]
step 2: token_ids passed to the processor = [['A', 'C'], ['B', 'D']]
final beams                                  = [['B', 'C', 'E'], ['B', 'D', 'E']]
step 2 histories, expected = [['B', 'C'], ['B', 'D']]
step 2 histories, observed = [['A', 'C'], ['B', 'D']]
AssertionError: logits processor was given token lists that are not the live beams
```

`token_ids[0]` at step 2 is `[A, C]`, which is not a hypothesis the search ever held. Slot 0 previously held `A`, and the new token for slot 0 (`C`) was appended to that slot's list, even though the beam it extends came from slot 1.

### Additional notes

Where it happens (links at `main` 0970204df7):

- `ModelEngine._execute_logit_post_processors` passes `request.get_tokens(beam_idx)` for each beam ([model_engine.py#L6582-L6585](https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM/blob/0970204df7e6b91790c0dfaf7eb986d4b5f9c4a3/tensorrt_llm/_torch/pyexecutor/model_engine.py#L6582-L6585)).
- After each non-final step the sampler appends each slot's new token to that slot's list, `add_token(req, new_tokens_list, beam_idx=beam_idx)` ([sampler.py#L1594-L1596](https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM/blob/0970204df7e6b91790c0dfaf7eb986d4b5f9c4a3/tensorrt_llm/_torch/pyexecutor/sampler/sampler.py#L1594-L1596), [sampler_common.py#L133-L141](https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM/blob/0970204df7e6b91790c0dfaf7eb986d4b5f9c4a3/tensorrt_llm/_torch/pyexecutor/sampler/sampler_common.py#L133-L141)). When the beams are reordered, a slot's list stops matching the beam in that slot.
- The corrected paths are

items.title: [BUG] SM100/SM103 ptr-array GEMM kernels size the per-SM tensormap workspace from the raw hw_info.sm_count, so a default KernelHardwareInfo causes out-of-bounds descriptor writes
items.author: elbourne12345
items.body_excerpt:
**Which component has the problem?** CUTLASS C++

**Describe the bug**

The Blackwell ptr-array and grouped GEMM kernels keep one set of TMA descriptors per SM in the global workspace and index that array on the device by SM id. The workspace is sized from the raw `args.hw_info.sm_count`, whose default is `0`, so a caller that leaves `KernelHardwareInfo` at its default gets a zero-byte tensormap workspace and the kernel then writes 128-byte descriptors through a null or undersized pointer.

Affected kernels:

- `include/cutlass/gemm/kernel/sm100_gemm_array_tma_warpspecialized.hpp`
- `include/cutlass/gemm/kernel/sm100_gemm_array_tma_warpspecialized_input_transform.hpp`
- `include/cutlass/gemm/kernel/sm100_gemm_array_tma_warpspecialized_mma_transform.hpp`
- `include/cutlass/gemm/kernel/sm103_blockscaled_gemm_array_tma_warpspecialized.hpp`

Taking the first file at `main` (59e3a33, v4.8.0) as the example:

- 349-359 `to_underlying_arguments()` computes a local `sm_count`, querying the device when the value is `<= 0`, but that local is used only in a trace message.
- 367, 371 size the epilogue and mainloop workspaces from `args.hw_info.sm_count` (the raw value), as do 461, 465 in `get_workspace_size()` and 486, 494 in `initialize_workspace()`.
- 392-399 store `args.hw_info` unchanged in `Params`, so the device sees the same raw value.
- 591-594 derive `sm_id` from `%smid` for ptr-array kernels and from the linear CTA id for grouped kernels, and 601-1448 pass `params.hw_info.sm_count` into `tensormaps_init()` as the stride between the A and B descriptor arrays.

The collectives size and index the same way: `sm100_mma_array_warpspecialized.hpp` 424-428 allocates `2 * sizeof(TmaDescriptor) * sm_count * NumTmaDescriptorsPerSm`, and 767-768 read `tensormaps[sm_idx * N]` and `tensormaps[(sm_idx + sm_count) * N]`. `sm100_epilogue_array_tma_warpspecialized.hpp` 375-381 and 1373-1420 do the same for the C/D descriptors.

Two distinct failures follow:

1. **ptr-array (`GemmUniversalMode::kArray`), default or reduced `sm_count`.** The launch grid for these kernels is the full output-tile grid and does not depend on `sm_count`, so the kernel launches normally. `can_implement()` succeeds and `get_workspace_size()` returns only the fusion/scheduler bytes. On the device every CTA writes its A and B descriptors to `tensormaps[%smid * N]`, both to the same slot because the B offset is `sm_count * N = 0`. With no workspace allocated this is an illegal address; with a fusion workspace present the descriptors land past the end of that allocation, which is silent corruption. A user-supplied `sm_count` below the device SM count fails the same way for every SM whose `%smid` is at or beyond that value, because `%smid` does not honor the smaller number. The trace text at 355-357 tells users of exactly this kernel not to specify an SM count.

2. **Grouped kernel, default `sm_count`.** The queried SM count is discarded, and `PersistentTileSchedulerSm90Params::get_grid_shape` (`tile_scheduler_params.h` 1725-1790) truncates the grid to `sm_count`, so the launch grid becomes zero-sized and `run()` fails with an invalid launch configuration. Not memory-unsafe, but `can_implement()` accepted the arguments and the device query is dead code.

**Steps/Code to reproduce bug**

Build any SM100 ptr-array GEMM (for example the configuration in `examples/75_blackwell_grouped_gemm` in `kArray` mode) and construct `Arguments` with a default-constructed `KernelHardwareInfo`, i.e. omit the line that the examples use:

```cpp
// examples/75_blackwell_grouped_gemm/75_blackwell_grouped_gemm.cu:576
// hw_info.sm_count = cutlass::KernelHardwareInfo::query_device_multiprocessor_count(hw_info.device_id);
cutlass::KernelHardwareInfo hw_info;   // sm_count == 0

typename Gemm::Arguments arguments{cutlass::gemm::GemmUniversalMode::kArray,
                                   problem_shape, mainloop_args, epilogue_args, hw_info};

auto workspace_size = Gemm::get_workspace_size(arguments);   // tensormap bytes == 0
cutlass::device_memory::allocation<uint8_t> workspace(workspace_size);
gemm.can_implement(arguments);                               // returns kSuccess
gemm.initialize(arguments, workspace.get());
gemm.run();                                                  // cudaErrorIllegalAddress
```

The same program with `hw_info.sm_count` set to the device SM count runs correctly. Under `compute-sanitizer` the invalid writes appear inside `tensormaps_init()`.

**Expected behavior**

Either the workspace is sized from the SM count the kernel actually observes on the device (the SM90 array kernels in `sm90_gemm_array_tma_warpspecialized_cooperative.hpp` 264-294 and 349-364 do exactly this: they query `query_device_multiprocessor_count()` when the field is `<= 0`, size both workspaces from the queried value, and store it in `Params`), or `can_implement()` rejects the configuration. Today a default `KernelHardwareInfo` is supported on Hopper and memory-unsafe on Blackwell.

**Environment details**

- Environment location: bare metal
- CUTLASS: `main` @ 59e3a33 (v4.8.0); the raw-`sm_count` sizing is present since the file's first release in v3.8.0. v4.0.0 added the device query in `to_underlying_arguments()` but never used the result, so the query has been dead code from v4.0.0 through 4.8.0.

**Additional context**

Every in-tree caller sets the field before calling the kernel, which is why CI does not see this: `test/unit/gemm/device/gemm_testbed_3x_ptr_array.hpp` 2078-2079, `examples/75_blackwell_grouped_gemm/75_blackwell_grouped_gemm.cu` 576, and the profiler through `tools/library/src/grouped_gemm_operation_3x.hpp` 234.

This was found by reading the host and device paths and cross-checking them against the SM90 array kernel and the tagged sources for v3.8.0 through v4.6.0. I do not have Blackwell hardware, so the reproducer above is written from the code rather than executed; the code sequence is the one the examples use, minus the `sm_count` ass

items.title: [BUG] SM90 blockwise FP8 GEMM reuses modified B scales across M waves
items.author: 1sgtpepper
items.body_excerpt:
## Which component has the problem?

CUTLASS C++

## Bug Report

**Describe the bug**

SM90 cooperative blockwise FP8 GEMM applies the preceding M wave's A scale again when processing the next M wave. With CTA tile 256×128×128 and scale granularity 128×64×128, `D[128,0]` is **1024 instead of 512**.

**Steps/Code to reproduce bug**

In a checkout of `59e3a3338d516ca6ce0e073af8da65289678a35c`:

```sh
curl -fL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/1sgtpepper/cutlass/75e7b4a8a2859c317209d81c91c5ab9158a573e7/test/regression/fp8_scale_wave.cu -o fp8_scale_wave.cu
nvcc -std=c++17 -O3 -lineinfo --expt-relaxed-constexpr \
  -gencode=arch=compute_90a,code=sm_90a \
  -Iinclude -Itools/util/include fp8_scale_wave.cu -o fp8_scale_wave
./fp8_scale_wave
```

Inputs are FP8 E4M3 ones, with A scales 2 and 4 across the row bands and B scales 1 and 2 across the column bands.

```text
minimal l=0 m=128 n=0 actual=1024 expected=512
minimal tile=256x128x128 scale=128x64x128 stages=3 problem=256x128x128x1 mismatches=16384 FAIL
```

**Expected behavior**

Each M wave multiplies its own A scale by the original B scale for the current K tile.

**Environment details (please complete the following information):**

- CUTLASS `59e3a3338d516ca6ce0e073af8da65289678a35c`, main as of September 8, 2026. The affected collective is byte-identical in `v4.8.0dev` and `v4.7.1`; these releases were not executed.
- H100 80GB HBM3, driver 580.95.05; CUDA 13.1.1.
- Modal cloud GPU, Ubuntu 24.04 container, Linux x86_64.

**Additional context**

The `ScaleMsPerWave == 1 && ScaleNsPerTile > 1` path modifies B-scale registers reused by successive M waves, in both the main loop and drain. Reloading B's original scales makes all ten `--all` cases pass; restoring the old code restores the same six failures.

items.title: [serve] Offer first-class support for `CapacityQueueRouter`
items.author: jeffreywang88
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

This issue tracks the work items to make `CapacityQueueRouter` a first-class supported router in Ray Serve.
- [ ] **Stability**: Stabilize at large scale (e.g. 512 replicas for each deployment under a `client -> parent -> child` deployment topology). Falling over to `PowerOfTwoChoicesRouter` should be seamless.
- [ ] **Cold start**: Probe queue length during `CapacityQueueRouter`'s normal operation so that when `CapacityQueue` actor faults occur, we can seamlessly fall back to power-of-two-choices router without facing queue length cache cold-start problems.
- [ ] **API changes**: Allow users to select between `CapacityQueueRouter` and `PowerOfTwoChoicesRouter`.
- [ ] **Observability**: Metrics for the hit rate, latency, fallback rate of `CapacityQueueRouter`. If `CapacityQueueRouter` doesn't converge post-fault, we need a systematic mechanism to figure out the root cause.
- [ ] **Documentation**: Guidance on when to choose `CapacityQueueRouter` vs. `PowerOfTwoChoicesRouter`.

A node lifecycle event relocated the Redis pod and its front-end HAProxy pod, which dropped the TCP endpoint behind `RAY_REDIS_ADDRESS`. `gcs_server` SIGSEGV'd (issue #53475), kubelet restarted the head container, and from there the pod entered a 4.5-hour CPU-saturated + memory-linear-leak state that ended in OOMKilled at 11.4 GB. Raising the memory limit to 14 → 24 → 28 GiB did not help — the first-container lifetime actually shortened each time (~70s → 26s → 24s, all OOMKilled with exit 137), meaning the backlog accumulated faster than the memory increases. The cascade only cleared after the operator swapped `RAY_REDIS_ADDRESS` to a fresh empty Redis and restarted the Serve controller. items.title: [Serve] [RFC] Computed Retry-After for backpressure rejections
items.author: vinay7373
items.body_excerpt:
## Motivation

PR #65193 added `BackpressureConfig`. Deployments can now reject backpressured requests with a 429 and a static `Retry-After` header. Each caller (proxy or `DeploymentHandle`) has its own request queue, and at the time of a backpressure rejection a static `Retry-After` value can be incorrect in both directions. If the queue is deep and the static value is too short, clients retry into another rejection, adding load exactly when the system is trying to shed it. If the queue drains fast and the value is too long, capacity sits idle while clients wait.

This proposal computes the `Retry-After` value from observed load. This makes the header a reliable estimate of when capacity will be available, instead of a number the operator guessed. This was the original shape of the production request behind #65193 and it fits the discussion there about making 429 the default at some point.

No OSS inference server does this today (TGI, Triton, NVIDIA Dynamo and TorchServe all reject without a retry hint). The closest prior art is cloud-side (Azure OpenAI's `retry-after-ms`, AWS's `x-amz-retry-after`) and per-client rate limiters, where the value can be exact because a rate window is a clock. Capacity recovery is not a clock, so here the value is an estimate at any layer.

## Goals

- An opt-in `BackpressureConfig` policy that computes `Retry-After` from load signals the rejecting component already has.
- Keep the rejection path as cheap as it is today. No RPCs, locks or extra work on reject-and-respond.
- Degrade gracefully: computed, else static, else no header. Never fail or delay a rejection.

## Non-goals

- Changing when requests are rejected. Admission control is a separate discussion.
- Guaranteeing admission at the suggested time. The header is a hint, not a reservation.
- Changing the default rejection status code. Tracked separately.
- Implementing any further policy, such as the cluster-informed one (see "Future policies").

## Proposed API

```python
from ray.serve.config import BackpressureConfig

@serve.deployment(
    max_queued_requests=64,
    backpressure_config=BackpressureConfig(
        status_code=429,
        retry_after_policy="queue_drain_rate",   # NEW: "static" (default) | "queue_drain_rate"
        retry_after_s=5,                         # static value; also the fallback for computed policies
    ),
)
```

`retry_after_policy` is a named policy instead of a bare `"auto"` so future strategies can be added without changing what existing configs mean.

## Proposed design

This design adds a new field to `BackpressureConfig` called `retry_after_policy`, and one new policy named `queue_drain_rate` that computes `Retry-After` from the rejecting component's observed queue depth and drain rate.

The overall mechanism has 3 basic aspects: (i) how to compute the `Retry-After` value (what the `queue_drain_rate` policy implements), (ii) where to compute it, and (iii) who stamps the header and emits it to the client.

These boil down to emission and estimation. Emission answers (iii) and is fixed: the rejecting component stamps the header. Estimation covers (i) and (ii): one shared implementation, invoked at the two places Serve rejects today, each feeding its own local signals.

### The `queue_drain_rate` policy (this proposal)

```
retry_after = ceil(observed_queue_depth / drain_rate)
```

- **The numerator is the depth observed at rejection.** It is at least `max_queued_requests`, since a rejection only fires once the queue has reached the cap, and occasionally a little above it: the router's check is not atomic, and replica-rejected requests re-enter the queue behind new arrivals. The raise site already holds this number (it is in the `BackPressureError` message today), so using the observed value costs nothing and is exact.
- **`drain_rate` is the live signal**: how fast the queue empties, updated at the end of every interval as `drain_rate = 0.3 * rate_over_last_interval + 0.7 * previous_drain_rate`. `rate_over_last_interval` is the fresh measurement: requests drained during the interval that just ended. `previous_drain_rate` is this same formula's output from the previous update, so it carries the whole history with older intervals fading out. The 70% weight on the trend keeps lumpy traffic from whipping the value around (completions land in bursts, so a single interval can read 0 or 3x the true rate), and the 30% on the fresh measurement keeps the estimate chasing real load changes within a few intervals. The split, the interval length and the warmup threshold are implementation constants with environment-variable overrides, like Serve's other internal tunables, not new `BackpressureConfig` fields. The update runs on a lightweight background timer in the component's existing metrics machinery (default 1s). An interval with zero completions counts as a real observation when work is in flight, since that is what slow drain looks like, but idle intervals (nothing running or queued) skip the update instead of decaying the rate. The rate counts as warm after a configurable minimum number of counted intervals; until then the fallback applies.
- **Two call sites, one implementation.** On the proxy path the router rejects; its drain rate is its own assignment throughput, from a monotonic counter added at the existing send event (the current per-replica counter is an in-flight gauge, so it can't provide a rate). The rate is fleet-blended: faster replicas take more assignments, so mixed hardware is priced in. On direct ingress the replica rejects; its drain rate is its own completion rate, and its queue is drained only by itself. Same formula, different local inputs, different values, each describing its own queue. A replica's value is a conservative upper bound, since a retry may be re-balanced to a replica that frees up sooner.
- **Clamp to [1, 60] seconds.** Common client SDKs ignore `Retry-After` above 60s.
- **Jitter (for example +/-20%) is applied in the shared heade

comments.author: johntaylor-cell
comments.body:
My main concern is how this RFC and direct-ingress work together.  Serve is moving toward direct-ingress with HAProxy as the default, and on that path the router is no longer the module that rejects the request.  HAProxy will sit between the client and Serve, and it already has retry-after functionality (as does Envoy).  Both implement it very differently from what the RFC proposes.  Their calculation is time-based so it is more exact than the proposed prediction.  It is also per-client, and HAProxy exposes queue-based metrics so the limit can fire only under real back pressure.  I suggest we provide a way to enable that functionality in HAProxy, which Serve already generates config for but does not use today.

If we also want retry-after on the router path (when direct-ingress is disabled), I would try to duplicate HAProxy's time-based functionality, rather than use a forecast. That is a larger change than this RFC scopes, since admission control is listed as a non-goal, but I think it is worth deciding explicitly rather than estimating.

comments.author: vinay7373
comments.body:
Thanks for the review. Breaking it down into where we agree and where we don't.

**Where we agree:**

1. The RFC did not cover the direct-ingress path. That was a real gap and I updated the RFC. Short version: on direct ingress the same policy runs at the replica, using its own queue depth divided by an EWMA of its own completion rate. Same formula, one shared estimator implementation, two call sites. A replica's queue is drained only by itself, so that vantage is even simpler than the router's.

2. Per-client rate limiting at the HAProxy layer is valuable. It answers "this client exceeded its quota", and its Retry-After can be exact because a rate window is a clock. That is complementary to this RFC, which answers "the deployment is out of capacity, here is when to come back". I would support that as a separate proposal and am happy to file it.

**Where we don't agree, and why:**

1. "HAProxy will sit between the client and Serve" as the rejector. Not for backpressure today. On the direct-ingress path the replica rejects the request (see the "Request dropped due to backpressure" emission sites in [replica.py on the ray-2.58.0 tag](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/ray-2.58.0/python/ray/serve/_private/replica.py)). HAProxy passes the replica's response through, and its errorfiles only rewrite HAProxy-generated errors. #65193 shipped 429 + Retry-After on this path, tested with `RAY_SERVE_ENABLE_DIRECT_INGRESS=1`.

2. "Functionality Serve already generates config for but does not use". I checked `haproxy_templates.py`: no stick-tables, no track-sc, no deny rules, no Retry-After anywhere in the generated config. Enabling this would be new work, not switching on something dormant.

3. "Their calculation is time-based so it is more exact than the proposed prediction". I checked the [HAProxy docs](https://www.haproxy.com/documentation/haproxy-configuration-tutorials/security/traffic-policing/) on this. HAProxy's computed Retry-After is `http-after-response set-header Retry-After %[src,table_expire(...)]`: the time until the client's stick-table rate-limit record expires. That is per-client policing, and it is exact because a rate window is deterministic. For capacity overload (server maxconn queue full, `timeout queue` expiring) the docs show no Retry-After computation: that 503 ships without a hint. The queue timer measures elapsed wait, not time until capacity returns. When capacity frees depends on service completions and arrivals, and no layer can know that exactly, including HAProxy, which cannot see how long the inference ahead of a request will take. Any capacity Retry-After is an estimate at every layer. That is why the RFC ships an acceptance criterion and telemetry to measure the estimate, instead of claiming exactness.

Rate limiting and capacity backpressure are different problems. An exact time-based Retry-After exists for the first and cannot exist for the second. This RFC is scoped to the second, now explicitly works on both ingress paths, and leaves room for a HAProxy rate-limiting proposal alongside it.

comments.author: vinay7373
comments.body:
@johntaylor-cell 

My thoughts on your a HA Proxy based admission control and what I see as limitations:

- As you mentioned the HAProxy queue resets on every reload and Serve reloads HAProxy on every replica-set change. So the primary queue evaporates exactly during autoscaling churn (your own finding).
- Composition traffic never passes HAProxy, so the Serve backstop must stay. That means 3 admission systems with 3 threshold vocabularies to keep coherent.
    - Users configuring three queueing layers instead of one: per-server `maxconn` plus timeout queue in HAProxy, `max_queued_requests` at handles, `max_ongoing_requests` at replicas. Three knobs at three levels in different units (connections vs requests, per instance vs per caller vs per replica) that all have to be sized against each other and re-sized as the cluster scales. Mis-size any pair and you get double queueing or shedding while replicas sit idle. That is more error prone, not simpler.
- The default proxy path gets nothing from it.
- Per-deployment BackpressureConfig granularity would have to be re-expressed in generated HAProxy config.
- Moving where queueing happens is an admission-control redesign, which this RFC explicitly scopes out as a non-goal.
- On jittered-static vs computed: 
    - jitter only spreads retries around a center, it cannot make the center reliable. With `retry_after_s` we already ship the option to set a fixed, guessed value at config time, so a jittered constant is not a new proposal, it is [#65193](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/pull/65193) plus jitter. Drain rate moves 10-100x across load regimes, so the constant is wrong exactly when it matters. A 5s center against a 60s real drain means every jittered retry comes back early and gets refused again. Guessing that constant is the problem this RFC exists to remove. So a computed value using drain rate is more reliable. And @suppagoddo 's suggestion for A/B against a jittered-static baseline will show it under real workloads and make this measurable.

And [@suppagoddo](https://github.com/suppagoddo) 's suggestion for A/B against a jittered-static baseline will show it under real workloads and make this measurable.

I have one last set of comments, but I think I have explored an HAProxy centric solution enough at this point.    A less invasive change as proposed in your RFC is likely the safest approach.  I do have two comments about the estimation calculation as presented below in #6 and #7.
1. The reload is really a gap.  There is no reason to wipe out the HAProxy state unless there is a configuration change that requires such a drastic step.  HAproxy can add/remove servers dynamically of course
2. If HAProxy did perform admission control (set per-server maxconn), composition traffic would become indirectly visible, since it slows the replica and HAProxy's queue fills behind it, at least while the replica holds the overflow rather than fast-rejecting it.
3. Yes, an HAProxy approach doesnt work if there is no HAProxy :slightly_smiling_face: Hopefully that path is rare as direct-ingress will become the default very soon
4. Yes, but entirely doable and not difficult
5. No reason to not explore admission control even though the RFC mentions it as a non-goal.  Seems limiting if we are trying to find best long-term soln
6. The estimator has three inputs and I do not think any of them hold up.  Queue depth is not an observation, a rejection only fires once depth has reached `max_queued_requests`, so it is always the configured cap.  Occupancy is zero for LLM deployments, where `max_ongoing_requests` defaults to a billion.  And I could not find any signal behind the backoff term.  That leaves the drain rate, which the RFC agrees carries the estimate, but the router has no counter for it today and the code that raises the rejection cannot reach the router state it would need.
7. Regarding adding jitter, today's static path has none, `retry_after_s` is emitted verbatim by every path through one helper.  That makes the A/B @suppagoddo suggested a comparison bet

comments.author: vinay7373
comments.body:
@johntaylor-cell took your 6 and 7 into the RFC:

On 6: you are right that queue depth is the configured cap at rejection, and right about occupancy. I checked: `serve.llm` sets `DEFAULT_MAX_ONGOING_REQUESTS = int(1e9)` (python/ray/llm/_internal/serve/constants.py), so occupancy against configured capacity reads zero. The saturation factor is dropped entirely and the formula is now `ceil(max_queued_requests / drain_rate)`. 

One clarification on the drain rate, since implementability was questioned: the router already counts assignments per replica (num_requests_sent_to_replicas, router.py:152) and the rejection is raised from a method on the same `RouterMetricsManager` that owns those counters, so the EWMA is a derivation over state the raise site already holds, not new plumbing.

On 7: agreed and adopted. Jitter moves into the shared header helper, so the static retry_after_s path gets it too, which both fixes today's verbatim emission and keeps the A/B fair. Good catch, credited in the RFC.

Separately, your reload observation (HAProxy state wiped on replica-set changes when dynamic server updates would do) is a real standalone improvement to the HAProxy ingress, worth its own issue regardless of this RFC.

comments.author: vinay7373
comments.body:
@suppagoddo thanks for your review, all of your points are in the updated RFC:

1. Renamed to queue_drain_rate, since the same policy runs at the router or the replica, whichever rejects.
2. On a local saturation factor for direct ingress: we ended up dropping the saturation factor everywhere instead. From @johntaylor-cell 's finding `serve.llm` defaults `max_ongoing_requests` to `1e9`, so occupancy measured against configured capacity reads zero for the main workload class, and the backoff term had no existing signal behind it. It isn't gone forever though: if the A/B data shows the simple formula consistently errs in a way a saturation signal would fix, that data is the justification to bring one back. Evidence first, term later.
3. EWMA warmup is configurable as an implementation constant with an environment-variable override, alongside the smoothing split and the interval length, same as Serve's other internal tunables. Deliberately not a new BackpressureConfig field, to keep the public API at two fields plus the policy name.
4. Adopted your measurement point: since retries can't be reliably correlated (new request IDs, different proxy, or no retry at all), the primary measure is suggested delay vs the locally observed queue drain time, with admitted-retry rate secondary where correlation does exist.
5. Your A/B against a jittered-static baseline is now the acceptance test itself.

comments.author: vinay7373
comments.body:
@abrarsheikh to summarize the whole review thread and the current state of RFC:

Updated the RFC based on the review so far and it came out simpler. 
One policy, `queue_drain_rate` which computes `retry_after` on rejection using below formula:
```
retry_after = ceil(max_queued_requests / drain_rate)
```
Where:
- `max_queued_requests`: the numerator is the configured cap (depth at rejection is always the cap) and 
- `drain_rate` is a smoothed measure of how fast the rejecting component's queue empties which is assignment throughput at the router, completion rate at the replica. 

The value is clamped to [1, 60]s and jittered in the shared header helper so the static path gets jitter too, falls back to the static retry_after_s when the rate isn't warm, and the acceptance test is an A/B against a jittered-static baseline measured on suggested delay vs observed local drain time.

comments.author: suppagoddo
comments.body: @abrarsheikh @vinay7373 - Can I take this feature implementation?

comments.author: JerryChaox
comments.body:
hello guys, some information and test for this RFC.

I tested the proposal on Ray 2.58.0 and found two implementation details worth checking before coding it.

First, num_requests_sent_to_replicas is an in-flight gauge: it increments on send and decrements on completion. It cannot directly provide assignment throughput, so the router likely needs a monotonic counter at the accepted-assignment event.

Second, router queue depth is not always equal to max_queued_requests at rejection. Internal replica rejection can cause requests to re-enter after new requests occupy temporarily freed slots. With a cap of 8, 1,418 of 17,270 router rejection events had an observed depth of 9–11. I did not observe this on the direct-replica path.

I also compared the computed policy with a tuned jittered-static baseline over 90 held-out distributed runs. Conditional local-drain header MAE was 1.865s for the computed policy and 1.141s for static 2s. The computed policy generated fewer attempts, so this looks like a precision versus retry-cost tradeoff rather than a clear winner.

comments.author: vinay7373
comments.body:
@JerryChaox Thanks for testing the approach and for those valuable findings. Here are my thoughts on each of them:

1. Agree (and my earlier comment was wrong on this) that `num_requests_sent_to_replicas` is an in-flight gauge, increments on send (`router.py:404`) and decrements on completion (`router.py:412`). I will fix this by adding a new monotonic assignment counter at the same send event. So the raise site and the counters live on the same object and the drain rate is still a derivation over local state.

2. This is a great find. Agreed. This finding makes the formula better: use the observed depth at rejection as the numerator instead of the configured cap. The raise site already holds that number, it is in the BackPressureError message today.

3. On your third observation, the A/B test: I see how a static value wins on a homogeneous workload, where a good constant like your 2s can be guessed or tuned in advance. But the whole purpose of this RFC is the case where the constant cannot be guessed in advance, because load regimes vary and move the drain rate. I'd like to know: a) Did drain time vary across your 90 runs? b) Was the 2s tuned per workload or once overall?

Your fewer attempts observation is the most interesting part. MAE weighs a 1s early and a 1s late suggestion equally, but the costs are not equal: early means a wasted attempt plus more load on a system that is already shedding, late means idle wait. So I think we should use a asymmetric or composite metric that penalizes wasted attempts (penalize early more than late).

comments.author: vinay7373
suppagoddo
comments.body: @vinay7373 - Sounds good, will start the implementation work!

comments.author: vinay7373
comments.body:
Acceptance criteria spec:

1. Ground truth: Each rejection records the observed depth D and the drain counter value at that moment. Ground truth T is the wall time until the counter advances by D: assignments at the router, completions at the replica on direct ingress. This measures what the header claims, that the observed backlog clears. It does not measure whether a specific retry gets admitted, since that depends on other clients' arrivals. T stays measurable under continuous overload because the counter keeps advancing even when the queue never dips below the cap.
2. Metric: An asymmetric loss between the suggested delay `s` and `T`: `0.75 * max(T - s, 0) + 0.25 * max(s - T, 0)`. One second too early costs 3x one second too late, because an early retry wastes an attempt and adds load while the system is shedding and a late one only waits, bounded by the clamp. The minimizer of this loss is the 75th percentile of the drain time distribution, so the estimator gets a concrete target. MAE is reported as secondary for comparability. Scoring is offline over logged pairs, on the pre-jitter post-clamp value.
3. Baseline: The comparison arm is jittered static, with the constant tuned only on calibration runs disjoint from the evaluation set (rule: 75th percentile of calibration drain times, one global constant). A per-scenario tuned static is also reported. Runs are open loop (clients ignore the header) with autoscaling off and a pinned replica set.

@suppagoddo For me to run the above acceptance test I'll need one structured record per rejection with `policy id, fallback rung used, observed depth, drain rate estimate and warm flag, pre-jitter and post-jitter values, and the counter value at rejection`. Plus the counter itself readable by a test harness at sub-second granularity. Everything already exists at the raise site or in estimator state; the cost is one log line on a path that already logs a warning today. Please make sure this record emission is part of your implementation.

Pass bar (proposal): 
- Computed beats the static baseline on the primary loss by at least 20% in aggregate across the scenarios
- is never more than 10% worse in any single scenario
- the undershoot rate lands at 25 +/- 10 points
- and cold start falls back to the static value cleanly.

cc. @JerryChaox @abrarsheikh @johntaylor-cell

comments.author: vinay7373
comments.body:
**AI serving regimes for the acceptance runs**

Now that the implementation is up for review (#66798), here are the regimes the acceptance runs will cover. The runs collect the metrics defined in my acceptance comment above. The scenarios its pass bar refers to are drawn from these regimes. I'm deriving the regimes from real-world AI serving, using two characteristics: load and completion.

What a regime is: An AI serving regime is a recurring pattern of load and completion at the component that rejects requests. Load is how requests arrive. Completion is how they finish: how long each one runs, how many run at once, and whether they finish one at a time or in batches.

**Why these two (load and completion)?**
Ground truth in the acceptance spec is the time for the drain counter to advance by the observed depth: assignments at the router, completions at the replica on direct ingress. Both count the completion process, seen from each vantage, since the router hands a queued request to a replica when one finishes. So completion sets the drain time directly. Load decides when the queue overflows and what the estimator sees between rejections, such as idle gaps. Latency is an outcome of both, not an input.

Completion is the important half in AI serving, because processing time is not known when a request arrives. A generative model decides its output length while it generates, and in production "the remaining output length of an LLM request is not conditioned on the generated length so far" [1]. Drain speed cannot be computed from what is in the queue. It has to be measured from completions.


**Completion regimes:** 
The estimator samples once per second, so what matters is how far apart completions arrive at that scale.

| Regime | Examples | Completions | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| W1 Real-time predictive | vision, ranking, LLM code completion | Dense: many per second | Latency bounds of 15 to 250 ms [2]. Code completion has a median output of 13 tokens [3] |
| W2 Batched execution | `@serve.batch`, dynamic batching | Grouped: a batch finishes together | Each response returns once its whole batch is evaluated [4] |
| W3 Interactive LLM | chat on continuous batching | Dense to moderate: seconds each, many at once | A median of 129 output tokens [3] at 20 to 50 tokens/s [5] |
| W4 Long-running LLM | reasoning, long context, agent steps | Sparse: minutes each, few at once | A mean of 3,880 output tokens [6]. Long contexts limit how many run at once [7] |

**Load regimes:**

| Regime | Arrivals | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| L1 Steady | A constant rate. The runs use fixed-interval schedules so repeated runs are comparable | MLPerf's Server scenario models online load with Poisson arrivals [2] |
| L2 Bursts and idle gaps | High-rate bursts separated by silence | API traffic is "aperiodic... characterized by burstiness" [8]. Short-term arrivals are "often bursty (CV > 1)" [1] |
| L3 Mix shift | A steady rate, but the request mix changes, so completions speed up or slow down | Services have "widely different prompt and token distributions" [3]. In one 48-hour window, 29 of 2,412 clients sent 90% of requests [1] |

**Scenarios:** 
|# | Cell | Completions | Expected drain time | Load |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| S1 | W1, L1 | every 0.25 s | 2 s | 2x drain |
| S2 | W3, L1 | every 2.5 s | 20 s | 2.5x drain |
| S3 | W1 to W3, L3 | every 0.25 s, then every 1 s | 4 s, then 16 s | 2x drain |
| S4 | W1, L2 | every 0.25 s during bursts | 4 s | 3x drain for 20 s, then idle for 25 s |
| S5 | W3, L1, mixed fleet | every 0.4 s, from one fast and one 4x slower replica | 10 s | 2.4x drain |
| S6 | W4, L1, beyond cap | every 8 s | 240 s | 4x drain |
| S7 | W1, L1, cold start | every 0.25 s | 4 s | 3x drain from the first second |
| S8 | W3, L1, pipeline | every 1 s at the inner deployment | 8 s | 3x drain |
| S9 | W2, L1 | 8 at once every 4 s | about 8 s | 2x drain |
| S10 | W4, L1 | every 8 s | about 48 s | 2x drain |

[1] ServeGen, NSDI'26: https://

items.title: [Serve] gRPC servers keep SO_REUSEPORT on with enable_so_reuseport=False, so direct ingress ports can be shared
items.author: xyuzh
items.body_excerpt:
### What happened + What you expected to happen

`start_grpc_server` takes `enable_so_reuseport`, and direct ingress replicas (`RAY_SERVE_ENABLE_HA_PROXY=1`) pass `False`, so that binding a port another process listens on fails and Serve allocates another port. The flag has no effect. The option reaches gRPC as a string, `("grpc.so_reuseport", str(int(enable_so_reuseport)))` in `python/ray/serve/_private/grpc_util.py`. gRPC reads `grpc.so_reuseport` as an integer and ignores a string, so SO_REUSEPORT stays on (gRPC's default). A second server then binds a port that is in use without an error, and the kernel splits new connections between the listeners.

Expected: with `enable_so_reuseport=False`, binding a port that is in use fails.

We hit this on a 12-replica gRPC deployment behind HAProxy after an in-place rolling update. The process of one replica, which the controller had allocated gRPC port 40010, also listened on 40011, the port of another replica:

```
LISTEN *:40010  users:(("ray::ServeRepli",pid=157869,fd=65))  ino:95078843
LISTEN *:40011  users:(("ray::ServeRepli",pid=157869,fd=67))  ino:95078844
LISTEN *:40011  users:(("ray::ServeRepli",pid=157968,fd=65))  ino:95012385
```

The second listener of pid 157869 had none of the deployment's servicers. Connections that the kernel gave it got `UNIMPLEMENTED: Method not found!` for every RPC, and about 8% of requests failed until we killed pid 157869 and Serve replaced the replica. The controller's log shows it allocated only 40010 to that replica, so it isn't clear from the logs how the second socket came about (replica INFO logs were off). Either way, the replica could bind 40011 next to the other replica only because both sockets had SO_REUSEPORT on. With the option passed as an integer, that bind fails instead.

### Versions / Dependencies

Ray 3.0.0.dev0 (6703877370); the same code is on master (49bb8191b1). grpcio 1.75.0, Python 3.12, Linux (EKS). Serve with `RAY_SERVE_ENABLE_HA_PROXY=1`.

### Reproduction script

```python
import asyncio
import socket

import grpc


def free_port():
    with socket.socket() as s:
        s.bind(("", 0))
        return s.getsockname()[1]


async def second_bind(value):
    port = free_port()
    first = grpc.aio.server(options=[("grpc.so_reuseport", value)])
    first.add_insecure_port(f"[::]:{port}")
    await first.start()
    second = grpc.aio.server(options=[("grpc.so_reuseport", value)])
    try:
        second.add_insecure_port(f"[::]:{port}")
        return "bound (port shared)"
    except RuntimeError:
        return "failed (port in use)"
    finally:
        await second.stop(0)
        await first.stop(0)


async def main():
    for value in ("0", 0):
        print(f"grpc.so_reuseport={value!r}: second bind {await second_bind(value)}")


asyncio.run(main())
```

Output on Linux with grpcio 1.75.0:

```
grpc.so_reuseport='0': second bind bound (port shared)
grpc.so_reuseport=0: second bind failed (port in use)
```

### Issue Severity

Medium: It is a significant difficulty but I can work around it.

items.title: [core][rdt] Add execution-ucx (Axon) as an RDT backend
items.author: Florentino-Ding
items.body_excerpt: ### Description I would like to propose adding [execution-ucx](https://github.com/MoFHeka/execution-ucx) (via Axon) as a new Ray Direct Transport (RDT) backend. execution-ucx is an asynchronous communication framework built on OpenUCX and the P2300 `std::execution` model. I have integrated it into Ray RDT through Axon, a C++ communication layer with Python bindings. ### Performance Results I benchmarked the execution-ucx backend against GLOO and NIXL using **Ray's official `rdt_single_node_benchmark`**, with CPU tensors ranging from 4 B to 1 GB. The results show that execution-ucx consistently achieves the lowest end-to-end latency across all tested tensor sizes. | Tensor Size | GLOO | NIXL | execution-ucx (Axon) | |---|---:|---:|---:| | 4 B | 5.92 ms | 9.59 ms | **5.63 ms** | | 150 KB | 5.89 ms | 10.20 ms | **5.63 ms** | | 1 MB | 6.43 ms | 11.10 ms | **6.28 ms** | | 100 MB | 179.5 ms | 238.0 ms | **143.1 ms** | | 1 GB | 1.72 s | 2.36 s | **1.37 s** | Compared with the existing backends: - **vs. NIXL:** 1.66–1.81× speedup across all tested tensor sizes. - **vs. GLOO:** Up to 1.26× speedup, with the largest improvements observed for 100 MB and 1 GB tensors. The stage-level breakdown also shows that execution-ucx spends less time in the RDT handoff stage, which accounts for a significant portion of the end-to-end latency. These results suggest that execution-ucx could be a promising alternative RDT backend, particularly for large CPU tensor transfers. **Benchmark stage breakdown:** ### Use Case Provide a lower-latency RDT backend for CPU tensor transfers between Ray actors, with the potential to extend support to GPU tensors and multi-node RDMA communication. ### References - [execution-ucx](https://github.com/MoFHeka/execution-ucx?utm_source=chatgpt.com) - [Related issue: UCCL as an RDT backend](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/issues/60433) I would appreciate feedback from the Ray maintainers on integrating this backend into RDT.

items.title: Illegal memory access in triton kernel and non-determinism codegen
items.author: xw285cornell
items.body_excerpt:
Hi team, we seem to identified an issue that triton is generating non-deterministic codegen results, and in certain cases (small chances) it seems to have illegal memory access due to out of bound access in shared memory. 
The triton code is fairly simple (shown below). We run the code many times (disabled pytorch's codegen cache) and it seems it produced different shared memory: 
Most of times: 
{"name": "triton__0d1d2d3d4", "shared": 2560, "num_warps": 4, "num_stages": 1}
Sometimes: 
{"name": "triton__0d1d2d3d4", "shared": 544, "num_warps": 4, "num_stages": 1}

So sometimes it only asks for 544 bytes for shared memory space which might lead to out of bound access to shared mem. We checked and ttir is the same across the two runs, but llir is different. Wondering if you can shed some lights on this (and whether the codegen is deterministic. Also this is still on llvm IR - not sure if it repros in MLIR. 

```
from torch._inductor.triton_ops.autotune import pointwise

@pointwise(
    size_hints=[262144, 64],
    tile_hint=TileHint.DEFAULT,
    filename="notebook",
    meta={
        "signature": {0: "*bf16", 1: "*fp32", 2: "*bf16", 3: "i32", 4: "i32"},
        "device": 0,
        "constants": {},
        "mutated_arg_names": [],
        "configs": [instance_descriptor(divisible_by_16=(0, 1, 2, 3), equal_to_1=())],
    },
)
@triton.jit
def triton_(
    in_ptr0,
    in_ptr1,
    out_ptr0,
    xnumel,
    ynumel,
    XBLOCK: tl.constexpr,
    YBLOCK: tl.constexpr,
):
    xnumel = 262144
    ynumel = 62
    xoffset = tl.program_id(0) * XBLOCK
    xindex = xoffset + tl.arange(0, XBLOCK)[:, None]
    xmask = xindex < xnumel
    yoffset = tl.program_id(1) * YBLOCK
    yindex = yoffset + tl.arange(0, YBLOCK)[None, :]
    ymask = yindex < ynumel
    x0 = xindex % 512
    x1 = xindex // 512
    y2 = yindex
    x3 = xindex
    tmp0 = tl.load(
        in_ptr0
        + (
            512
            + x0
            + (1536 * x1)
            + (786432 * y2)
            + (786432 * (((x0 + (512 * x1)) // 262144)))
        ),
        xmask & ymask,
    ).to(tl.float32)
    tmp1 = tl.load(in_ptr1 + (512 + x0), xmask)
    tmp2 = tmp1.to(tl.float32)
    tmp3 = tmp0 + tmp2
    tmp4 = 2.8284271247461903
    tmp5 = tmp3 / tmp4
    tl.store(
        out_ptr0 + (y2 + (62 * x3) + tl.zeros([XBLOCK, YBLOCK], tl.int32)),
        tmp5,
        xmask & ymask,
    )
```

items.title: Discussion: First-class image warmup workflow for AIBrix model workloads
items.author: googs1025
items.body_excerpt:
## Proposal

Add a first-class `ModelWarmup` workflow for AIBrix model workloads.

The initial scope is intentionally small: preload large inference/runtime images onto nodes before rollout or scale-out. This addresses cases where traffic arrives while a newly-created Pod is still waiting for the container runtime to pull and unpack images.

This issue is for design discussion. The API and controller behavior are not finalized.

## Business value

Image pulling is a major source of cold-start latency for model-serving workloads. It is especially visible during:

- autoscaler scale-out, when a new replica lands on a node without the required image cache;
- StormService or RoleSet rolling updates, when the new revision is not yet ready but traffic is already increasing;
- manual capacity preparation, where operators want to warm nodes before exposing them to serving traffic.

A first-class workflow should make image warmup observable through Kubernetes status and provide a verify-before-rollout/scale workflow.

## Proposed MVP

Introduce a standalone `ModelWarmup` CRD under `model.aibrix.ai/v1alpha1`.

```yaml
apiVersion: model.aibrix.ai/v1alpha1
kind: ModelWarmup
metadata:
  name: qwen-image-warmup
spec:
  targets:
  - nodes:
      names:
      - gpu-node-a
      - gpu-node-b
  - nodeSelector:
      matchLabels:
        resource-pool.aibrix.ai/name: latency-pool
  - workload:
      ref:
        apiVersion: orchestration.aibrix.ai/v1alpha1
        kind: StormService
        name: qwen
      subTarget:
        roleName: prefill

  imagePreload:
    images:
    - registry.example.com/vllm@sha256:...
    - registry.example.com/aibrix-runtime@sha256:...
    pullSecrets:
    - name: registry-secret

  policies:
    parallelism: 8
    globalTimeoutSeconds: 1800
    retryLimit: 2
    ttlSecondsAfterFinished: 3600
```

## Target selection

All of the following target sources should be supported:

1. **Explicit nodes**: a list of node names.
2. **Node labels, capabilities, or resource pools**: a Kubernetes `LabelSelector`, for example an AIBrix resource-pool label. This mode should discover matching nodes added later for autoscaler scale-out.
3. **AIBrix workloads**: resolve nodes from `StormService`, `RoleSet`, `Deployment`, `ModelClaim`, or `ModelAdapter` Pods, with role-level filtering such as `prefill` or `decode` where applicable.

Multiple target entries are allowed. The controller should take the union of all resolved targets and deduplicate by node name. This allows operators to combine a resource pool, a workload's current nodes, and explicitly reserved nodes.

A workload reference describes the current workload placement. It does not by itself guarantee coverage of future scale-out nodes; use a node selector/resource-pool target for that purpose.

## Execution model

The controller should:

1. Resolve all target sources.
2. Union and deduplicate target nodes.
3. Calculate a deterministic revision from the target and image configuration.
4. Create one node-pinned warmup Job per target node and revision.
5. Run one short-lived regular container per unique image so image pulls can proceed independently.
6. Update per-node and aggregate status from Job completion.
7. Reconcile newly matching nodes, failed Jobs, stale targets, retries, and TTL cleanup.

Warmup Jobs should use `nodeName` or required node affinity, support the target node's taints and architecture, use configured pull secrets, and avoid requesting GPU resources for image-only warmup. Image entrypoints should be overridden so an inference server does not start accidentally.

A Job is preferred over a bare Pod because it provides retry and completion semantics and can recreate a deleted warmup Pod.

## Suggested status

```yaml
status:
  phase: Pending|Running|Succeeded|Failed|Degraded
  observedRevision: ...
  desiredNodes: 2
  activeNodes: 1
  succeededNodes: 1
  failedNodes: 0
  startTime: ...
  completionTime: ...
  targets:
  - nodeName: gpu-node-a
    source: NodeSelector
    phase: Succeeded
    jobName: qwen-image-warmup-gpu-node-a
    reason: ImagePreloadSucceeded
    message: ...
  conditions: []
```

Image references should preferably be immutable digests, or the controller should record the resolved digest. A changed image list or target configuration must create a new revision and invalidate the previous result.

## MVP boundaries

The first implementation focuses on image preloading only. It should not yet include:

- model artifact/file download;
- engine startup or inference warmup;
- generic arbitrary commands or custom actions;
- automatic rollout blocking or autoscaler mutation;
- direct runtime sidecar RPC integration.

The status and API should remain extensible for later artifact, engine, and precheck stages. Existing StormService, RoleSet, ModelClaim, and PodAutoscaler behavior must remain unchanged unless warmup integration is explicitly enabled.

## Why keep warmup independent?

Warmup is useful before rollout, scale-out, and manual capacity preparation. A standalone resource provides reusable target selection, independent lifecycle and status, and a foundation for future integration with workload controllers without coupling the first implementation to a single workload type.

## Open questions

- Should the kind remain `ModelWarmup`, or should the image-only MVP use `ModelImageWarmup`?
- Should `StormService`, `RoleSet`, and `NodeSelector` be the initial supported target sources, with other workload kinds added later?
- Should failed Jobs be retained by default until TTL cleanup?
- Should the default failure behavior be fail-closed, degraded success, or require an explicit policy?

items.title: [Feature][ModelClaim][Residency] Add per-claim Sleep Policy overrides
items.author: googs1025
items.body_excerpt:
### Feature Description and Motivation

Related umbrella RFC: #2290.

ModelClaim idle sleep is currently configured on the warm-pool Deployment through
the `pool.aibrix.ai/policy` annotation. When the pool sets
`lifecycle.sleepAfterSeconds`, every eligible vLLM ModelClaim engine owned by that
Deployment uses the same timeout. An individual claim cannot declare that it:

- must remain awake;
- needs a different idle timeout from the pool default; or
- should sleep after an idle period even when the pool has no lifecycle policy.

This prevents latency-sensitive and long-tail models from sharing one warm pool
with different availability policies. The current workarounds are to disable idle
sleep for the entire pool or move always-on models into a separate GPU pool. The
first loses HBM reclamation; the second reduces the value of high-density pooling.

### Use Case

One B300 warm pool hosts:

```text
online-chat  -> must remain awake
batch-coder  -> sleep after 10 minutes idle
evaluation   -> sleep after 2 minutes idle
```

The pool should continue to own the GPU Pods and KV-reclaim policy while each
ModelClaim can express its own sleep requirement.

### Proposed Solution

Add an optional sleep policy under `ModelClaimSpec.residencyPolicy`:

```yaml
spec:
  residencyPolicy:
    sleepPolicy:
      mode: PoolDefault
```

Initial modes:

| Mode | Semantics |
| --- | --- |
| `PoolDefault` | Inherit the Deployment lifecycle policy; do not sleep automatically when the pool has no lifecycle policy |
| `Never` | The pool policy must not automatically sleep this claim |
| `AfterIdle` | Use the claim's own `idleTimeout` |

Examples:

```yaml
spec:
  residencyPolicy:
    sleepPolicy:
      mode: Never
```

```yaml
spec:
  residencyPolicy:
    sleepPolicy:
      mode: AfterIdle
      idleTimeout: 15m
```

Effective-policy precedence:

```text
ModelClaim sleepPolicy
    > Deployment lifecycle policy
    > no automatic sleep
```

The claim sleep policy overrides lifecycle sleep only. It must not change the
pool's KV-reclaim policy.

### API Validation

- `mode` is one of `PoolDefault`, `Never`, or `AfterIdle`.
- `AfterIdle` requires a positive `idleTimeout`.
- `PoolDefault` and `Never` reject `idleTimeout`.
- `AfterIdle` initially supports vLLM only.
- Existing claims without `residencyPolicy` retain their current behavior.

### Implementation Boundary

This is an API/controller change:

- add ModelClaim API types, CRD schema, and generated artifacts;
- add an effective sleep-policy resolver;
- resolve the claim policy before issuing Sleep;
- skip automatic Sleep for `Never`;
- use the claim timeout for `AfterIdle`, including when the Deployment has no
  lifecycle annotation;
- preserve existing request-metric, ClaimRef UID, status, and topology safety
  checks.

No Python runtime change is required. The runtime already exposes idempotent
Sleep, activity metrics, phase, ClaimRef, and last-transition observations. No
Gateway behavior change is required for this track.

### Priority

1. **P1: `Never`** — solve the concrete opt-out requirement for critical models.
2. **P1: compatibility and safe convergence** — unset policies remain unchanged,
   and controller restarts must not sleep a `Never` claim.
3. **P2: `AfterIdle`** — add claim-specific idle timeouts.
4. **P2: observability, documentation, and E2E coverage**.

The issue is P2 while ModelClaim remains experimental, but should become P1
before production readiness or GA.

### Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Unset policies and `PoolDefault` preserve current pool behavior.
- [ ] A `Never` claim is never selected for automatic Sleep.
- [ ] Other claims in the same pool can still sleep normally.
- [ ] `AfterIdle` uses the claim's `idleTimeout`.
- [ ] `AfterIdle` works without a Deployment lifecycle annotation.
- [ ] Claim sleep policy does not affect KV reclaim.
- [ ] Invalid combinations are rejected by CRD validation.
- [ ] Controller restart preserves the effective policy.
- [ ] Unit and integration tests cover mixed policies in one pool.
- [ ] No Python runtime wire-protocol change is introduced.

### Area

Orchestration (controllers, CRDs)
